FM patients performed worse on the Semantic Verbal Fluency Test than healthy controls, indicating cognitive impairment.
No significant differences were found between FM and HC groups in Mediterranean diet adherence, sleep quality, or anthropometric variables (body fat %, water %, metabolic age, waist-to-hip ratio).
A PERMANOVA on the combined covariate set (using Euclidean distance) showed no significant differences between FM and HC groups, supporting the absence of confounding bias.
Overall gut microbiota composition (β-diversity) differed significantly between FM patients and healthy controls.
Shannon α-diversity of gut microbiota was significantly lower in FM patients compared to healthy controls.
Chao1 index of species richness did not differ significantly between FM and HC groups.
A significantly higher proportion of FM patients tested positive for methanogenic SIBO compared to healthy controls.

No significant beta-diversity differences were found based on the specific type of SIBO detected.

Correspondence analysis showed a tendency toward greater microbial dysbiosis as pain scores (NRS-11) increased, with pain intensity being the covariate that most effectively separated FM and HC groups.
The genus Akkermansia was significantly increased in FM patients compared to HC by ANCOM-BC differential abundance analysis.
The genus Oscillospira was significantly increased in FM patients and this difference was robust in sensitivity analysis; it was also linked to constipation in this population.
The genus Methanobrevibacter was significantly increased in FM patients, correlating with SIBO and methane overproduction prevalent in this group.
The genus Erysipelatoclostridium, an opportunistic pathogen, was significantly increased in FM patients.
An uncultured genus from the Christensenellaceae family was significantly increased in FM patients and showed strong positive correlations with Methanobrevibacter.
The genus Anaerotruncus showed an upward trend in FM patients with FDR just below 0.1, and this difference was robust in sensitivity analysis.
The genus Clostridia_UCG-014 showed a decreasing trend in FM patients, but this difference was not statistically significant.
Clostridia_UCG-014 showed extensive co-occurrence correlations with other bacterial genera in HC, but these correlations were entirely absent in the FM group's co-occurrence network.
Despite showing lower relative abundance than in HC, Prevotella_9 and Faecalibacterium acted as primary hubs of bacterial correlation networks specifically within the FM group.
In the HC group, the genus Dialister showed no significant correlation with the genus Christensenellaceae.
The majority (75%) of FM patients presented with gastrointestinal complaints such as constipation and abdominal bloating.
Ruminococcus, a genus known to stimulate peripheral serotonin production via tryptophan/phenylalanine metabolism, was found reduced in the FM cohort.
The FM cohort showed increased Lactobacillus and Escherichia abundance, contrasting with prior studies linking low GABA to reduced Lactococcus/Enterococcus abundance.

Lower GABA levels have been associated with reduced pressure-pain thresholds and increased sleep problems in FM, per cited literature.

Elevated glutamate concentrations have been reported in the insula, hippocampus, and posterior cingulate cortex of FM patients, correlating with enhanced pain perception via NMDA receptor overactivity.

Fibromyalgia patients exhibit significantly lower serum serotonin levels than healthy controls, associated with greater symptom severity including pain, anxiety, and depression.

Ruminococcus abundance was reduced in the FM cohort; this genus normally stimulates peripheral serotonin production by metabolizing dietary phenylalanine and tryptophan into precursors that promote serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis in enterochromaffin cells.
R. gnavus has been shown to enhance peripheral serotonin production through activation of the trace amine-associated receptor 1 (TAAR1).

A 27 kDa protein-derived peptide produced by Prevotella has been reported to mediate Th1 cell immune responses, relevant to Prevotella's role as a rheumatoid arthritis pathobiont discussed as a comorbidity mechanism in FM.
Increased Methanobrevibacter abundance correlates with SIBO and methane overproduction, conditions reported to be prevalent in 56.76% of the FM population studied.
In this study's population, Oscillospira, elevated in FM, was also associated with constipation, a common gastrointestinal symptom of fibromyalgia.

Unlike prior reports of positive co-abundance among Oscillospira, Ruminococcaceae, RF39, Rikenellaceae, Akkermansia, and Christensenellaceae, this FM cohort showed reduced abundance of Ruminococcaceae, Rikenellaceae, and RF39 alongside increased Oscillospira, Akkermansia, and Christensenellaceae.

Lactobacillus, found increased in the FM cohort, is capable of producing significant amounts of glutamate under specific metabolic conditions, potentially contributing to excitatory-inhibitory neurotransmitter imbalance.
IBS-SSS total scores were significantly higher in IBS-only and FM+IBS patients than in FM-only patients, indicating GI symptom severity is driven primarily by IBS.
Global Severity Index (GSI) scores on the SCL-90-R showed a progressive increase from IBS to FM to FM+IBS, with the comorbid group showing the highest overall psychopathological distress.
SCL-90-R Obsessive-Compulsive, Depression, Anxiety, and Hostility subscale scores all showed a progressive increase from IBS to FM to FM+IBS.
SCL-90-R Somatization subscale scores differed significantly between IBS and FM, and between IBS and FM+IBS, but not between FM and FM+IBS.
SF-36 Physical Component Summary (PCS) scores differed significantly among groups, with FM patients reporting the lowest physical health scores, FM+IBS intermediate, and IBS patients the highest.
SF-36 Mental Component Summary (MCS) scores gradually declined from IBS to FM to FM+IBS, with a significant difference between IBS and FM+IBS.
The WHOQOL-BREF physical domain score was significantly lower in FM+IBS patients compared to IBS-only patients.
No significant differences were found in the WHOQOL-BREF psychological domain among the FM, IBS, and FM+IBS groups.
The WHOQOL-BREF social relationship domain showed a significant difference between FM and FM+IBS groups.
FM+IBS patients scored significantly lower than IBS-only patients on the WHOQOL-BREF environmental domain.
IBS-SSS total score positively correlated with the SCL-90-R Somatization subscale across the sample.
IBS-SSS total score positively correlated with the SCL-90-R Anxiety subscale across the sample.
IBS-SSS total score negatively correlated with the WHOQOL-BREF physical health domain.

A multivariable regression model showed somatization and diagnostic group jointly explained half the variance in IBS-SSS score, with somatization being the strongest independent predictor of GI symptom severity.
FM-only patients, despite not meeting Rome IV criteria for IBS, reported mild GI symptoms, suggesting subthreshold functional bowel disturbance intrinsic to the FM phenotype.
Abdominal bloating severity, an IBS-SSS item, differed significantly only between the FM and FM+IBS groups among the individual questionnaire items.
FM-only patients scored in the severe FM category (48-68) on the FIQ-R, while FM+IBS patients scored in the very severe category (>68), indicating greater disease impact with GI comorbidity.
Both FM and FM+IBS groups had mean Fatigue Severity Scale scores above the clinical threshold of 4.67, indicating significant fatigue in both groups.
Mean pain intensity assessed with the VAS was very high in both FM-only and FM+IBS groups.
Digital tender point examination showed widespread tenderness with a median of 18 positive points in both FM and FM+IBS groups.
All three patient groups (FM, IBS, FM+IBS) showed high perceived stress levels on the PSS, with no significant differences among them.

Fibromyalgia was selected as a study phenotype because it involves a diagnostic delay averaging 5-7 years, is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring rheumatology referral, and shows highly heterogeneous ICD-10 coding ranging from specific (M79.7) to nonspecific myalgia codes.
Of the six phenotypes tested, fibromyalgia had the lowest optimal SFI-aware calibration strength parameter (alpha=0.5), compared to alpha=2.5 for dementia, adult ADHD, and geriatric bipolar disorder.

Fibromyalgia exhibited a distinct alpha-sensitivity pattern in which performance peaked at a low calibration strength and degraded at higher alpha values, unlike complex phenotypes that improved monotonically with increasing alpha.

SFI-aware calibration improved F1-score by 4.2% for fibromyalgia relative to uncalibrated predictions, a comparatively modest gain attributed to an already-reasonable uncalibrated baseline (F1=0.625).

For fibromyalgia, SFI-aware calibration and Platt scaling produced essentially equivalent F1 scores, but SFI-aware calibration achieved superior AUC gain (+5.2% vs 0%) and Brier score improvement (-14.8% vs +5.4% for Platt scaling, which worsened Brier score).
Expected Calibration Error for fibromyalgia decreased by 3.5% under SFI-aware calibration, indicating a modest improvement in bin-level calibration.
Brier score decomposition for fibromyalgia showed a 35% increase in resolution (discrimination) and an overall 15% reduction in Brier score under SFI-aware calibration.

Statistical comparison between SFI-aware calibration and Platt scaling for fibromyalgia showed a negligible effect size (mean difference near zero), indicating equivalent performance for this comparatively well-calibrated, low-heterogeneity phenotype, though both methods substantially outperformed isotonic regression.

Across the six phenotypes evaluated (including fibromyalgia), the specificity and contextual concordance components of the Signal Fidelity Index showed near-perfect correlation, though the authors retained both due to conceptually distinct underlying denominators.

Across all six phenotypes and 3,550 synthetic datasets, SFI-aware calibration produced consistent improvements over uncalibrated predictions (F1 +4.2% to +34.9%, AUC +4.6% to +40%) without ever degrading performance below the uncalibrated baseline.

Traditional baseline calibration methods, particularly isotonic regression, showed unstable and often severely degraded performance (near-chance AUC, large F1 losses) when applied to unlabeled target populations across phenotypes, in contrast to SFI-aware calibration which never degraded below baseline.
In patients presenting with anaphylaxis or systemic mast cell activation symptoms, 4% (15/381) had detectable KIT D816V mutation in peripheral blood.
Most (80%) of the KIT D816V-positive patients had basal serum tryptase levels below 20 ng/mL, indicating that low tryptase does not exclude clonal disease.
Most KIT D816V-positive patients (73%) presented with severe (Ring-Messmer grade III/IV) anaphylaxis.

Combining KIT D816V-positive cases with additional patients diagnosed with clonal mast cell disease based on elevated tryptase and follow-up, the total prevalence of clonal mast cell disease was 8% (29/381) among patients with anaphylaxis or systemic MCA symptoms.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HaT) was present in 36% (138/381) of patients with anaphylaxis or systemic mast cell activation symptoms.
Prolonged (3 h), but not acute (15 min), selective CysLT2R agonism with NM-LTC4 desensitizes LTD4-induced CysLT1R-mediated ERK phosphorylation in human cord blood mast cells.

CysLT2R-selective antagonists HAMI-3379 and BayCysLT2 do not alter LTD4-induced ERK phosphorylation alone but completely reverse the NM-LTC4-induced desensitization, confirming CysLT2R signaling specificity.

In HEK293 CysLT1R/CysLT2R double transfectants, CysLT2R signaling desensitizes both ERK phosphorylation and calcium flux downstream of CysLT1R, but in mast cells only ERK (not calcium flux) is desensitized, indicating cell-type-specific signaling differences.

Prolonged (60 min) but not acute CysLT2R stimulation potentiates forskolin-induced adenylate cyclase (cAMP) activation, a novel 'AC superactivation' phenomenon that is independent of Gi protein deletion.

CysLT2R does not directly activate Gs proteins but strongly potentiates cAMP accumulation in response to Gs-linked receptors (EP2R, EP4R, β2AR, IP), increasing maximal responses 3- to 5-fold and enhancing receptor autoactivity even without exogenous ligand.
Mouse CysLT2R shows a rank order potency for cAMP potentiation of LTD4 > LTC4 > NM-LTC4 > LTE4, with LTD4 being the most potent ligand.

The asthma/atopy risk-associated CysLT2R M201V coding variant shows markedly diminished LTD4-induced (and modestly diminished LTC4-induced) AC superactivation and PKA activation compared to wild-type CysLT2R.
The oncogenic uveal melanoma-associated CysLT2R L129Q variant shows strong ligand-independent (constitutive) potentiation of forskolin-induced cAMP accumulation and PKA dissociation.

CysLT2R-dependent AC superactivation requires Gβγ subunits: overexpression of GRK2 or GRK3 (which sequester Gβγ) markedly diminishes potentiation of cAMP accumulation, while GRK5/6 (which lack Gβγ-binding) have no effect.

Prolonged CysLT2R stimulation induces direct recruitment of Gβγ to the AC2 isoform, a process independent of EP2R co-expression but abolished without exogenous Gs proteins, supporting a direct Gβγ-AC macromolecular complex mechanism.
Cell-permeable cAMP analog (dibutyryl cAMP) and forskolin dose-dependently inhibit LTD4-induced ERK activation and PGD2 generation by human cord blood mast cells.

Combined shRNA knockdown of both PKA catalytic subunits α and β (PRKACA and PRKACB), but not either alone, blocks cAMP-induced desensitization of LTD4-induced ERK phosphorylation, indicating functional redundancy between the two PKA catalytic subunits.

The PKA inhibitor H89, but not the EPAC inhibitor ESI-09, reverses the NM-LTC4-induced desensitization of LTD4-induced ERK activation and PGD2 generation in mast cells, confirming a PKA-dependent (not EPAC-dependent) mechanism.

NM-LTC4-selective CysLT2R activation at the dose/duration used does not affect IgE/anti-IgE-induced mast cell degranulation (LAMP-1 expression) or PGD2 production, indicating CysLT2R's inhibitory effect is specific to CysLT1R-mediated activation rather than FcεRI-mediated activation.

Mast cell-specific deletion of Cysltr2 amplifies Df-induced allergic lung inflammation in female mice, with significantly higher BAL fluid total cells, eosinophils, and lung ILC2 counts compared to littermate controls; males showed only a non-significant trend.

MC-Cysltr2 deletion selectively increases BAL fluid PGD2, soluble ST2, and lung Il5 transcript expression in female mice without altering IL-5, IL-13, MMCP-1 protein, several other cytokine transcripts, or serum IgE in either sex.

BAL fluid cysteinyl leukotriene concentrations are significantly higher in female mice than male mice in the Df-induced allergic lung inflammation model, consistent with known sex differences in leukotriene generation.

The CysLT1R antagonist montelukast reverses the amplified type 2 lung inflammation (BAL total cells/eosinophils, lung ILC2 and mast cell expansion, CysLT and PGD2 levels) seen in female MC-Cysltr2 KO mice, confirming that the excess inflammation is CysLT1R-dependent.

In PGE2-insufficient (Ptges-/-) mice, the protective effect of MC-CysLT2R is lost: MC-Cysltr2 KO mice on the Ptges-/- background show no significant differences from littermate controls in inflammation parameters, indicating MC-CysLT2R's protective effect requires endogenous PGE2/EP2R signaling.
APP/PS2 transgenic mice showed increased mast cell density and a higher degranulation ratio within the primo vascular system compared to controls.
Atomic force microscopy revealed irregular alignment of primo subvessels and interstitial spaces, increased surface roughness, and loss of spatial periodicity in AD model mice.
Scanning electron microscopy showed a significant increase in the density and diameter of primo pores in AD model mice, along with reduced fiber structure diameter.
Behavioral testing confirmed cognitive impairments characteristic of Alzheimer's disease in APP/PS2 transgenic mice, validating the model used for downstream PVS analysis.
Overall, 53.8% (50/93) of patients across all chronic pain diagnoses reported some subjective benefit from low-dose naltrexone (LDN).
Among patients with fibromyalgia, widespread pain, or central sensitization (n=27), 55.6% reported symptom relief with LDN.
Among patients with mast cell activation syndrome (n=7), 71.4% reported benefit from LDN for pain.
Among patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (n=9), 66.7% reported benefit from LDN, particularly reduction in fatigue.
Among patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (n=5), 60% reported benefit from LDN, consistent with a prior retrospective study showing 74% benefit in 218 participants.
Benefit for low back pain (27.3%) and neuropathic pain (50%) with LDN was more modest than other diagnostic categories in this cohort.
Among the 7 patients with arthralgia, arthritis, or osteoarthritis, mean response rate to LDN was 71.4%, though a prior RCT in arthritis found no significant analgesic difference vs placebo.
A prior RCT of LDN in fibromyalgia found no difference from placebo in pain intensity or pressure pain threshold, but conditioned pain modulation was significantly different with LDN versus placebo.
Adverse effects were reported in 49.5% (46/93) of patients taking LDN, most commonly nausea (18 patients, 12 transient), with none classified as serious or life-threatening.
Among the 43 patients who stopped LDN or did not report efficacy, 21 discontinued due to lack of efficacy and 25 stopped due to adverse effects that may have precluded benefit.
Across responders, the most frequently relieved symptom was pain (49 patients), followed by fatigue (25 patients) and brain fog (6 patients).

TLR4 receptors are present on mast cells and type 1 macrophages, immune cells that release inflammatory mediators implicated in nociception, providing a plausible mechanism for LDN's antinociceptive effect via TLR4 antagonism.

Naltrexone is theorized to exhibit a biphasic dose-response (hormesis), with weak agonist effects at low doses upregulating opioid receptors and beta-endorphins, versus receptor inhibition at high doses.
Among patients with mast cell activation syndrome and pelvic pain, response rates (71.4% and 66.7% respectively) were congruent with prior evidence limited to case reports of success.
BLG-specific IgE was significantly elevated in BLG-sensitized mice compared to sham controls regardless of sex or thioperamide treatment.
Thioperamide treatment did not alter the sensitization-induced elevation of BLG-specific IgE levels.
BLG-sensitized female mice produced significantly higher levels of allergen-specific IgG1 than sensitized males, suggesting sex-differential antibody responses.
Plasma histamine plus N-methylhistamine levels were significantly increased in BLG-sensitized mice of both sexes compared to sham mice, and thioperamide did not reduce this peripheral elevation.
Thioperamide-treated male BLG-sensitized mice showed slightly greater grip strength than vehicle-treated sensitized males, an effect not seen in females.
Neither BLG sensitization nor thioperamide treatment altered anxiety-like behaviors (time in center zone, center entries) in the open field test in either sex.
Vehicle-treated male BLG-sensitized mice spent significantly more time immobile in the tail suspension test than sham males, indicating increased depression-like behavior.
Thioperamide treatment prevented the development of depression-like behavior in male BLG-sensitized mice, significantly reducing time immobile compared to vehicle-treated sensitized males.
Vehicle-treated BLG-sensitized male mice showed reduced discrimination index in the novel object recognition test compared to sham males, indicating impaired recognition memory.
Thioperamide treatment improved recognition memory in male BLG-sensitized mice, significantly increasing the discrimination index compared to vehicle-treated sensitized males.
Total dural mast cell number was significantly increased specifically in BLG-sensitized male mice compared to sham males, with a sex-specific pattern.
BLG sensitization markedly increased degranulated dural mast cell numbers in male mice compared to sham males and to female BLG mice.

Thioperamide significantly reduced the percentage of degranulated IgE-positive dural mast cells in BLG-sensitized female mice compared to vehicle-treated sensitized females, an effect largely absent in males.
Histamine plus N-methylhistamine levels were significantly elevated in the frontal cortex and thalamus of BLG-sensitized male mice compared to sham males, but not in females.
HNMT enzyme levels were significantly increased by BLG sensitization in the frontal cortex and thalamus of vehicle-treated male mice, but not affected in females.
Thioperamide treatment reduced the sensitization-induced elevation of HNMT in the frontal cortex and thalamus of male BLG mice.

BLG-sensitized male mice showed significantly reduced myelin (FluoroMyelin) and neurofilament heavy chain immunofluorescence signals in the anterior cingulate cortex compared to sham males, indicating cortical demyelination and axonal integrity loss; no such change occurred in females.
Thioperamide treatment preserved myelin and axonal integrity in the anterior cingulate cortex of BLG-sensitized male mice, preventing the sensitization-induced demyelination.

LC-MS quantification (measuring HA alone, without NMHA) detected decreased histamine levels in the brains of BLG-sensitized male CMA mice, contrasting with the ELISA (HA+NMHA) result, suggesting elevated brain HA was rapidly metabolized to NMHA.
Toluidine blue staining showed a marked increase in dermal mast cell numbers in LL37-induced rosacea-like lesions compared to control skin.
mRNA and secreted protein levels of β-hexosaminidase, histamine, IL-6, TNF-α, CCL2, CXCL10 and MMP-9 were significantly higher in LL37-treated mouse skin than in PBS controls.
Transcriptome sequencing of LL37-induced lesional skin versus control skin identified 2166 differentially expressed genes, with 1511 upregulated and 655 downregulated.
GSEA and KEGG pathway analysis of the LL37-induced skin transcriptome showed significant enrichment of Toll-like receptor signaling and JAK/STAT signaling pathways.
Western blot confirmed increased protein expression of TLR2, MyD88, JAK2 and STAT3 in skin lesions of LL37-treated mice compared to controls.
Immunofluorescence showed increased numbers of c-kit-labeled mast cells and elevated TLR2, p-JAK2, and p-STAT3 fluorescence intensity within mast cells of LL37-treated lesions compared to controls.
Both intragastric and topical ruxolitinib treatment significantly reduced redness score/area, dermal inflammation, mast cell infiltration, and degranulation-related mediators in LL37-induced mice.
In LUVA human mast cells, 4 µM LL37 incubated for 24 hours significantly increased β-hexosaminidase release, establishing the dose/time used for subsequent experiments.

LL37 significantly increased β-Hex, histamine, IL-6, TNF-α and other cytokine release from LUVA mast cells, an effect not seen with scrambled LL37, indicating specific LL37-driven mast cell degranulation.
Transmission electron microscopy of LL37-treated mast cells showed marked reduction in electron-dense granules with vacuole-like structures, confirming morphological degranulation.
In LUVA cells, LL37 rapidly increased JAK2 and STAT3 phosphorylation at 1 hour, followed by increased TLR2 and MyD88 expression at 24 hours; scrambled LL37 produced no such changes.
LL37 (FITC-labeled) colocalized with the mast cell membrane marker Dil, whereas scrambled LL37 did not; TLR2 knockdown significantly reduced LL37 membrane colocalization.
Co-immunoprecipitation confirmed a direct physical interaction between LL37 and TLR2.
TLR2 knockdown suppressed LL37-induced MyD88 expression and prevented LL37-induced increases in IL-6, TNF-α, CCL2, CXCL10, MMP-9, β-Hex, and histamine in mast cells.
Ruxolitinib suppressed LL37-induced JAK2 and STAT3 phosphorylation as well as β-Hex release and cytokine production in mast cells.
Niclosamide, used to inhibit STAT3 phosphorylation, significantly reduced LL37-induced release of β-Hex and degranulation-related cytokines in mast cells.

MyD88 overexpression rescued the decline in JAK2 phosphorylation caused by ruxolitinib, while MyD88 knockdown significantly reduced JAK2 and STAT3 phosphorylation, indicating MyD88 acts upstream of JAK2/STAT3.

Molecular docking between the Death domain of MyD88 and the FERM domain of JAK2 produced an optimal binding model with a docking score of -239.48 and confidence score of 0.8569, indicating a high probability of direct protein-protein interaction.
Proximity ligation assay and co-immunoprecipitation confirmed a physical interaction between MyD88 and JAK2 in mast cells following LL37 treatment.

In a small open-label trial, four weeks of topical ruxolitinib cream significantly improved erythema and papules in rosacea patients, with reductions in CEA, PSA, and GFSS scores and only mild, transient adverse effects.
Ruxolitinib treatment suppressed LL37-induced JAK2 and STAT3 phosphorylation in mast cells along with reduced β-hexosaminidase release and cytokine production.
Niclosamide, a STAT3 phosphorylation inhibitor, significantly inhibited LL37-induced release of β-hexosaminidase and degranulation-related cytokines in mast cells.

MyD88 overexpression rescued the ruxolitinib-induced decline in JAK2 phosphorylation, whereas MyD88 knockdown significantly reduced JAK2 and STAT3 phosphorylation, indicating MyD88 acts upstream of JAK2/STAT3.
Ruxolitinib treatment attenuated the increased release of mast cell degranulation markers, including β-hexosaminidase, histamine, and related cytokines, that was induced by MyD88 overexpression.
Molecular docking of the MyD88 Death domain and the JAK2 FERM domain predicted a high-probability physical interaction, with a docking score of -239.48 and a confidence score of 0.8569.
Proximity ligation assay demonstrated that MyD88 physically interacts with JAK2 in mast cells following LL37 treatment.
Co-immunoprecipitation experiments confirmed a direct protein-protein interaction between MyD88 and JAK2 in mast cells.

In a small clinical trial of 10 rosacea patients, four weeks of topical ruxolitinib significantly improved erythema and papules, reflected by reductions in Clinician's Erythema Assessment, Patient's Self-Assessment, and Global Flushing Severity Scale scores.
Topical ruxolitinib was well tolerated in rosacea patients, with most reporting only mild, transient itching or burning during the first week and no severe adverse events.
Preconditioning human bronchial smooth muscle cells with IL-13 for 24 h increased calcium flux responses triggered by histamine and LTD4.
Protectin D1 reversed the IL-13-induced increase in calcium flux responses to histamine and LTD4 in bronchial smooth muscle cells.
Maresin 1 reversed the IL-13-induced increase in calcium flux responses to histamine and LTD4 in bronchial smooth muscle cells.
Lipoxin A4, resolvin D2, and maresin-conjugate in tissue repair 3 (MCTR3) did not reverse the IL-13-induced increase in calcium flux, unlike PD1 and MaR1.
In isolated human bronchi preconditioned with IL-13, contractions induced by histamine and LTD4 were amplified compared to untreated bronchi.
When added acutely during myography (not as a 48h preconditioning), PD1 and MaR1 had no effect on histamine- or LTD4-induced airway contractility.
PD1 attenuated the IL-13-induced enhancement of airway contractions triggered by mast cell activation.
Antagonism of the CysLT1 receptor did not influence the anti-hyperreactive effect of the SPMs (PD1/MaR1), suggesting their action is not mediated via CysLT1 signalling.
Chemo-informatic analysis revealed structural similarities between PD1 and MaR1 that may explain why these two SPMs, but not the other tested mediators, exert the anti-hyperreactive action.
Anastrozole treatment increased mast cell numbers and tryptase levels in the plantar tissue of mice.
Depleting mast cells with compound 48/80 prevented anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia, muscle strength loss, and the increase in plantar mast cell number.
Mast cell stabilisation with ketotifen fumarate prevented anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia and muscle strength loss.
The tryptase inhibitors nafamostat and gabexate reduced anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia and muscle strength loss.
PAR2 antagonists ENMD-1068 and AZ3451 reduced anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia and muscle strength loss.

Global PAR2 knockout mice and sensory neuron-specific PAR2 (Nav1.8) knockout mice did not develop mechanical allodynia or muscle strength loss after anastrozole treatment, demonstrating PAR2 is required for this pain phenotype.

Local sub-nociceptive doses of PAR2 agonists (tryptase, trypsin, or the peptide agonist 2F) enhanced anastrozole-induced mechanical sensitivity in wild-type mice, an effect reduced by pre-treatment with the PAR2 antagonist AZ3451, while PAR2-/- and PAR2 Nav1.8-/- mice given anastrozole did not respond to these agonists.
Tryptase inhibitors nafamostat and gabexate reduced anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia and muscle strength loss in mice.
PAR2 inhibitors ENMD-1068 and AZ3451 reduced anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia and muscle strength loss.
Global PAR2 knockout (PAR2-/-) mice did not develop anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia or muscle strength loss.
Sensory neuron-specific PAR2 knockout (PAR2 Nav1.8-/-) mice did not develop anastrozole-induced mechanical allodynia or muscle strength loss, implicating sensory neuronal PAR2 in the pain mechanism.

Local sub-nociceptive doses of PAR2 agonists (tryptase, trypsin, or the synthetic peptide 2F) enhanced anastrozole-induced mechanical sensitivity in wild-type mice, an effect reduced by pre-treatment with the PAR2 antagonist AZ3451.
PAR2-/- and PAR2 Nav1.8-/- mice treated with anastrozole did not respond to local sub-nociceptive doses of PAR2 agonists, confirming PAR2-dependence of the sensitisation effect.
Transcriptomic analysis of rosacea skin lesions (GSE65914) showed significant enrichment of the cGAS/STING signaling pathway compared to normal skin.
LL37 triggers oxidative stress that damages mitochondria in mast cells, leading to mitochondrial DNA leakage into the cytosol.
Leaked mitochondrial DNA in the cytosol activates the cGAS/STING/NF-κB signaling pathway, driving mast cell degranulation.
Scavenging ROS with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) significantly reduced LL37-induced mast cell activation.
Blocking mPTP opening with cyclosporin A (CsA) significantly reduced LL37-induced mast cell activation.
Blocking mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening with cyclosporin A (CsA) significantly reduced LL37-induced mast cell activation in vitro.
Targeted chemical degradation of STING using SP23 significantly reduced LL37-induced mast cell activation in vitro.
Topical application of CsA cream suppressed cGAS/STING/NF-κB signaling in dermal mast cells and alleviated rosacea-like dermatitis in an LL37-induced mouse model.
Topical application of SP23 cream suppressed cGAS/STING/NF-κB signaling in dermal mast cells and alleviated rosacea-like dermatitis in an LL37-induced mouse model.
Transmission electron microscopy revealed damaged mitochondrial ultrastructure in mast cells following LL37 exposure, consistent with mitochondrial stress and dysfunction.
Plasma MRGPRX2 levels were significantly higher in AR patients than in healthy controls.
ROC curve analysis showed excellent discriminative ability of plasma MRGPRX2 for distinguishing AR patients from healthy controls.
Plasma MRGPRX2 levels did not correlate with age in AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 was significantly higher in patients with moderate-to-severe AR symptoms than in those with mild symptoms.
Plasma MRGPRX2 moderately differentiated moderate-to-severe from mild AR patients by ROC analysis.
Plasma MRGPRX2 levels correlated positively with VAS symptom scores across all AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 correlated positively with total IgE levels in AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 correlated positively with Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS) in AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 correlated positively with rhinorrhea score in AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 correlated positively with nasal congestion score in AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 correlated positively with nasal itching score in AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 did not correlate with age, disease duration, histamine levels, sneezing score, ocular itching, or tearing score.
Plasma MRGPRX2 did not correlate with allergen-specific IgE levels (house dust mite, cockroach, dog dander, mold, Artemisia, peanut, crab, shrimp).
In the IgE-negative AR subgroup, plasma MRGPRX2 strongly discriminated AR patients from healthy controls.
In the IgE-positive AR subgroup, plasma MRGPRX2 strongly discriminated AR patients from healthy controls.
In the IgE-negative subgroup, plasma MRGPRX2 moderately-to-well differentiated mild from moderate-to-severe AR (higher AUC than IgE-positive subgroup).
Plasma MRGPRX2 correlated with TNSS specifically in IgE-negative AR patients but not in IgE-positive patients.
The correlation between plasma MRGPRX2 and VAS symptom scores was significantly stronger in IgE-negative AR patients than in IgE-positive AR patients.
Plasma MRGPRX2 levels did not differ by sex among AR patients.
Concomitant allergic comorbidities (chronic urticaria, allergic asthma, atopic dermatitis) and family history of atopy were not associated with plasma MRGPRX2 differences.
Plasma MRGPRX2 levels did not differ between total IgE/sIgE-positive AR patients and IgE-negative AR patients overall.

The authors state that fatigue and myalgia were highly prevalent and clinically meaningful symptoms identified in their prior analysis of small fiber neuropathy patients, defining a 'myalgic' SFN subgroup distinct from pain-centric presentations.

The authors propose that immune dysfunction and small fiber abnormalities documented in ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, and Long COVID may share mechanisms with the 'myalgic' SFN subgroup identified in their study.

The authors note that most current SFN symptom assessment scales focus almost exclusively on painful symptoms, risking underrecognition of patients in whom fatigue, myalgia, or dysautonomia predominate.
In a cohort of 203 SFN patients, only 20% had severe neuropathic pain, forming an 'algesic' subgroup.
The remaining 80% of the SFN cohort had significant fatigue, myalgia, and generalized weakness with no or only mild neuropathic pain.
Most SFN patients experienced autonomic symptoms—most commonly dry eyes, dry mouth, and GI dysmotility—prior to skin biopsy, compared with healthy controls.
In the 'myalgic' cluster (60% of the cohort), fatigue was more severe than neuropathic symptoms, and weakness and myalgia were significantly more severe than burning pain.
Autonomic symptoms were present across all three identified symptom clusters in the SFN cohort.
SFN was confirmed by reduced epidermal nerve fiber density even in patients with mild or absent neuropathic pain.

At least 50% of patients with POTS and Long COVID, and nearly one-third of patients with ME/CFS, were found to have small fiber neuropathy when assessed via skin biopsy, QSART, corneal microscopy, or microneurography.

Autoimmune conditions and abnormal autoimmune markers were commonly reported in SFN cohorts, suggesting an autoimmune/immune-mediated etiology also implicated as a major mechanism in POTS, Long COVID, and ME/CFS.
Both twins carry a pathogenic GLA variant (c.298A>T) that introduces a premature stop codon, producing a truncated α-galactosidase A enzyme associated with the classic Fabry disease phenotype.

Quantitative sensory testing in twin 1 showed markedly elevated vibratory detection thresholds in both upper and lower extremities (percentile >97.5), indicating vibratory hyposensitivity consistent with small fiber/large fiber sensory involvement.
Twin 1 showed significantly reduced heat pain thresholds with a leftward shift in the thermoalgesic curve, indicating heat hyperalgesia.
24-hour Holter monitoring in twin 1 revealed sinus tachycardia and reduced heart rate variability, suggesting autonomic nervous system involvement.
Twin 2 also showed significantly elevated vibratory detection thresholds in both upper and lower extremities, with all other sensory thresholds remaining normal.
Holter monitoring in twin 2 also demonstrated decreased heart rate variability, with other cardiac, metabolic, and imaging studies unremarkable.
Both patients were started on enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant agalsidase beta due to the presence of small fiber neuropathy, per international Fabry disease guidelines.
Neuropathic pain management with pregabalin was initiated in both patients as a second-line option, chosen over sodium channel blockers due to a better pediatric safety profile.

Both patients reported a subjective reduction in neuropathic and autonomic symptoms after starting ERT combined with symptomatic pain management, but this could not be objectively verified since no validated pain or autonomic assessment scales were used.
Per cited literature, neuropathic pain affects up to 40% of individuals under age 18 with Fabry disease, and pain attacks occur in 58% of affected girls.

Both twins presented with gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain with constipation in twin 1, diarrhea in twin 2) alongside acroparesthesia, consistent with Fabry disease-related small fiber/autonomic GI involvement.
The Survey of Autonomic Symptoms (SAS) total score and subscores improved with high-dose long-term IVIG therapy while symptoms worsened in the usual-care control group.
The composite QASAT-total autonomic/small-fiber score improved with IVIG while it changed little in controls.
Pain (PNRS) scores decreased in the IVIG arm while pain worsened in controls.
Total NTSS-6 sensory symptom score did not significantly differ between IVIG and control arms overall.
Specific NTSS-6 subscores (burning frequency, numbness frequency, numbness intensity) were significantly reduced in the IVIG arm.
Cardiovagal heart rate response to deep breathing improved with IVIG in one statistical model but was not significant in the other.
The relative percent decline in cerebral blood flow velocity during tilt was paradoxically worse in the IVIG group despite overall improvement in other measures.
Epidermal nerve fiber density at the proximal thigh improved in both groups but improved substantially more with IVIG.
QASAT orthostatic cerebral blood flow response score, autonomic failure score, and ENFD score all improved with IVIG, while the end-tidal CO2 score did not differ.
At baseline, patients who chose IVIG therapy had a significantly higher proportion of abnormal inflammatory/autoimmune markers than the control ASFN group.
Electrochemical skin conductance was lower in the IVIG group when unadjusted for weight, but no difference remained after adjusting for weight (the measure used for QASAT grading).

At baseline there were no significant differences between IVIG and control ASFN groups in cardiovascular autonomic testing (deep breathing, Valsalva, tilt table) or raw blood pressure/heart rate/CBFv data.
There was no baseline difference in skin biopsy epidermal or sweat gland nerve fiber density between IVIG and control groups at proximal and distal sites.
Adverse events related to high-dose long-term IVIG were common, mostly mild-to-moderate, with headache being the most frequent side effect.
Nearly a quarter of IVIG-treated patients required a brand change due to side effects not resolved by premedication/fluid adjustment.

ASFN patients had a heterogeneous pattern of preceding infections and elevated inflammatory/autoimmune markers, including Lyme disease/post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome and tick-borne coinfections.

The authors propose that ASFN pathophysiology involves autoreactive B-cell mediated neurodegeneration, molecular mimicry, and/or dysimmunity, and that IVIG acts via multiple immunomodulatory mechanisms including neutralizing autoantibodies and reducing complement-mediated and endothelial inflammation.

Across 196 gut microbial taxa and 15 chronic pain phenotypes, 101 gut microbiota-chronic pain pairs showed potentially robust causal associations, with 48 taxa acting as risk factors and 53 as protective factors.
Three gut microbial taxa showed potential causal associations with small fiber neuropathy risk.

Among 206 brain white-matter structural connectivity traits tested, 127 showed potentially robust causal associations with the 15 chronic pain phenotypes, with 73 acting as risk factors and 54 as protective.
Five brain structural connectivity traits showed potential causal associations with small fiber neuropathy.

Genetically predicted higher connectivity from the right-hemisphere control network to the pallidum was associated with increased risk of small fiber neuropathy and idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy.
Genetically predicted higher connectivity from the right-hemisphere control network to the nucleus accumbens was associated with decreased risk of small fiber neuropathy and intercostal neuropathy.

Right-hemisphere somatomotor network-to-putamen connectivity was protectively associated with small fiber neuropathy but risk-increasing for diabetic neuropathy, showing a bidirectional effect across pain phenotypes.

Genetically predicted genus Parabacteroides abundance was inversely associated with alcohol-induced polyneuropathy but positively associated with cluster headache risk, indicating bidirectional effects across pain phenotypes.
Genus Candidatus Soleaferrea was associated with increased risk of postherpetic neuralgia but decreased risk of migraine.
Genus Veillonella showed a protective association with postherpetic neuralgia but increased risk of sciatica.
Genus Christensenellaceae R.7 group increased the risk of diabetic neuropathy while decreasing the risk of migraine with aura.
Genetically predicted phylum Tenericutes abundance was associated with reduced risk of alcohol-induced polyneuropathy, surviving Bonferroni correction.
Genetically predicted class Bacteroidia and order Bacteroidales abundance were associated with increased risk of thoracic spine pain, surviving Bonferroni correction.
Genetically predicted order Bifidobacteriales and family Bifidobacteriaceae abundance were associated with lower migraine risk, surviving Bonferroni correction.
Genetically predicted connectivity from the right-hemisphere salience/ventral attention network to the putamen was associated with decreased risk of sciatica, surviving Bonferroni correction.
Genetically predicted connectivity from the left-hemisphere dorsal attention network to the pallidum was associated with reduced migraine risk, surviving Bonferroni correction.

Right-hemisphere control-network-to-accumbens connectivity negatively mediated the association between genus RuminococcaceaeUCG010 and intercostal neuropathy risk, accounting for about 15% of the total effect.
Right-hemisphere SAN/VAN-to-putamen connectivity positively mediated the association between genus Eubacterium brachy and sciatica risk, accounting for about 27% of the total effect.

Two inter-network connectivity phenotypes (left VN-to-right SAN/VAN and left SAN/VAN-to-right SAN/VAN) each positively mediated the association between genus Ruminiclostridium6 and sciatica risk, accounting for ~23% and ~19% of the total effect respectively.

Left-hemisphere SAN/VAN-to-right-hemisphere control-network connectivity positively mediated the association between genus Marvinbryantia and migraine risk, accounting for about 18% of the total effect.

Right-hemisphere SAN/VAN-to-right-hemisphere default mode network connectivity mediated the relationship between genus Parabacteroides and cluster headache, accounting for about 8% of the total effect.

Left-hemisphere-to-right-hemisphere visual network connectivity positively mediated the association between genus Senegalimassilia and diabetic neuropathy risk, accounting for about 10% of the total effect.

Left-hemisphere control-network-to-putamen connectivity negatively mediated the associations between order Pasteurellales and family Pasteurellaceae abundance and atypical facial pain risk, each accounting for about 10% of the total effect.

Genetically predicted structural connectivity from the right-hemisphere control network to the pallidum was causally associated with increased risk of both small fiber neuropathy and idiopathic peripheral autonomic neuropathy.
Genetically predicted connectivity from the right-hemisphere control network to the nucleus accumbens was associated with reduced risk of both small fiber neuropathy and intercostal neuropathy.
Right-hemisphere somatomotor network-to-putamen connectivity showed bidirectional causal associations, being protective for small fiber neuropathy but a risk factor for diabetic neuropathy.

A cited cross-sectional case-control study found markedly reduced abundance of Helicobacteraceae, Ruminococcaceae, and Veillonellales taxa in patients with postherpetic neuralgia compared to healthy controls.
A cited mouse model of diabetic neuropathy showed significant reductions in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium along with an increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio.

A cited clinical case-control study in patients with painful diabetic neuropathy found elevated Firmicutes, Actinobacteria, Escherichia-Shigella, Clostridium, Megasphaera, and Ruminococcus, with decreased Bacteroidetes, Bacteroides, and Faecalibacterium compared to matched controls.

A cited systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed that chronic pain patients overall exhibit significantly lower relative abundance of Helicobacteraceae, Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Prevotella.
Cited studies found that probiotic supplementation with Lactobacillus acidophilus, Lactobacillus bulgaricus, and Bifidobacterium improved quality-of-life scores in migraine patients.
A cited non-randomized controlled trial found that a 12-week probiotic intervention in migraine patients significantly reduced migraine frequency and severity.
A cited placebo-controlled RCT with 63 migraine participants demonstrated that probiotic treatment significantly reduced migraine severity scores.

A cited double-blind RCT found that 10-week supplementation with 14 probiotic strains reduced frequency and severity of episodic migraine attacks, and an 8-week intervention alleviated symptoms of chronic migraine.
PHN patients were found in a cited study to have significantly lower serum butyrate levels compared to healthy controls.
A cited animal study found that butyrate administration significantly reduced neuropathic pain behaviors in a chronic constriction injury model.
A cited study found that transplanting gut microbiota from healthy donors into a cisplatin-induced neuropathic pain mouse model significantly alleviated pain behaviors within 21 days.
Patients with postherpetic neuralgia show decoupling between the DMN, salience network, and visual network, along with altered intra-DMN connectivity.
Patients with trigeminal neuralgia exhibit disrupted connectivity between the default mode network and the salience/attention network.

Chronic migraine sufferers show enhanced connectivity between the hypothalamus and both the DMN and dorsal visual network, with reduced intra-DMN connectivity, correlating with heightened pain sensitivity.
Patients experiencing bone metastasis pain demonstrate dysfunctional activity within the DMN and salience network.
A cited study of migraine and trigeminal neuralgia patients found increased DAN connectivity in chronic craniofacial pain, with especially pronounced somatomotor-DAN coupling in TN patients.
Patients with sciatica show increased connectivity between the amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex, potentially mediating pain catastrophizing and attentional bias.

Marked activation of amygdala and hypothalamic-limbic pathways occurs during cluster headache attacks, with impaired limbic function in patients with comorbid affective disorders worsening headache frequency and severity.
A cited animal study found that gut microbiota alleviated mechanical allodynia in mice with oxaliplatin-induced chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.

A cited study found that fecal microbiota transplantation from rats with spared nerve injury into germ-free mice exacerbated neuropathic pain symptoms and induced depressive- and anhedonia-like behaviors, contradicting a beneficial gut-microbiota-to-pain relationship.
Using the described protocol (20 μm cryosections, PGP9.5 immunofluorescence) in control mice, average intraepidermal nerve fiber counts were approximately 15 ± 5 fibers per two glabrous footpads.
No significant difference in fiber density was found between the two distal glabrous footpads (#2 and #3) sampled from the same paw.
IENFD quantification showed high inter-rater reliability between two independent blinded evaluators (r > 0.9) with mean standard deviation below 10% across samples.
PGP9.5 immunostaining also enabled clear visualization of Meissner corpuscles, mechanoreceptors in the dermal papillae associated with C fibers.

The authors' previous protocol used suboptimal sampling (central paw), thicker sections, and different antibody/permeabilization settings, resulting in weak PGP9.5 staining, low image resolution, and inconsistent fiber identification that required larger sample sizes to achieve statistical significance.

Reported control IENFD values vary widely across rodent studies, ranging from approximately 32-39 fibers/mm in dietary studies to around 15 fibers/mm in other reports, likely reflecting differences in section thickness and quantification criteria.
3D cleared-tissue imaging methods for IENFD quantification typically yield lower fiber densities than traditional 2D section-based counting.
In addition to intraepidermal nerve fibers and Meissner corpuscles, PGP9.5 immunostaining was also observed to highlight sweat glands in the footpad skin.
Among all tested oral immune adjuvants, LPS elicited the most pronounced clinical allergic symptom scores following IRC allergen challenge.
LPS-adjuvanted rats showed the lowest mean rectal temperature after IRC challenge compared to the blank control group.
All immune adjuvant groups showed elevated serum IgE, IgG, IgA, IgD and IgM compared with the blank group, with LPS producing the highest levels of all Ig classes.
Serum mMCP-1 was significantly elevated in all immune adjuvant groups relative to blank controls, with the LPS group showing the greatest increase.
Serum MCT was significantly elevated in all immune adjuvant groups compared with the blank group, with LPS showing the highest levels followed by chitosan (CHI).
Plasma histamine was elevated in the LPS group and most other adjuvant groups (except Zn(OH)2) relative to the blank group, reflecting mast cell degranulation.
LPS administered without IRC antigen did not independently trigger allergic reactions, except for a significant reduction in serum IgD.

Rats given LPS plus IRC challenge showed the highest levels of all measured allergy biomarkers (Ig classes, mMCP-1, MCT, HIS) with statistically significant increases, confirming LPS enhances IRC allergenicity.
No significant differences were observed in spleen or thymus cytokine levels between the blank group and the LPS+IRC group, indicating a gut-localized rather than systemic immune response.
Splenic CD8+ T cell and mast cell number/distribution did not significantly differ between blank and LPS+IRC groups on histological analysis.
IgG, IgA, and IgM levels were significantly higher in all intestinal segments (duodenum through colon) in the LPS+IRC group compared to blank and LPS-control groups.
IgE and IgD were significantly elevated in most intestinal segments of the LPS+IRC group, with the jejunum showing the most pronounced increase.
sIgA was significantly elevated specifically in the jejunum and ileum of the LPS+IRC group compared with blank and control groups.
Intestinal histamine levels were significantly elevated in the jejunum and ileum of the LPS+IRC group, consistent with mast cell degranulation-driven allergic pathophysiology.
Complement C3 and C4 levels were significantly elevated in intestinal segments (notably jejunum and ileum) of the LPS+IRC group compared with blank and LPS-control groups.
The jejunum showed the strongest convergence of elevated IgE, IgD, sIgA, and histamine, identifying it as the primary site of mucosal immune activation in the LPS-induced IRC allergy model.
Chitosan (CHI) adjuvant produced the second most pronounced elevation in immunoglobulin levels after LPS, likely via enhanced antigen-presenting cell activity and T-cell activation.
Activation of TRPV4 suppressed gastrointestinal motility in vivo.
TRPV4 was found to be expressed in enteric glial cells (EGCs).
TRPV4 activation inhibited GI motility by promoting Enteric Gliosis, encompassing EGC proliferation, activation, and neuroinflammation.
TRPV4 activation promoted intracellular Ca2+ signaling in enteric glial cells.
TRPV4 is required for CaCl2-, CaSR-, and ATP-mediated regulation of Ca2+ signaling and gliosis in enteric glial cells.
TRPV4 activation promoted Enteric Gliosis and corrected abnormal GI motility in a pathological diarrhea model in vivo.
Parvovirus B19 infection was significantly more common in connective tissue disease (CTD) patients with interstitial lung disease (ILD) than in those without ILD.
Hypertension was significantly more prevalent in CTD patients with ILD than in those without ILD.

No significant differences were found between CTD patients with and without ILD in age, sex distribution, smoking status, disease duration, CMV, COVID-19, herpes zoster infection, diabetes mellitus, or cardiovascular disease.
Co-administration of B19V NS1 with bleomycin resulted in a higher lung fibrosis score than bleomycin alone in mice.
Lung hydroxyproline (collagen deposition) content was significantly higher in mice given B19V NS1 plus bleomycin than in mice given bleomycin alone.
B19V NS1 administration significantly increased TGF-beta expression in lung tissue compared with bleomycin treatment alone.
B19V NS1 administration significantly increased collagen I positive cells in lung tissue compared with bleomycin treatment alone.
B19V NS1 increased the proportion of neutrophils in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid compared with bleomycin treatment alone.
B19V NS1 significantly increased Cit-H3 (a NETosis marker) expression in lung tissue compared with bleomycin alone.
B19V NS1 significantly increased MPO expression in lung tissue compared with bleomycin alone, and MPO remained elevated even after nintedanib treatment in the NS1 group.
IL-18 expression in lung tissue was significantly increased in mice given B19V NS1 plus bleomycin compared with bleomycin alone, consistent with inflammasome activation.
IL-17A expression in lung tissue was significantly increased in mice given B19V NS1 plus bleomycin compared with bleomycin alone.
BALF levels of TNF-alpha, KL-6, and IL-6 were significantly elevated in both bleomycin and bleomycin+NS1 groups compared with PBS controls.

Nintedanib treatment significantly reduced fibrotic and inflammatory markers (TGF-beta, collagen I, IL-18, IL-17A, Cit-H3, MPO, TNF-alpha, KL-6, IL-6, hydroxyproline, fibrosis score) and restored lung weight in both bleomycin and bleomycin+NS1 mouse groups.

Nintedanib did not fully reverse NS1-exacerbated pathology; MPO and hydroxyproline levels, and neutrophil proportions, remained elevated in the BLM+NS1+nintedanib group compared with BLM+nintedanib alone.

The authors conclude that B19V NS1 exacerbates bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis mainly through inflammasome activation and neutrophil-driven responses, providing a mechanistic link between B19V infection and ILD progression.
Cyclobenzaprine 30 mg/day produced only marginally greater pain reduction than 10 mg/day, and higher dose was judged to add no meaningful benefit while increasing side effects.
Cyclobenzaprine 30 mg/day was associated with a substantially higher adverse event rate than the 10 mg/day dose.
Cyclobenzaprine 30 mg/day reduced Hamilton Depression Scale scores from baseline.
The multi-strain probiotic VSL#3 did not significantly reduce composite GI symptoms (abdominal pain, bloating, meteorism) compared to placebo in FMS-IBS patients.
VSL#3 probiotic had no significant impact on physical health-related quality of life (SF-36 PCS) versus placebo.
VSL#3 probiotic showed no significant effect on depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) or insomnia severity (ISI) compared to placebo.
A 4-week excitotoxin-free (MSG-restricted) diet significantly reduced fibromyalgia-related pain.
The excitotoxin-free diet also significantly reduced IBS-related pain.
An MSG challenge worsened fibromyalgia pain relative to the excitotoxin-free diet phase.
MSG challenge worsened Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire-Revised (FIQR) scores compared to elimination diet.
The excitotoxin-free diet improved IBS-related quality of life, which reversed upon MSG re-challenge.
Mindfulness-based therapy achieved sustained improvement in physical health (SF-36 PCS) at 3 and 15 months.
Mindfulness therapy decreased anxiety/depression and health anxiety scores.
Mindfulness therapy reduced somatic symptoms less than enhanced usual care did.
Pregabalin 450 mg/day reduced pain scores more than placebo in FMS patients, with efficacy consistent across comorbidity subgroups.
Patient global impression of change with pregabalin was clinically meaningful, though certainty of evidence was very low.
Pooled meta-analysis across interventions showed high heterogeneity in adverse event rates, with an overall pooled adverse event rate of 39.7%.
Subgroup analysis found males receiving 30 mg cyclobenzaprine had a much higher adverse event rate than females receiving 10 mg.
Overall GRADE assessment rated evidence for all critical outcomes (pain VAS, FIQR, side effects) as very low certainty due to imprecision, risk of bias, publication bias, and indirectness.
The critiqued study reported a 200-marker EpiSwitch 3D chromatin conformation biomarker panel with 92% sensitivity and 98% specificity for distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls.
The critiqued study's diagnostic model was based on a retrospective cohort of only 47 ME/CFS patients, raising concerns about generalizability of the biomarker panel.
A Phase III clinical trial of rituximab in ME/CFS failed to meet its primary endpoints, undermining its use as a therapeutic comparator based on shared IL-2 pathway biomarkers.
The critiqued study frames immune dysregulation, including elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines and natural killer (NK) cell dysfunction, as a hallmark of ME/CFS.

The critiqued study reported network overlap between ME/CFS biomarkers and pathways involved in multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, citing shared IL-2, IL-10, CD4, and TLR signaling elements, though this letter argues the claim is speculative given the pleiotropic, non-specific nature of these markers.

The letter notes that oxygen-ozone autohemotherapy has shown promise in peer-reviewed literature for alleviating fatigue and disability in ME/CFS, an alternative therapy omitted from the critiqued study's discussion.
Multiple cited studies found a reduced relative proportion of the phylum Firmicutes in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Multiple cited studies found an increased relative proportion of Bacteroidetes in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, described as a lower Bacteroidetes/Firmicutes ratio.
Anti-inflammatory bacterial genera Faecalibacterium, Bifidobacterium, and Roseburia are reported to be decreased in ME/CFS patients.
Decreased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance is proposed as a potential diagnostic biomarker for ME/CFS.
A single study reported reduced levels of the butyrate-producing genus Anaerostipes in ME/CFS patients.

Two studies found increased abundance of Alistipes in ME/CFS patients, a genus with a possible pathogenic role in anxiety, depression, and chronic fatigue syndrome despite some protective effects in other diseases.
Kitami et al. identified Coprobacillus, Eggerthella, and Blautia abundances as the strongest microbiome features distinguishing ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.
A culture-based study found increased levels of D-lactic acid-producing Streptococcus and Enterococcus spp. in ME/CFS patients, implicated in neurological impairment and cognitive dysfunction.

Several studies found higher levels of LPS and anti-LPS antibodies in peripheral blood of ME/CFS patients compared with controls, supporting a 'leaky gut' / metabolic endotoxemia mechanism that activates TLR-4 signaling and pro-inflammatory cytokine release.

Reduced abundance of the butyrate-producing species Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Eubacterium rectale is linked to disrupted intestinal barrier function and promotion of intestinal inflammation in ME/CFS.
HPA axis dysfunction in ME/CFS patients is associated with lower cortisol levels, reduced daily cortisol variation, and a weakened stress response, worsening fatigue presentation.

Elevated oxidative stress biomarkers (isoprostane, oxidized LDL, iso-prostaglandin F2) together with lowered glutathione levels indicate impaired antioxidant capacity in ME/CFS, potentially contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction and ATP synthesis impairment.

Autoreactive immune cells producing autoantibodies against β2-adrenergic and M3 acetylcholine receptors have been detected in some ME/CFS patients, supporting an autoimmune component to disease pathogenesis.
In a small group of ME/CFS patients given probiotics containing Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, no meaningful changes in fatigue levels or physical activity were observed.
A study found probiotics reduced systemic inflammatory markers CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6 in ME/CFS patients.

In a study by Kenyon et al. comparing FMT to oral pro-/prebiotics in 42 ME/CFS patients with comorbid IBS, 17 of 21 FMT recipients reported improvements and 7 reported complete restoration of quality of life and daily functioning.
Another study found FMT to be a safe treatment for ME/CFS but it did not relieve symptoms or improve quality of life.

In a mouse model, Astragalus polysaccharide alleviated CFS symptoms by increasing SCFA (especially butyrate) levels via gut microbiota regulation, thereby influencing oxidative stress and inflammation in the brain.
A systematic review found insufficient evidence that ME/CFS patients benefit from elimination or modified diets for symptom relief.
Approximately 87% of patients recovering from acute SARS-CoV-2 infection report symptoms similar to ME/CFS, which is proposed to explain the rise in ME/CFS cases during the COVID-19 pandemic.
GI complaints, particularly IBS, are frequently reported by ME/CFS patients, with 35% taking medications to manage these symptoms.
ME/CFS is highly disabling, with up to 75% of affected people unable to work and 25-29% homebound or bedbound.

Results on tryptophan/kynurenine pathway metabolites in ME/CFS are conflicting; some researchers hypothesize insufficient kynurenine production from tryptophan disturbs CNS, GI, and immune function, while other diseases with overlapping symptoms show elevated kynurenine and its metabolites, and gut bacteria-driven dysbiosis may alter tryptophan/phenylalanine metabolite production along the gut-brain axis.
A meta-analysis estimated global ME/CFS prevalence at nearly 0.9% when using the CDC-1994 (Fukuda) case definition.
The review proposes that immunosenescence in ME/CFS drives chronic low-grade inflammation and SASP factor release that impair immune cell function.
Immune aging changes are proposed to impair endothelial nitric oxide production and cerebral blood flow regulation in ME/CFS.
Immunosenescence-related vascular changes may contribute to blood-brain barrier breakdown in ME/CFS.
Brain hypoperfusion and oxidative stress are proposed to impair neuronal energy metabolism and synaptic plasticity in memory-related brain networks in ME/CFS.
The proposed mechanism results in reduced ATP availability, excitotoxicity, and neurotransmitter imbalance contributing to cognitive decline in ME/CFS.
The review proposes a novel conceptual 'immune-vascular-cognitive axis' linking peripheral immune aging to central neural dysfunction in ME/CFS.

The review highlights cytokine blockade, nitric oxide enhancement, immune modulation, and acupuncture as therapeutic strategies that may ameliorate neurovascular impairments and cognitive symptoms in ME/CFS.

Meta-analysis of pooled studies found a significant difference with a large effect size between ME/CFS patients and controls on verbal working memory tasks, indicating impaired verbal working memory in ME/CFS.
No significant difference was found between ME/CFS individuals and controls on visual working memory task performance.
When verbal working memory was broken down into span/attentional control subtasks, the significant impairment in ME/CFS patients relative to controls remained consistent.

When visual working memory was broken down into object/spatial subtasks, no significant difference between ME/CFS patients and controls remained, consistent with the overall visual working memory finding.

The ether-linked glycerophosphocholine PC(O-38:4) was the only lipid to remain significant after multiple-comparison correction, being markedly reduced in ME/CFS LCLs and almost perfectly separating cases from controls.
DG(36:2) was the most elevated lipid detected, and combining its levels with PC(O-38:4) produced near-perfect PCA clustering of ME/CFS versus HC LCLs.
Across the entire non-polar lipidome, the majority of detected lipids showed elevated levels in ME/CFS LCLs compared to HC LCLs.

Six lipid classes (triglycerides, diglycerides, fatty acids, phosphatidylglycerols, lyso-phosphatidylcholines and phosphatidylethanolamines) had significantly more than the chance-expected proportion of lipids elevated in ME/CFS LCLs.
Triglycerides and diglycerides were significantly over-represented among all significantly altered lipids relative to their proportional occurrence in the whole dataset.
Across all di-acyl lipids, the number of double bonds correlated negatively with fold change in ME/CFS LCLs, indicating a shift toward greater lipid saturation.

On a per-class basis, fold change correlated positively with acyl chain carbon count in SM but negatively in PG and ether PS, and correlated positively with double bond count in DG but negatively in PE and PG.
BioPAN pathway analysis of the lipidomic dataset identified 135 lipid pathways and reactions as significantly suppressed or activated in ME/CFS LCLs compared with HCs.

PTDSS1 (phosphatidylserine synthase 1), a BioPAN-predicted gene product, was found upregulated at both the transcript and protein level in ME/CFS LCLs, with protein levels 57.64% higher than controls.

PTDSS1 was previously reported (in a 2016 GWAS cited by the authors) to carry one of the SNPs most strongly associated with ME/CFS diagnosis, supporting a potential genetic link to the observed PTDSS1 overexpression.
None of the 306 detected polar metabolites reached significance in ME/CFS versus HC LCLs after Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons.

An exploratory (uncorrected p<0.05) pathway analysis of the polar metabolome identified vitamin B6 metabolism, thiamine metabolism, and steroid hormone biosynthesis as dysregulated pathways in ME/CFS LCLs.

Cholesterol sulphate, the metabolite driving the steroid hormone biosynthesis pathway signal, was elevated in ME/CFS LCLs, consistent with increased membrane rigidity and potentially linked to reduced CYP2D6 activity.
Pyridoxal was the specific metabolite responsible for the vitamin B6 metabolism pathway signal in the polar metabolome of ME/CFS LCLs.

Thiamine was the specific metabolite responsible for the thiamine metabolism pathway signal, an essential cofactor for BCAA, tryptophan, carbohydrate, TCA cycle, and pentose phosphate pathway enzymes implicated in ME/CFS.

Joint pathway analysis integrating metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics and transcriptomics (female data) highlighted 15 metabolic pathways likely dysregulated in ME/CFS LCLs, with glycerophospholipid metabolism showing the greatest number of hits.

Eicosadienoic acid, an upstream metabolite of eicosanoid precursors, was the highest-ranked feature by p-value in the polar metabolite fraction of ME/CFS LCLs, though it did not survive multiple-comparison correction.

Detected members of the SLC27A fatty acid transporter family showed no differential expression between ME/CFS and HC LCLs in the gene expression datasets, suggesting the lipid accumulation is unlikely to be driven by these transporters.
SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus have been directly shown to induce senescence in endothelial cells.
Endothelin-1 (ET-1) levels are significantly higher in patients with ME/CFS and long COVID compared with controls.
Multiple endothelial senescence-associated markers, including VEGF-A, VCAM-1, ICAM-1, PAI-1, IL-8, MCP-1, and FGF-2, are elevated in ME/CFS and long COVID patient cohorts.
Natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxicity, which is important for clearing senescent cells, is reduced in patients with ME/CFS.
Complement system dysfunction, which normally aids in senescent cell clearance, is implicated in the pathophysiology of ME/CFS and long COVID.
Plasma levels of chitotriosidase and stathmin 1, both suggestive of cellular senescence induction, were increased in hospitalised COVID-19 patients three months after infection.
Indications of T-cell senescence have been observed in both long COVID patients and COVID-19 survivors.
Increased levels of fibronectin, a component of the endothelial SASP linked to fibrosis, have been reported in ME/CFS and long COVID patients.
Thickening of the capillary basement membrane has been observed in long COVID patients, suggesting impaired substance exchange across the vasculature.
Plasma from ME/CFS patients was shown to downregulate nitric oxide (NO) expression in healthy endothelial cells in vitro, indicating a circulating factor that impairs endothelial function.
There is initial evidence of decreased nitric oxide expression and eNOS function in patients with ME/CFS.
Heterogeneous fibrinaloid microclots, dysregulated platelets, and abnormal clotting kinetics are observed in ME/CFS and long COVID patient cohorts.
Senescent endothelial cells express HLA-E, which engages the inhibitory NKG2A receptor on NK and CD8+ T cells, enabling evasion of immune-mediated clearance.
Treatment with senolytic drugs that eliminate senescent cells improved survival in mice infected with coronaviruses, supporting a role for senescent cells in driving acute disease pathology.
Reduced cerebral blood flow and reduced perfusion of certain brain regions and organs have been documented in both ME/CFS and long COVID patient cohorts.
Multiple viruses implicated in ME/CFS and long COVID—including SARS-CoV-2, EBV, HHV-6, influenza A, enteroviruses, and parvovirus B19—are capable of directly infecting endothelial cells.
Gut dysbiosis coupled with increased intestinal permeability and microbial translocation has been documented in both ME/CFS and long COVID.
Herpesvirus RNA and protein have been detected in the central nervous system of ME/CFS patients, suggestive of CNS viral infection.
Peripheral endothelial senescence has been shown to impact blood-brain barrier integrity and cognitive function, suggesting neurological symptoms could arise from peripheral vascular senescence.
Disruption of blood-brain barrier integrity and function has been demonstrated in long COVID patient cohorts.
ET-1 binds the endothelin B receptor on myoblasts, inhibiting skeletal muscle myogenesis and reducing expression of MyoD, MyoG, and MyHC in cultured muscle cells.
PAI-1, a component of the endothelial SASP, inhibits skeletal myogenesis and promotes fibrosis, compromising muscle regenerative capacity.
PACVS patients developed symptoms a mean of 5 days (range 0-33, SD 9) after COVID-19 vaccination, supporting a temporal association between vaccination and symptom onset.
The MECFS group had a mean symptom onset of 9 days after SARS-CoV-2 infection and the LC group a mean of 11 days, both showing a temporal association with acute infection.
The MECFS group had a higher rate of severe-critical acute COVID-19 infection compared to the LC group (18.3% vs 8.5%).

Among PASC patients later vaccinated, only 14.3% reported worsening of PASC symptoms after vaccination while 6.5% reported improvement, suggesting overall low risk of symptom exacerbation from subsequent vaccination.
Nearly half (46.4%) of PACVS patients met screening criteria for ME/CFS, indicating substantial clinical overlap between the two syndromes.
PACVS patients reported significantly higher rates of atypical chief complaints (peripheral neuropathy, tinnitus, rash) as their most debilitating symptom compared to MECFS and LC groups.
The MECFS group reported significantly higher symptom rates across all organ systems, particularly neurologic symptoms, compared to the LC group, even after controlling for demographic factors.
Tinnitus was reported at a significantly higher rate in the PACVS group than in MECFS and LC groups.
MECFS and PACVS patients reported markedly lower perceived preillness health (median 37.5% and 40%, respectively) compared to LC patients (median 65%), indicating greater functional impairment.
The majority of MECFS (80.3%) and PACVS (70.5%) patients reported moderate to severe functional limitations, whereas most LC patients (60.0%) reported negligible to occasional functional limitations.
Plasma histamine was abnormal in 42.7% of the total lab-analysis cohort, suggesting possible mast cell activation across PASC/PACVS groups.

Cytokine panel abnormalities were present in 60.7% of the total lab-analysis cohort, and were significantly more common in MECFS than LC patients (78.1% vs 48.8%, OR 3.14, P = .02), remaining significant after adjustment for demographics.
IL-10 was the most commonly abnormal cytokine across all three groups, abnormal in 41.6% of the lab-analysis cohort, suggesting a compensatory anti-inflammatory response.
TNF-alpha was elevated in 19% of MECFS patients and 21% of PACVS patients, consistent with pro-inflammatory cytokine activation.
IFN-gamma was elevated in 22% of MECFS patients, and z-score analysis confirmed a significant between-group difference for IFN-gamma.

C-reactive protein positivity was low overall (5.1%) and did not differ significantly between MECFS (11.9%), PACVS (0%), and LC (1.6%) groups, despite elevated cytokines, indicating CRP is a poor screening marker for the immune dysregulation seen in these conditions.
HSP-70 autoantibody positivity was elevated in both MECFS (18.75%) and PACVS (35.71%) groups, far exceeding the reported general population rate of 5-8%.

Anticardiolipin IgM (ACL) positivity was significantly higher in PACVS (42.9%) compared to LC (11.6%), and also elevated in MECFS (15.63%) versus a general population rate of approximately 9%, with confirmatory z-score significance.
U1-RNP autoantibody positivity was significantly higher in PACVS (21.4%) than LC (2.3%), with an odds ratio of 10.55 that remained significant after adjusting for demographic factors.
Patients with post-COVID condition showed significantly reduced whole-brain ATP/PCr ratios in a cluster centered on the cingulate cortex compared with fully recovered controls.
Region-of-interest analysis showed consistent ATP/PCr reductions across the anterior cingulate cortex, midcingulate cortex, and posterior cingulate cortex in PCCo patients.
Lower ATP/PCr ratios specifically in the anterior cingulate cortex correlated with poorer cognitive performance on neuropsychological testing in PCCo patients.
Exploratory analysis found a trend toward higher intracellular pH in the midcingulate cortex of PCCo patients.

A significant negative correlation between intracellular pH and ATP/PCr ratio in the midcingulate cortex was observed only in PCCo patients and not in controls, suggesting disease-specific bioenergetic dysregulation.

Subgroup analysis showed that PCCo patients meeting diagnostic criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome exhibited similar cerebral bioenergetic metabolic alterations as the broader PCCo cohort.
CFS/IBS patients had a significantly elevated Dysbiosis Index and reduced fecal bacterial (Shannon) diversity compared with healthy controls.
Serum iron levels were significantly lower in CFS/IBS patients than in healthy controls at baseline.
Probiotic intervention significantly increased serum iron levels, restoring them to control range.
Urinary 3-indoxyl sulfate, a marker of bacterial tryptophan catabolism/leaky gut, was markedly elevated in CFS patients versus controls with a large effect size.
The 3-IS/TRP ratio, reflecting diversion of tryptophan to bacterial indole pathways, was significantly increased in patients at baseline.
Quinolinic acid, a neurotoxic NMDA receptor agonist, was markedly elevated in CFS patients relative to controls at baseline.
The neuroprotective metabolite kynurenic acid was significantly reduced in CFS patients versus controls at baseline.
Xanthurenic acid, a marker of vitamin B6-dependent kynurenine flux, was significantly elevated in CFS patients with a large effect size.
The neuroprotective-to-neurotoxic KYNA/QA balance was severely reduced in CFS patients at baseline versus controls.
Urinary tryptophan availability was significantly lower in CFS patients at baseline, while KYN/TRP ratio was increased, suggesting enhanced IDO/TDO activity.
Absolute 5-HIAA concentration did not differ from controls, but the 5-HIAA/TRP serotonin turnover ratio showed a borderline elevation in patients.
The 12-week multi-strain probiotic intervention significantly decreased xanthurenic acid levels with a large effect size, improving in the great majority of patients.
Quinolinic acid showed a nominal decrease after probiotic treatment but did not remain statistically significant after multiple-comparison correction.
Probiotic treatment significantly increased neuroprotective kynurenic acid, with the majority of patients showing improvement, and the KYNA/QA balance improved with a large effect size.
Probiotic treatment significantly reduced urinary 3-indoxyl sulfate and the 3-IS/TRP ratio, indicating reduced bacterial tryptophan catabolism.
5-HIAA levels increased significantly after probiotic treatment, indicating enhanced serotonin turnover, while tryptophan showed a non-significant increasing trend.
After treatment, 3-indoxyl sulfate levels were no longer significantly different from healthy controls, with effect size shrinking from large to small/negligible.
Post-treatment xanthurenic acid returned to a range statistically indistinguishable from healthy controls.
Kynurenic acid levels, initially depressed, were restored post-treatment and showed no significant difference from healthy controls.
