Quinolinic acid remained significantly elevated in treated patients compared to controls, retaining a large effect size, indicating an incompletely resolved neurotoxic burden.
Tryptophan availability remained significantly lower in treated patients compared to controls, suggesting ongoing substrate depletion despite probiotic supplementation.
Probiotic intervention produced a continuous, highly significant reduction in fatigue severity (FSS) across all timepoints, with a 40.3% mean reduction by week 12.
By week 12, the vast majority of patients achieved remission (FSS below diagnostic threshold), compared to less than half at baseline.
The Minimally Clinically Important Difference (≥10-point FSS reduction) was achieved by the large majority of patients following probiotic treatment.
Gastrointestinal bloating and abdominal pain improved in most participants after probiotic treatment, but constipation worsened in a minority, requiring temporary laxative use.
Sleep disturbances remained the most refractory symptom, persisting in the majority of patients despite substantial reductions in daytime fatigue.

After 12 weeks of probiotic treatment, urinary 3-indoxyl sulfate levels in CFS patients were no longer significantly different from healthy controls, indicating normalization of this bacterial overgrowth marker.
Post-treatment xanthurenic acid levels in CFS patients returned to the range observed in healthy controls, suggesting attenuation of excess kynurenine pathway flux.
Kynurenic acid levels, initially depressed in CFS patients, were restored after treatment and no longer differed significantly from healthy controls.

Despite probiotic treatment, quinolinic acid remained significantly elevated in CFS patients compared to healthy controls, retaining a large effect size and indicating incomplete metabolic normalization.
The neuroprotective KYNA/QA ratio remained significantly lower in treated CFS patients than in healthy controls, indicating that neurotoxic burden was reduced but not eliminated by treatment.

Post-treatment urinary tryptophan availability remained significantly lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls, suggesting persistent substrate depletion or malabsorption despite probiotic therapy.
Probiotic treatment produced a continuous and highly significant reduction in fatigue severity across all assessment time points over 12 weeks.
By week 12, nearly all patients achieved fatigue remission (FSS below the diagnostic threshold), a large increase from the proportion in remission at baseline.
A large majority of patients met the minimally clinically important difference threshold for fatigue improvement after the probiotic intervention.
Gastrointestinal complaints, specifically bloating and abdominal pain, improved in the majority of patients following probiotic treatment.
Constipation worsened in a subset of patients during probiotic treatment, requiring temporary laxative use, in contrast to the general symptom improvement.
Sleep disturbances were the most treatment-refractory symptom, persisting in most patients despite substantial reductions in daytime fatigue.
A greater treatment-associated increase in urinary tryptophan was correlated with a larger reduction in fatigue severity scores.
Patients with the greatest increase in tryptophan showed a dose-dependent, monotonically greater reduction in fatigue scores compared to those with the smallest increase.

The authors interpret the elevated KYN/TRP ratio and high downstream kynurenine metabolites as evidence of robust, chronic immune-mediated IDO activation in CFS, which contradicts the 'Metabolic Trap' hypothesis of a functional IDO block.
Tuina plus usual care produced a significantly greater reduction in overall fatigue severity (CFQ-11 total score) than usual care alone at 4 weeks.
Tuina plus usual care significantly reduced physical fatigue subscale scores compared with usual care alone at 4 weeks.
Tuina plus usual care significantly reduced mental fatigue subscale scores versus usual care alone, but the effect was smaller and was attenuated in a fully-adjusted sensitivity model.
A significantly higher proportion of Tuina-group participants achieved the minimal clinically important difference (≥3-point CFQ reduction) than controls.
Tuina plus usual care significantly reduced anxiety symptom scores (HADS-Anxiety) compared with usual care alone at 4 weeks.
There was no significant between-group difference in depressive symptoms (HADS-Depression) at 4 weeks.
No significant between-group difference was found in bodily pain (SF-36 Bodily Pain subscale) at 4 weeks.
No significant between-group difference was found in physical functioning (SF-36 Physical Function subscale) at 4 weeks, possibly due to a ceiling effect from high baseline scores.
Tuina plus usual care significantly improved overall sleep quality (PSQI total score) compared with usual care alone.
The PSQI sleep duration subscale showed a significant improvement with Tuina that remained significant after Bonferroni correction.
The PSQI sleep disturbance subscale improved with Tuina but did not remain statistically significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
The PSQI daytime dysfunction subscale improved nominally with Tuina but did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction.
Subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep efficiency, and sleep medication use PSQI subscales showed no significant between-group differences.
No serious adverse events occurred in either group, and only two Tuina-group participants experienced transient, self-limiting local pain that resolved without treatment.

The authors hypothesize, but did not test, that Tuina's effects on fatigue, anxiety, and sleep in CFS may involve neuroendocrine regulation and oxidative stress pathways, including tryptophan-serotonin metabolism and antioxidant capacity.
A 10-year-old boy presented with violaceous pretibial plaques, hypermobile joints, and periodontal disease with mobile teeth, consistent with periodontal Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (pEDS).

The patient exhibited atypical features seen in other connective tissue diseases, including mitral valve prolapse, severe myopia, esotropia, tortuous optic nerves, and partial empty sella turcica, suggesting the phenotypic spectrum of pEDS may be broader than previously recognized.
Neither parent of the patient met the diagnostic criteria for pEDS, raising questions about inheritance pattern in this case.
The scoping review identified 36 studies (mostly case reports, 56%) encompassing 9,479 patients with HSD/hEDS undergoing surgical interventions, with a female majority.

Surgical interventions in HSD/hEDS patients spanned nine specialties, most commonly orthopaedic, followed by neurosurgery, maxillofacial, gynaecology, thoracic, dental, endocrine, ophthalmology, and vascular surgery.
Most studies on surgical interventions in HSD/hEDS were limited by small sample sizes and lack of long-term follow-up, restricting definitive clinical conclusions.
There is a gap in qualitative research adequately capturing the surgical experiences of patients with HSD/hEDS.

A 56-year-old female with EDS Type III who failed conservative management underwent a novel meniscal allograft arthroplasty ('Taco Technique') for right CMC (basal joint) arthritis, with no intraoperative or postoperative complications and favorable functional recovery by six months.
Due to joint defects from impaired collagen synthesis, patients with EDS often develop basal joint (CMC) arthritis, making this a recognized comorbidity of the condition.

In a study by Hevesi et al. of nine EDS patients with CMC arthritis, operative management resulted in significant reduction in pain and increased grip strength over time, whereas nonoperative management (NSAIDs, splints, steroid injections) showed no significant change in grip strength or pinch and a decreasing trend in range of motion.
A systematic review found that EDS patients who underwent orthopedic procedures suffered high rates of persistent pain, joint instability, and repeated joint dislocation.

In a prior case report, an 18-year-old female EDS patient with joint instability treated with trapezial opening wedge osteotomy and volar ligament reconstruction was pain-free with joint stability and an 18 kg improvement in grip strength at two-year follow-up.

A prior case report of a 56-year-old male with CMC arthritis managed with bilateral tendon interposition arthroplasty and thermal capsular shrinkage reported excellent pain relief at two months and no pain with return to normal activity and improved grip/pinch strength at one year.

A prior case report of a 58-year-old female with suspected EDS and bilateral CMC arthritis treated with CMC arthroplasty and ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction reported near full range of motion by six weeks and high satisfaction at three months postoperatively.
Nearly half of the 77 male dental hygiene students studied (46.6%, n=36) exhibited joint hypermobility based on the modified Beighton criteria used.
37.7% (n=29) of participants scored positive on Beighton criterion 1 (passive dorsiflexion of the little finger beyond 90°).
46.8% (n=36) of participants met both Beighton criterion 2 (thumb-to-forearm apposition) and the added criterion 3 (index finger distal interphalangeal joint flexibility).
Students positive for Beighton criterion 1 (little finger hyperdorsiflexion) had significantly lower clinical periodontal instrumentation performance scores than those negative for it.
Students positive for both Beighton criterion 2 and the added index-finger criterion 3 had markedly lower clinical performance scores than those negative for both.
Linear regression analysis confirmed a significant relationship between Beighton hypermobility scores and periodontal instrumentation clinical performance ratio.
The patient carried a heterozygous germline missense variant in TGFBR2, consistent with a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

Lung parenchyma showed alveolar septa with irregularly dilated and tortuous capillary proliferation resembling pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis, accompanied by hemosiderin-laden macrophages in air spaces.
Pulmonary muscular arteries and veins showed irregular dilatation and tortuosity with fragmented and disorganized elastic fibers.
The resected lung showed a ruptured bulla/bleb with localized distal acinar emphysema contiguous with the bullous lesion, consistent with the cause of spontaneous pneumothorax.

The authors propose that aberrant TGF-beta signaling together with deranged extracellular matrix formation underlies both the dilated/tortuous pulmonary vasculature and the emphysematous/bullous changes causing pneumothorax in LDS lungs.
Postoperative lateral center edge angle (LCEA) was significantly higher in patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder compared to non-HSD patients after periacetabular osteotomy.
Postoperative anterior wall index (AWI) was significantly higher in patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder compared to non-HSD patients after periacetabular osteotomy.

Patient-reported outcome scores (Modified Harris Hip Score, Nonarthritic Hip Score, International Hip Outcome Tool, Hip Dysfunction and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score) did not differ significantly between HSD and non-HSD patients at preoperative, 1-year postoperative, or most recent follow-up timepoints after PAO.
Patient-reported satisfaction with surgery after PAO was significantly higher in the HSD group than the non-HSD group.
Among 43 pediatric patients with generalized hypermobility spectrum disorder evaluated for Chiari malformation type 1, 43.8% were also found to have a Chiari 1.5 malformation.
Syringomyelia was present in 32.6% of the G-HSD cohort evaluated for Chiari malformation type 1.
Patients with a pB-C2 distance of 9 mm or greater were significantly more likely to require operative Chiari decompression.
Presence of a Chiari 1.5 malformation subtype was significantly associated with a greater likelihood of undergoing operative Chiari decompression in G-HSD patients.
Presence of syringomyelia was significantly associated with a greater likelihood of undergoing operative Chiari decompression in G-HSD patients.
Of the patients who underwent surgery, most received a suboccipital decompression with duraplasty rather than without it.
Surgical treatment consisted of suboccipital decompression with duraplasty in the majority of operated patients (8 of 12, 66.6%).
Ventral decompression was not required for any patient with G-HSD and Chiari malformation over the follow-up period.
Occipitocervical fusion was not required for any patient in the cohort regardless of preoperative anatomical characteristics such as pB-C2 distance.
At a mean postoperative follow-up of 38.2 months, 94.1% of operated patients had improvement or resolution of their preoperative symptoms.
All patients with syringomyelia in this cohort had improvement or resolution of their preoperative syrinx after surgical decompression.

In the electroacupuncture (EA) group, greater improvement in pressure-pain tolerance was significantly correlated with greater reduction in widespread pain, while no such relationship existed in the sham mock-laser (ML) group.
In the mock-laser sham group, there was no significant relationship between changes in pressure-pain tolerance and widespread pain.
The strength of the correlation between pressure-pain tolerance change and widespread pain change was significantly greater in the EA group than in the ML group.
Neither EA nor ML produced statistically significant pre-to-post changes in pressure-pain tolerance or widespread pain, though there was substantial inter-individual variability in change scores.

A whole-brain activation analysis found significant group differences between EA and ML in how pain-evoked activation changes in bilateral S1, left posterior midcingulate cortex, and left precuneus related to widespread pain changes; in EA, greater activation in all four regions was associated with larger widespread pain reductions, whereas in ML the effect was reversed, particularly in the left precuneus.

In the EA group, activation in right S1, left posterior midcingulate cortex, and left precuneus was significantly correlated with improvements in pressure-pain tolerance, an effect not seen in the ML group.

Mediation analysis showed that activation changes in S1 (bilateral), left pMCC, and left precuneus each significantly mediated the relationship between increased pressure-pain tolerance and reduced widespread pain in the EA group.

In the EA group, increased task-modulated functional connectivity between the right anterior insula and a left S1 cluster during pressure-pain was strongly associated with greater reductions in widespread pain.

In the EA group, increased functional connectivity between left and right S1 clusters was correlated with reduced widespread pain, but this pathway did not reach significance as a mediator and was not retained in the final model.

In the ML (sham) group, reductions in widespread pain were associated with decreased functional connectivity between the right anterior insula and a left precuneus cluster, suggesting a top-down default mode network mechanism.

Mediation analysis showed that increased functional connectivity between left S1 and right anterior insula mediated the relationship between S1 activation and reductions in widespread pain following EA treatment.

A serial mediation model showed that increased pressure-pain tolerance led sequentially to increased S1 activation, then strengthened S1-right anterior insula connectivity, ultimately reducing widespread pain in the EA group; reversing the mediator order (connectivity before activation) was not significant.

In the ML sham group, reduced functional connectivity between the precuneus and right anterior insula mediated the relationship between decreased precuneus activation and reduced widespread pain, consistent with a top-down default mode network mechanism.

Overall, electroacupuncture appears to reduce fibromyalgia pain via a bottom-up mechanism linking improved pressure-pain tolerance to reduced widespread pain through S1 activation and S1-anterior insula connectivity, while sham mock-laser operates through a distinct top-down precuneus/DMN-related mechanism.
Kinesiophobia prevalence in sickle cell disease patients (mean TSK score of 30.48) was comparable to that seen in patients with chronic back pain and fibromyalgia.
In women with sickle cell disease, kinesiophobia showed a significant positive correlation with depressive symptoms measured by the Beck Depression Inventory.
In women with sickle cell disease, kinesiophobia showed a strong positive correlation with depressive symptoms measured by the CESD-r.
In men with sickle cell disease, no significant relationship was observed between kinesiophobia and depression on the Beck Depression Inventory.
In men with sickle cell disease, no significant relationship was observed between kinesiophobia and depression on the CESD-r.
The authors propose that the relationship between kinesiophobia and depression in sickle cell disease is mediated by psychomotor retardation, somatization, and pain catastrophizing behaviors.
The patient's serum tryptase was elevated during a symptomatic flare-up, contributing to her diagnosis of mast cell activation syndrome.
Urine N-methylhistamine was elevated during the patient's symptomatic flare-up, supporting the MCAS diagnosis.

Gastric biopsy showed normal mucosa but increased mast cells scattered in the lamina propria on KIT (CD117) stain, with no eosinophils seen, supporting a mast cell disorder rather than eosinophilic GI disease.
Switching from omeprazole to famotidine (an H2 antihistamine) improved the patient's acid reflux and abdominal cramping at 4-week follow-up.
The patient had a good symptomatic response to Cromolyn (mast cell stabilizer) and H1 antihistamines but required additional H2 antihistamines to control GI symptoms.
A minority of MCAS/mastocytosis cases have a genetic basis involving the KIT D816V mutation, which leads to aberrant CD25 expression on mast cells with or without concurrent mastocytosis.

The Vienna consensus defines MCAS diagnosis via three mandatory criteria: recurrent symptoms in ≥2 organ systems, an event-related rise in serum tryptase above baseline (formula: baseline × 1.2 + 2 ng/mL), and clinical response to anti-mast cell therapy.

WHO diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis require 1 major + 1 minor or ≥3 minor criteria, with minor criteria including tryptase >20 ng/mL, KIT D816V mutation, aberrant CD25/CD2 expression, and >25% atypical/spindle-shaped mast cells.
Normal tissue contains ≤15 mast cells per high-power field, but this count can reach up to 100/HPF in mastocytosis on KIT staining.
A higher number of mast cells has been observed in irritable bowel syndrome, though the etiology remains unclear.
Mast cells located near enteric nerve terminals are activated by neuropeptides such as substance P, and their degranulation can worsen GI motility and cause abdominal symptoms.

In guinea pig colon experiments, histamine exposure triggered persistent, recurring cycles of mucosal secretion and muscle contraction that entirely depended on the enteric nervous system, acting as a paracrine neuromodulator from enteric mast cells responding to antigens or dorsal root ganglion input.

Enteric neurons express 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 receptors on mucosal terminals that are activated by serotonin released from enterochromaffin cells, initiating propagating action potentials involved in GI motility.
The patient's GI symptom severity was exacerbated during periods of psychological stress, and dietary elimination strategies were ineffective.
Autosomal mosaic chromosomal alterations, particularly mosaic loss events, were significantly more frequent in schizophrenia patients compared to controls.
Autosomal mosaic chromosomal alterations, particularly mosaic loss events, were significantly more frequent in bipolar disorder patients compared to controls.
The association between mosaic loss and schizophrenia was much stronger in the young-age subgroup than in the overall cohort.
The association between mosaic loss and bipolar disorder was much stronger in the young-age subgroup than in the overall cohort.
The strength of association between mosaic loss events and both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder increased with higher cell fraction of the mosaic event.
High cell fraction mosaic loss events showed a statistical interaction with polygenic risk score in predicting schizophrenia.
Antigen stimulation induced transient dephosphorylation (activation) of SSH1 in RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Antigen stimulation induced sustained dephosphorylation (inactivation) of LIMK1/2 in RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Pretreatment with the SSH inhibitor D3 blocked antigen-induced cofilin dephosphorylation, confirming SSH1's role in cofilin activation.
Pretreatment with the LIMK inhibitor BMS-5 suppressed cofilin rephosphorylation, confirming LIMK1/2's role in cofilin inactivation.
D3 pretreatment alone induced cellular spreading and plasma membrane ruffling in resting mast cells and significantly promoted antigen-induced degranulation.
SSH1 colocalized with histamine-containing secretory granules in resting mast cells, and this colocalization diminished following antigen stimulation.
The LIMK inhibitor BMS-5 suppressed antigen-induced IL-4 secretion from mast cells more efficiently than the SSH inhibitor D3.

LIMK1 interacted with ERK1/2 following antigen stimulation, and BMS-5 pretreatment reduced this interaction as well as ERK1/2 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation, suggesting LIMK positively regulates cytokine secretion via ERK1/2 activation.
LAD2 mast cells were shown to express high surface levels of MRGPRX2 along with the stem cell factor receptor CD117.
Compound 48/80 activated LAD2 cells in a dose-dependent manner, with 2.5 µg/mL producing approximately 50% of total β-hexosaminidase release.
Substance P activated LAD2 cells in a dose-dependent manner, with 5 µM producing approximately 30% of total β-hexosaminidase release.
Cortistatin-14 activated LAD2 cells in a dose-dependent manner, with 5 µM producing approximately 40% of total β-hexosaminidase release.
MRGPRX2 activation increased tryptase secretion, CD63/CD107a surface exposure, and ERK phosphorylation in LAD2 cells, confirming degranulation.
The known MRGPRX2 antagonists C8, C9, and resveratrol each significantly inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated degranulation of LAD2 cells across β-hexosaminidase, tryptase, CD63, and CD107a readouts.
C8 and resveratrol were more effective inhibitors of MRGPRX2 activation than C9, particularly for substance P- and CST-14-induced degranulation.
Oat kernel extract at the tested concentrations did not impact LAD2 mast cell viability over 24-72 hours.
Oat extract pre-exposure significantly and dose-dependently reduced c48/80-induced degranulation of LAD2 cells, with 100 ppm being the most effective concentration.
All tested exposure durations of 100 ppm oat extract significantly reduced MRGPRX2 activation, with 2 hours of pre-exposure producing the most pronounced reduction in degranulation.

Oat extract pre-exposure significantly reduced LAD2 mast cell degranulation induced by c48/80, substance P, and CST-14, measured by β-hexosaminidase and tryptase release and CD63/CD107a surface expression.
Oat extract pre-exposure reduced MRGPRX2-induced ERK phosphorylation in LAD2 cells as shown by Western blot.

Oat extract significantly reduced MRGPRX2 activation induced by the additional agonists LL37 (G-protein-biased), PAMP-12, and ZINC-3575, indicating modulation of both balanced and biased ligand responses.
In a PathHunter β-arrestin recruitment assay using MRGPRX2-transfected CHO cells, oat extract efficiently inhibited MRGPRX2 activation, confirming the effect is not specific to LAD2 cells.
Primary mast cells (skin and blood-derived) released significantly more tryptase upon MRGPRX2 activation than LAD2 cells.
Primary mast cells exhibited substantial donor-dependent variability in β-hexosaminidase, tryptase, CD63, and CD107a responses to MRGPRX2 ligands.

Oat extract pre-exposure significantly reduced ligand-induced degranulation in primary human skin mast cells and blood-derived mast cells, measured by β-hexosaminidase and tryptase release and CD63/CD107a surface expression.
Oat extract pre-exposure reduced phosphorylated ERK levels in blood-derived mast cells stimulated with c48/80 or substance P, confirming reduced downstream signal transduction.
Oat extract pre-exposure completely inhibited release of the chemokine CCL2 (MCP-1) induced by c48/80, substance P, and CST-14 in both LAD2 cells and primary skin mast cells.

In a 45-year-old woman with antihistamine-refractory CSU, initiation of semaglutide (for glucose intolerance) led to complete resolution of urticaria activity within 3 weeks, sustained over 20 months.
In a 44-year-old woman with antihistamine-refractory CSU, tirzepatide started for weight reduction led to marked decrease in urticarial activity within 3 weeks, sustained over 18 months.

In Case 1, marked weight loss (13.5 kg over 3 months) accompanied semaglutide therapy and coincided temporally with CSU remission, though weight loss continued gradually beyond the initial 3-week symptom resolution.

GLP-1RA are reported in the literature to inhibit NF-κB signaling, reduce IL-6 and TNFα, and promote M2 macrophage polarization, mechanisms proposed to underlie their anti-inflammatory effects relevant to CSU.

In animal models of asthma, GLP-1RA suppress IL-33 release, limit ILC2 proliferation, and decrease IL-5 and IL-13 production, indicating downregulation of Th2-driven inflammation, a mechanism proposed as possibly relevant to CSU.
In stimulated human eosinophils, GLP-1RA reduced production of IL-4 and IL-13, cited as further mechanistic support for potential Th2 modulation.

GLP-1 receptors have been identified on several immune cells including ILC2, regulatory T cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, macrophages, and on mast cells in rodents, though human mast cell expression data are conflicting.

A recent cited study demonstrated potential benefit of GLP-1RA in patients with mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), supporting the concept that GLP-1 signaling may influence mast cell-driven diseases including CSU.
Prior studies cited show a higher prevalence of obesity among CSU patients compared to healthy controls, although association with metabolic syndrome remains debated.
Cited data indicate that women with CSU present with more comorbidities than men, including asthma, thyroid disease, obesity, autoimmune conditions, gastrointestinal disorders, and depression.

Case 1 had Hashimoto's thyroiditis with high anti-TPO antibodies and low IgE, suggesting the autoimmune type IIb CSU endotype, which together with history of angioedema typically predicts poor response to antihistamines and even omalizumab, making her rapid GLP-1RA response notable.

Case 2 did not fit either the autoallergic (aiTI) or autoimmune type IIb (aiTIIb) CSU endotype based on basic tests, yet still responded rapidly to GLP-1RA, suggesting a mechanism independent of these classic endotypes, possibly a direct effect on mast cell degranulation threshold.

The authors note that dupilumab, which acts on the Th2 pathway, improves CSU only gradually, contrasting with the rapid response seen with GLP-1RA in their cases, arguing against Th2 pathway inhibition as the explanation for the rapid improvement observed.
Oral esculetin reduced Evans blue dye extravasation in DNP-HSA-induced passive cutaneous anaphylaxis, indicating decreased vascular permeability.
Esculetin treatment diminished ear thickness (a measure of edema) in the PCA model.
Toluidine blue staining showed esculetin suppressed mast cell degranulation at the local allergic reaction site in the PCA model.
Esculetin mitigated OVA-induced hypothermia (rectal temperature drop) in the active systemic anaphylaxis model.
OVA challenge substantially increased serum histamine, and esculetin administration significantly attenuated this elevation.
OVA sensitization increased serum total IgE, and esculetin significantly attenuated this elevation.
OVA sensitization increased serum OVA-specific IgE, and esculetin significantly attenuated this elevation.
OVA sensitization increased serum IL-4, and esculetin significantly attenuated this elevation.
In IgE/DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells and mBMMCs, esculetin reduced histamine release in a concentration-dependent manner.
Esculetin reduced β-hexosaminidase release from activated RBL-2H3 cells and mBMMCs in a concentration-dependent manner.
Esculetin (10 µM) significantly inhibited phosphorylation of the Src-family kinases Lyn and Fyn and the downstream kinase Syk in IgE/DNP-HSA-stimulated RBL-2H3 cells.
Esculetin significantly reduced intracellular calcium levels in a concentration-dependent manner in both RBL-2H3 cells and mBMMCs following IgE/DNP-HSA stimulation.
Esculetin (100 nM) significantly suppressed phosphorylation of PI3K, Akt, and PLCγ1 in activated mast cells, linking its calcium-lowering effect to inhibition of this signaling cascade.
Esculetin pretreatment significantly suppressed IL-4 and TNF-α gene expression in RBL-2H3 cells and BMMCs in a concentration-dependent manner.
Esculetin pretreatment significantly reduced IL-4 and TNF-α cytokine secretion from mast cells in a concentration-dependent manner as measured by ELISA.
Esculetin (10 µM) significantly suppressed phosphorylation of NF-κB p65 and IκBα in IgE/DNP-HSA-activated mast cells, linking FcεRI signaling suppression to reduced cytokine transcription.

RBL SX-38 cells engineered to lack alpha-gal and passively sensitized with AGS patient sera showed a 3-fold increase in CD63+ cells upon alpha-gal antigen stimulation compared with cells sensitized with control serum.
Certain individual human alpha-gal-specific IgE clones, when used to passively sensitize the cells, promoted CD63 upregulation upon alpha-gal antigen stimulation (antigen-dependent activation).
Certain alpha-gal-specific human IgE clones also caused CD63 upregulation independent of alpha-gal antigen exposure, suggesting antigen-independent basophil/mast cell activation.
Cells sensitized with pooled AGS sera released the degranulation marker beta-hexosaminidase even without alpha-gal antigen stimulation, indicating antigen-independent mediator release.

In contrast to pooled AGS sera, cells sensitized with individual alpha-gal sIgE clones alone showed no beta-hexosaminidase release above background, indicating these clones alone were insufficient to trigger full degranulation.
Skin fibroblasts constitutively release sST2 protein at extremely high levels compared to mast cells, a discrepancy not explained by mRNA expression differences.
sST2 protein levels are partly reduced via degradation mediated by mast cell proteases, explaining the mismatch between high fibroblast-derived sST2 protein and mast cell mRNA levels.
sST2 deficiency did not affect IL-33- and/or IgE plus antigen-stimulated mast cell activation in vitro.
Constitutively high levels of sST2 suppress food allergies in mice by inhibiting IL-33-dependent expansion and enhanced degranulation of jejunum mast cells.
Bone marrow chimeric mice studies showed circulating sST2 under steady-state conditions is derived almost equally from hematopoietic and nonhematopoietic cell sources.
Increased circulating sST2 in food-allergic mice was possibly and partly derived from fibroblasts stimulated by locally released IL-4 and IL-13.

Unsupervised PCA of supernatant metabolomics showed clear segregation of pRBC samples by storage time, with PC1 explaining 26.6% of variance and defining distinct clusters for Week 0, Weeks 1-2, and Weeks 3-6.
A Random Forest model trained to predict storage week from metabolite profiles achieved perfect classification at Week 0 but declining accuracy at later weeks, yielding an overall OOB error of 0.646.

Methionine underwent early and substantial depletion in RBC supernatant during storage, reaching near-depletion by the end of the second metabolic phase, consistent with its role in supporting methylation-based proteostasis.
Linear modeling with donor ID as a blocking factor and Week 0 as reference identified 118 of 188 quantified metabolites that significantly changed in concentration during 42-day storage.
Glycine was among the top metabolites with increased concentration in RBC supernatant over storage, alongside C18:1 and C18:2 acylcarnitines and histidine.
Hexoses (glucose sum) were among the top metabolites with decreased concentration in RBC supernatant during storage, along with methionine, SM C18:1, and lysoPC a C16:1.
Red cell distribution width (RDW-SD and RDW-CV) increased significantly with storage duration, reflecting progressive anisocytosis and declining RBC deformability during cold storage.
Supernatant C18:1 (oleic acid) acylcarnitine showed a statistically significant positive correlation with RDW-SD, a marker of storage-induced RBC damage.
Supernatant C18:2 (linoleic acid) acylcarnitine was significantly positively correlated with RDW-SD, consistent with membrane lipid degradation during storage.

A calculated glutathione-turnover index (Gly/(Glu+Gln)) increased monotonically throughout storage, indicating that export and extracellular gamma-glutamyl cycling of used glutathione outpaces the diminishing intracellular substrate supply.

Human skin mast cells cultured with 10% supernatant from 6-week-stored pRBC units showed significantly greater degranulation (beta-hexosaminidase release) than those exposed to fresh (Week 0) supernatant.

C18 acylcarnitine, a known mast-cell activator that promotes histamine release and intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, significantly accumulated in RBC supernatant over extended storage, potentially contributing to allergic transfusion reaction risk.

Median serum MRGPRX2 concentration did not differ significantly between patients with drug-induced immediate hypersensitivity reactions, patients with Hymenoptera venom-induced reactions, and healthy controls.
Serum MRGPRX2 concentration was not associated with reaction severity, the specific causative agent, or serum tryptase level among patients with immediate hypersensitivity reactions.

The authors concluded that serum MRGPRX2 concentration was not a risk factor for the investigated drug- and venom-induced immediate hypersensitivity reactions and does not support its use as a predictive biomarker.
Plasma concentrations of 5-lipoxygenase-derived lipid mediators were significantly higher in CSU patients than in non-atopic control subjects.
5-HETE was identified as the strongest independent plasma marker distinguishing CSU patients from non-atopic controls in a stepwise regression model.
5-HETE significantly upregulates IgE-dependent activation of basophils and mast cells.
Changes in plasma 12-HEPE levels before and after omalizumab treatment significantly correlated with changes in basophil counts.
12-HEPE significantly inhibits TNF-α/IFN-β-induced CCL2 mRNA expression in human keratinocytes, suggesting a role in limiting basophil recruitment.
Plasma 12-HEPE concentration significantly increased after omalizumab treatment in treatment responders but not in non-responders.
Small fiber neuropathy is frequently detected in Parkinson's disease and may occur before overt motor symptoms appear.
Long-term levodopa therapy has been linked to peripheral neuropathy, attributed to metabolic disturbances including vitamin B12 depletion and elevated homocysteine.
Pathogenic variants in PRKN, DJ1, PINK1, GBA, and ATP13A2, which cause parkinsonian syndromes, have also been associated with peripheral nerve involvement.
Several inherited peripheral neuropathies caused by variants in FIG4, LRSAM1, SLC25A46, DNAJB2, and AARS present with overlapping parkinsonian features.
Standard diagnostic screening for classic causes of distal sensory polyneuropathy (DSP) fails to identify a cause in roughly a third to a half of patients, termed initially idiopathic DSP (iiDSP).
Multiple large case series and two small passive-transfer studies suggest that autoimmunity may be a prevalent cause of initially idiopathic DSP, particularly for small-fiber neuropathy.
Concomitant rheumatologic conditions, including often undiagnosed Sjögren's syndrome, predispose patients to autoimmune small-fiber/sensory neuropathies.
Autoantibody panels are almost never useful in identifying autoimmune causality in idiopathic distal sensory polyneuropathy.

Uncontrolled studies suggest that apparently autoimmune distal sensory polyneuropathy sometimes responds to corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulins, and plasmapheresis, though these cannot be prescribed indiscriminately due to risk, cost/availability, and lack of controlled trials and guidelines.
Small-fiber sensory/autonomic disturbances in DSP can cause premature fatigue, neuropathic pain and itch, postural orthostatic tachycardia, and gastrointestinal distress.
The pooled prevalence of at least one post-COVID neuromuscular disease or related symptom declined from 36% in the acute phase to 8% at 24 months.
Myalgia prevalence steadily declined from 35% in the acute phase to 8% at two years post-COVID.
Guillain-Barré syndrome showed a trend towards lower prevalence across successive follow-up time points after COVID-19.
Other muscle diseases also showed a trend towards lower prevalence over successive follow-up time points after COVID-19.
Neuropathic pain prevalence remained high and nearly unchanged over follow-up, from 31% in the acute phase to 25% at 12 months.

Small fiber neuropathy was one of fourteen specific post-COVID neuromuscular conditions/symptoms assessed for long-term prevalence and trajectory, though the abstract does not report a specific pooled prevalence value for it.
oxLDL treatment of resting (M0) THP-1-derived macrophages caused more than a sixfold increase in TNF-α secretion compared to untreated M0 macrophages, approaching M1-like levels.
M2-like polarized macrophages secreted TNF-α at levels as low as untreated M0 macrophages, indicating an anti-inflammatory secretory profile.
Conditioned medium from oxLDL-treated M0 macrophages doubled the number of firmly adherent THP-1 monocytes on an endothelial monolayer compared to medium from untreated M0 macrophages.
M2-like macrophages secreted the highest levels of TGF-β1, roughly 3-fold higher than M0 and 5.5-fold higher than M1-like macrophages.

oxLDL, native LDL, and IL-6 each modestly increased TGF-β1 secretion from resting M0 macrophages, significantly higher than levels seen in M1-like macrophages, suggesting a hybrid rather than pro-inflammatory-only shift.

In M1-like macrophages, combined LDL+IL-6 or oxLDL treatment produced a 4.8- to 5.0-fold increase in TGF-β1 secretion, reaching 86-90% of the M2-like level, indicating a shift toward a hybrid Mox-like phenotype.
In M2-like macrophages, treatment with IL-6, LDL, LDL+IL-6, or oxLDL slightly reduced TGF-β1 secretion relative to untreated M2-like cells.
Recombinant TGF-β1 significantly increased LUVA human mast cell motility and induced positive directional chemotaxis, in contrast to control, M0, and M1-like conditions.
M2-like macrophage conditioned medium enhanced mast cell motility and chemotaxis comparably to recombinant TGF-β1, while M1-like conditioned medium did not induce chemotaxis.

M1-like macrophages treated with LDL+IL-6 or oxLDL (forming a Mox-like phenotype) induced mast cell motility exceeding that induced by recombinant TGF-β1 alone, and chemotaxis comparable to M2-like macrophages.

Prior work by the authors showed that a subclinical concentration of oxLDL significantly enhances TNF-α secretion from resting macrophages while also activating human mast cells, evidenced by a 2.5-fold increase in histamine release.
The paper cites literature indicating IL-6 has been implicated as a potential contributor to Alzheimer's-disease-like symptoms in patients with long COVID.

The paper cites a Phase III clinical trial in which masitinib, a dual mast cell/microglia activation inhibitor, showed significant clinical benefit in patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
PCA of cranial landmark coordinates showed a significant difference in cranial shape between Tgfbr2G357W/+ and Tgfbr2+/+ mice at all four postnatal ages.
Cranial centroid size (a measure of overall skull size) was significantly smaller in Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice than wild-type at all four ages.
Orbital spacing (width of frontal bone between orbits) was significantly larger in Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice than wild-type at 24w and 6w.
The ventral length of the skull was significantly reduced in Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice at all four developmental stages, appearing more severe at earlier stages.
Mandibular shape differed significantly between genotypes across all ages, with the mutant mandible overall shortened, most severely at the proximal end (condyloid process, coronoid process, angle).

Condyle length was reduced in mutant mice at 2 weeks but became increased at 6 and 24 weeks, indicating an age-dependent reversal of directionality (condylar hyperplasia with osteophyte formation at later ages).
Significant directional (left-right) asymmetry of cranial and mandibular shape was found in Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice across all age groups, more so than in wild-type mice.

Cranial doming was observed in mutant mice, corroborated by a significant reduction in the angle between the frontal and nasal bones and between the parietal and interparietal bones, consistent with an anteriorly shortened, curved skull.

Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice showed cranial suture microfusions/full fusions and palatal fusion not seen in wild-type mice, features consistent with craniosynostosis and high-arched palate reported in human LDS patients.

Female Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice exhibited significantly more severe reduction of the nasal-frontal angle, ventral skull length, and mandibular length than males, indicating sexual dimorphism in craniofacial phenotype severity.
The effect of sex on the degree of cranial asymmetry was statistically significant at 12 and 24 weeks, and on mandibular asymmetry at 2, 6, and 24 weeks, in Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice.

No statistically significant sexual dimorphism was detected in overall cranial or mandibular shape or centroid size across age stages in Tgfbr2G357W/+ mice, despite the sex-specific severity differences observed in specific measurements.
In the LDS2 human cohort, downslanting palpebral fissures were observed in 18/26 (69.2%) of patients, most of whom (61%) were female.
The Craniofacial Abnormality Index (CAI) score tended to be higher in female LDS2 patients (median CAI=14) than males (median CAI=12), indicating greater craniofacial anomaly burden in females.
The skeletal intermaxillary sagittal discrepancy (ANB) was significantly more severe in female LDS2 patients than males.

3D PCA of craniofacial shape in the LDS2 human cohort showed statistically significant directional asymmetry and a significant effect of sex on craniofacial shape, with females showing greater variability and more outliers.

Case-series imaging of three female and one male LDS2 patients with distinct TGFBR2 kinase-domain variants showed that nasal tip deviation was due to underlying skeletal asymmetry of the nasal bone and nasal cavity base, more severe in females than in the male patient, consistent with nasal bone asymmetry seen in the Tgfbr2G357W/+ mouse model.

Cephalometric analysis of the LDS2 human cohort confirmed shorter anterior cranial base length, decreased midface length and maxillary projection, decreased mandibular length and projection, and increased maxillomandibular sagittal discrepancy compared to normative population values.

The mouse model showed high phenotypic variability in craniofacial shape, contrasting with the uniform, fully penetrant phenotype (100% cleft palate, 100% mandibular shortening) seen in prior Tgfbr2 conditional knockout mouse models, and instead recapitulating the variable expressivity seen in human LDS2 patients.
Aged human gingival fibroblasts showed reduced α11 integrin mRNA (76%) and protein (33%) compared with fibroblasts from younger donors.
Aged human gingival fibroblasts showed reduced TGF-β1 mRNA (34%) and protein (40%) compared with fibroblasts from younger donors.
TGF-β transcriptional activity, measured by a gene reporter assay, was reduced by 38% in fibroblasts from older donors compared with younger donors.

TGF-β1 treatment increased α11 integrin mRNA 3.6-fold and protein 45% in fibroblasts from younger donors, but produced no change in α11 integrin expression in fibroblasts from older donors, indicating a loss of TGF-β1 responsiveness with aging.
Gingival wounds in older mice showed 61% lower collagen deposition than wounds in younger mice.
Gingival wounds in older mice showed 48% lower collagen alignment/organisation than wounds in younger mice.
Gingival wounds in aged mice showed reduced collagen fiber alignment/organisation compared with wounds in young mice.
TGF-β1 expression was markedly reduced in gingival wounds of aged mice compared with young mice.
The paper notes that IBS is a condition frequently associated with fibromyalgia and was present as a comorbidity in the reported case.

The 2016 ACR Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria requires a Widespread Pain Index ≥7 with Symptom Severity Scale ≥5 (or WPI 4-6 with SSS ≥9), pain in at least four of five body regions, and symptoms persisting at least three months.
The AAPT 2019 Diagnostic Criteria for Fibromyalgia require pain in at least six of nine body sites, moderate to severe sleep problems or fatigue, and symptoms present for at least three months.

In the reported case, standard inflammatory, autoimmune, and endocrine laboratory tests (ESR, CRP, vitamin B12, folate, anti-CCP, rheumatoid factor, TSH) were all normal, supporting fibromyalgia as a diagnosis of exclusion.

The patient exhibited severe bilateral tenderness on tender point assessment in nine paired regions (posterior shoulder, upper back, epicondyle, wrist, hand, low back, posterior thigh, popliteal, knee), rated 10/10 in intensity, supporting the fibromyalgia diagnosis.
The patient was prescribed pregabalin and tramadol for pain management instead of an SNRI, due to concern for serotonin syndrome given concurrent sertraline use.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has been shown to improve pain in fibromyalgia by increasing patient awareness and motivating exercise to reduce pain intensity.
Consistent aerobic and resistance exercise are linked to improved pain tolerance and quality of life in fibromyalgia patients.

Novel therapies for fibromyalgia including cannabinoids, ketamine, lidocaine infusions, melatonin, low-dose naltrexone, and psychedelics are supported by limited evidence and warrant further research.

Multiple concurrent comorbidities (bipolar II disorder, major depressive disorder, PTSD, IBS, cardiomyopathy, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, hidradenitis suppurativa, and melanoma) complicated the diagnostic work-up of fibromyalgia in this patient.

Socioeconomic stressors, including financial difficulties, unemployment, and limited access to quality healthcare, likely contributed to and exacerbated the patient's fibromyalgia symptoms and delayed treatment-seeking.
Binding and internalization of the ACE2-SARS-CoV-2 complex leads to functional downregulation of membrane ACE2 enzymatic activity.

Ang-(1-7) signaling through the Mas receptor activates PI3K/Akt and exerts vasodilatory, anti-proliferative, anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory effects including inhibition of TGF-β, adhesion molecules, and NF-κB.
In Vero E6 cells, NO donors DETA-NONOate and S-nitrosoglutathione reduced SARS-CoV-2 binding to ACE2 and subsequent viral replication, likely via S-nitrosylation of spike protein cysteines.
NO S-nitrosylates viral cysteine proteases including the main protease (Mpro), impairing SARS-CoV-2 replication analogous to mechanisms seen in SARS-CoV-1.
Hypertension was reported in 30-50% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients and significantly increased mortality risk.
Endothelial biomarkers including endothelin-1, von Willebrand factor, and soluble adhesion molecules are elevated in hypertensive COVID-19 patients, reflecting systemic endothelial damage.
A cohort study identified obesity as an independent predictor of severe COVID-19 in patients younger than 60 years.
Diabetes was present in 20-30% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients and was associated with greater disease severity and mortality.
Acute myocardial injury with troponin elevation occurred in up to 20-30% of critically ill COVID-19 patients with metabolic syndrome comorbidities.
ACE2 expression and NO signaling decline with aging and are lower in males, which may partly explain higher COVID-19 mortality in older men.
Increased iNOS activity/levels have been reported in severe COVID-19, correlating with ventilatory failure and cardiac injury.
In experimental ischemic stroke models, ACE2-deficient mice show larger infarcts, greater neuronal apoptosis, and more pronounced blood-brain barrier damage.
Reduced ACE2 levels have been detected in brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid in Alzheimer disease.
Increased Ang II/AT1 activity in the substantia nigra contributes to neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neuron loss in Parkinson disease.
Meta-analyses indicate that approximately 30-40% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients present with neurological symptoms including headache, anosmia, encephalopathy, stroke, or seizures.
In a retrospective cohort of over 230,000 patients, 33% received a neurological or psychiatric diagnosis within 6 months of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Obesity has emerged as a predictor of more severe and persistent cognitive symptoms in long COVID.

Small randomized studies of L-arginine (± vitamin C) improved flow-mediated dilation, 6-minute walk distance, and fatigue in long COVID, and reduced need for respiratory support/length of stay in hospitalized patients.
Early clinical testing of Mas-axis augmentation in severe COVID-19 showed acceptable safety but no consistent efficacy on hard clinical outcomes.
Clinical studies in severe COVID-19 suggest inhaled NO improves oxygenation parameters and reduces viral replication, but without a consistent survival benefit.
Experimental work shows S-nitrosocaptopril releases captopril and NO/NO2, combining ACE inhibition with NO donation for a cardioprotective and potentially neuroprotective profile.
Il33 was the most highly enriched wound-healing-associated transcript in oral versus skin fibroblasts from public scRNA-seq datasets, showing a 15-log2fold increase in aggregate expression.
IL-33+ fibroblasts in mouse palatal gingiva co-localized with PI16+ reticular fibroblasts at ~70% frequency, whereas SCA1+ submucosal fibroblasts made up less than 10%.

Nuclear IL-33 immunopositivity in connective tissue was drastically reduced on day 2 post-wounding and only partially recovered to ~50% of baseline by day 6, indicating rapid release from oral fibroblasts upon injury.
Extracellular IL-33 protein concentration in wound tissue supernatant peaked on day 2 post-wounding and was non-detectable at other time points.
Fibroblast-specific deletion of IL-33 (ΔIL33Col1a2) caused delayed epithelial gap closure on day 2 and reduced re-epithelialized area on days 2 and 4 post oral wounding compared to controls.
Fibroblast IL-33 deletion mice showed reduced COL3A1 protein deposition and impaired granulation tissue turnover in oral wounds on days 4 and 6 post wounding.
Fibroblast-specific IL-33 deletion had no impact on scalp skin wound epithelial gap closure or collagen matrix formation on day 4, contrasting with its effect in oral mucosa.

Keratinocyte-specific IL-33 deletion did not alter epithelial gap closure, KRT14+ area, granulation tissue, COL3A1+ area, or CD45+ cell numbers in oral wounds, indicating fibroblast- rather than keratinocyte-derived IL-33 drives the phenotype.
Nearly 90% of ST2+ cells in early oral wounds were CD45+ leukocytes, not EPCAM+ epithelial or PDGFRA+ fibroblast cells, implicating an indirect leukocyte-mediated IL-33 signaling mechanism.

Recombinant IL-33 addition to primary oral keratinocytes or fibroblasts did not alter keratogenesis or collagen production gene expression in vitro, and siRNA knockdown of Il33 in oral fibroblasts had little effect on collagen gene expression, supporting an indirect signaling mechanism.
Among ST2+ leukocyte clusters in oral wounds, Treg cells accounted for ~40% of total Il1rl1+ cells, more than mast cells or ILC2s.

MIF and TGF-β1 expression were reduced in FOXP3+ Treg cells from IL-33 deletion mice compared to controls, confirmed by scRNA-seq violin plots and flow cytometry mean fluorescent intensity in day 2 wounds.

The monocyte cluster showed the most drastic 2.6-fold decrease in cell numbers in IL-33 fibroblast-deletion mice compared to controls, with associated Vegfa expression in this cluster linked to angiogenesis.
Stimulating isolated splenic Treg cells with recombinant IL-33 enhanced MIF mRNA and protein levels, an effect prevented by IL-33 neutralization with soluble ST2 decoy receptor.
In Transwell assays, IL-33-primed Treg cells significantly increased monocyte migration compared to vehicle or IL-33-neutralized groups, an effect blocked by neutralizing MIF or CD74 antibodies.
ΔIL33Col1a2 mice had significantly reduced CD74+LY6C+ monocytes, VEGFA+LY6C+ monocyte numbers, and CD31+ blood vessel numbers in oral wounds compared to control littermates.
Anti-inflammatory gene expression in the M2 macrophage cluster was significantly reduced in IL-33 deletion mice compared to controls, while pro-inflammatory M1 genes were similar or upregulated.

Co-culturing IL-33-primed Treg cells with bone marrow-derived macrophages increased Arginase-1+ M2 macrophage numbers under M2-polarizing conditions, an effect blocked by TGF-β1-neutralizing antibody.

Diphtheria toxin-induced Treg cell ablation in Foxp3-DTR mice delayed epithelial gap closure, decreased COL3A1+ area, reduced angiogenic monocytes and M2 macrophages, and lowered MIF/TGF-β1 tissue levels and CD31+ blood vessels in oral wounds.

Local injection of recombinant MIF and TGF-β1 into oral wounds of Treg-ablated mice rescued CD74+LY6C+ monocyte and F4/80+CD206+ macrophage numbers, blood vessel numbers, and COL3A1+ area compared to saline injection.

In human tissue, IL-33 was mainly expressed in CD31+ endothelial cells in the upper lamina propria and in PI16+ reticular fibroblasts in the deeper lamina propria of gingiva, contrasting with human skin where suprabasilar epithelial cells and hair follicle niches were the major IL-33 source and skin PI16+ fibroblasts minimally expressed IL-33.

In human healing gingival biopsies (4 days after implant abutment removal), FOXP3+MIF+ and FOXP3+TGFB1+ double-positive Treg cells were significantly more abundant in the deeper lamina propria than the upper layer, with MIF puncta ~20/cell and TGFB1 puncta ~2/cell in deep-layer Treg cells.
NK cells from ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced PregS-evoked TRPM3 ion channel current amplitude compared to NK cells from healthy controls.
Ononetin-suppressed current amplitude in NK cells was significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, confirming impaired TRPM3 function.
A significantly smaller proportion of NK cells from ME/CFS patients were sensitive to the TRPM3 antagonist ononetin compared with NK cells from healthy controls.

ANCOVA analysis showed that laboratory site (NCNED vs UWA) did not significantly confound TRPM3 current or ononetin amplitude results, confirming reproducibility of the finding across two independent laboratories.
Total white cell count was significantly reduced in ME/CFS participants compared to healthy controls.
Neutrophil count was significantly reduced in ME/CFS participants compared to healthy controls.
NK cell isolation purity did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and healthy control samples, confirming comparable cell quality between groups.
All eight SF-36 quality of life domains were significantly reduced in ME/CFS participants compared with healthy controls.
All six WHODAS disability domains were significantly increased in ME/CFS participants compared with healthy controls, indicating greater functional disability.

Employment status differed significantly between groups, with only 13.9% of ME/CFS patients in full-time employment compared to 63.4% of healthy controls, and 25% of ME/CFS patients reporting illness/disability as their employment status versus none in HC.
The majority (80%) of ME/CFS patients in this cohort reported an infectious episode as the trigger for disease onset, consistent with prior literature.
Fatigue, pain, and sleep disturbances were reported by 100% of the ME/CFS cohort, while cognitive difficulties, sensory disturbances, and immune disturbances were also highly prevalent.
Cardiovascular symptom prevalence differed significantly between ME/CFS patients recruited at the Griffith (Queensland) versus UWA (Western Australia) sites.

Prior in vitro studies cited in the discussion found that overnight naltrexone treatment restored impaired TRPM3 ion channel function in NK cells from ME/CFS and long COVID patients, supporting naltrexone as a potential TRPM3-targeted therapeutic.
A novel intronic SNP (rs2179311) near CAMK1G, predicted to functionally affect HSD11B1, was associated with decreased extra-large VLDL phospholipids specifically in the ME/CFS cohort.
A novel SNP (rs13203202) upstream of CARMIL1, predicted to affect SCGN, was associated with decreased total fatty acids specifically in the ME/CFS cohort.
A novel intronic SNP (rs12402423) within the long intergenic non-coding RNA LINC01701 was associated with increased free cholesterol in LDL specifically in the ME/CFS cohort.

An intronic SNP downstream of CETP, predicted to affect NLRC5, was significantly associated with total cholines, small HDL particle concentration, and VLDL free cholesterol uniquely in the ME/CFS cohort.

A missense CPS1 variant (rs1047891) showed the strongest functional-impact association in ME/CFS, being linked to reduced glycine levels, and this SNP was also significant in the DecodeME case-control GWAS.
A synonymous MYRF variant (rs174535) was associated with sphingomyelin levels in both ME/CFS and healthy controls, and was also significant in the Million Veteran Program case-control GWAS.
In the ME/CFS cohort, mGWAS identified 112 significant SNP-region-biomarker associations, involving 27 unique SNPs mapping to 15 genes across 8 metabolic biomarker groups.

In healthy controls, the mGWAS yielded 4,114 significant SNP-biomarker associations across 861 SNPs mapping to 366 genes, including stop-loss variants in LPL and SCARB1 each linked to multiple biomarkers.

Twenty-three SNPs mapping to 12 genes were significantly associated with metabolic biomarkers in both ME/CFS and healthy controls, spanning urea cycle, lipid metabolism, fatty acid metabolism, glycosylation, innate immunity, solute transport, retinoic acid synthesis, and signal transduction pathways.
None of the four unique ME/CFS mGWAS SNPs reached genome-wide significance in seven prior case-control ME/CFS GWAS, though rs13203202 (SCGN) showed nominal significance in five of seven studies.

Genetic effect sizes on metabolic biomarkers showed only moderate correlation between ME/CFS and healthy controls after winner's curse adjustment, suggesting differing genetic regulation of metabolism between groups.
Heterogeneity testing identified 65 SNP-biomarker associations with significantly different effect sizes between ME/CFS and healthy controls, with high between-group variance.
rs10951261 near ADAP1 showed opposite-direction effects on ApoB levels in ME/CFS versus healthy controls, suggesting divergent immunogenetic regulation of lipid metabolism.

rs4752983 near NR1H3 (encoding LXRα, a regulator of cholesterol efflux and macrophage inflammation) showed opposite-direction effects on large HDL particle concentration in ME/CFS versus healthy controls.
rs10432735 near CD40 showed opposite-direction effects on cholesteryl esters in large LDL particles between ME/CFS and healthy controls.

Minor allele frequencies of significant SNPs did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and controls after correction for multiple testing; only rs4968318 (EFCAB13) and rs1260333 (GCKR) showed nominal differences.

Unsupervised decomposition of mGWAS summary statistics revealed five molecular functions—including apolipoprotein binding, lipoprotein lipase activity, monoamine transmembrane transporter activity (implicating SLC18A1), triglyceride binding, and triglyceride lipase activity—enriched across all 24 latent genetic components in ME/CFS.

A latent genetic component (Component 5) capturing VLDL variation was enriched for both pro- and anti-inflammatory pathways (leukocyte-mediated immunity, neutrophil degranulation) via NLRC5, LPL, and AQP9, and for TGF-β-related signaling (glycosaminoglycan and SMAD binding).

A latent genetic component (Component 18) capturing VLDL variation was enriched for collagen receptor activity and muscle alpha-actinin binding through DDR1, suggesting a possible link to connective tissue and mechanotransduction dysfunction in ME/CFS.
Of 135 NMR metabolic biomarkers screened, 87 differed significantly between ME/CFS and healthy controls after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

Genes involved in ATP-generating pathways (amino acid metabolism, glycolysis, ketone metabolism) were significantly associated with biomarkers in healthy controls but not detected as significant in ME/CFS, consistent with attenuated genetic effects on energy metabolism in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS participants had significantly higher BMI than healthy controls.
C-reactive protein was significantly higher in ME/CFS cases than in healthy controls, consistent with low-grade systemic inflammation.
ME/CFS cases had lower testosterone levels than healthy controls.
Hand grip strength (both left and right) was markedly lower in ME/CFS cases compared with healthy controls.
Comorbid irritable bowel syndrome was present in 9.9% of the ME/CFS cohort, among several other comorbidities reported.
Migraine was reported as a comorbidity in 6.5% of ME/CFS cases in this cohort.
The minor allele frequency of a missense EFCAB13 variant, rs4968318, was nominally higher in ME/CFS than in healthy controls.
The minor allele frequency of an intronic GCKR-proximal variant, rs1260333, was nominally higher in ME/CFS than in healthy controls, though this did not survive multiple-testing correction.

DeGAs decomposition identified monoamine transmembrane transporter activity, involving SLC18A1 (a gene not individually significant in the mGWAS), as enriched across all 24 latent components, suggesting a broader monoaminergic signaling disruption in ME/CFS.

DeGAs component 18, which captured VLDL biomarker variation, was enriched for collagen receptor and alpha-actinin binding activity via DDR1, suggesting impaired mechanotransduction and connective tissue involvement.

DeGAs component 5, capturing VLDL biomarker variation, was enriched for both pro- and anti-inflammatory processes including leukocyte-mediated immunity and neutrophil degranulation, involving NLRC5, LPL and AQP9, alongside TGF-β-related signaling.

DeGAs component 6, capturing 82.5% of fatty acid biomarker variation, was enriched for linoleoyl-CoA desaturase and omega-6 fatty acid desaturase activity, implicating FADS2-related fatty acid metabolism.

NR1H3 (encoding LXRα), which regulates cholesterol efflux, bile acid synthesis and macrophage anti-inflammatory activity, showed a significant effect-size difference between ME/CFS and controls for its association with large HDL particle concentration.

A CD40-mapped variant, rs10432735, showed opposite-direction effects on cholesteryl esters in large LDL particles between ME/CFS and healthy controls, indicating differential immunogenetic regulation of lipid metabolism.
An ADAP1-mapped variant, rs10951261, showed a significant heterogeneity in its effect on ApoB levels between ME/CFS and healthy controls.

Healthy-control-only genetic associations mapped to ATP-production pathways (amino acid metabolism, glycolysis, ketone metabolism) that were absent in the ME/CFS mGWAS, suggesting attenuated genetic signal for energy metabolism genes in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS individuals in the UK Biobank exhibited elevated glycoprotein acetyls, a composite biomarker of systemic inflammation associated with various inflammatory conditions.
Loss of MYRF transcription factor function disrupts myelin production, a mechanism the authors link to demyelination previously observed in ME/CFS via MRI and plasma catalytic antibody studies.
HSD11B1 had been previously implicated in ME/CFS through a different SNP (rs846906) identified by a candidate gene study, corroborating the current mGWAS finding of HSD11B1 involvement via rs2179311.

The CPS1-glycine association, significant in both ME/CFS and HC, is interpreted as reflecting hepatic urea cycle function, consistent with prior metabolomic reports of reduced ornithine and citrulline suggesting inefficient ammonia detoxification in ME/CFS.
The coefficient of variation (CV) of handgrip strength was previously shown not to be an appropriate method for determining sincerity of effort, being inflated in weaker or injured individuals.

In healthy volunteers tested under full-effort, reduced-effort, and simulated-injury conditions, CV did not differ significantly between conditions even though other testing modalities did distinguish them.
In closely spaced repeated handgrip trials, ME/CFS patients show a steeper decline in force than healthy individuals, and this decline correlates with disease severity.

The fatigability-based exclusion criterion used in the original analysis removes subjects with the largest force decline, who arguably represent more severe ME/CFS disease, producing selective attrition that could distort variance estimates and obscure true group differences.
The letter authors report they were unable to reproduce the participant numbers of the original study using the publicly available dataset, even after applying the stated exclusion criteria.

The author reiterates that submaximal handgrip contractions in ME/CFS patients are not evidence of insincere effort or poor motivation, but likely reflect higher-order factors such as pain, kinesiophobia, and low motor self-efficacy.

The author argues that if lower strength invariably caused higher coefficient of variation (CV), healthy females (who have ~62% of healthy males' mean grip strength) would show substantially higher CV than males, which is not observed.

The author clarifies the methodology for the fatigability subgroup analysis: index of fatigability (IF) values from sessions 1 and 2 were averaged per healthy control, and only ME/CFS participants within ±2 SD of the gender-specific mean IF of healthy controls were included.
In healthy controls, functional connectivity between the right caudate nucleus and right cerebellum 10 increased from the Pre to the Post cognitive fatigue condition.
In healthy controls, functional connectivity between left amygdala and cerebellar vermis 9 increased during the Post cognitive fatigue condition compared to Pre.
In healthy controls, functional connectivity between cerebellar vermis 6 and the posterior cingulate cortex increased during the Post cognitive fatigue condition.
In healthy controls, functional connectivity between cerebellar vermis 7 and the right midbrain increased during the Post cognitive fatigue condition.
In long COVID patients, functional connectivity between the left nucleus accumbens and cerebellar vermis 3 was significantly reduced during the Pre cognitive fatigue condition.
In long COVID patients, functional connectivity between the medial prefrontal cortex and left hippocampus increased during the Post cognitive fatigue condition.

In ME/CFS patients, functional connectivity between the brainstem left cuneiform nucleus and right medulla increased significantly during the Post cognitive fatigue condition, with no significant connectivity in Pre.
Compared to healthy controls, long COVID patients showed significantly reduced functional connectivity between the left amygdala and cerebellar vermis 7 during Pre.
Compared to healthy controls, long COVID patients showed significantly reduced functional connectivity between right cerebellum 9 and the anterior cingulate cortex during Pre.
Compared to healthy controls, long COVID patients showed significantly reduced functional connectivity between the left medulla and left hippocampus during Pre.

During Post, long COVID patients showed reduced functional connectivity between left nucleus accumbens and vermis 3, while healthy controls showed increased connectivity between right cerebellum 7b and vermis 6.

Compared to healthy controls, ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased functional connectivity between the right rostro-prefrontal cortex hub of the salience network and the posterior cingulate cortex during Pre.

Compared to healthy controls, ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased functional connectivity between the left lateral parietal cortex node of the default mode network and cerebellar vermis 7 during Pre.
Compared to healthy controls, ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced functional connectivity between the right rostro-prefrontal cortex and left lateral parietal cortex during Pre.
During Post, healthy controls showed increased functional connectivity between right thalamus and left midbrain, and between right cerebellum 7 and vermis 6, relative to ME/CFS patients.

During Pre, ME/CFS patients showed increased functional connectivity between the posterior cingulate cortex and cerebellar vermis 9 compared to long COVID patients, who showed no significant connectivity in Pre.
During Post, long COVID patients showed significantly increased subcortical functional connectivity involving bilateral thalamus and putamen compared to ME/CFS patients.
During Post, long COVID patients' left putamen showed hyperconnectivity with the left amygdala but reduced connectivity with the posterior cingulate cortex, compared to ME/CFS patients.

In ME/CFS patients, duration of illness positively correlated with FC between right hippocampus and vermis 4&5, and between right hippocampus and cerebellum 6, during the Pre condition, but negatively correlated with right hippocampus-vermis 4&5 FC during Post.
No significant correlation was found between duration of illness and functional connectivity in long COVID patients, possibly reflecting their much shorter disease course.
In ME/CFS patients, functional connectivity between cerebellum 6 and the left caudate nucleus was strongly negatively correlated with cognitive deficit scores during Post.
In ME/CFS patients, functional connectivity between the left supramarginal gyrus and amygdala was strongly negatively correlated with cognitive deficit scores during Pre.

In long COVID patients, functional connectivity between the right supramarginal gyrus and left cerebellum 7, and between right SMG and left red nucleus, positively correlated with cognitive deficit scores during Pre.
No sex-based differences in functional connectivity were observed among the three cohorts (HC, pwME/CFS, pwLC).

Overall, reduced functional connectivity was a prevalent feature in both long COVID and ME/CFS patients during repeat cognitive fatigue task fMRI, while healthy controls consistently showed increased connectivity between regions.

A five-factor latent structure (IBS, musculoskeletal pain, depression, anxiety, and general malaise) best captured the combined diagnostic symptoms of internalizing and functional disorders in a large general population sample.
ME/CFS and fibromyalgia symptoms did not form their own distinct diagnostic dimensions, but were instead distributed across a musculoskeletal pain dimension and a general malaise dimension.
Post-exertional malaise, considered the hallmark symptom of ME/CFS, loaded onto the musculoskeletal pain dimension rather than the general malaise dimension.

ME/CFS symptoms tender lymph nodes, sore throat, and headache, together with the IBS symptom abdominal pain, clustered with transdiagnostic symptoms in the general malaise latent dimension, despite being largely isolated in a prior symptom network analysis.

Six of the nine ME/CFS diagnostic symptoms loaded onto the general malaise dimension, which also captures symptoms common to depression and anxiety, indicating a close relationship between ME/CFS and internalizing disorders.
Current fibromyalgia diagnosis showed the strongest association with the musculoskeletal pain symptom dimension.
Current ME/CFS diagnosis was moderately associated with the musculoskeletal pain symptom dimension, though less strongly than fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Older age was positively associated with the musculoskeletal pain symptom dimension.
Chronic stress in the past year was strongly associated with the general malaise symptom dimension.
All ID and FD diagnoses were significantly associated with the general malaise symptom dimension, with the strongest association for fibromyalgia and weakest for major depressive disorder.
The IBS symptom dimension was associated most strongly with current IBS diagnosis and only weakly with all other demographic, lifestyle, stress, and comorbid diagnosis variables.

Chronic stress remained significantly associated with all five symptom dimensions even after removing illness-related chronic stress items in a sensitivity analysis, indicating the association was not solely driven by illness-related stress.

Among latent symptom dimensions, depression and anxiety were most strongly correlated; the general malaise dimension correlated strongly with anxiety, musculoskeletal pain, and depression, while the IBS dimension was weakly correlated with all other dimensions.
The IBS symptom dimension was distinct from the other four dimensions, showing only weak correlations with the musculoskeletal pain, depression, anxiety, and general malaise dimensions.
Point prevalence of current diagnoses in the general population sample was highest for fibromyalgia and generalized anxiety disorder, and lowest for major depressive disorder and ME/CFS.

Transdiagnostic symptoms shared across ID and FD diagnostic criteria (fatigue, concentration difficulty, unrefreshing sleep, trouble sleeping) were the most commonly reported symptoms in the general population sample.
In the EFA, the depression and anxiety symptom factors were the most strongly correlated of the five dimensions.
The general malaise symptom factor was strongly correlated with the anxiety, musculoskeletal pain, and depression factors.
The IBS symptom factor was only weakly correlated with the other four symptom dimensions, indicating a relatively distinct pattern.
The IBS symptom factor was most strongly associated with current IBS diagnosis and only weakly with all other risk factors and diagnoses.
The musculoskeletal pain symptom factor was most strongly associated with FM diagnosis, followed by osteoarthritis, ME/CFS diagnosis, and older age.

Compared with the depression factor, the anxiety symptom factor showed stronger associations with female sex and chronic stress, while the depression factor showed stronger associations with younger age, BMI, and acute stress.
The general malaise symptom factor was strongly associated with chronic stress and with all ID and FD diagnoses, with the largest association for FM and the smallest for MDD.

A sensitivity analysis removing illness-related chronic stress items yielded results comparable to the main model, with chronic stress remaining significantly associated with all five symptom factors.
Post-exertional malaise, often considered the hallmark ME/CFS symptom, loaded on the musculoskeletal pain dimension rather than the general malaise dimension.
Point prevalence of diagnostic status in the full sample was highest for FM and GAD and lowest for MDD and ME/CFS.
Overlapping symptoms (fatigue, concentration difficulty, unrefreshing sleep, trouble sleeping) were the most commonly reported symptoms in the general population sample.

Six of the nine ME/CFS diagnostic symptoms loaded on the general malaise dimension, which also captures symptoms common to MDD and GAD, indicating a close relationship between ME/CFS and internalizing disorders.

Sore throat, a ME/CFS diagnostic symptom, has been shown in prior population-based research to be equally prevalent among those meeting and not meeting ME/CFS criteria, suggesting limited diagnostic specificity.
Individuals with MDD who report fatigue, a high-loading symptom in the general malaise dimension, have previously been shown to have a significantly increased risk of functional disorders.
The five-factor CFA model fit better than models without covariates, and adding external risk factors and diagnoses accounted for additional variance in the symptom dimensions.

The authors clarify that the 30 ng/mL SMPDL3B threshold was derived using a k-fold cross-validated Random Forest model on the Canadian dataset, avoiding circularity by separating training and validation folds.

The SMPDL3B threshold's discriminative performance was preserved in an independent Norwegian ME cohort with a categorical, clinician-assigned severity outcome, supporting generalizability of the original model rather than requiring cohort-specific recalibration.

The authors acknowledge that the 100 µM saxagliptin concentration used in their original mechanistic assays is supraphysiological, employed only to ensure consistency across structurally related DPP-4 inhibitors in a proof-of-concept context.

Combining 4,000 µM myo-inositol with a much lower, near-clinically-relevant dose of saxagliptin (0.5 µM) reproducibly modulated membrane-bound SMPDL3B in Jurkat T cells, suggesting myo-inositol enhances saxagliptin's effect at pharmacologically plausible concentrations.

PBMC viability remained stable (80–89%) across all treatment conditions including saxagliptin, vildagliptin, and linagliptin, with no differences from vehicle-treated samples, indicating the observed SMPDL3B modulation is not due to cytotoxicity.

In the absence of commercially available isoform-selective PI-PLC activity assays, the authors used a combined approach of PLCXD1 expression, total PI-PLC quantification, and SMPDL3B redistribution to support a PI-PLC-mediated mechanism.

This is a protocol for a randomized, waitlist-controlled trial testing whether a 6-week course of CP003, a lingzhi (Ganoderma lucidum)-containing supplement, reduces fatigue in patients with CFS/ME or post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome, with no results yet available.

The paper's background states that patients with CFS/ME often have elevated cytokine levels and evidence of impaired immune function, such as decreased natural killer cell activity, compared to healthy individuals.
The background notes that patients with CFS/ME may have reduced antioxidant levels or impaired antioxidant defenses, contributing to oxidative stress and reduced cellular energy (ATP) production.

Both CFS/ME and post-COVID-19 fatigue are associated with persistent immune activation, elevated proinflammatory cytokines and autoantibodies, and downregulation of hypothalamic-pituitary axis activity.
