Baseline fatigue VAS scores differed significantly between the two crossover study periods, indicating a carryover effect that necessitated separate analysis of each period.
In Period 1, ketamine infusion was associated with a 21.0% decrease in fatigue VAS scores from baseline to 3 days post-infusion.
In Period 2, ketamine infusion was associated with a 10.9% decrease in fatigue VAS scores from baseline to 3 days post-infusion.
In Period 1, midazolam infusion (active comparator) was associated with a 17.7% decrease in fatigue VAS scores from baseline to 3 days post-infusion.
In Period 2, midazolam infusion was associated with a 12.6% decrease in fatigue VAS scores from baseline to 3 days post-infusion.
No statistically significant difference in fatigue VAS reduction was observed between ketamine and midazolam in either study period.
In the ketamine group, the largest reduction in fatigue VAS score occurred at 1 day post-infusion during Period 1, showing a 38.7% decrease from baseline.

The ketamine arm's 21.0% reduction in fatigue VAS score from pre-infusion to 3 days post-infusion in Period 1 exceeded the pre-specified 20% efficacy threshold used as the primary outcome, despite not reaching statistical significance versus midazolam.

Fatigue was described as a prevalent symptom across chronic illnesses including cancer survivorship, fibromyalgia, ME/CFS, and systemic lupus erythematosus, with a substantial impact on quality of life.
92.5% of individuals in a tertiary pain clinic cohort met criteria for moderate (71.3%) or severe (21.2%) Bodily Distress Syndrome (BDS), far exceeding general-population prevalence estimates.
77.0% of participants reported at least four non-pain symptoms (mean 7.18, SD 4.26) after excluding pain-related BDS items, indicating BDS symptom burden extends well beyond pain itself.
Severe BDS was significantly more common among women (23.7%) than men, with BDS severity differing significantly by gender.
Severe BDS was more common among individuals with lower education (24.7% in primary education vs 17.6% in higher tertiary education).
Severe BDS was more common among individuals not working (24.5%) than those employed (16.2%).
Severe BDS was associated with a longer duration of persistent pain compared to lower severity groups.
Severe BDS was associated with slightly younger age, but no age difference was found between the no-BDS and moderate-BDS groups.
Higher BDS severity was associated with more severe insomnia symptoms on the Insomnia Severity Index, confirmed in adjusted ANCOVA and regression models.
Higher BDS severity was associated with greater fatigue severity on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire, confirmed in adjusted ANCOVA and regression models.
Higher BDS severity was associated with greater pain catastrophizing on the Pain Catastrophizing Scale, confirmed in adjusted ANCOVA and regression models.
Higher BDS severity was associated with greater psychological distress (anxiety, depression, somatization) on the HSCL-25, confirmed in adjusted ANCOVA and regression models.
Higher BDS severity was associated with greater perceived injustice related to chronic pain on the Injustice Experience Questionnaire, confirmed in adjusted ANCOVA and regression models.
Higher BDS severity was associated with greater baseline pain-related disability on the modified Oswestry Disability Index, confirmed in adjusted ANCOVA and regression models.
Higher BDS severity was associated with lower health-related quality of life on the EQ-5D Index and VAS, confirmed in adjusted ANCOVA and regression models.
Higher baseline BDS symptom burden predicted greater pain-related disability at 12-month follow-up, even after adjusting for baseline disability and demographic variables.
Higher baseline BDS symptom burden predicted poorer perceived global improvement (PGIC) at 12-month follow-up, after adjustment for demographic covariates.

Individuals excluded from BDS analyses due to incomplete checklist data had higher baseline disability than those included, suggesting overall symptom burden in the analyzed sample may be underestimated.

An alternative single-organ/multi-organ BDS classification produced the same group distribution as the standard severity categories, suggesting overall symptom burden may be more informative than which specific clusters are affected.
Chronic fatigue syndrome was significantly more prevalent in the combined psoriasis/PsA study group than in healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia was significantly more common in the combined psoriasis/PsA study group compared to healthy controls.
Tension headache/migraine was significantly more common in the psoriasis/PsA study group than in healthy controls.
Restless leg syndrome was less frequent in the psoriasis/PsA study group than in healthy controls.
Within the whole cohort, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome were significantly more common among patients with clinically significant central sensitization (CSI≥40) than those without.
Irritable bowel syndrome was significantly more frequent among patients with clinically significant central sensitization (CSI≥40).

Fibromyalgia was significantly more prevalent in the psoriatic arthritis group than in the psoriasis-only group, while chronic fatigue syndrome prevalence was similarly high in both groups without a stated significant difference.
Central sensitization was present in 68% of psoriasis patients versus 35.8% of PsA patients, a significant difference favoring higher central sensitization burden in psoriasis.
Neuropathic pain, assessed via S-LANSS and pain DETECT questionnaires, was detected in 50% of psoriasis patients and 60.4% of PsA patients.
General disease-related pain (VAS) correlated strongly and positively with the central sensitization inventory score, pain DETECT score, S-LANSS score, and ESR.

In psoriatic arthritis, active disease (not achieving minimal disease activity) was associated with higher central sensitization inventory scores, neuropathic pain scores, and pain measures than inactive disease.
Minimal disease activity status in psoriatic arthritis was strongly associated with central sensitization score in a linear logistic regression model.
Diagnosis of hEDS/HSD was substantially delayed, with symptom onset in childhood, treatment first sought in the late 20s, and formal diagnosis not made until the mid-40s.
Comorbid diagnoses were highly prevalent among women with hEDS/HSD, with most reporting seven or more comorbid conditions.
SF-36 assessment showed high symptom burden and poor overall health-related quality of life, with physical domain scores worse than mental domain scores.

Multiple factors including symptom severity, treatment restrictions, environmental factors, comorbidities, and interactions with health care providers were associated with HRQOL in women with hEDS/HSD.
A case of spontaneous celiac artery dissection led to the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Patellofemoral instability affects over half of patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to systemic connective tissue abnormalities combined with joint-specific biomechanical issues.

Gait alterations from patellofemoral instability can overload the fibular head and aggravate proximal tibiofibular joint symptoms, while proximal tibiofibular joint instability can increase lateral stress on the patella and worsen maltracking, creating compounded symptoms when both occur together.
Combining MPFL reconstruction with tibial tubercle osteotomy produces better outcomes than MPFL reconstruction alone when the TT-TG distance is elevated.

Allograft tendons for MPFL reconstruction produce similar redislocation and satisfaction rates as autografts but significantly reduce donor site morbidity, making them preferable in patients with connective tissue disorders such as hEDS.

Tibial tubercle osteotomy can correct patellar tracking via anteriorization, medialization, and distalization, but anteriorization achieved is often less than planned intraoperatively, whereas medialization and distalization are more reliably achieved.

MPFL reconstruction combined with tibial tubercle osteotomy may not adequately correct patellofemoral malalignment in patients with severe trochlear dysplasia, so trochleoplasty should be added in those severe cases.

Lateral retinacular lengthening outperforms lateral release, particularly when combined with tibial tubercle medialization, by reducing lateral overtensioning and medial instability risk and improving patellar tracking control.

Anatomic reconstruction of the proximal tibiofibular joint using suspensory fixation devices is preferred over rigid screw fixation because it eliminates joint micromotion, avoids hardware complications like screw breakage, and removes the need for tendon grafts, simplifying surgery and reducing morbidity.
A biomechanical study found that a single-button suspensory fixation construct is sufficient to stabilize the proximal tibiofibular joint in cases of instability.
In this patient with hEDS, the tibial tubercle was medialized 15 mm during combined MPFLR/TTO/PTFJ stabilization surgery to achieve a target TT-TG distance of approximately 5 mm.

Intraoperative assessment after the combined MPFL reconstruction, tibial tubercle osteotomy, and proximal tibiofibular joint stabilization confirmed reduced lateral patellar quadrant excursion, full knee flexion to 120°, and unimpeded tracking in the trochlear groove.
The dog's skin extensibility index (SEI) was 17%, above the normal canine threshold of less than 14.5%, confirming skin hyperextensibility.

Morphometric analysis of skin biopsies showed the dermal elastin component increased to 28.3% of total collagen and elastic fibrous tissue area, more than double the ~12% typically seen in most species and humans.

Histopathology showed collagen fibers were largely preserved with only minor fragmentation and disarrangement, contrasting with the marked elastic fibre pathology and with typical collagen-abnormal canine EDS cases.

The combination of near-normal collagen with marked elastic fibre hypertrophy/fragmentation was interpreted as suggestive of a classical-like EDS phenotype caused by Tenascin-X (TNXB) deficiency, though genetic testing was not performed.

A previously published canine case reported two rare TNXB variants, each inherited from a different parent, in a dog with suspected TNXB-linked EDS, but without accompanying histopathological findings.
The dog developed a severe, permanent bilateral knee flexion contracture severely limiting mobility, a feature the authors state has not been previously reported in canine EDS.
The dog exhibited extreme blood vessel fragility, a feature the authors note is not well documented in canine EDS literature, with only one other published case reporting severe vascular fragility.
The dog died from hypovolemic shock and cardiac arrest following spontaneous hernial rupture with major blood vessel damage ten days after the first consultation.

The paper contrasts the present TNXB-suggestive case with the more commonly reported canine EDS mechanisms: COL5A1 mutations causing type V collagen abnormalities and ADAMTS2 mutations causing defective procollagen processing and collagen fibril formation.
Patients with EDS had an elevated risk for nearly all of the 18 gynecologic and 6 obstetric diagnoses assessed compared with age-matched patients without EDS.
Among the diagnoses examined, EDS patients showed the greatest increase in risk for urogynecologic conditions relative to non-EDS controls.
EDS patients had an increased risk for benign gynecologic diagnoses compared with age-matched controls without EDS.
EDS patients had an increased risk of adverse obstetric outcomes compared with age-matched controls without EDS.
EDS patients received more fertility care than age-matched controls without EDS.

The patient showed elevated lip mobility (47th percentile vs a 27% norm) and hypermobility of 1.7 mm compared to an ideal of 0 mm, consistent with a hypermobile upper lip contributing to her gummy smile.
Miniscrew-supported archwire mechanics produced approximately 3 mm of absolute intrusion of the maxillary anterior teeth.
Treatment reduced the Ricketts Maxillary Height angle from 62° to 56°, indicating successful correction of vertical maxillary excess.
Mandibular counterclockwise autorotation reduced the Go-Gn-SN angle from 40.5° to 32°, normalizing the patient's hyperdivergent facial profile.
The treatment achieved a Class I molar relationship with 2 mm overbite and 2 mm overjet, correcting the initial shallow overbite (1 mm) and reduced overjet (1 mm).

The authors hypothesize that altered tooth position may modify lip elevator muscle activity via periodontal proprioception, potentially reducing gummy smile by decreasing elevator muscle hyperactivity.

Fascial network adaptations such as SMAS layer redistribution are proposed to contribute to improved lip posture after orthodontic treatment, though the authors note this requires further confirmation.

A genetically confirmed COL3A1 variant consistent with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was identified in a patient with thoracoabdominal aortic hypoplasia (midaortic syndrome) and multiple aortic and visceral aneurysms.

Open surgical thoracoabdominal type II aortic replacement using a multimodal neuro- and organ-protective approach (CSF drainage, MEP monitoring, selective distal perfusion, and targeted blood product/volume management) achieved a complication-free thoracoabdominal reconstruction in a patient with COL3A1-related vascular EDS and midaortic syndrome.
Postoperatively the patient developed an anastomotic stenosis of the right renal artery, which required subsequent interventional endovascular treatment.

There was no significant difference between the hypermobility and non-hypermobility groups in the change in total pain frequency or any individual body-part pain frequency before versus after bariatric surgery.

In participants without hypermobility, pain frequency significantly decreased after metabolic and bariatric surgery compared with before surgery in the neck, lumbar spine, hips, knees, ankles, and feet/toes.
In participants with hypermobility, no significant change in pain frequency was observed for any body part between pre- and postoperative assessments.
In participants without hypermobility, the number of painful body parts significantly decreased after surgery compared with before surgery.
In participants with hypermobility, no significant change was observed in the number of painful body parts after surgery.
There was no significant difference between the hypermobility and non-hypermobility groups in the change in number of painful body parts after surgery.
Postoperatively, 15 of 74 participants (20%) self-reported joint hypermobility according to the Five-Part Questionnaire, while 59 (80%) did not.

Six participants who did not report hypermobility before surgery reported hypermobility after surgery, while one participant transitioned from hypermobile to non-hypermobile, suggesting weight loss may alter perceived joint stability.

Participants with hypermobility tended to maintain pain levels in load-bearing joints such as hips and knees after surgery, whereas pain in these regions decreased in the non-hypermobility group, possibly reflecting underlying joint instability less responsive to weight-loss-related load reduction.
Presence of joint hypermobility significantly predicted presence of bipolar affective disorder, with a fivefold increase in odds.
Likely autism, as screened by the RAADS-R, was much more prevalent in the bipolar affective disorder group than in the comparison group.
Likely ADHD, as screened by the Wender Utah Rating Scale, was much more prevalent in the bipolar affective disorder group than in the comparison group.
Meeting the threshold for likely autism was strongly associated with a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder.
Meeting the threshold for likely ADHD was strongly associated with a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder, with a larger effect size than for autism.

Mediation analysis indicated that autistic traits, ADHD traits, and pooled neurodivergent characteristics statistically mediate the relationship between joint hypermobility and bipolar affective disorder.
Keratoconus has been anecdotally associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, as some patients with joint hypermobility and skin hyperelasticity also present with keratoconus.

A 2021 resequencing study of 34 candidate genes in about 745 keratoconus patients versus 810 controls found significant enrichment of rare variants in the EDS-associated genes COL5A1, COL12A1, TNXB, and ZNF469, supporting a shared genetic etiology between keratoconus and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Within the same resequencing study, the strongest single-variant association with keratoconus was a common variant in COL12A1 (collagen XII).
Gene-based burden testing in the same cohort also implicated COL2A1 (collagen II) as associated with keratoconus.

Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in ZNF469 or PRDM5 cause Brittle Cornea Syndrome, an EDS-like connective tissue disorder featuring extreme corneal thinning (200-450 μm or less) with risk of spontaneous rupture.

Evidence for rare, damaging ZNF469 coding variants in sporadic keratoconus is inconsistent: early screenings were largely negative, while some later cohorts reported enrichment of rare ZNF469 variants.

COL5A1 and COL12A1 mutations underlie classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, TNXB mutations cause a tenascin-X-deficient form of EDS, and ZNF469 is linked to brittle cornea syndrome, an EDS-like condition — the same genes implicated in keratoconus.

COL5A1 is one of the most consistently replicated keratoconus risk loci across GWAS and case-control studies, with biological plausibility from its role in collagen fibrillogenesis and corneal structure — the same gene implicated in classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The authors suggest that identifying TNXB or COL5A1 mutations in keratoconus patients could prompt clinical screening for systemic Ehlers-Danlos-related manifestations such as mitral valve prolapse or vascular fragility.
Patients with generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥5) had nearly triple the odds of developing future contralateral patellar instability after ipsilateral MPFL reconstruction.
Skeletal immaturity at the time of ipsilateral MPFL reconstruction was independently associated with increased odds of future contralateral patellar instability.
Recurrent (versus first-time) patellar dislocation in the ipsilateral knee was independently associated with increased risk of future contralateral patellar instability.
Trochlear dysplasia in the ipsilateral knee (assessed via trochlear depth on MRI) was independently associated with increased odds of future contralateral patellar instability.

Patella alta in the ipsilateral knee (assessed via Caton-Deschamps index) was included in the final model but its confidence interval crossed 1, indicating borderline/non-significant association with future contralateral patellar instability.
Overall, about one-third of knees that underwent ipsilateral MPFL reconstruction subsequently developed contralateral patellar instability.

A composite prediction model combining the five identified risk factors estimated contralateral patellar instability risk ranging from 9.2% with none of the risk factors present to 77.8% when all five were present.
TMJ effusion on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of palpation pain at the lateral pole of the TMJ.
Degenerative joint disease seen on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of TMJ crepitation.
Thickening of the lateral pterygoid muscle insertion (pterygoid double disc sign) on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of TMJ crepitation.
Degenerative joint disease on MRI was significantly associated with decreased odds of clinical condylar hypermobility, suggesting degenerative changes restrict joint movement.
A glenoid fossa height greater than 6 mm on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of clinical condylar hypermobility.
TMJ effusion on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of uncorrected mandibular deviation on opening.
TMJ effusion on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of palpation pain in the medial pterygoid muscle.
Mandibular condyle subluxation on MRI was strongly associated with increased odds of palpation pain in the medial pterygoid muscle.
Abnormal (flattened/folded/convex) disc morphology on MRI was associated with decreased odds of palpation pain in the lateral pterygoid muscle.
A side-to-side difference in TMJ space width greater than 1 mm was associated with decreased odds of palpation pain in the lateral pterygoid muscle (i.e., symmetric spacing favored bilateral pain).
Degenerative joint disease on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of palpation pain in the masseter muscle.
Anterior disc displacement with reduction on MRI was significantly associated with increased odds of palpation pain in the temporalis muscle.
Abnormal disc morphology (e.g., flattened disc) on MRI was significantly associated with decreased odds of palpation pain in the temporalis muscle.
Uncorrected deviation on clinical exam predicted the presence of joint effusion on MRI, but with poor model discrimination.
Palpation pain in the medial pterygoid muscle predicted the presence of joint effusion on MRI, but with poor model discrimination.
Clinical condylar hypermobility was associated with a lower likelihood of degenerative joint disease on MRI, though model discrimination was poor.
Palpation pain in the masseter muscle was associated with higher odds of degenerative joint disease on MRI, though model discrimination was poor.
Clinical condylar hypermobility reduced the likelihood of anterior disc displacement without reduction on MRI, in one of the two models with acceptable diagnostic value in this study.
Palpation pain in the masseter muscle increased the likelihood of anterior disc displacement without reduction on MRI, in one of the two models with acceptable diagnostic value in this study.
Uncorrected deviation on clinical exam predicted medial disc displacement on MRI, but the model showed very poor discrimination.
TMJ crepitation predicted lateral pterygoid muscle insertion thickening on MRI, though model discrimination was poor.
Palpation pain in the medial pterygoid muscle predicted mandibular condyle subluxation on MRI, though model discrimination was poor.
Clinical condylar hypermobility increased the likelihood of detecting an elevated (>6 mm) glenoid fossa on MRI, but was only a weak predictor.
Palpation pain in the temporalis muscle was a significant negative predictor of abnormal disc morphology on MRI in the logistic regression model.
The logistic regression model combining condylar hypermobility with anterior disc displacement without reduction demonstrated acceptable diagnostic performance by ROC analysis.
The logistic regression model combining masseter muscle palpation pain with anterior disc displacement without reduction also demonstrated acceptable diagnostic performance by ROC analysis.
Most ROC-derived AUC values for the clinical-sign-to-MRI-diagnosis predictive models were below 0.5, indicating the models performed worse than chance at predicting MRI findings from clinical signs.

Comparison of the two directions of regression modelling showed that eight associations between clinical symptoms and MRI signs were reciprocal (bidirectionally predictive), while eight others held in only one direction, indicating that an MRI abnormality may explain a clinical sign without the clinical sign being able to predict the MRI abnormality.

The authors' own regression analysis found that TMJ clicking was not a significant predictor of radiologically confirmed anterior disc displacement with reduction, consistent with prior reports that clicking sounds do not reliably imply disc reduction.
All three probands with 19p13.11 microduplication exhibited neurodevelopmental delay, ADHD, and speech delay.
Joint hypermobility, short stature, and craniofacial anomalies were overlapping clinical features shared across the three probands with 19p13.11 duplication.
Patient-specific manifestations beyond the shared phenotype included haematological abnormalities, musculoskeletal asymmetries, and cardiac findings.

The 19p13.11 duplicated regions spanned 1.2-1.6 Mb and encompassed 41-49 protein-coding genes, several with high predicted triplosensitivity scores linked to autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental and skeletal disorders.

Patient 1, who carried the largest duplication and whose CNV overlapped 76% with those of Patients 2 and 3, showed more extensive systemic involvement, suggesting a dosage-dependent relationship between duplication size and phenotype severity.
Pubourethral and external urethral ligament plication achieved an objective cure rate of 71.4% at six-month follow-up with no complications.
Total Incontinence Quality of Life (I-QOL) scores improved significantly from preoperative to postoperative assessment following ligament plication surgery.
All I-QOL subscales, including behavioral limitation, psychosocial impact, and social isolation, showed significant improvement after surgery.
Composite success criteria combining objective and subjective outcomes classified 46.9% of patients as complete success, 42.9% as partial success, and 10.2% as treatment failure.
The procedure was associated with a short operative time and a high rate of same-day discharge, supporting a favorable safety and efficiency profile.
A de novo heterozygous BICRA frameshift variant, initially classified as VUS and later reclassified as pathogenic, was confirmed as the cause of Coffin-Siris syndrome 12 in this patient.

The patient developed severe gastrointestinal dysmotility progressing from infantile constipation to functional megacolon and recurrent bowel obstruction, ultimately requiring total colectomy, an expansion of the known BICRA-related CSS12 phenotype.
The patient experienced recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces at age 19 due to bilateral apical bullous lung disease, a previously unreported pulmonary complication of BICRA-related CSS12.

The patient exhibited generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score 6/9) with recurrent knee dislocations during adolescence, contributing to the connective-tissue phenotype associated with BICRA-related CSS12.
Psoriatic arthritis in this patient responded well to adalimumab, a novel autoimmune manifestation reported within the BICRA spectrum.

The patient was diagnosed with growth hormone deficiency and short stature in early childhood and received recombinant growth hormone therapy for two years, with partial improvement in growth velocity.
The patient developed portal-vein thrombosis, treated successfully with anticoagulation and later resolved, representing a previously unreported vascular complication in BICRA-related CSS12.

A heterozygous COL1A1 missense variant inherited from the unaffected father was identified but classified as benign/tolerated by in silico tools and not considered causative of the patient's connective-tissue phenotype.

Truncating (frameshift/nonsense) BICRA variants are associated with more severe multisystem involvement including growth impairment, connective tissue findings, and visceral complications, compared to missense variants which may cause milder phenotypes.

Loss of BICRA function destabilizes the non-canonical BAF (ncBAF) chromatin-remodeling complex, leading to global dysregulation of developmental gene programs; the authors hypothesize this may also disrupt smooth muscle and connective tissue transcriptional programs.
Cognitive testing at age 11 demonstrated mild-to-moderate intellectual disability with full-scale IQ approximately 75, verbal comprehension 69, and working memory 86.
FMS patients consistently show decreased heart rate variability, indicating reduced vagal tone and impaired autonomic flexibility.

FMS is associated with a chronic low-grade inflammatory state, with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α) and reduced anti-inflammatory IL-10 in serum and cerebrospinal fluid, correlating with pain, fatigue, and cognitive symptoms.

In a Phase I/II open-label trial, implanted left cervical VNS in 14 treatment-resistant FM patients resulted in 5 of 12 completers meeting composite efficacy criteria for pain, function, and well-being improvement at 3 months, with some patients no longer meeting FM diagnostic criteria by 11 months.

In a pilot RCT of 60 female FM patients, taVNS combined with home-based exercise improved SF-36 subdomains (physical function, social functioning, pain) more than exercise alone, but between-group differences were not statistically significant overall.

A single-arm open-label pilot trial of taVNS (AVNT) in 18 FM patients showed significant improvements in symptom severity (rFIQ) and sleep quality (PSQI), but no significant change in serum BDNF levels.
Serum BDNF levels showed no significant change following taVNS treatment in FM patients, despite clinical symptom improvement.

In a four-arm RCT of 116 adults with severe FM comparing active/sham taVNS and active/sham meditative-based diaphragmatic breathing, ultra short-term HRV (primary outcome) showed no significant differences between groups, and no correlation was found between HRV changes and pain intensity, though trends toward reduced FM severity were seen in both active treatment groups.
taVNS has been shown to enhance heart rate variability and reduce TNF-α and IL-6 levels, indicating anti-inflammatory and autonomic-regulating effects, based on broader neuromodulation literature.

A published trial protocol proposes a large-scale, sham-controlled RCT of non-invasive transcutaneous cervical and auricular VNS in 136 FM patients, assessing pain, fatigue, sleep, depression, HRV, and inflammatory cytokines, comparing two stimulation sites that both project to the NTS.
Pairwise LDSC showed positive genetic correlations among fibromyalgia, insomnia, depression, and anxiety GWAS, ranging from 0.55 to 0.84.
A common factor model fit well the genetic covariance matrix of fibromyalgia, insomnia, depression, and anxiety, supporting a shared genetic factor (mvFibroPsych).
Standardized factor loadings for fibromyalgia, insomnia, depression, and anxiety onto the latent factor ranged from 0.63 to 0.94.
The multivariate GWAS of mvFibroPsych identified 49 lead SNPs across 43 independent genome-wide significant loci, of which 32 were novel relative to the individual input GWAS.
One genome-wide significant SNP, rs1245129, showed significant cross-trait heterogeneity, indicating trait-specific rather than shared effects at this locus.

The lead SNP rs4865477 reached genome-wide significance for mvFibroPsych despite non-significant marginal effects in all individual input GWAS, consistent with a pure common-factor effect rather than trait-specific heterogeneity.
MAGMA gene-set analysis showed enrichment of mvFibroPsych-associated genes in pathways related to synaptic function.
MAGMA tissue-expression analysis identified brain and pituitary tissues as the most significantly enriched tissues for mvFibroPsych-associated genes.
Phenome-wide LCV analysis of 1,266 traits found 133 phenotypes with |GCP| > 0.6 and significant FDR-corrected causal relationships with mvFibroPsych.
mvFibroPsych genetic liability showed a strong positive causal association with substance use as a coping mechanism for anxiety.
mvFibroPsych genetic liability showed a positive causal association with chronic back pain (3+ months).

Several somatic conditions—irregular/excessive menstruation, deep vein thrombosis, syncope and collapse, synovitis/tenosynovitis, and urinary tract/kidney infection—showed GCP values below -0.6, suggesting they act as upstream causal contributors to mvFibroPsych genetic liability.

Brain-wide Mendelian randomization found that higher fractional anisotropy in the splenium of the corpus callosum was causally associated with reduced odds of mvFibroPsych, suggesting white matter integrity may be protective.
Bidirectional Mendelian randomization found no significant causal effect of mvFibroPsych genetic liability on brain imaging-derived phenotypes.
Proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (SMR-HEIDI) identified five plasma proteins—UBE2L6, VWC2, BTN3A2, FES, and HSPA1A—with a true positive causal association with mvFibroPsych risk.

VWC2 showed a significant, consistent positive causal association with mvFibroPsych across the primary UKB-PPP dataset and three independent validation cohorts (deCODE, FENLAND, INTERVAL), prioritizing it as a candidate blood biomarker.

Brain eQTL SMR-HEIDI analysis found higher brain expression of SLC12A5 (encoding KCC2) was associated with increased risk of mvFibroPsych, potentially via impaired chloride homeostasis and GABAergic signaling.
Brain eQTL SMR-HEIDI analysis found lower brain expression of BPTF, a NURF chromatin-remodeling complex subunit, was associated with increased mvFibroPsych risk.
Brain eQTL SMR-HEIDI analysis found lower FURIN expression was associated with increased mvFibroPsych risk, possibly reflecting reduced buffering of neuroinflammatory processes.

Brain mQTL SMR-HEIDI analysis found that increased DNA methylation at CD40 (cg09053081) was positively associated with mvFibroPsych risk, suggesting altered methylation drives dysregulated CD40 expression and maladaptive immune responses.
Brain mQTL SMR-HEIDI analysis identified DNA methylation of AMZ1, GSDME, and TMEM258 as significantly associated with mvFibroPsych risk.

Brain sQTL SMR-HEIDI analysis found that alternative splicing of CD40 was positively associated with mvFibroPsych risk, opposite in direction to its negative expression association, suggesting isoform-specific effects.
Brain sQTL SMR-HEIDI analysis identified significant splicing variants in AREL1, ARHGAP19, BPTF, CD40, and OTOA associated with mvFibroPsych.
CD40 was implicated across gene expression, DNA methylation, and splicing QTL layers, positioning it as a key candidate regulatory gene in mvFibroPsych molecular etiology.
Positional and eQTL gene mapping in FUMA prioritized 342 protein-coding genes as associated with mvFibroPsych.

Sensitivity analyses with alternative three-trait and pairwise Genomic SEM models showed fibromyalgia retained significant, non-redundant factor loadings, indicating its contribution to the shared genetic architecture is not solely driven by the more highly-powered psychiatric traits.
DNA methylation at the AMZ1 locus (cg23627948) was significantly associated with mvFibroPsych risk in the methylation QTL SMR analysis.
Increased DNA methylation at cg27436603 in GSDME was negatively associated with mvFibroPsych risk.
Methylation at cg18171955 in TMEM258 was negatively associated with mvFibroPsych risk.
Splicing QTL SMR analysis identified five genes (AREL1, ARHGAP19, BPTF, CD40, and OTOA) with significant splicing variants causally associated with mvFibroPsych.

CD40 splicing variation showed a positive association with mvFibroPsych risk, contrasting with a negative association observed for CD40 gene expression, suggesting alternative splicing generates functionally distinct isoforms.

Bidirectional Mendelian randomization found no significant causal effect of mvFibroPsych genetic liability on brain imaging-derived phenotypes, suggesting brain structural changes are more likely upstream causes than consequences.
Among the 43 genome-wide significant loci, only rs1245129 showed evidence of cross-trait heterogeneity (Cochran's Q), indicating a trait-specific rather than shared effect at that locus.

The lead SNP rs4865477 reached genome-wide significance for the mvFibroPsych latent factor despite non-significant marginal effects (|Z|<1.96) in all four individual-trait GWASs, consistent with a pure common-factor effect rather than trait-specific heterogeneity.
Gene prioritization via positional and eQTL mapping in FUMA identified 342 protein-coding genes associated with the mvFibroPsych latent factor.

Among SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with independent genome-wide significant loci, 54.9% were mapped to genes by positional proximity and 48.1% via eQTL mapping, while none were mapped via chromatin interaction.

The mvFibroPsych GWAS showed an attenuation ratio of approximately -0.908 (from LDSC intercept 0.812 and genomic control λGC 1.207), an atypical negative value the authors attribute to multivariate phenotype sparsity, cohort heterogeneity, or conservative correction rather than confounding.

Sensitivity analyses using three-trait and pairwise sub-models confirmed that fibromyalgia retained statistically significant factor loadings across all configurations, indicating it contributes stable, non-redundant shared genetic variance despite its smaller sample size relative to the psychiatric traits.

Insomnia showed moderate genetic correlations with the other three traits but had a lower factor loading onto the common factor than depression and anxiety, suggesting a partly distinct genetic basis potentially involving circadian or metabolic pathways.

Previously reported borderline-significant fibromyalgia-specific loci from FinnGen (rs139332433 and rs56132815) did not replicate in the mvFibroPsych multivariate model, likely because the latent factor captures shared rather than disorder-specific genetic effects.

Meta-analysis of the four phenotypes yielded effective sample sizes of 17,827 for fibromyalgia, 115,173 for insomnia, 391,264 for depression, and 191,496 for anxiety disorder, which were used as inputs to the Genomic SEM common factor model.

Fibromyalgia, considered the typical phenotype of nociplastic pain, can co-occur with axial spondyloarthritis and is associated with increased symptom burden and reduced efficacy of anti-inflammatory therapies.
Female patients with axial spondyloarthritis report more widespread pain, show higher rates of central sensitization, and have worse response to biologic therapies compared with male patients.
Central sensitization is described as a key mechanism of nociplastic pain that amplifies pain and reduces responsiveness to treatment.
Neuropathic pain, although less common in axial spondyloarthritis, can arise from structural complications and requires targeted therapeutic approaches distinct from anti-inflammatory treatment.

The authors hypothesize that some COVID-19 'quorum deaths' represent fatal angioedema or anaphylaxis misclassified as primary respiratory failure or cardiac arrest, especially when urticaria or an identifiable allergen is absent.

The authors propose that in COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2-associated endothelial injury converges with mast cell activation disorders and complement system maladaptation to form a self-amplifying mast cell-endothelium-complement axis capable of causing terminal vascular collapse without prominent systemic inflammation.
The authors recommend early postmortem serum tryptase sampling as a practical approach to detect mast cell activation contributing to sudden death in COVID-19 cases.
The authors recommend postmortem complement studies, including C4 and C1-inhibitor levels, to identify complement system maladaptation contributing to fatal angioedema in COVID-19.

The authors propose targeted genetic testing for SERPING1 variants associated with hereditary angioedema as part of a postmortem workflow for COVID-19-associated deaths with suspected occult angioedema.
The authors propose testing for the KIT D816V variant, a marker of clonal mast cell disease, as part of postmortem investigation of suspected mast-cell-driven deaths in COVID-19.

The authors suggest that fatal angioedema or anaphylaxis in COVID-19 may be misclassified as primary respiratory failure or cardiac arrest, especially in the absence of urticaria or an identifiable allergen.

The authors argue that integrating these forensic investigations could reduce misclassification of cause of death, strengthen pharmacovigilance, and support pandemic-era risk stratification and equity.

In a cyclophosphamide-induced rat model of acute IC/BPS, IL-4 correlated positively with IL-1β and TNF-α correlated with IL-1β in the early phase, while IL-5, IL-6, and IFN-γ emerged as key mediators in later stages.
MCP-1, eotaxin, MIP-1β, TNF-α, and PGE2 differentiated healthy individuals from IC/BPS patients, while IL-8, CXCL10, BDNF, IL-6, and RANTES served as effective biomarkers for IC/BPS.
CXCL10 was confirmed as a diagnostic biomarker for interstitial cystitis, particularly among patients with Hunner's lesions.
Combining IL-6 with the methylhistamine/creatinine ratio yielded a sensitivity of 70.0% and specificity of 72.4% for diagnosing interstitial cystitis.

Bladder instillation with 0.4 M potassium chloride elicited urgency/frequency/pain symptoms in 4.5% of healthy individuals versus 70% of IC patients, 18% of heparin-treated IC patients, and 100% of radiation cystitis patients.

IC patients show defects in keratin-18, keratin-20, and uroplakin expression along with reduced proteoglycan core proteins (perlecan, biglycan, decorin, syndecan-1), potentially correlating with dysregulated FGF, TGF-β, PDGF, and VEGF signaling.

Pyroptosis of uroepithelial cells releases IL-1β and IL-18 via GSDMD pore formation, activating NF-κB and MAPK signaling to upregulate the fibrosis genes TGF-β, COL1A1, and COL3A1, contributing to bladder wall fibrosis.
Suppression of GSDMD expression or function has been shown to attenuate bladder inflammation and fibrosis, supporting targeting of inflammatory mediators as a therapeutic strategy.

Mast cells in the bladder submucosa can be activated by SCF, NGF, bacterial/viral superantigens, substance P, immunoglobulin aggregates, acetylcholine, and neuronal signals, releasing histamine, kinins, proteases, cytokines, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and nitric oxide upon degranulation.
The presence of mast cells in the bladder submucosal layer is a characteristic histological hallmark of IC/BPS with Hunner's lesions.
Urine levels of IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-13 were significantly increased in IC/BPS patients with Hunner's lesions.
Plasma levels of IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α were increased in cohorts of patients with interstitial cystitis.
Anti-TNF-α therapy with adalimumab produced significant reductions in validated IC symptom indices without notable adverse effects.
Increased expression of TNF-α, VEGF, CD31, and TGF-β has been observed in IC/BPS patients, with elevated VEGF concentrations linked to bladder inflammatory processes and abnormal angiogenesis.

Bladder tissue from IC patients showed a 50-fold increase in plasma cells and 28-fold increase in B cells compared to unaffected controls, alongside elevated urinary IL-6, and these were positively correlated with disease severity.
More than 30% of IC patients exhibit immunoglobulin light chain restriction, providing further evidence of B-cell clonal expansion.
APRIL and BAFF gene expression levels significantly correlate with the extent of B-cell clonal proliferation in interstitial cystitis.
Patients with interstitial cystitis were 1.66 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis than controls, suggesting shared features with autoimmune disease.

Bladder tissue in interstitial cystitis exhibits Th1/Th17-polarized immune responses marked by significant overexpression of IFN-γ and upregulation of IL-17A, along with elevated TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-17A mRNA levels.

A one standard deviation increase in TLR-4-mediated inflammatory response was associated with a 1.59-fold increased likelihood of extrapelvic pain in IC/BPS patients, with a borderline association with lower pressure pain thresholds and a significant correlation with elevated plasma IL-6.

In a cyclophosphamide-induced rat model of acute IC/BPS, IL-4 correlated positively with IL-1β and TNF-α correlated with IL-1β in the early phase, while IL-5, IL-6, and IFN-γ became key mediators in later stages.
Ketamine and its urinary metabolites directly damage the urinary tract epithelium, making ketamine-induced cystitis a viable model for simulating interstitial cystitis clinically.

IC/BPS shows considerable symptom and comorbidity overlap with functional somatic syndromes including irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome, and migraine, particularly in patients without Hunner's lesions.

Nearly 90% of IC/BPS patients report symptom sensitivity to dietary factors, with citrus fruits, tomatoes, vitamin C, artificial sweeteners, coffee, tea, carbonated/alcoholic beverages, and spicy foods commonly exacerbating symptoms, while calcium glycerophosphate and sodium bicarbonate tend to alleviate them.

Endoscopic low-dose triamcinolone injections produced favorable outcomes in IC patients by suppressing NF-κB and reducing expression of IL-6, MCP-1, and IL-8, with a good safety and simplicity profile.
Cyclosporine A, a Level V AUA-guideline treatment for IC/BPS, demonstrated efficacy by reducing T-cell signaling activity and decreasing IL-2 and IFN-γ synthesis.
Phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitors, which simultaneously suppress TNF-α and IL-6, are proposed to have potential therapeutic value for interstitial cystitis, though this remains unvalidated.
Stem cell therapy, using either adult or pluripotent stem cells, can differentiate into urinary tract epithelial tissue, mitigate inflammation, and enhance bladder function metrics in IC/BPS.

Mendelian randomization analysis revealed a positive correlation between the risk of interstitial cystitis and gut microbiota taxa including Butyricimonas, Coprococcus, Lactobacillales, Lentisphaerae, and Bilophila wadsworthia.

Certain gut microbial taxa, including Desulfovibrio piger, Oscillibacter unclassified, and Ruminococcus lactaris, appear to exert a protective effect against the development of interstitial cystitis, per Mendelian randomization analysis.
More than 30% of IC patients exhibit light chain restriction, providing further evidence of B-cell clonal expansion in interstitial cystitis.
Gut microbial community composition (beta diversity) differed significantly between patients with SM and healthy controls after accounting for dietary confounders.
Beta dispersion (variability of microbial composition) was significantly greater among patients with SM than HCs, indicating a more unstable/variable gut microbiome in SM.
Alpha diversity metrics of the gut microbiome did not differ between SM patients and HCs and did not correlate with KIT D816V allele burden or serum tryptase.
Bacteroidetes relative abundance was significantly higher in patients with SM compared with HCs.
Overall Firmicutes abundance and the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio did not differ between SM and HC, despite differences in Bacteroidetes abundance.

Although overall Firmicutes abundance was unchanged, the community composition of Firmicutes alone differed between SM and HC, while Bacteroidetes composition alone did not, indicating Firmicutes compositional shifts drive SM dysbiosis.
At the ASV level, 20 Firmicutes ASVs were higher and 22 were lower in SM, while 6 Bacteroidetes ASVs and 1 Actinobacteria ASV were higher in SM compared with HCs.
At the genus level, Negativibacillus, Ruminococcaceae UCG005, and Ruminococcaceae NK4A214 (Firmicutes) and Escherichia-Shigella (Proteobacteria) were lower in patients with SM than HCs.

Multiple Firmicutes genera (Eisenbergiella, Hungatella, Granulicatella, Anaerotruncus, Clostridium innocuum group, Tyzzerella, Faecalitalea, Flavonifractor, Oscillibacter, an unclassified Ruminococcaceae) and the Actinobacterium Eggerthellaceae were higher in patients with SM than HCs.
Anaerotruncus, already elevated in SM, showed a positive correlation with both serum tryptase and KIT D816V allele frequency.
Ruminococcaceae NK4A214, already reduced in SM, showed a negative correlation with both KIT D816V allele frequency and serum tryptase.
Bilophila, Peptostreptococcaceae, Lachnospiraceae FCS020 group, and Roseburia showed a negative correlation with serum tryptase levels.
Barnesiella, Ruminococcaceae UBA1819, Enterococcus, Clostridium innocuum group, and Candidatus Stoquefichus showed a positive correlation with serum tryptase levels.
Agathobacter, Ruminococcaceae UCG005, and Coprococcus 3 negatively correlated with KIT D816V allele frequency, while Lachnospiraceae ASF356 positively correlated with KIT D816V.
PICRUSt2 functional gene prediction identified 60 differentially abundant predicted genes between HCs and patients with SM, spanning carbohydrate, SCFA, and virulence-related metabolism.
Predicted genes for short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)/butyrate metabolism and lysine fermentation (a butyrate-producing pathway) were enriched in patients with SM, along with an SCFA transporter gene.

Predicted genes encoding virulence factors, including antimicrobial resistance, competence, hemolysin transport, and complement C5 degradation, were enriched in the gut microbiome of patients with SM.
GI symptoms and bone-related symptoms in SM correlated with dietary fiber intake: bone pain was associated with lower soluble fiber intake, and osteopenia with lower energy intake from added sugars.
Abdominal pain and nausea in SM patients were associated with lower consumption of total and insoluble dietary fiber, and both symptoms negatively correlated with Mastocytosis Quality-of-Life scores.

Nausea in SM patients was associated with lower consumption of lactose and iron, and lactose intake negatively correlated with intestinal fatty acid binding protein (I-FABP), a marker of gut barrier integrity.
Patients with a history of anaphylaxis consumed more animal protein than those without a history of anaphylaxis.
Dietary calcium consumption positively correlated with liver fat content (FibroScan-controlled attenuation parameter) and was higher in SM patients with obese BMI.
Dietary fat intake positively correlated with serum tryptase, while consumption of vegetable protein negatively correlated with KIT D816V allele frequency in SM patients.

Predicted gut microbial functional gene composition was significantly associated with dietary fat, carbohydrate, and protein intake in patients with SM but not in HCs, suggesting greater diet-sensitivity of the SM gut microbiome.
Microbial beta diversity (community composition) differed significantly with dietary consumption of vegetable protein and lactose, independent of sex, age, or race.
Predicted gene composition of the gut microbiome was associated with dietary intake of fat, carbohydrate, and total protein in patients with SM but not in healthy controls.
Predicted peptidase-encoding genes differed between SM and HCs, with the peptidase Streptogrysin B lower and a C5a peptidase (which degrades complement protein C5) higher in patients with SM.
Two genes involved in polyketide synthesis were higher in the predicted gut microbiome gene set of patients with SM compared with HCs.

Predicted genes for glycan biosynthesis in the context of lipopolysaccharide production were lower in patients with SM, while penicillin-binding protein 2X, involved in peptidoglycan synthesis and antimicrobial resistance, was higher.

Patients with SM were enriched in predicted genes encoding two-component signaling systems, including beta lactamase class C, OmpR family sensor histidine kinases, and response regulators, suggesting enhanced microbial capacity to adapt to environmental stress and antibiotics.
Genes for transcriptional regulation of amino acid transport, lipid metabolism (dhaKLM), and cell wall sugar utilization (murPQ) were lower in patients with SM compared with HCs.
Most predicted transporter genes and type II toxin-antitoxin system antitoxins (CcdA, PrlF) were lower in patients with SM, suggesting reduced microbial defense against phage infection and toxins.

Unlike a previous study of the SM gut microbiome that found lower alpha diversity (Shannon Index) in SM patients, this study did not observe differences in alpha diversity metrics between SM and HCs, a discrepancy attributed to differences in cohort geography, symptom severity, diet, or disease management.

The lower abundance of Escherichia-Shigella in SM patients, likely representing nonpathogenic Escherichia, aligns with a prior study showing reduced colony-forming units of nonpathogenic E coli in SM patients, and is notable because E coli can inhibit mast cell degranulation.
Patients with SM have previously been reported to have decreased gut barrier integrity, which the authors suggest could underlie altered production of microbial metabolites observed in this study.
Serum tryptase was markedly elevated immediately after the anaphylactic event and normalized within 24 hours, confirming systemic mast cell activation.

Complement studies showed normal C1 esterase inhibitor antigen and function but low C4 and C1q levels, helping exclude hereditary angioedema while not matching the classic CARPA anaphylatoxin pattern.

The patient's course of prior mild reaction to perflutren lipid microspheres followed by severe first-time anaphylaxis to sulfur hexafluoride lipid microspheres supports cross-reactivity between the two ultrasound-enhancing agents.
PEG-4000, the main excipient of sulfur hexafluoride lipid microspheres, is proposed as the shared antigenic trigger driving IgE-mediated cross-reactivity and severity of anaphylaxis in this case.

A multicenter analysis reported that severe hypersensitivity reactions (cardiopulmonary involvement) to sulfur hexafluoride lipid microspheres occurred in 0.0848% of administrations, with critical reactions in 0.0330%, and notable intercenter variability.
Perflutren lipid microspheres carries a lower reported incidence of severe hypersensitivity (0.0114%) and critical reactions (0.0010%) compared with sulfur hexafluoride lipid microspheres.

An American Society of Echocardiography analysis found that patients experiencing adverse reactions to sulfur hexafluoride lipid microspheres were statistically more likely to have received a PEG-containing mRNA COVID-19 vaccine, particularly the Moderna formulation, and this patient had received both Moderna and Pfizer mRNA vaccines.

Premedication with oral prednisone, diphenhydramine, and montelukast allowed the patient to safely undergo a subsequent left heart catheterization with iodinated contrast without any hypersensitivity reaction.

Emergency treatment with CPR, intravenous epinephrine, norepinephrine infusion, methylprednisolone, diphenhydramine, famotidine, and fluids achieved return of spontaneous circulation within approximately 2 minutes of anaphylaxis-induced PEA arrest.

Although the patient's coronary artery disease and elevated tryptase raised suspicion for Kounis syndrome (allergic acute coronary syndrome), absence of dynamic ECG changes, normal troponins, and stable coronary anatomy argued against this as the primary cause of the cardiac arrest.

The pattern of prior sensitizing exposure with escalating reaction severity, together with elevated and normalizing tryptase, was judged more consistent with an IgE-mediated mechanism than with CARPA, although lack of anaphylatoxin (C3a/C5a/sC5b-9) measurements limited definitive exclusion of CARPA.
Initiation of CPAP therapy for severe obstructive sleep apnea led to significant improvement in the patient's exertional capacity and daytime fatigue.
TSLP expression is elevated in asthma patients compared with healthy controls and correlates with disease severity and exacerbation risk.
Phase III trials cited in the paper report that tezepelumab significantly reduces the risk of asthma exacerbations in severe asthma regardless of endotype.
The authors hypothesize that tezepelumab's inhibition of TSLP-driven activation of ILC2 cells, eosinophils, and mast cells may contribute to resolving acute severe asthma exacerbations.
Bronchoalveolar lavage confirmed Influenza A infection as the likely trigger of the near-fatal asthma exacerbation.

After five days of unsuccessful VV-ECMO weaning attempts, the patient received azithromycin and a single 210 mg subcutaneous dose of tezepelumab, following which the PaO2/FiO2 ratio progressively improved and VV-ECMO was discontinued 72 hours later, with extubation two days after tezepelumab administration.
Forced oscillation technique testing twelve days after spontaneous breathing showed reduced reactance and increased resistance at 5 Hz, both of which improved one month after discharge.
Left MCA mean flow velocity increased significantly after venous sinus stenting.
Right MCA mean flow velocity increased significantly after venous sinus stenting.
Left MCA pulsatility index decreased after stenting but did not reach statistical significance.
Right MCA pulsatility index decreased after stenting but did not reach statistical significance.
ICA time to peak contrast opacification showed a mean reduction after stenting that was not statistically significant.
ACA time to peak contrast opacification showed a mean reduction after stenting that was not statistically significant.
MCA time to peak contrast opacification showed only a slight, non-significant change after stenting.
Time to peak contrast opacification in the middle cerebral artery showed only a slight, non-significant increase after venous sinus stenting.
Venous sinus stenosis in this cohort was most frequently located at the transverse-sigmoid sinus junction.

Diabetic patients with peripheral neuropathy (DPN) had significantly reduced corneal sensitivity, requiring a higher air-pulse pressure threshold to detect stimulation compared to patients without DPN.
When corneal sensitivity was categorized into esthesiometry levels, a higher proportion of DPN patients showed hypesthesia, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Patients with DPN reported markedly more severe dry eye symptoms on the OSDI questionnaire than those without DPN.
Tear osmolarity did not differ significantly between diabetic patients with and without DPN.
Schirmer I test results (aqueous tear production) did not differ significantly between DPN and non-DPN groups.
Percentage of meibomian gland dropout did not differ significantly between diabetic patients with and without DPN.
Noninvasive tear break-up time (NIBUT) did not differ significantly between DPN and non-DPN diabetic patients.
Tear MMP-9 positivity was numerically more frequent in patients with DPN than without, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Among patients with corneal sensory impairment, a significantly higher proportion were MMP-9-positive compared to those without corneal sensory impairment.
A significant negative correlation was found between tear osmolarity and corneal sensitivity (mbar), indicating that patients with reduced corneal sensitivity tend to have higher tear osmolarity.

In a multivariable regression adjusting for MMP-9 and age, the presence of DPN was independently associated with higher corneal sensitivity thresholds, indicating reduced sensitivity independent of these confounders.
MMP-9 positivity was independently and significantly associated with reduced corneal sensitivity in the multivariable regression model.
Age was not significantly associated with corneal sensitivity in the adjusted regression model.
Patients with DPN had a significantly longer duration of diabetes than those without DPN.
iNOS is reported to be highly expressed in scleroderma skin lesions.
In a bleomycin-induced scleroderma mouse model, iNOS knockout mice showed alleviated scleroderma progression compared to wildtype mice.
iNOS deletion reduced inflammatory factor expression in keratinocytes and decreased neutrophil infiltration in the bleomycin-induced scleroderma model.
In fibroblasts stimulated with TNF-alpha and IL-1beta (cytokines mainly produced by keratinocytes and neutrophils), iNOS deletion attenuated fibroblast activation.
Pharmacological inhibition of iNOS significantly reduced the severity of scleroderma skin lesions in the mouse model.
Persons exposed to giardiasis or cryptosporidiosis in a drinking water contamination event had a 3.4-fold increased risk of IBS symptoms 3 years postinfection compared with unexposed persons.
At 6 years postinfection, risk for IBS symptoms after giardiasis or cryptosporidiosis remained elevated at 3.4-fold, with a slight decrease seen between years 3 and 6.
At 10 years postinfection, giardiasis/cryptosporidiosis exposure was associated with a 4.7-fold increased odds of IBS symptoms compared with unexposed persons.

In a separate drinking water contamination event, persons affected by giardiasis, campylobacteriosis, or norovirus had nearly 3-fold increased odds of IBS onset 1 year later compared with unaffected persons.

Insurance database analysis showed the 1-year incidence of IBS was substantially higher in persons with prior giardiasis than in those without, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.9 after controlling for anxiety, depression, and healthcare use.
A pooled analysis of cohort studies found documented giardiasis increased the odds of developing IBS more than 5-fold compared with uninfected persons.

Female sex, younger age, antibiotic exposure, severity of initial infection, prior mental health diagnosis, somatization, and treatment-refractory giardiasis were reported as risk factors for postinfectious IBS onset.
A systematic review found increased odds of postinfectious functional dyspepsia onset 6 months after a gastrointestinal infection compared with controls.
A cohort study of active-duty military personnel found an increased risk of postinfectious functional dyspepsia after prior giardiasis compared with controls.
Prior giardiasis was associated with an increased risk of gastroesophageal reflux in a cohort study.
Persons with prior giardiasis showed increased prevalence of bloating and nausea compared with those without prior giardiasis.
An estimated 30% of persons with prior giardiasis experience long-term extraintestinal symptoms including joint pain, fatigue, cognitive/sensory impairment, and musculoskeletal complaints.
US healthcare/insurance claims analysis found 51% higher odds of arthritis or joint pain within 6 months of giardiasis compared with controls.
A systematic review reported that postgiardiasis arthritis prevalence was higher among children under 18 years of age compared with adults.
A follow-up study after a Norway water contamination event found persons with history of giardiasis had a 4-fold increased risk of ME/CFS compared with controls at 3 years postexposure.
At 6 years postexposure to the Norway giardiasis outbreak, fatigue risk decreased slightly but remained higher than in unexposed persons.
Approximately 5% of persons developed ME/CFS-like symptoms after resolution of giardiasis acquired during the 2004 Norway water contamination event.
Chronic fatigue syndrome was associated with overactive bladder in both giardiasis-exposed and unexposed persons, with similar odds ratios in both groups.
A Norway outbreak study found a higher prevalence of fibromyalgia 10 years postgiardiasis in case-patients compared with persons with no prior giardiasis, with nearly 3-fold increased odds.
Children with more than one intestinal parasite infection in Ethiopia had increased odds of stunting compared with children without such infections.
Persistent giardiasis within the first 6 months of life was associated with deficits in both weight and length at 24 months of age in a large multi-country study of children.
Fecal presence of Giardia in infants aged 3-6 months and 9 months was associated with a mean difference of approximately 0.3 SD lower height-for-age Z-score at 2 years of age in a Pakistan study.
Giardiasis before 2 years of age predicted lower social and intelligence quotients and poorer growth at 3 years of age in a study from southern India.
A longitudinal Peru cohort study of ~140 children found lower IQ scores in children who had more than one episode of giardiasis annually compared with children with one or no infections.
Giardiasis during a child's first 2 years of life is associated with cognitive impairment up to 7 years later, independent of physical growth effects.

The authors report the first clinically documented case linking isolated hypoglycemic brain injury to transient but profound gut dysmotility via a hypothesized blood-brain-barrier-mediated neurohumoral cascade.
Animal studies cited show that acute glucose deprivation activates hypothalamic CRH neurons within 5 minutes, which then induces colonic hypermotility via vagal efferent signaling.
Population-based cohorts cited report that 23% to 41% of severe hypoglycemic survivors experience persistent gastrointestinal symptoms.

The patient developed acute-onset, painless, large-volume watery diarrhea (Bristol Type 7) 24 hours after the hypoglycemic coma, occurring 3-4 times daily without nocturnal symptoms, fever, hematochezia, tenesmus, or abdominal pain.

Cardiovagal function testing (HRV 15 bpm, Valsalva ratio 1.8) and sudomotor function (electrochemical skin conductance 75 μS) were normal, excluding diabetic autonomic neuropathy as a cause of the diarrhea.
Loperamide, dosed up to 8 mg/day, provided only minimal symptom relief for the post-hypoglycemic diarrhea.
Adjunctive smectite and Saccharomyces boulardii, added on day 4, yielded no substantial benefit for the diarrhea.
A trial of cholestyramine, targeting possible bile acid malabsorption and initiated on day 6, did not produce a meaningfully greater reduction in stool frequency.
The diarrhea persisted until it abruptly resolved on day 11 post-hypoglycemia, with sustained normalization of stool consistency at 3-month follow-up.

The authors propose the 24-hour latency to diarrhea onset corresponds to experimental evidence of secondary neuronal apoptosis in the nucleus tractus solitarius occurring 18 to 36 hours post-hypoglycemia.

The authors propose that hypoglycemia-induced CRH surge activates colonic mast cells via CRH-R1 receptors, a mechanism reportedly visualized in humans by confocal endomicroscopy showing real-time mast cell degranulation during hypoglycemic stress.
The proposed neuroimmune interaction is stated to increase intestinal permeability 2.3-fold within 6 hours through histamine-mediated upregulation of claudin-2.

The authors note that profound diarrhea after hypoglycemic coma contrasts with the constipation or gastroparesis more commonly observed after other acute brain injuries such as stroke, suggesting a distinct pathophysiology.

Rodent studies cited show enteric glial cells initiate proliferation via GDNF/RET kinase signaling within 72 hours of vagal injury, peaking at day 7-10, a timeline the authors align with the patient's day 11 recovery.

The authors propose a 'transient autonomic crisis' model whereby acute glucose deprivation reversibly silences glucose-sensitive dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus neurons expressing high-density GLUT2 transporters, which fire erratically below 2.8 mmol/L glucose.

The authors propose that CRH antagonists such as verucerfont, currently in phase II trials for irritable bowel syndrome, could offer a targeted therapeutic intervention by blocking the hypothalamic-mast cell axis in post-hypoglycemic gut dysfunction.
The authors advocate for structured symptom tracking using the 'HYPO-GI score' to quantify frequency and stool consistency of post-hypoglycemic diarrhea.
Fecal calprotectin and elastase levels were within normal limits, excluding intestinal inflammation and pancreatic insufficiency as causes of the diarrhea.
Plasma concentrations of the MASP-2/C1Inh complex, a marker of lectin complement pathway activation, were significantly higher in long COVID patients than healthy convalescent controls.

Plasma C1s/C1Inh, a classical pathway activation marker, was modestly but significantly elevated (13%) in long COVID patients relative to healthy convalescent controls, consistent with prior ELISA findings.
In the prior cohort study, MASP-1/C1Inh, the only lectin pathway marker assessed, was not significantly elevated in long COVID patients versus healthy convalescent controls.
A four-marker panel comprising MASP-2/C1Inh, TCC, iC3b, and properdin was identified as optimally predictive of long COVID status with an AUC of 0.796.
Sequential combinations of classical pathway markers (C4, C1q, C1s/C1Inh) were poorly predictive of long COVID compared to lectin/alternative/terminal pathway markers.
In the prior cohort, alternative pathway markers (iC3b, Ba) and terminal pathway markers (C5a, TCC) were predictive of long COVID with a combined AUC of 0.785.
Properdin, a positive regulator of the alternative pathway released from neutrophil secondary granules during inflammation, was elevated in long COVID patients and contributed to disease prediction.

The authors propose that lectin pathway activation via MASP-2, which has factor Xa-like coagulation activity (cleaving prothrombin and factor XII), may mechanistically link complement activation to the endothelial damage and coagulopathy seen in long COVID.

A previous study of acute COVID-19 (cited) found MASP-1/C1Inh elevated in acute COVID-19 patients versus uninfected individuals, with the acute-COVID median value closely matching the level seen in this study's healthy convalescent group, suggesting prolonged elevation regardless of long COVID status.
A pre-donation 500 mL isotonic drink did not significantly reduce in-session vasovagal reactions with loss of consciousness compared with standard plain water.
Extending post-donation chair rest from 2 to 3 minutes did not significantly reduce in-session vasovagal reactions with loss of consciousness.

A modified applied muscle tension (AMT) exercise showed a borderline increase in odds of vasovagal reaction with loss of consciousness, with the confidence interval only marginally excluding no effect, and was not deemed a clear benefit.
A psychosocial intervention using preparatory materials did not significantly reduce in-session vasovagal reactions with loss of consciousness compared with no materials.
Overall, none of the four interventions jointly showed a clear reduction in the primary outcome of in-session vasovagal reaction with loss of consciousness.

Absolute event rates for the primary outcome (vasovagal reaction with loss of consciousness) were nearly identical between intervention and no-intervention periods, at 10.7 vs 10.5 per 10,000 donations respectively.

Results for the secondary outcome of total in-session vasovagal reactions (with and without loss of consciousness) were similar to the primary outcome findings, showing no clear intervention benefit, although absolute event rates were higher for this broader outcome.

ME/CFS participants reported worse fatigue on all five MFI-20 domains, greater symptom burden on CDC-SI, and worse functional impairment on all eight SF-36v2 subscales compared with non-fatigued controls.
Plasma C3 levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than non-fatigued controls, and higher C3 was associated with increased odds of ME/CFS in adjusted regression models.
The Bb-to-C3 ratio, an index of alternative pathway activation relative to abundance, was significantly lower in ME/CFS compared to controls.

BMI was the most consistent demographic covariate, showing significant positive associations with seven of nine measured complement proteins (CRP, C3, C3a, C5a, Factor B, Factor D, Factor H), strongest for C3.
Sex was significantly associated with CRP and Factor B plasma levels, with lower levels observed in males.
Factor H showed the most extensive inter-protein correlation profile of the complement panel, correlating strongly with C3 and Factor B but not with Bb.
Higher plasma C3 levels were consistently associated with greater symptom burden, increased fatigue, and lower functioning scores across CDC-SI, MFI-20, and SF-36.
CRP showed the largest beta coefficients across multiple MFI-20 and SF-36 domains but explained only a modest proportion of variance in CRP levels (R2~0.32).
The rs17611 SNP in C5 was a top pQTL for C5a plasma levels, replicating a previously validated pQTL association and serving as an internal positive control.
The rs800292 SNP in CFH showed a progressive decrease in plasma Bb levels with increasing copies of the T allele under an additive model.
The G allele of rs17759529 in DPP4 was associated with higher C3 levels in homozygous carriers, a top-ranked pQTL for CRP and C3.
The T allele of rs1061170 (CFH), the minor C allele at rs9332739 (C2), and the T allele at rs4151667 (CFB, in LD with rs9332739) were each associated with significantly lower Bb levels.

Sixteen SNPs overlapped between the 3192 complement-protein-associated SNPs and 48 previously reported ME/CFS-associated SNPs, with 11 acting in the complement cascade and the remainder in T cell signaling, chemokine, GPCR, and TNF superfamily pathways.
The trans-pQTL rs3020729 in CD8A (a miRNA-binding variant) was significantly associated with higher levels of both CRP and C3.
The missense variant rs9550987 in TNFRSF19 was associated with decreased C3 and Factor H levels.

Combined genotypes of rs9332739 (C2) and rs1061170 (CFH), ordered by increasing ME/CFS-risk allele count, showed opposing trends: the double-risk genotype (CG-TT) had the lowest Bb, highest C3, and highest proportion of ME/CFS cases.
Across 27 disease-associated SNPs, the ME/CFS odds ratio strongly correlated with the pQTL beta for C3, indicating that increasing genetic risk for ME/CFS is associated with higher circulating C3.

Disease odds ratio showed an inverse relationship with Bb pQTL beta values across 30 SNPs (R2=0.328), strengthening to near-perfect correlation (R2=0.965) when restricted to 6 complement-pathway SNPs, indicating ME/CFS genetic risk is linked to reduced Bb.
In a non-genetic ROC model, CRP, Factor B, and C3 had the highest predictive power for ME/CFS status (AUC 0.75, 0.75, and 0.69 respectively), but only C3 reached statistical significance.
Stratifying subjects by heterozygosity at rs9332739 (C2) and rs800292 (CFH) improved discrimination of ME/CFS status, yielding an AUC of 0.84 in a subgroup of 71 subjects.

Within genotype-restricted heterozygous subgroups (CFShet vs NFhet), CRP and C3 achieved improved AUCs of 0.85 and 0.84 respectively, with Factor H and C3a also improved (AUC 0.78 and 0.74) relative to the non-stratified model.

Six SNPs across five genes (CFB, CFH, C2, MMP10, PIK3R5) overlapped between the complement pQTL dataset and UK Biobank fatigue-related GWAS traits, with consistent direction of effect (risk allele and OR) between datasets.

The rs394811 variant in PIK3R5 was the only overlapping SNP specifically matching the UK Biobank's designated Chronic Fatigue Syndrome group, while CFB, CFH, and C2 variants overlapped with broader fatigue/malaise and post-viral fatigue phenotypes.

Three cis-acting intronic pQTLs decreased circulating C3 levels via their minor alleles and were strong individual predictors of illness status, though subjects homozygous for the major alleles (higher C3) were not associated with ME/CFS.

Multiple pQTLs in the TRAF1/C5 region on chromosome 9 influenced circulating C5a levels but were not associated with ME/CFS status; one such variant, rs7037673, has been reported as a C5 expression pQTL in prefrontal cortex tissue.
At Week 12, the intervention group (active vitamin D plus replacement therapy guidance) showed significantly greater reduction in ME/CFS symptom count than the control group (alfacalcidol alone).
Serum 25(OH) vitamin D levels increased substantially in the intervention group but did not improve in the control group at Week 12.
A significantly higher proportion of intervention-group participants no longer met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria (<8 symptoms) at Week 12 compared with controls.
Time-to-event Cox regression showed the intervention group achieved <8 ME/CFS symptoms significantly faster than the control group.

Higher baseline MCHC was independently associated with a lower likelihood of achieving remission from ME/CFS (<8 symptoms), potentially reflecting reduced red blood cell deformability and impaired microvascular perfusion.

In a subgroup with prior COVID-19 vaccination as the triggering event (PVS), vitamin D replacement therapy guidance produced a larger reduction in ME/CFS symptom count versus control than in the PASC subgroup.

In the PASC subgroup, vitamin D replacement therapy guidance also reduced ME/CFS symptom count relative to control, though with a smaller effect size and wider confidence interval than the PVS subgroup.
In the intervention group, immune symptoms had the highest improvement rate at Week 12, followed by pain and sleep problems.
A far greater proportion of individual symptoms resolved by Week 12 in the intervention group than in the control group.
At screening, all enrolled participants exhibited pathologic fatigue, sleep problems, and autonomic symptoms, reflecting the diagnostic core of ME/CFS in this cohort.

One control-group participant experienced serious adverse events (acute pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer) during the trial, with causality to the active vitamin D preparation ruled out; no cases of severe hypercalcemia or clinically significant renal impairment occurred.

In a small sensitivity subgroup of participants enrolled from sites other than the primary study site, a trend toward symptom improvement with intervention was seen but did not reach statistical significance.
In a 33-year-old man with post-COVID ME/CFS, 12 weeks of electroacupuncture-based deep peroneal nerve (vagal reflex) stimulation reduced total MFI fatigue score by more than 50%, from 71 to 31.

General fatigue and reduced activity MFI subscales showed the greatest absolute reductions (−9 points each), with general fatigue falling below the diagnostic cut-off at week 8 and reduced activity at week 12.
Mental fatigue and reduced motivation subscales showed the largest proportional improvements after EA vagal stimulation, decreasing 63.6% (11 to 4) and 61.5% (13 to 5), respectively.
Daily flu-like symptom duration (headache, chills, myalgia) decreased markedly from baseline to week 12 of EA vagal stimulation.
No adverse events were observed during the 12-week course of EA-based vagal stimulation in this ME/CFS case.

Following the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, newly diagnosed ME/CFS incidence reportedly increased about 15-fold, and infected individuals had nearly five-fold higher hazard of developing ME/CFS than non-infected populations.
Evidence cited in this review suggests elevated IL-1β as part of altered cytokine profiles in ME/CFS.
Evidence cited in this review suggests elevated IL-6 as part of altered cytokine profiles in ME/CFS.
Evidence cited in this review suggests elevated IL-10 as part of altered cytokine profiles in ME/CFS.
Approximately 78% of ME/CFS patients with GI symptoms report that these symptoms worsen following physical or cognitive exertion, supporting a link between GI dysfunction and post-exertional malaise.

A larger synbiotic supplementation RCT (n=463, 24 weeks) in Long COVID reported statistically significant anti-fatigue effects compared with placebo, whereas a smaller synbiotic trial (n=26, 12 weeks) did not.

An RCT of Sijunzi decoction (herbal medicine) in Long COVID showed significant improvements in fatigue and general wellness, accompanied by increased abundance of Pediococcus acidilactici correlating with reduced fatigue and GI symptoms.
A preliminary fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) RCT in ME/CFS (n=11) did not yield statistically significant fatigue improvement compared with placebo.
