Ten sessions of kanshoho, a low-pressure muscle relaxation technique, over 2.5 months led to complete resolution of Long COVID/ME-CFS symptoms with marked improvement in fatigue, functional status, and mood disturbance scores.
Sertraline (50 mg/day), continued initially during kanshoho treatment, was later tapered and discontinued at the patient's request without any clear worsening of symptoms.
Prior up-titration of sertraline to 50 mg/day and trials of other symptomatic medications by a previous physician did not produce meaningful improvement in the patient's Long COVID/ME-CFS symptoms.
The paper questions whether the RACGP HANDI recommendation of incremental (graded) physical activity for chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis may be causing harm to patients.

scRNAseq showed depletion of naive CD4+ T cells (cluster 0) and naive CD8+ T cells (cluster 6) with expansion of effector CD4+ (cluster 2) and effector CD8+ (cluster 3) subsets in LC patients compared to recovered individuals.

LC patients had a significantly higher T cell exhaustion module score, and GSEA showed the exhaustion gene signature enriched among CD8 T cell clusters, with CTLA4, ENTPD1 and TOX among the most highly ranked genes.
FOXP3 expression was substantially reduced both across total PBMCs and specifically within the Treg cluster in LC patients, despite unchanged Treg cluster frequency.
MAIT cells (cluster 13) were reduced in frequency in LC patients, driven primarily by loss of naive MAIT subpopulations while activated MAIT subclusters relatively increased.
All three identified γδ T cell subpopulations (cluster 17) were depleted in LC patients compared to recovered individuals.

NK cell frequency (cluster 4) was reduced and NK activation module score was significantly lower in LC patients, with decreased IFNG, NKG7, KLRD1, KLRF1, PRF1, IL2RB, GZMA, GNLY, NCR1, and BCL2 but increased CD69, GZMB, LAMP1, KLRB1, RIPK1, and CASP8 expression.

Classical monocytes (cluster 1) were the most transcriptionally affected immune subset in LC, showing the largest number of DEGs and strong enrichment of TNFα/NFκB signaling, type I/II interferon responses, and complement pathways.

Monocytes from LC patients showed a reduced phagocytosis-associated gene score but an elevated cytokine-associated gene score compared to recovered controls, indicating a phenotypic shift toward pro-inflammatory rather than phagocytic function.
LDN cluster (cluster 18) was expanded in LC patients, with a transcriptionally distinct activated subcluster (elevated MME and CXCL8) specifically expanded.
Platelets (cluster 21) were markedly expanded in LC patients, with two subclusters both expanded and upregulated platelet-activation-associated genes.

B cell subsets (clusters 5, 8, 15) shifted toward an activated phenotype in LC, with naive B cell genes higher in recovered individuals and activation genes (CR2, CD69, FOXP1, CD40, JUN, FOS) higher in LC patients; clusters 5 and 15 were expanded in LC.

RELN was broadly expressed across immune cell types and consistently upregulated in LC patient PBMCs, confirming prior bulk RNAseq findings and suggesting Reelin as a potential biomarker linking neuroinflammation to LC cognitive symptoms.
MEIS2, expressed primarily in basophils, was paradoxically downregulated in LC patients' PBMC scRNAseq despite being upregulated in prior bulk whole-blood RNAseq.
PTPRU, GMPR, WDR62, MUC12, and AIRE, previously reported as downregulated in bulk whole-blood RNAseq of LC patients, were paradoxically upregulated in PBMC scRNAseq.

OLFM1 (mainly in monocytes/DCs) and OLFM2 (diffusely expressed) were downregulated in LC patient PBMCs, consistent with prior bulk RNAseq, while none of 25 upregulated olfactory receptor genes from bulk RNAseq were detectable in PBMC scRNAseq, suggesting a non-immune cell source.

Hormone receptor genes ESR1, ESR2, AR and NR3C1 were significantly upregulated in PBMCs of female LC patients compared to recovered females, confirming prior bulk RNAseq findings, with NR3C1/AR/ESR2 highest in pre-B cells and ESR1 highest in plasma cells.
Plasma Galectin-9 levels were significantly elevated in LC patients compared to recovered individuals, confirming previous reports.
MAIT cells from LC patients exhibited significantly higher TIM-3 (HAVCR2) surface expression (MFI) by flow cytometry compared to recovered individuals.

In vitro treatment of PBMCs from LC patients with recombinant Gal-9 (0.5 μg/ml overnight) enhanced MAIT cell apoptosis and reduced MAIT cell proportion; this effect was partially but significantly reversed by co-administration of lactose (30 mM), a known Gal-9 antagonist.

γδ T cells from LC patients showed elevated TIM-3 expression and increased baseline apoptotic potential; overnight rGal-9 treatment promoted γδ T cell depletion via enhanced apoptosis in LC patients but not in the recovered group.

Flow cytometry confirmed a significant reduction in the frequency of CD8+CD26hi MAIT-associated T cells (expressing CD161, TCR Vα7.2, IL-18Rα) in LC patients versus recovered individuals, in agreement with scRNAseq data.

Reanalysis of an independent idiopathic ME/CFS scRNAseq dataset showed higher T cell activation score in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls, but no significant difference in T cell exhaustion score, contrasting with the LC-ME/CFS cohort where exhaustion was elevated.
In contrast to the LC-ME/CFS cohort, FOXP3 expression was upregulated in idiopathic ME/CFS patients relative to healthy controls in the reanalyzed dataset.

MAIT cells in idiopathic ME/CFS patients exhibited a higher activation score than healthy controls, without a change in subcluster proportions, paralleling the MAIT activation phenotype seen in LC-ME/CFS.

In contrast to the reduced NK cell activation and altered subset composition seen in LC-ME/CFS, no significant difference in NK cell activation was observed between idiopathic ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
In contrast to the LC-ME/CFS cohort, no significant differences in monocyte activation or cytokine gene scores were found between idiopathic ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Although overall basophil cluster frequency was unchanged, basophil activation-associated gene scores were significantly lower in LC patients, with an activated subcluster proportionally reduced.
Among participants meeting diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia, only 25.2% reported having received an actual FM diagnosis.
Among participants meeting diagnostic criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, only 14.2% reported having received a CFS diagnosis, the lowest labelling rate of the three FSS.
Among participants meeting diagnostic criteria for irritable bowel syndrome, 47.6% reported having received an IBS diagnosis, the highest labelling rate of the three FSS.
Female sex was positively associated with receiving a diagnostic label among those meeting FSS diagnostic criteria.
Lower education level was positively associated with receiving an FSS diagnostic label.
Having psychiatric diagnoses other than anxiety or depression was positively associated with receiving an FSS diagnostic label.
Somatic comorbidities were positively associated with receiving an FSS diagnostic label.
Higher healthcare use was positively associated with receiving an FSS diagnostic label.
Older age was negatively associated with receiving a diagnostic label among those meeting FSS diagnostic criteria.
Smoking was negatively associated with receiving a diagnostic label among those meeting FSS diagnostic criteria.
Depressive or anxiety disorders were negatively associated with receiving a diagnostic label among those meeting FSS diagnostic criteria.
Individuals who received an FSS diagnostic label had lower quality of life than those meeting criteria but without a label.
Individuals who received an FSS diagnostic label reported higher health anxiety than those meeting criteria but without a label.
Individuals who received an FSS diagnostic label had reduced physical work capacity compared to those meeting criteria but without a label.
Receiving an FSS diagnostic label was not associated with mental work capacity, unlike its association with reduced physical work capacity.

A lightweight random forest model using BPCA imputation, NearMiss undersampling, 10 biomarkers, and 3 covariates (BMI, age, gender) achieved high diagnostic accuracy for CFS versus both healthy and overlapping-condition controls.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal relationship between blood urea levels and CFS.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal relationship between total protein levels and CFS.
Mendelian randomization identified a causal relationship between glucose and CFS, and higher glucose levels were associated with worsened CFS symptoms.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal relationship between total bilirubin levels and CFS.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal relationship between blood urea levels and CFS.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal relationship between total protein levels and CFS.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal relationship between total bilirubin levels and CFS.
Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal relationship between vitamin D levels and CFS.
The study designed a control group that included both healthy individuals and patients with CFS-overlapping conditions, unlike prior studies, to improve diagnostic specificity.

Systematic comparison of 7 missing value imputation methods, 9 feature selection techniques, and 11 machine learning/deep learning models identified BPCA imputation, NearMiss undersampling, and random forest classification as the optimal pipeline combination for CFS diagnosis.
The client's fatigue severity, measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale, decreased from severe (6.8) to moderate (4.2) after 10 weekly sessions of HeartSpeak Lite for BodyWork.
Perceived stress, measured by the PSS-10, decreased from 29 to 19 over the 10-week intervention period.
Within individual sessions, subjective distress dropped sharply from a pre-session range of 7-8/10 to a post-session range of 1-2/10.
No adverse effects were reported by the client during or following the 10-session HeartSpeak Lite for BodyWork intervention.

Alongside symptom score improvements, the client showed functional gains including increased mobility, reduced back pain, ability to resume light activities and short walks, and gradual sleep improvement.

The authors hypothesize that fascia, as a sensory-rich interoceptive tissue, may store implicit emotional memory and that felt-sense engagement with fascia can facilitate memory reconsolidation underlying symptom improvement.
PLWNT Qigong exercise significantly reduced total fatigue scores (MFI-20) from baseline to week 8 in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome.
PLWNT Qigong exercise produced statistically significant improvements in GSRS subtype scores compared with baseline in CFS patients.
PLWNT Qigong exercise significantly improved MFI-20 subtype scores from baseline in CFS patients.
Gut microbiota alpha diversity changed significantly from baseline to week 8 in the PLWNT group, accompanying clinical improvement.
Compared with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), PLWNT showed no significant difference in changes of MFI-20, GSRS scores, or gut microbiota alpha and beta diversity, supporting non-inferiority.
Combining hEDS and HSD patients, 69 serum proteins (50 upregulated, 19 downregulated) were differentially expressed compared to healthy controls.
In an independent comparison, 54 proteins (19 downregulated, 35 upregulated) were differentially expressed in hEDS patients versus controls.
In HSD patients versus controls, 49 proteins were differentially expressed, with 3 downregulated and 46 upregulated.
Direct comparison of serum protein levels between hEDS and HSD patients revealed no significant differentially expressed proteins, supporting a shared molecular profile.
No significant serum protein differences were found between Italian and American hEDS patients, or between Italian and American HSD patients, supporting cohort aggregation.

Random Forest analysis of the 69 DEPs identified MYOC, NUDT5, and CLEC10A as the most important proteins for classifying hEDS/HSD patients versus controls, with the affected-classification probability peaking at 0.60 with low MYOC and high CLEC10A.
LASSO regression applied to the 69 DEPs selected a refined 17-protein panel capable of discriminating hEDS/HSD patients from healthy controls.

Among the 17 LASSO-selected proteins, MYOC, TOP2B, and INPPL1 were the most informative for classification, with the probability of being classified as affected reaching 0.70 when MYOC was low and TOP2B/INPPL1 were high.
MIF was the most highly upregulated protein in hEDS/HSD serum, a cytokine implicated in synovial/cartilage destruction in rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
Three carbonic anhydrase family members (CA1, CA2, CA3) were upregulated in hEDS/HSD serum and may contribute to a pro-inflammatory state linked to inflammatory joint disease.
The 19 downregulated DEPs were enriched for functions in eosinophil/macrophage chemotaxis, leukocyte proliferation, blood vessel morphogenesis, and ECM organization.

Serum levels of SIRT2, NTRK2, MYOC, and SOD1 — proteins involved in Schwann cell development, differentiation, and myelin sheath formation — were abnormal in hEDS/HSD patients, suggesting involvement of peripheral nervous system regulatory pathways relevant to comorbid small fiber neuropathy.
BANK1, a B-cell scaffold protein implicated in autoantibody production in SLE, was noted among the dysregulated immune-related proteins in hEDS/HSD serum.
CD69, an early leukocyte activation marker with pro-inflammatory effects in autoimmune disease, was among the dysregulated proteins found in hEDS/HSD serum.
A classification tree using the 69 DEPs identified MYOC, BLVRB, and MAX as the primary discriminative splits, with terminal nodes reaching up to 78% probability of being classified as affected.

Functional enrichment of the 69 DEPs identified positive regulation of MAPK cascade, response to oxidative stress, Schwann cell development, regulation of T cell activation, and inflammatory response to antigenic stimulus as the most significantly affected biological processes.

The paper appears to address timely diagnosis and management of gynaecological bleeding in adult patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, but no specific quantitative or mechanistic findings are given in the title alone.
The paper describes a surgical screening protocol for craniocervical instability in a case series of 347 patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and other connective tissue disorders.
Genetic testing after recurrent pseudoaneurysm formation identified a pathogenic COL3A1 mutation confirming vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

In a patient with underlying (later diagnosed) vEDS, TEVAR for a ruptured thoracic aortic isthmus aneurysm was followed one month later by vascular graft/endograft infection complicated by an aortobronchial fistula and aortic/tricuspid valve vegetations.

The patient developed multiple recurrent pseudoaneurysms at anastomotic and graft junction sites over 15 months despite repeated surgical/endovascular reinterventions and negative infectious workups, culminating in fatal rupture.
Family cascade genetic screening after the index case identified the pathogenic COL3A1 mutation showed that the patient's siblings were negative for the mutation.

The paper cites historical data that median survival in vEDS cohorts is approximately 51 years and that outcomes are strongly influenced by mutation type, with glycine substitutions associated with worse outcomes.
At 5 minutes post-injection, delta sensation scores did not differ significantly between EDS and healthy participants.
At 15 minutes post-injection, EDS participants reported significantly higher residual sensation (delta sensation score) than healthy controls, indicating reduced lidocaine effect.
At 30 minutes post-injection, EDS participants continued to show significantly higher residual sensation than healthy controls, consistent with shorter anesthetic duration.
There was no significant difference between EDS and healthy participants in the proportion achieving categorical 'anesthesia' at 5 minutes post-injection.
A significantly smaller proportion of EDS participants experienced adequate categorical anesthesia at 15 minutes post-injection compared with healthy controls (60% vs 84%).
A significantly smaller proportion of EDS participants experienced adequate categorical anesthesia at 30 minutes post-injection compared with healthy controls (53% vs 80%).

The proband carries a paternally inherited missense variant c.766C>T (p.Arg256Trp) in B3GALT6, classified as likely pathogenic by ACMG criteria and located within the galactosyltransferase catalytic (GalT) domain.
The proband also carries a maternally inherited missense variant c.962G>A (p.Cys321Tyr) in B3GALT6, classified as a variant of uncertain significance under ACMG criteria.
The proband presented with loose/lax skin, scoliosis and kyphosis, generalized joint hypermobility, and delayed motor development consistent with EDSSPD2.
Pooled literature review of 18 live-born EDSSPD2 patients (including the proband) found scoliosis in 88.9%, generalized hypotonia in 83.3%, and soft/lax skin in 66.7%.
In the same pooled EDSSPD2 cohort, prenatal skeletal abnormalities were noted in 22.2% of patients and cervical instability in 16.7%.
Among 18 live-born patients with B3GALT6-related EDSSPD2, soft and lax skin was reported in two-thirds of cases.
Prenatal ultrasound detected skeletal abnormalities in about one-fifth of EDSSPD2 patients before birth.
A minority of EDSSPD2 patients presented with cervical spine instability.

One reported EDSSPD2 patient died at 18 months of age from hypoxia due to tracheomalacia and tracheal compression secondary to severe scoliosis, indicating a life-threatening respiratory complication of this disorder.
Across 23 reported B3GALT6 variant sites associated with EDSSPD2, missense variants were far more common than nonsense variants.
Adults with chronic pain/chronic fatigue had markedly higher odds of screening positive for likely autism than the non-clinical comparison group.
Adults with chronic pain/chronic fatigue had markedly higher odds of screening positive for likely ADHD than the non-clinical comparison group.
Joint hypermobility, a marker of variant connective tissue, significantly mediated the association between neurodivergent traits (likely autism/ADHD) and chronic pain/chronic fatigue.
43% of children with functional neurological disorder had generalized joint hypermobility using a Beighton score cutoff of 4 or more.
Using the stricter Beighton cutoff of 6 or more, 24% of children with functional neurological disorder still showed generalized joint hypermobility.
Elbow hyperextension was the most frequently observed hypermobility feature, present in 56.6% of the FND cohort.
The total Beighton score was independently associated with higher severity on the 24-item Children's Somatic Symptoms Inventory.
The total Beighton score was independently associated with a greater number of limbs affected by functional neurological disorder symptoms.
A higher Beighton score was positively associated with greater pain reported after the six-minute walk test.
Ulnar nerve instability (recurrent subluxation/dislocation at the elbow) has a reported incidence of 10%-31% in children and is bilateral in more than half of affected cases.
Among children exhibiting all five Wynne-Davies signs of ligamentous laxity, 25% had ulnar nerve dislocation and 76% had subluxation, per Zaltz et al.

In the reported child, medial K-wire pin insertion during crossed-pinning fixation of a Gartland IIb supracondylar fracture caused an iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury with paresthesia, altered sensation, and painful incomplete clawing of the ring and little fingers.

Dynamic ultrasound of the contralateral, uninjured elbow confirmed bilateral ulnar nerve instability (subluxation/dislocation) in this child, despite the absence of any of the five Wynne-Davies signs of ligamentous laxity.

Prompt surgical exploration, K-wire removal, and soft-tissue decompression of the entrapped, devascularized ulnar nerve led to immediate return of vascularity and complete restoration of motor and sensory function within 4 weeks.
Iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury following crossed K-wire fixation of supracondylar humeral fractures has a reported risk ranging from 2% to 20% due to the medial pin.
Lateral-only pin configurations have been reported to yield comparable outcomes to crossed K-wire fixation in terms of fixation instability and rate of ulnar nerve injury.
In approximately one third of children, the ulnar nerve may lie at the tip of or anterior to the medial epicondyle during elbow flexion, increasing risk of iatrogenic injury during medial pinning.
Rasool reported that in one of six cases of iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury from medial pin placement, the nerve was hypermobile and found fixed anterior to the medial epicondyle.
Right-to-left shunt was detected by thermodilution in 133 of 151 (90%) PFO patients evaluated before closure.
Shunt magnitude was stratified into three severity groups: >20% in 41 patients (28%), 10%-20% in 33 patients (22%), and <10% in 49 patients (40%).
Greater atrial septal separation during Valsalva maneuver was associated with shunt size >10%.
Greater atrial septal separation during respiration was associated with shunt size >10%.
Greater amplitude of interatrial septal displacement was associated with shunt size >10%.
A greater amount of contrast media reaching the left atrium was associated with shunt size >10%.
Patients with a right-to-left shunt greater than 10% showed increased hypermobility of the interatrial septum compared with those with smaller shunts.
After PFO closure, exercise work capacity increased in patients with a shunt of 20% or greater, whereas it decreased in patients with a shunt under 10%.
Migraine occurrence decreased in a subset of patients following PFO closure.
In patients who had exercise-induced desaturation before closure, oxygen saturation normalized after PFO closure, though this had no effect on exercise capacity.

The review found that tDCS-related MRI findings were heterogeneous across disorders, with baseline brain structure implicated as a predictor in major depressive disorder, functional connectivity changes observed in schizophrenia and alcohol use disorder, and motor network modulation seen in stroke, though effect strength and direction varied across studies.
Aquatic exercise-based interventions produced a significant overall improvement in nighttime sleep quality compared to control conditions across patients with chronic diseases.
The mode of aquatic exercise significantly moderated the sleep quality effect size, with recreational aquatic therapy most effective and aquatic resistance training least effective.
Patient population was the strongest significant moderator of aquatic exercise effect size on sleep quality, explaining a large proportion of between-study variance.
In the fibromyalgia subgroup, aquatic exercise did not significantly improve sleep quality compared with control conditions.
In the post-COVID syndrome subgroup, aquatic exercise significantly improved sleep quality compared with control conditions, with efficacy comparable to the Parkinson's disease reference group.
Neither mean age, intervention duration, nor training frequency showed a statistically significant association with the sleep quality effect size of aquatic exercise.
There was no significant difference in aquatic exercise effect size on sleep quality depending on whether the control group received land-based exercise or no exercise.
Excluding the single preprint study from the meta-analysis reduced the pooled sleep quality effect size from 0.825 to 0.691, but overall statistical significance was unchanged.
High-dose tryptophan (100 µM) produced the highest proportion of Th1 (CXCR3+) differentiation among CD4+ T cells under IFN-γ induction, with a significant concentration-dependent increase.
Under IFN-γ induction, Th2 cell differentiation did not differ significantly across the four tryptophan concentration groups.
Under IL-4 induction, baseline (25 µM) tryptophan produced the highest Th2 (CCR4+) differentiation, which progressively decreased as tryptophan concentration increased.
Notch1 and Jagged1 protein expression increased in a tryptophan concentration-dependent manner in CD4+ T cells, being highest in the high-tryptophan group.
IL-2 and IFN-γ secretion by CD4+ T cells were significantly higher in the high-tryptophan group than in medium-high, regular, and baseline tryptophan groups.
IL-4 secretion by CD4+ T cells was significantly lower in the high-tryptophan group compared to the other tryptophan concentration groups.
T-bet mRNA expression in CD4+ T cells was highest in the high-tryptophan group, indicating enhanced Th1-associated transcriptional activity.
GATA3 mRNA expression was highest in the baseline (25 µM) tryptophan group, consistent with a Th2-associated transcriptional program under low tryptophan availability.
mTOR mRNA expression in CD4+ T cells was highest under high-tryptophan conditions, suggesting nutrient-sensing pathway activation accompanies the Th1 shift.
IDO1 and TDO mRNA expression in CD4+ T cells were highest under high-tryptophan conditions, likely reflecting increased substrate availability driving catabolic enzyme expression.

In IgE-activated LAD2 mast cells, culturing in high-tryptophan medium markedly attenuated tryptase expression and altered its subcellular distribution compared to IgE-activated controls, implying reduced histamine release.

Tryptophan's suppression of mast cell histamine release is partially dependent on IDO1/TDO enzymatic activity: pharmacological inhibition with HY-149,411 abolished the tryptophan-mediated suppression, equalizing histamine levels across MHS, RS, and HS groups, while the baseline (BS) group retained significantly lower histamine.

IgE specific to Bet v 7 induced dose-dependent mast cell degranulation in primary human mast cells sensitized with patient sera, with 5 of 8 evaluable patients showing 10-35% CD63-positive activation peaking at 0.1-1 µg/mL.
Serum sIgE levels to Bet v 7 and Ara h 18 showed an almost perfect positive correlation across 100 children with seasonal allergic rhinitis.
Pre-incubation with rBet v 7 strongly inhibited IgE binding to Ara h 18 and vice versa in ImmunoCAP inhibition assays using three selected sera, confirming bidirectional IgE cross-reactivity.
Serum Bet v 7-specific IgE levels correlated strongly with the magnitude of mast cell activation (peak CD63 expression at 1 µg/mL rBet v 7) across the tested patients.

Amino acid sequence alignment and AlphaFold2 structural modeling showed 91% identity (155/171 residues) and near-identical 3D structure (TM-score 0.99346) between Bet v 7 and Ara h 18, explaining their extensive IgE cross-reactivity.
Mild heat treatment (60°C, 10 min) of rBet v 7 did not significantly reduce its ability to induce mast cell activation compared with untreated protein.
Exposure of rBet v 7 to human saliva did not significantly change its capacity to induce mast cell activation relative to untreated protein.
Addition of trypsin to saliva reduced rBet v 7-induced mast cell activation, demonstrating that the allergen is susceptible to enzymatic proteolysis despite resisting native saliva alone.

Higher temperature heat treatment (80°C and 100°C) progressively reduced Bet v 7's ability to induce mast cell activation, with a significant overall temperature effect and large effect sizes for high-temperature comparisons.
Children selected for cyclophilin sensitization (100-patient subset) had higher rates of anaphylaxis and atopic dermatitis, and higher total IgE, than the full 1263-patient PAN-PED cohort.

Very low concentrations of rBet v 7 (as low as 10 ng/mL) were sufficient to trigger robust mast cell activation in the stem cell-derived mast cell assay, a sensitivity exceeding previous skin prick test or RBL-based reports.
An initially observed association between Bet v 7 sensitization and asthma comorbidity in the PAN-PED survey was no longer significant after multivariate adjustment.

Ten SAR patients sensitized to Bet v 7 but negative for profilins, PR-10, and nsLTPs showed no clinical oral allergy syndrome at the time of sampling, raising doubt about the direct clinical impact of cyclophilin-specific IgE.

Authors propose that a single plant cyclophilin (e.g., Bet v 7) could serve as a diagnostic surrogate for detecting sensitization to plant cyclophilins broadly, given near-identical sIgE measurements to Bet v 7 and Ara h 18.
In LPS-induced septic cardiomyopathy mouse hearts, mast cells showed increased degranulation and proliferation, with increased tryptase expression, compared to controls.
Serum and cardiac CXCL4 protein levels were significantly increased in septic cardiomyopathy mice compared to controls.
Mast cell stabilizer Sodium Cromoglycate (CS) reduced cardiac inflammatory cell infiltration and significantly increased survival rate in septic cardiomyopathy mice.
Mast cell stabilization with CS significantly reduced elevated serum/cardiac IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α levels seen in LPS-induced septic cardiomyopathy mice.
Mast cell stabilization with CS reduced serum myocardial injury markers CK-MB, AST, and LDH that were elevated in septic cardiomyopathy mice.
Inhibiting mast cell activation with CS reduced CXCL4 protein expression in heart tissue and serum of septic cardiomyopathy mice.
Inhibiting mast cell activation with CS was reported to further reduce cardiac SLC7A11 and GPX4 protein levels, as measured by western blot.
Inhibiting mast cell activation with CS reduced lipid peroxidation marker 4-HNE and oxidative stress markers (MDA/SOD) in heart tissue and serum of septic cardiomyopathy mice.
TUNEL staining co-localized with CD68 showed macrophage cell death within the hearts of septic cardiomyopathy mice, suggesting macrophage ferroptosis occurs in vivo.
Ferroptosis inhibitor Fer-1 reduced cardiac inflammatory cell infiltration and improved survival in septic cardiomyopathy mice.
SLC7A11 and GPX4 protein expression was decreased in the hearts of septic cardiomyopathy mice, consistent with active ferroptosis.
Transcriptomic profiling of CXCL4-treated macrophages showed significant enrichment of ferroptosis-related genes compared to untreated controls.

CXCL4 treatment of macrophages significantly reduced SLC7A11 and GPX4 gene and protein expression in vitro, and this reduction was reversed by the ferroptosis inhibitor Fer-1, which also reduced cellular iron content.

CXCL4 treatment significantly reduced expression of phagocytosis genes CD36 and MERTK in macrophages, and this reduction was reversed by Fer-1, while phagocytosis genes MRC1 and LRP1 were unaffected; macrophage microbead phagocytosis assays showed the same pattern.
CD36 protein and gene expression was reduced in heart tissue of LPS-treated septic cardiomyopathy mice, and was restored by ferroptosis inhibitor Fer-1 treatment.

CXCL4 reduced macrophage viability and increased ROS levels, effects that were reversed by the p53 inhibitor Pifithrin-α (PFT-α); PFT-α also modulated SLC7A11 and GPX4 expression, implicating p53 in CXCL4-induced macrophage ferroptosis.

STAT3 inhibitor Niclosamide increased macrophage viability, reduced ROS levels, increased SLC7A11/GPX4 protein expression, and reduced p53 protein expression in CXCL4-treated macrophages, supporting STAT3 as an upstream regulator of p53-mediated ferroptosis.

In vivo, STAT3 inhibitor Niclosamide and p53 inhibitor PFT-α each alleviated cardiac inflammatory damage, improved survival, reduced serum CK-MB/AST/LDH, and increased SLC7A11/GPX4 protein expression in septic cardiomyopathy mice; Niclosamide also reduced cardiac p53 protein expression.

Investigational therapies targeting the KIT D816V mutant receptor in ongoing clinical trials have shown ability to improve symptoms, decrease mast cell burden, and improve quality of life in nonadvanced systemic mastocytosis.
Investigational therapy targeting siglec-8 has shown potential to reduce symptoms in small patient cohorts with nonadvanced systemic mastocytosis.
Investigational therapy targeting mTOR has shown potential to reduce symptoms in small patient cohorts with nonadvanced systemic mastocytosis.
Targeted therapy against interleukin-6 did not show sufficient benefit and results did not support further pursuit of this approach in nonadvanced systemic mastocytosis.
A clinical trial targeting Bruton tyrosine kinase in nonadvanced systemic mastocytosis is ongoing, with no published efficacy or safety data yet available.
Rothia and Staphylococcus species isolated from human saliva and jejunum degrade the immunodominant peanut allergens Ara h 1 and Ara h 2 in vitro.
Microbial degradation of Ara h 1 and Ara h 2 by Rothia/Staphylococcus generates protein fragments with reduced IgE binding and limited mast cell activation.
Mice colonized with Rothia showed reduced local and systemic Ara h 1 and Ara h 2 allergen levels and dampened anaphylaxis after peanut challenge.
In clinical studies, peanut-degrading bacteria including Rothia were more abundant in peanut-allergic patients who showed better tolerance to allergen exposure.
Human saliva and jejunum harbor peanut-degrading bacteria capable of metabolizing immunodominant allergens Ara h 1 and Ara h 2.
Decursin suppresses mast cell activation by directly targeting Fyn kinase, a key upstream signaling molecule in the FcεRI pathway.
Decursin inhibits activation of key upstream signaling molecules in the FcεRI-mediated degranulation pathway of mast cells.
In a murine passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) model, Decursin significantly inhibited the IgE-mediated anaphylactic response.
In a murine passive systemic anaphylaxis (PSA) model, Decursin exerted significant inhibitory effects on the systemic anaphylactic response.

Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics (age, sex, BMI, coronary risk factors, labs, LVEF, ECG findings, culprit lesion, medications, outcomes) did not differ significantly between allergy-associated and non-allergy-associated ACS patients.

Post-PCI beta-blocker use was descriptively lower in the anaphylactic allergy-ACS subgroup than in the non-anaphylactic subgroup (100% vs 50%), though the table reports this as not statistically significant.
Serum total IgE levels were significantly higher in allergy-associated ACS patients than in non-allergic ACS patients, although values overlapped substantially between groups.
Serum IgE levels did not significantly differ between the non-anaphylactic and anaphylactic allergy-associated ACS subgroups.
Plasma histamine levels were significantly higher in allergy-associated ACS patients than in non-allergic ACS patients.
Plasma histamine levels did not significantly differ between the non-anaphylactic and anaphylactic allergy-associated ACS subgroups.
Plasma histamine levels in healthy non-allergic volunteers were lower than in either ACS group, provided as an exploratory reference range.
Daytime parasympathetic (HF) heart rate variability power was significantly lower in allergy-associated ACS patients than in non-allergic ACS patients.
Nighttime HF power did not significantly differ between allergy-associated and non-allergic ACS groups.
The daytime LF/HF ratio, indicating relative sympathetic predominance, was significantly higher in allergy-associated ACS patients than in non-allergic ACS patients, with a large effect size.
The nighttime LF/HF ratio was significantly higher in allergy-associated ACS patients than in non-allergic ACS patients, with sympathetic predominance remaining robust despite limited sample size.
HF power and LF/HF ratio did not significantly differ between the non-anaphylactic and anaphylactic allergy-associated ACS subgroups.
Bee venom exposure was significantly more frequent as the identified allergen in patients with anaphylactic allergy-associated ACS than in those without anaphylaxis.

The time from allergen exposure to symptom onset was markedly shorter in anaphylactic allergy-associated ACS than in non-anaphylactic cases, confirming closer temporal association with acute onset in the former.
The time from allergen exposure to ACS diagnosis was markedly shorter in the anaphylactic subgroup than in the non-anaphylactic subgroup.
A Time-Relation grade indicating symptom onset within 4 hours of allergen exposure was significantly more common in anaphylactic than non-anaphylactic allergy-associated ACS patients.

In one case report, adding an antihistamine to beta-blocker therapy for a patient with frequent PVCs reduced PVC burden from 12.3% to 8.0%, reduced PVC runs, and was associated with a nighttime increase in HF power suggesting partial restoration of circadian autonomic rhythm; the authors caution this does not imply causality.
OFE significantly inhibited compound 48/80-induced degranulation (β-hexosaminidase release) in LAD2 human mast cells and primary rat peritoneal mast cells.
OFE rapidly and reversibly decreased cytoplasmic Ca2+ ([Ca2+]c) levels in mast cells independent of Mrgpr signaling activation.
OFE promoted uptake of mitochondrial Ca2+ ([Ca2+]m), which was identified as the mechanism by which it lowers cytoplasmic Ca2+ among the four classical Ca2+ removal pathways tested.
OFE did not affect the activity of plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase, sarco/endoplasmic Ca2+-ATPase, or the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, ruling these out as mechanisms of Ca2+ reduction.
In vivo, OFE alleviated compound 48/80-induced vascular leakage in an animal model of pseudo-allergic reaction.
In vivo, OFE alleviated compound 48/80-induced scratching behavior, a symptom correlate of pseudo-allergic pruritus.
In vivo, OFE alleviated compound 48/80-induced hypothermia, a systemic anaphylactoid response marker.
Incubation of isolated human small bronchi with IL-33 for 48 hours increased the maximal contractile force to anti-IgE challenge by 62% compared with buffer control.
IL-33 pre-incubation increased the maximal contractile force to hyperosmolar mannitol challenge by 78% in isolated human small bronchi.
IL-33 doubled antigen-IgE-induced prostaglandin D2 release from bronchial segments compared with buffer control.
IL-33 pretreatment enhanced degranulation and release of cysteinyl leukotrienes and prostaglandin D2 from isolated primary human lung mast cells stimulated with anti-IgE or mannitol.
Unlike IL-33, TSLP had no effect on bronchial contraction, mast cell degranulation, or mediator release in response to anti-IgE or mannitol challenge.
Unlike IL-33, IL-25 had no effect on bronchial contraction, mast cell degranulation, or mediator release in response to anti-IgE or mannitol challenge.
The period prevalence of sesame allergy increased threefold from early childhood to school age, with most new cases developing after 36 months of age.
Children who had sesame allergy at 7-12 years had larger skin prick test wheal sizes to sesame at 36 months and at 7-12 years compared to sesame-sensitised but tolerant children.
Sesame-specific IgE levels were higher from 12 months onwards in children who had sesame allergy at 7-12 years compared to sensitised-but-tolerant children.
Ses i 1-specific IgE (a sesame seed allergen component) levels were higher from 12 months onwards in children with sesame allergy at 7-12 years compared to sensitised-but-tolerant children.
Mast cell activation test responses to sesame showed small but statistically significant differences between sesame-allergic and sesame-sensitised-tolerant children.
A larger increase in sesame-specific IgE and Ses i 1-specific IgE levels between 12 and 36 months predicted development of new sesame allergy by 7-12 years of age.
A greater rise in sesame-specific IgE and Ses i 1-specific IgE between 12 and 36 months was predictive of developing new sesame allergy by 7-12 years.

Among 301 children followed longitudinally, sesame allergy outcomes at 7-12 years comprised 4 with persistent allergy, 10 with new-onset allergy, 1 who outgrew allergy, and 286 who remained sesame-sensitised but tolerant.
H. pylori infection is positively associated with metabolic syndrome, and eradicating the bacterium affects MetS-related parameters.
H. pylori is described as an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease, and its eradication is considered cardiovascularly safe.
A meta-analysis found a positive correlation between H. pylori infection and both metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance.
H. pylori infection is an independent risk factor for MetS-related non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and correlates with increased steatosis severity.
Active H. pylori infection is independently positively associated with severity of MetS-related NASH, and with IR, dyslipidemia, and arterial hypertension.
H. pylori-derived VacA is chemotactic toward bone marrow-derived mast cells and induces them to produce pro-inflammatory cytokines.
Stress-induced corticotropin-releasing hormone activates mast cells to release chymase/tryptase, IL-8, and VEGF, which disrupt the blood-brain barrier and contribute to neurodegenerative pathology.
Mast cell activation, by mediating blood-brain barrier damage, contributes to cognitive impairment.
H. pylori infection is linked to arterial stiffness, an early atherosclerosis marker associated with MetS-related hypertension and a predictor of CVD complications and mortality.

H. pylori DNA has been detected in atherosclerotic plaques, and H. pylori infection is associated with carotid plaque onset in adults without prior CVD, suggesting a role in atherosclerosis pathogenesis.
H. pylori-related galectin-3 elevation is positively associated with metabolic syndrome and connected to higher all-cause mortality, particularly heart failure and cardio-cerebrovascular mortality.
Galectin-3 is associated with severe cardiovascular outcomes and all-cause mortality in MetS-related type 2 diabetes independently of conventional risk factors.
Plasma LPS levels were 76% higher in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus than in controls, consistent with a role for gut bacterial LPS in metabolic inflammation.
H. pylori eradication significantly reduces total cholesterol, LDL-C, and fibrinogen while increasing HDL-C, alongside improvements in hypertension, insulin resistance, BMI, and oxidant status.
Ghrelin, an appetite-stimulating hormone, is elevated in individuals with H. pylori infection and may contribute to increased food intake and obesity.
Patients with H. pylori infection show significantly higher mast cell counts in the gastric mucosa compared to normal subjects, accompanied by increased apoptotic epithelial cells.
Mast cell infiltration in gastric epithelium is significantly higher in H. pylori-infected individuals but diminishes after successful eradication therapy.
An in vitro study found that H. pylori enhances histamine release by murine serosal mast cells.
Rat peritoneal mast cells express leptin and adiponectin receptors; leptin induces mast cell migration and secretion of histamine, cysteinyl leukotriene, and CCL2.
Unlike leptin, adiponectin induces mast cells to produce anti-inflammatory IL-10, in addition to promoting mast cell migration.
Increased mast cell abundance is associated with symptomatic carotid artery disease and with prevalence of future adverse cardiovascular events.
Serum tryptase concentrations are significantly increased in patients with acute coronary syndromes, and intraplaque mast cell numbers rise upon atherosclerotic plaque destabilization.
The number of intraplaque mast cells in carotid plaques is independently associated with the prevalence of clinical cardiovascular adverse events.
Mast cell degranulation increases rapidly after cardiac injury, reaching approximately 80% within one week.
Mast cell-derived chymase is linked to atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability.
Eradication regimens supplemented with probiotics have been established for over 15 years to increase H. pylori eradication rates and reduce treatment side effects.
Next-generation probiotic supplementation reduced insulin resistance, plasma cholesterol, and risk of liver dysfunction/inflammation, but showed no significant change in gut microbiota composition.
Insulin resistance is associated with atrial fibrillation and with a twofold increase in cardiovascular outcomes, including stroke.
Late heart-to-mediastinum ratio (l-H/M) on 123I-mIBG scintigraphy was reduced in asymptomatic TTR mutation carriers compared with healthy controls.
l-H/M was further reduced in symptomatic ATTRv patients compared with asymptomatic carriers and healthy controls, indicating progressive cardiac sympathetic denervation with disease severity.
Delta-PADO (years from predicted age of disease onset) correlated with early heart-to-mediastinum ratio (e-H/M) in asymptomatic carriers.
Delta-PADO correlated with the early summed score (ESS) on 123I-mIBG imaging in asymptomatic carriers.
Delta-PADO correlated with the late summed score (LSS) on 123I-mIBG imaging in asymptomatic carriers.
Half of the asymptomatic TTR mutation carriers already showed reduced lower-limb intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy, indicating subclinical small fiber neuropathy.
Cutaneous silent period latencies, a measure of A-delta small fiber function, were prolonged or absent in advanced ATTRv cases.
IL-17 levels were elevated in the colon of TNBS-induced fibrosis model mice compared to controls.
Gamma delta T cell numbers were increased in the intestinal tissue of the fibrosis model mice relative to controls.
Fibroblast numbers/activity were increased in the model group compared to controls, consistent with fibrotic progression.
Treatment with an anti-IL-17A antibody attenuated intestinal fibrosis and reduced IL-17, gamma delta T cell, and fibroblast levels in the mouse model.
Treatment with an anti-gamma delta TCR monoclonal antibody (clone GL3) attenuated intestinal fibrosis and reduced IL-17, gamma delta T cell, and fibroblast levels.
In vitro, model fibroblasts showed increased IL-17, alpha-SMA, and collagen expression, which was further increased by Transwell co-culture with gamma delta T cells.

The TGF-beta/Smad signaling pathway was activated with upregulated connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) in the model group in vivo, and antibody intervention inhibited this pathway, consistent with in vitro results.
TGFB3 mRNA and protein were significantly upregulated in myocardial tissue from human heart failure patients compared to controls.
Plasma TGFB3 concentration positively correlated with plasma NT-proBNP levels in an independent cohort of cardiology patients.
TGFB3 expression was significantly elevated in myocardial tissue from patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy compared to controls in publicly available RNA-seq datasets.
TGFB3 mRNA and protein were significantly increased in the myocardium of mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction (TAC) compared to sham controls, along with elevated plasma TGFB3.
Tgfb1 mRNA was the most highly expressed TGF-β isoform in TAC hearts, exceeding levels of Tgfb2 and Tgfb3.

Single-cell/single-nucleus RNA-seq and cell fractionation data show that TGFB3 upregulation under pathological stress (TAC) occurs predominantly in cardiomyocytes rather than fibroblasts, whereas fibroblasts are the main source under physiological conditions.
Angiotensin II (AngII) treatment significantly induced TGFB3 expression in primary cardiomyocytes and the HL-1 cardiomyocyte cell line.

Cardiomyocyte-specific Tgfb3 knockout mice (Myh6-Cre) showed no significant difference in ejection fraction, fractional shortening, cardiac output, heart weight, or fibrosis-associated gene expression compared to controls under basal physiological conditions.

Inducible cardiomyocyte-specific Tgfb3 deletion prior to TAC exacerbated cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibrosis 8 weeks post-surgery, with reduced ejection fraction and fractional shortening compared to controls.
Plasma TGFB3 levels were significantly decreased in mice with cardiomyocyte-specific Tgfb3 knockout after TAC, indicating myocardium as a major source of systemic TGFB3 in this model.
Transcriptomic profiling of cardiomyocyte-specific Tgfb3 knockout hearts revealed 37 upregulated and 102 downregulated genes, with fibrosis mediators CTGF and SERPINE1/SERPINF1 markedly upregulated.
Recombinant TGFB3 attenuated TGFB1-induced activation of primary cardiac fibroblasts, reducing expression of CTGF and SERPINE1 compared to TGFB1 alone.

Conditioned media from TGFB3-deficient cardiomyocytes increased fibroblast activation marker α-SMA and expression of CTGF and SERPINE1 in wild-type cardiac fibroblasts compared to media from wild-type cardiomyocytes.
Co-stimulation with TGFB3 significantly diminished TGFB1-induced phosphorylation of SMAD3 and suppressed TGFB1-induced transcriptional activation in a Smad-responsive luciferase reporter assay.
Co-immunoprecipitation showed that TGFB3 competitively inhibited TGFB1 binding to TGFBR2 in a dose-dependent manner in primary cardiac fibroblasts.

Recombinant TGFB3 treatment did not significantly alter SMAD7 expression, indicating that TGFB3's inhibition of TGFB1-induced SMAD3 phosphorylation is not mediated by SMAD7, contrary to a prior proposed mechanism.
Duration of diabetes was significantly longer in T2DM patients with constipation compared to those without, though this lost significance in multivariate analysis.
Fasting C-peptide (FCP) was significantly lower in the constipation group than in the non-constipation group in univariate comparison, but not an independent factor in multivariate analysis.
Total cholesterol (TC) was significantly higher in the constipation group and remained a significant independent factor in multivariate logistic regression.
LDL-C was significantly higher in the constipation group and remained a significant independent factor in multivariate logistic regression.
HbA1c was significantly higher in the constipation group in univariate analysis but did not remain an independent factor in multivariate regression.
Time in Range (TIR), a continuous glucose monitoring metric, was significantly lower in T2DM patients with constipation and remained an independent associated factor in multivariate regression.

Coefficient of Variability (CV), a glycemic variability metric from continuous glucose monitoring, was significantly higher in T2DM patients with constipation and remained an independent associated factor in multivariate regression.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy was more prevalent among T2DM patients with constipation than those without.
Diabetic nephropathy was more prevalent among T2DM patients with constipation than those without.
Diabetic retinopathy, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and peripheral vascular disease did not significantly differ in prevalence between constipation and non-constipation T2DM groups.
ROC curve analysis showed TIR had modest predictive value for constipation in T2DM patients (AUC=0.6646).
ROC curve analysis showed CV had modest predictive value for constipation in T2DM patients (AUC=0.6726).
Combining TIR and CV improved predictive value for constipation risk in T2DM patients compared to either metric alone (AUC=0.7350).
T2DM patients with constipation had significantly higher Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index (GCSI) scores, indicating more severe upper GI symptoms, compared to non-constipated patients.
Intestinal sensitivity (VSI) scores were significantly higher in T2DM patients with constipation compared to non-constipated patients.
Patient Assessment of Upper Gastrointestinal Symptom Severity Index (PAGI-SYM) scores were significantly higher in the constipation group, indicating greater GI symptom severity.
Patient Assessment of Quality of Life Index (PAGI-QOL) scores were significantly higher in the constipation group, indicating greater negative impact on quality of life.
Intestinal muscularis resident macrophages isolated from mouse muscularis expressed α1, α2, β1, and β2 adrenergic receptors.
LPS stimulation significantly increased nitric oxide (NO) production in the macrophage-like cell line J774.1.
Activation of α1 adrenergic receptors attenuated the LPS-induced increase in NO production.
Activation of β1 adrenergic receptors attenuated the LPS-induced increase in NO production in J774.1 macrophages.
Activation of β2 adrenergic receptors attenuated the LPS-induced increase in NO production in J774.1 macrophages.
Activation of α2 adrenergic receptors enhanced the LPS-induced NO response, in contrast to α1/β1/β2 activation.
Norepinephrine suppressed the LPS-induced increase in NO production, and this suppression was reversed by β1/β2 receptor antagonists.
Inhibition of adenylate cyclase reversed the NO suppression induced by a non-selective β receptor agonist, implicating cAMP signaling downstream of β-adrenergic receptors.
Norepinephrine suppressed the LPS-induced increase in nitric oxide production by J774.1 macrophage-like cells.
Blockade of beta1/beta2 adrenergic receptors reversed the norepinephrine-induced suppression of LPS-stimulated NO production, confirming a beta-adrenergic mechanism.

Inhibiting adenylate cyclase reversed the suppression of LPS-induced NO production caused by a non-selective beta receptor agonist, indicating cAMP-dependent signaling downstream of beta-adrenergic receptors.
In ex vivo intestinal segments, electrical stimulation of sympathetic nerves alone did not significantly alter LPS-induced iNOS mRNA expression.
Combining electrical sympathetic stimulation with a non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonist significantly enhanced LPS-induced iNOS expression in intestinal segments.
Combining electrical sympathetic stimulation with a selective beta1-adrenergic antagonist significantly enhanced LPS-induced iNOS expression in intestinal segments.
Administration of 3 doses of 5-Fluorouracil caused a significant decrease in circulating leukocyte counts, confirming induction of immunosuppression.
L-Glutamine supplementation was associated with progressive body weight gain in immunosuppressed mice, whereas vehicle-treated controls lost weight.
Histological counting showed L-Glutamine treatment reduced the overall number of inflammatory cells infiltrating the peritoneal implant compared with control.
Flow cytometry showed L-Glutamine reduced the overall frequency of CD45+ leukocytes within the implant compared with control.
Among the reduced CD45+ population, L-Glutamine-treated animals showed a higher relative proportion of neutrophils than controls.
L-Glutamine-treated animals showed a higher relative proportion of macrophages within the CD45+ population than controls.
L-Glutamine-treated animals showed a higher relative proportion of lymphocytes within the CD45+ population than controls.
L-Glutamine treatment reduced the number of Caspase-3-positive (apoptotic) cells in the peritoneal implant compared with control, indicating an anti-apoptotic effect.
L-Glutamine reduced myeloperoxidase activity (a marker of neutrophil infiltration/activation) in the peritoneal implant compared with control.
L-Glutamine reduced NAG activity (a marker of activated macrophage/mononuclear cell accumulation) in the peritoneal implant compared with control.
L-Glutamine treatment lowered TNF-alpha production in the peritoneal implant compared with control.
L-Glutamine treatment reduced the number of mast cells in the peritoneal implant compared with control.
L-Glutamine reduced the number of newly formed blood vessels within the peritoneal implant compared with control.
L-Glutamine treatment significantly lowered VEGF levels in the peritoneal implant compared with control.
L-Glutamine treatment reduced total collagen area in the peritoneal implant, with a more fragmented, greenish (type III-predominant) collagen fiber appearance compared with control.
L-Glutamine treatment reduced levels of the pro-fibrogenic cytokine TGF-beta1 in the peritoneal implant compared with control.

Diffusion-based neuroinflammation imaging showed significantly lower NII-HR (hindered water ratio, reflecting extracellular tissue edema) in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls across several association, commissural and projection white matter fibres.
NII-RF, indicating inflammation-related cellularity, was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls across association, commissural, and projection white matter fibres.
NII-FF, indicating apparent axonal density, was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls in widespread white matter fibre tracts.
NII-derived fractional anisotropy was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls across widespread white matter fibre tracts.

NII-derived axial diffusivity (NII-AD) and mean diffusivity (NII-MD) showed a regionally heterogeneous pattern, being both increased and decreased in different white matter tracts in ME/CFS relative to controls.
No significant group differences were found in NII-RD between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Conventional DTI-derived axial diffusivity (DTI-AD) was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls in several white matter fibre tracts.
There were no significant group differences in DTI-FA, DTI-MD or DTI-RD between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

Across all participants, NII-RF showed significant positive associations with mental health scores (SF-36 MCS) in major white matter tracts that overlapped with regions of group-level NII-RF reduction in ME/CFS.

Across all participants, NII-RF showed significant positive associations with disability level (Bell's Disability Scale) in major white matter tracts overlapping with regions of ME/CFS-related NII-RF reduction.

NII-AD in commissural fibres (corpus callosum body/genu) and the anterior corona radiata was significantly positively associated with mental health scores among all participants, overlapping with areas of reduced NII-AD in ME/CFS.

NII-MD in commissural fibres (corpus callosum body/genu) and projection fibres (superior and anterior corona radiata) was significantly positively associated with mental health scores among all participants.
Within the ME/CFS patient group, NII-FF was significantly negatively associated with disease severity in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus and right posterior corona radiata.
No significant associations were found between any DTI-derived metrics and clinical measures (MCS, PCS, PSQI, BDS, disease severity), in contrast to NII-derived metrics.

Both post-infectious ME/CFS (PI-ME/CFS) and gradual onset ME/CFS (GO-ME/CFS) subgroups showed the same pattern of lower NII-RF and higher NII-FF compared with healthy controls, supporting pooling of subtypes for the main analysis.
ME/CFS patients had significantly worse anxiety and depression scores, worse SF-36 mental and physical health, worse sleep quality, and higher disability compared to healthy controls.
Among participants who had severe ME/CFS at 6 months post-infectious mononucleosis, 81% still met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria at the 7-year follow-up.
Among participants with moderate or lingering symptoms at 6 months post-infectious mononucleosis, only about one-third still met ME/CFS criteria at the 7-year follow-up.
Approximately 30% of ME/CFS cases are linked to a preceding Epstein-Barr virus infection that caused infectious mononucleosis.
Flow cytometry showed small EVs strongly expressed tetraspanins, with only minor differences between ME/CFS patients and healthy donors.
Proteomic profiling identified hemoglobin subunit alpha as an altered EV cargo protein in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Proteomic profiling identified insulin-like growth factor-binding protein acid labile subunit as an altered EV cargo protein in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Small RNA sequencing and qPCR showed significant downregulation of hsa-let-7b-5p in plasma EVs from post-COVID-19 ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Reduced hsa-let-7b-5p expression in EVs correlated with impaired physical functioning and increased fatigue, pain, and immune activation in ME/CFS patients.
Combined exercise (aerobic plus resistance/other modalities) ranked highest among 13 exercise modalities for improving physical function as measured by the 6-Minute Walk Test.
Aerobic exercise ranked highest among all modalities for reducing anxiety symptoms as measured by the HADS-A subscale.
Combined exercise ranked highest among all modalities for reducing depressive symptoms as measured by the Beck Depression Inventory.
High-intensity interval training (HIIT) ranked highest among all modalities for improving health-related quality of life as measured by the SF-36.
HIIT ranked highest among all modalities for reducing disease impact as measured by the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire.
Aquatic exercise ranked highest among all modalities for reducing pain as measured by the Visual Analog Scale.
Meta-regression showed that the type of exercise intervention had a greater influence on treatment outcomes than session frequency or intervention duration.
Pre-existing chronic illness was the only independent factor significantly associated with severe acute COVID-19 in children, conferring almost sixfold higher odds.
BMI showed a positive but statistically non-significant trend toward association with severe acute COVID-19 after adjustment for other covariates.
Only 1.7% (12 of 698) of children with PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection met the study's criteria for long COVID (symptoms >4 weeks).
Children who developed long COVID were significantly older than those who did not.
Chronic illness was significantly more common among children who developed long COVID compared to those who did not.
Prevalence of long COVID showed a severity-dependent gradient across the acute COVID-19 disease course, rising from 0% after asymptomatic infection to 50% after severe courses.
Long COVID prevalence was associated with age group/type of childcare setting, rising across older school levels.
No significant associations were found between long COVID and sex, socioeconomic status, migration background, BMI, or repeated quarantine episodes.
Only nine participants (1.2%) reported symptoms persisting beyond 12 weeks, aligning more closely with the WHO post-COVID-19 condition definition.
The most frequently reported long COVID symptoms in children were fatigue, sleep disturbances, and problems concentrating, with prevalence declining over time.

The authors interpret the stepwise rise in persistent post-acute symptoms with acute disease severity (0% to 50%) as an exploratory signal potentially relevant to ME/CFS-like sequelae in children after severe COVID-19, while stating that causality cannot be established from cross-sectional data.
Approximately 5% of COVID-19 patients experience persistent neurological sequelae, predominantly affecting young or middle-aged working adults.
The review states that women are disproportionately affected by long neuro-COVID sequelae compared to men.

The most common neurological symptoms of long neuro-COVID include persistent cognitive impairment ('brain fog'), chronic fatigue syndrome, neuroinflammation (motor or autonomic), anxiety, and depression.
An estimated 15% of COVID-19 cases globally continue to have symptoms persisting beyond the acute infection phase.
Up to 79% of people with Long COVID exhibit autonomic dysfunction consistent with POTS.
Approximately 4–5% of people with Long COVID meet formal ME/CFS diagnostic criteria or report ME/CFS-type symptoms such as post-exertional malaise.
Mast cell activation syndrome is reported more frequently among individuals with Long COVID-associated POTS, suggesting links between MCAS, POTS, and ME/CFS.

Within four months of ICD-10 code U09.9 activation in the US, 78,525 Long COVID patients were identified in a large private-payer dataset, most of whom had not been hospitalised during acute infection.
Women were diagnosed with Long COVID more frequently than men in the US claims-based surveillance cohort.
A substantial proportion of the identified Long COVID patients in the US claims dataset had no pre-existing chronic conditions.
A 2025 national survey found that half of respondents with prior COVID-19 infection and two-thirds of those with Long COVID reported moderate to severe impacts on their capacity to work.
Fewer than half (47%) of surveyed participants had been referred to a Long COVID clinic, with a median waiting time of 90 days.
The perceived usefulness of advice from Long COVID clinics for supporting symptom understanding and management was rated low, with a median score of 3 out of 10.
Emerging evidence suggests metformin may reduce the risk of developing Long COVID among people with overweight or obesity.
Modifiable predictors identified for developing Long COVID include acute-phase fatigue, muscle or joint pain, shortness of breath, dysgeusia, and chest pain.
A systematic review found a median recovery time of 14 days after acute COVID-19, extending up to 12 weeks in some cases.

Twenty currently active multidisciplinary Long COVID clinical services were identified across Australia, comprising six public and fourteen private services, distributed across most states with none in the Northern Territory.

Three newly published or updated Long COVID guidelines (Australia's NSW ACI, US CDC, Canada's CAN-PCC) all received AGREE II overall quality ratings of 5–6 out of 7, with excellent inter-rater agreement.
Editorial independence was a weakness for the Australian and US guidelines, as neither reported funding sources or declared conflicts of interest, whereas the Canadian guideline was more transparent.

ICD-10-AM adopted the WHO code G93.3 for post-viral fatigue syndrome including ME/CFS since 1998, but Australian services and clinical guidelines have failed to keep pace with this coding pathway, leaving many patients without coordinated care.

In June 2024 the Australian Government committed $1.1 million to the NHMRC to develop new clinical guidelines for ME/CFS that will also reference Long COVID, POTS, and fibromyalgia, with public consultation scheduled for late 2027.

Between 2024 and 2025, the Australian Government committed $50 million through the Medical Research Future Fund to support Long COVID research with a focus on lived experience and translational impact.
Polysomnography with transcutaneous CO2 monitoring showed sleep-related hypoventilation with TcCO2 exceeding 55 mmHg for 13.7 minutes, despite no sleep disordered breathing.

The patient's polysomnogram revealed a normal apnea-hypopnea index and respiratory disturbance index, indicating the absence of obstructive sleep disordered breathing despite a moderate pretest probability for OSA.
BPAP titration at 9/5 cm H2O maintained TcCO2 below 55 mmHg with an improved baseline of 45 mmHg, and the patient reported improved breathing during titration.
After one to two months of consistent BPAP use, the patient's serum CO2 levels decreased compared to pre-treatment values.
Despite good BPAP compliance and lower serum CO2 levels, the patient continued to experience persistent excessive daytime sleepiness, considered multifactorial.

The patient's chronic opioid use (hydromorphone and oxycodone for at least three years) for EDS-related pain was identified as a major risk factor for central respiratory depression contributing to hypoventilation.
Pulmonary function testing revealed severely reduced maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures, suggesting significant respiratory muscle weakness in this patient with hypermobile EDS.
Pulmonary function testing showed a decrease in supine forced vital capacity greater than 10%, suggesting diaphragmatic weakness, despite normal spirometry.

Contrary to typical expectations, TcCO2 elevations did not worsen during REM sleep; instead, the maximum TcCO2 occurred during NREM or wake stages, possibly because baseline respiratory muscle weakness was already severe.
Neither the baseline diagnostic PSG nor the BPAP titration study showed evidence of nocturnal hypoxemia.
The patient reported a history of possible (unconfirmed) scoliosis, which may restrict chest wall motion and contribute to hypoventilation via reduced tidal volumes and minute ventilation.

The authors propose that sleep-related hypoventilation may be an under-recognized systemic manifestation of hypermobile EDS, distinct from the muscle atonia described in rarer spondylodysplastic and myopathic EDS subtypes.
Patients with non-vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes had a significantly higher prevalence of temporomandibular disorders than healthy controls.
Gingivitis prevalence was significantly higher in patients with non-vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes compared to healthy controls.
Lingual parafunction (e.g., tongue habits) was significantly more frequent in patients than controls.
Atrophy of the lingual frenulum was markedly more common in patients with non-vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes than in controls.
Atrophy of the inferior labial frenulum was significantly more frequent in patients than in controls.
Dental pulpal retractions were significantly more frequent in patients with non-vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes than in controls.
Dental root hypoplasia was significantly more frequent in patients with non-vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes than in controls.
Bi-allelic deleterious variants in OLA1 were identified in fourteen individuals from nine families presenting with a hypermobility-neurodevelopmental disorder and distinctive facial features.
The joint hypermobility phenotype seen in some affected individuals led clinicians to a diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Proband-derived fibroblasts confirmed the loss-of-function nature of the OLA1 variants, recapitulating impaired cell migration and proliferation previously reported in OLA1-deficient cells.
Neurons derived from proband fibroblasts showed impaired adhesion and cytoskeletal control, suggesting a mechanism underlying the abnormal neurodevelopment seen in probands.
Modeling ola-1 deficiency in C. elegans showed reduced neurite numbers compared to wild-type animals.
Transcriptomic analysis of ola-1-deficient C. elegans indicated dysregulation of key signaling pathways leading to suppression of microtubule dynamics and axon regrowth.
Mutant ola-1-deficient worms showed crippled regenerative competence (impaired axon regeneration) compared to wild-type controls.
OLA1 was described as regulating cell-matrix adhesion by modulating focal adhesion kinase (FAK) levels, thereby influencing cytoskeletal dynamics and cell motility.
The disorder is proposed to follow an autosomal-recessive inheritance pattern, consistent with bi-allelic OLA1 variants identified across nine families.
All 32 patients with vEDS carried disease-causing variants in COL3A1 identified through exome sequencing.
Among 32 vEDS patients, 27 exhibited respiratory system involvement, with pneumothorax (50.0%) and hemoptysis (43.8%) being the most common respiratory symptoms.
Patients in the pulmonary hemorrhage (PH) and pneumothorax/hemothorax (P/HTX) groups were younger on average than the OTHER group, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Extrapulmonary vascular complications occurred significantly less often in the PH and P/HTX groups compared with the OTHER group, though this may be confounded by age.
Inflammatory markers (WBC, neutrophils, CRP, ESR) were within normal range across vEDS patients, indicating a non-inflammatory mechanism underlying pulmonary hemorrhage.

Only one patient among those tested for autoantibodies (ANA and ANCA) had a positive ANA, and no pathogens were detected in bronchoalveolar lavage from patients undergoing bronchoscopy, supporting a non-autoimmune, non-infectious mechanism for pulmonary hemorrhage in vEDS.
Patients with pulmonary hemorrhage were significantly more likely to undergo invasive diagnostic procedures than other groups, including biopsies performed solely for diagnostic purposes.

Patients with pulmonary hemorrhage had a significantly higher rate of misdiagnosis as infection or vasculitis, leading to ineffective antibiotic, antiparasitic, antituberculous, or corticosteroid treatment.
Chest CT abnormalities in vEDS most commonly included spontaneous pneumothorax/hemothorax and pulmonary bulla/emphysema, with nodules present in 14 patients, most showing cavitation and halo sign.

Adoption of an empirical clinical-imaging-genetic diagnostic approach prioritizing pulmonary hemorrhage recognition and genetic testing since 2022 significantly shortened diagnostic duration for vEDS compared with before 2022.
Misdiagnosis rate for vEDS decreased significantly after implementation of the empirical diagnostic approach in 2022.
Aortic dissection requiring surgery occurred during pregnancy in 1.8% (4/226) of deliveries among women with Marfan-related disorders.
Aortic dissection occurred during postpartum hospitalization in 2.7% (6/226) of deliveries among women with Marfan-related disorders.
Within one year after delivery, 2.7% (6/226) of cases required re-hospitalization for aortic dissection, indicating persistent postpartum risk.

Cabergoline, used to elect against breastfeeding within 2 days postpartum in 6.6% of cases, was not associated with a significant difference in postpartum aortic dissection incidence compared with non-users.
Vascular EDS, caused by deleterious variants in COL3A1, is one of the most common heritable connective tissue disorders underlying spontaneous coronary artery dissection.
SCAD-vEDS patients had a lower average age at SCAD onset compared with the general/non-vEDS SCAD population, though this should be interpreted cautiously given small cohort size.
A higher proportion of males was observed among SCAD-vEDS patients than is typical for SCAD, which predominantly affects women.
Systemic (extra-cardiac) features consistent with vEDS were present in most, but not all, cases of SCAD-vEDS identified via the systematic review.

Clinical and angiographic differences between SCAD-vEDS and SCAD-nonvEDS groups were insufficient to reliably distinguish SCAD-vEDS from the general SCAD population, meaning clinical assessment alone will miss some cases and wider genetic testing may be warranted.
Using the Beighton Score cut-off of ≥5, 50.1% of the validity sample (308/615) was classified as GJH-positive.
Using the 5PQ-CN cut-off of ≥2, 56.4% of the validity sample (347/615) was classified as GJH-positive.
GJH classification differed significantly between the 5PQ-CN and BS diagnostic methods, indicating discordance between the two screening approaches.
The 5PQ-CN showed moderate overall diagnostic accuracy (72.19%), sensitivity 78.57%, specificity 65.80%, and an AUC of 0.722 relative to the Beighton Score reference standard.
The 5PQ-CN had a positive predictive value of 69.74% and negative predictive value of 75.37% relative to the Beighton Score.
5PQ-CN item 2 showed the strongest association with BS-defined GJH among all items, with an odds ratio of 8.09.
5PQ-CN item 4 did not significantly distinguish GJH-positive from GJH-negative participants, unlike the other four items.
5PQ-CN item 5 (self-perceived joint hypermobility) had the lowest odds ratio among items that significantly distinguished BS-defined GJH status.
Test-retest of the 5PQ-CN over a 7-day interval showed substantial agreement for dichotomous diagnosis (Cohen's kappa=0.703) and moderate reliability for total score (ICC=0.707).
Item-level test-retest reliability of the 5PQ-CN was moderate to substantial (kappa 0.442-0.664), with items 2 and 3 showing significant response shifts between rounds (McNemar p<.001).

GJH prevalence in this young Chinese cohort was higher than typically reported in Western cohorts, attributed to age, higher proportion of women, ethnicity, and sports/flexibility training background.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was identified as one of the systemic conditions with dermatologic manifestations described in case reports/series of complications following facial or scalp cosmetic procedures.
Increases in shoulder external rotation strength were associated with improved self-reported shoulder function after adjustment for covariates.
Increases in shoulder scaption strength were associated with improved self-reported shoulder function after adjustment for covariates.
Increases in shoulder scaption strength were associated with a small reduction in self-reported shoulder pain.
For every 10% increase in external rotation strength, patients had higher adjusted odds of reporting an important perceived improvement in physical symptoms.
For every 10% increase in scaption strength, patients had higher adjusted odds of reporting an important perceived improvement in physical symptoms.
For every 10% increase in external rotation strength, patients had greater adjusted odds of reaching the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) in shoulder function.
For every 10% increase in scaption strength, patients had greater adjusted odds of reaching the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) in shoulder function.
No testing position (external rotation, internal rotation, scaption) strength change was significantly associated with reaching MCID in shoulder pain.
Changes in internal rotation strength were not associated with any of the self-reported outcomes (function, pain, or perceived effect).
High-load progressive resistance training (HEAVY) produced greater increases in shoulder strength across the three movements than low-load home-based exercise (LIGHT).
Both HEAVY and LIGHT groups reported improved shoulder function and reduced pain, with a greater proportion of the HEAVY group reaching MCID for function and pain.
A post hoc subgroup analysis found no interaction between the HEAVY and LIGHT groups in the observed strength-symptom associations.
Based on the adjusted linear model, patients needed an approximate 80% increase in external rotation strength to reach the MCID in shoulder function, a threshold few participants reached.
An increase above 100% in scaption strength was needed to reach the MCID in pain, a threshold rarely achieved by participants.

In the primary RCT, both high-load and low-load shoulder exercise resulted in clinically meaningful improvements in shoulder function at 16 weeks, with an 8.3% absolute between-group difference favoring high-load exercise.

Activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain was reported by 28.36% of school-aged children attending pediatric outpatient clinics in the past month, with the back, shoulders, and knees most commonly affected.
Older children (12-15 years) had a higher prevalence of activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain than younger children (8-11 years).
Female sex was associated with significantly higher prevalence of activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain compared to males.
Among children with activity-limiting pain, average pain intensity on a numeric rating scale was moderate, indicating clinically relevant discomfort.
Children with activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain missed an average of 2.38 school days in the past month, and over half experienced sleep disturbances about three nights per week.

Among children with pain, task-specific difficulty was greatest for play, followed by carrying school bags, climbing stairs, and walking, indicating meaningful interference with age-appropriate physical function.
