Daily screen time exceeding two hours was an independent predictor of activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain.
Backpack loads exceeding 10% of body weight were an independent predictor of activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain.
Low or moderate physical activity level was an independent predictor of activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain.
Generalized joint hypermobility (Beighton score ≥4) was an independent predictor of activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain.

Higher foot posture index (more pronated) and higher BMI, along with reduced lower-limb strength and Y-Balance scores, were also associated with increased odds of pain, but with milder effect sizes than the top predictors.

The combination of excessive backpack load and generalized joint hypermobility showed a synergistic interaction, producing the strongest risk of activity-limiting musculoskeletal pain among all factors tested.

Stratified analysis showed the association between hypermobility and pain was much stronger in children carrying heavy backpack loads (>10% body weight) than in those with lighter loads, with a significant interaction by mechanical load.

ROC-derived thresholds for quadriceps strength (<132 N) and Y-Balance composite score (<81 cm) identified children with activity-limiting pain with moderate sensitivity/specificity, proposed as preliminary clinical screening cut-offs.

In bivariate comparisons, children with activity-limiting pain showed significantly greater joint hypermobility, more pronated foot posture, higher BMI, and reduced lower-limb strength and dynamic balance compared to pain-free peers.
In bivariate comparisons, children with activity-limiting pain reported more screen time, heavier backpack loads, and lower physical activity levels than pain-free peers.

Fixing the pelvis and thorax (FPT) during the wiper exercise produced greater infraspinatus muscle activity than no fixation or pelvis-only fixation, in both individuals with and without scapular dyskinesis.

The FPT (pelvis and thorax fixation) condition produced significantly greater shoulder external rotation strength than the no-fixation or pelvis-only fixation conditions, regardless of scapular dyskinesis status.
No significant difference in infraspinatus muscle activity was found between the no-fixation and pelvis-only fixation conditions during the wiper exercise.
Unlike muscle activity, shoulder external rotation strength differed significantly between the no-fixation and pelvis-only fixation conditions.
The authors state that weakness of the infraspinatus muscle may contribute to shoulder hypermobility and joint subluxation.
Visual dependence scores derived from the VR-based and PC-based Rod and Disk Tests showed only a weak, non-significant correlation when the head was in the neutral position.
A significant moderate correlation between VR-based and PC-based visual dependence was found only when the head was rotated 45° to the left.
When the head was rotated 45° to the right, the correlation between VR-based and PC-based visual dependence was not significant.
Bland-Altman analysis showed a small (<1°) mean bias with the VR-based system trivially overestimating visual dependence relative to the PC-based system across all head positions.
The VR-based Rod and Disk Test showed poor intra-rater test-retest reliability across all three head positions in healthy participants.
The PC-based Rod and Disk Test showed poor to moderate intra-rater test-retest reliability across the three head positions, the first reported reliability data for this reference test.
Despite poor ICC, the VR-based RDT demonstrated relatively small measurement error, with a standard error of measurement of approximately 0.7° and a minimal detectable change of 1.8–2.2°.

Mast cells are the primary effector cells driving anaphylaxis in humans, and elevated levels of mast-cell mediators such as tryptase and histamine have been detected during anaphylactic episodes.
Activated basophils may theoretically contribute to anaphylaxis symptoms by secreting mediators including histamine and leukotrienes.

The major activator of mast cells/basophils in anaphylaxis is allergen-specific IgE acting through cross-linking of its high-affinity receptor (FcεRI); other non-IgE pathways of direct mast-cell activation have also been described.
The estimated lifetime prevalence of anaphylaxis in the general population is approximately 0.3% to 5.1%.
Mortality from anaphylaxis is low, at less than 1 death per million population per year, despite impact on quality of life.
Global incidence of anaphylaxis is reported to range from 50 to 112 episodes per 100,000 person-years, with pediatric incidence ranging much more widely (1-761 per 100,000 person-years).
A recent meta-analysis estimated global anaphylaxis incidence at approximately 46 cases per 100,000 people per year, increasing annually by about 7.4%.

The three most common triggers of anaphylaxis are food (predominantly in children, especially cow's milk, peanuts, and tree nuts), drugs (predominantly in adults, especially beta-lactam antibiotics and NSAIDs), and insect venom (Hymenoptera), varying by age and geography.

Serum tryptase is the most reliable laboratory marker supporting a diagnosis of anaphylaxis, with an increase of 20% above basal level plus 2 mcg/L suggestive of acute mast cell activation, although it may not rise in all cases.

Intramuscular epinephrine administered in the lateral mid-thigh is the current first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, providing rapid pharmacological action while avoiding the overdose risks of intravenous administration.

Intranasal epinephrine, delivered as a nasal spray, has been shown to provide blood levels and cardiovascular effects comparable to traditional intramuscular injections, offering a needle-free alternative, though no head-to-head trials versus injectable epinephrine have been published.

H1-antihistamines and corticosteroids have traditionally been used in anaphylaxis treatment, but their benefit is unclear and they are insufficient to reverse an anaphylactic reaction; their use should not delay or substitute epinephrine administration.

In up to 10% of anaphylaxis cases, no exact cause can be identified, and such cases are labeled idiopathic anaphylaxis, an exclusion diagnosis requiring rule-out of mast-cell disorders (eg, basal tryptase elevation, C-kit mutations).

Therapeutic approaches such as antihistamines, corticosteroids, and omalizumab have been used to prevent recurrence of anaphylaxis, but the supporting evidence is low, based on anecdotal cases or small series.

Anti-ganglioside antibodies have been detected in up to 65% of neuropathies associated with celiac disease, consistent with the anti-GD3 positivity observed in this patient.

Anti-ganglioside antibodies become negative in only approximately half of celiac patients with neurological manifestations following gluten withdrawal, which may explain persistence of anti-GD3 antibodies at 5 months of GFD in this patient.

Rigamonti et al. described two patients with motor neuropathy associated with celiac disease who demonstrated clinical and electrophysiological improvement following initiation of a gluten-free diet, supporting a direct pathogenic link between gluten exposure and motor neuropathy.

A retrospective US study of 39 patients reported significant neurological improvement under a gluten-free diet, and two prospective Italian studies confirmed that adherence was associated with clinical improvement while nonadherence resulted in neurological deterioration.

Lee and colleagues reported a patient initially diagnosed with motor neuron disease whose progressive weakness and fasciculations were ultimately attributed to celiac disease, with subsequent clinical improvement on a gluten-free diet.
QD-NS inhalation significantly reduced TGF-beta levels in the lungs compared with the silica-induced diseased group in both preventive and treatment regimens.
QD-NS inhalation significantly reduced lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels in the lungs compared with the silica-induced diseased group in both preventive and treatment aspects.
QD-NS inhalation significantly reduced alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels in the lungs compared with the silica-induced diseased group in both preventive and treatment aspects.
QD-NS inhalation reduced pulmonary infiltration of lymphocytes, granulocytes, monocytes, and total WBC in both co- and post-treatment regimens relative to the diseased group.
Inhaled QD-NS demonstrated better anti-fibrotic efficacy than orally administered QD-NS, attributed to targeted lung delivery.
Fibromyalgia was convincingly/very suggestively associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
IBS was convincingly/very suggestively associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
Recurrent urinary tract infection was strongly associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis was strongly associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
Anxiety was convincingly/very suggestively associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
Depression was convincingly/very suggestively associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
Systemic inflammation was convincingly/very suggestively associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
Allergy/atopy was convincingly/very suggestively associated with increased odds of vulvodynia.
Interstitial cystitis showed suggestive evidence of association with vulvodynia with a large effect size.
Endometriosis showed suggestive evidence of association with vulvodynia.
Younger age was suggestively associated with lower odds of vulvodynia (i.e., older age increased risk, or younger age was protective depending on direction interpretation) per the pooled eOR below 1.
Acute restraint stress produced a significant increase in mean arterial pressure across multiple experimental cohorts.
Acute restraint stress consistently produced tachycardia (increased heart rate) across cohorts.
Acute restraint stress decreased tail skin temperature, used as an indirect index of sympathetically-mediated cutaneous vasoconstriction.
Non-selective NOS inhibition within the lateral hypothalamus using L-NAME significantly reduced the restraint-evoked pressor (MAP) response.
Non-selective NOS inhibition (L-NAME) in the LH reduced restraint-evoked tachycardia during both the restraint and recovery periods.
L-NAME microinjection into the LH did not alter the restraint-evoked decrease in tail skin temperature, indicating no effect on cutaneous sympathetic vasoconstriction.
Selective nNOS inhibition (NPLA) in the LH enhanced the heart rate (tachycardic) response during restraint stress, without affecting the pressor or tail skin temperature responses.
Selective iNOS inhibition (1400W) within the LH did not affect restraint-evoked MAP, HR, or tail skin temperature responses.
Local delivery of the NO donor NOC-9 into the LH decreased the restraint-evoked tachycardic response without affecting the pressor or tail skin temperature responses.

Immunohistochemistry confirmed the presence of numerous nNOS-expressing (nitrergic) neurons within the lateral hypothalamus, in regions corresponding to the microinjection sites used in the pharmacological experiments.

The divergent effects of non-selective NOS inhibition (L-NAME, reduced pressor/tachycardic responses) versus selective nNOS inhibition (NPLA, enhanced tachycardia only) suggest that a NOS isoform other than nNOS (proposed to be eNOS) mediates the facilitatory L-NAME effect on pressor and tachycardic responses in the LH.
Mice with BON-1 neuroendocrine tumor liver metastases showed impaired acetylcholine-induced vasodilation of mesenteric arteries compared with vehicle-treated mice, most pronounced in males.
Mice with BON-1 neuroendocrine tumor metastases showed impaired serotonin-mediated vasodilation of mesenteric arteries compared with vehicle controls, most pronounced in males.

Nitric oxide synthase inhibition (L-NAME) and 5-HT receptor blockade attenuated serotonin-induced vasodilatory responses only in vehicle-treated mice, not in NET-bearing mice, suggesting reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and altered 5-HT receptor action in NET mice.
Incubation of mesenteric arteries with serotonin reduced vasopressin-mediated vasoconstriction.
Liver metastases of BON-1 neuroendocrine tumor cells were confirmed by histology, chromogranin A expression, and presence of ALDH1-positive cancer stem cells.
Exercise therapy significantly reduced IBS Symptom Severity Score (IBS-SSS) compared with non-exercise controls across five pooled RCTs.
Pooled analysis of four RCTs found no statistically significant difference in IBS-specific quality of life (IBS-QOL) between exercise and control groups.
Pooled analysis of five RCTs found no statistically significant effect of exercise on anxiety symptoms in IBS patients compared with controls.
In one included RCT (Fani et al.), exercise intervention significantly improved IBS-QOL scores compared with control.
In one included RCT (Daley et al.), exercise intervention showed a statistically significant negative effect on IBS-QOL score relative to control.
Two included RCTs (Chao et al. and D'Silva et al.) found no statistically significant improvement in IBS-QOL scores with exercise versus control.
Allam et al. and Taneja et al. each found that exercise significantly reduced anxiety scores in IBS patients compared with control.
Kuttner et al., D'Silva et al., and Tavakoli et al. found no statistically significant effect of exercise on anxiety scores in IBS patients.
In a basic rat study, exercise training increased resting activity of vagal preganglionic neurons and enhanced their excitatory response during exercise, indicating exercise increases vagal tone.
A basic study measuring fingertip blood flow found increased sympathetic activity in patients with IBS, suggesting autonomic abnormalities contribute to IBS pathogenesis.

A separate meta-analysis of 40 intervention studies (1,253 participants) found that exercise training reduced muscle sympathetic nerve activity, with greater reductions in those with higher baseline sympathetic activity (dose-response relationship).

A basic science study found that exercise reduces expression of the serotonin transporter in specific brain regions (e.g., rostral ventromedial medulla), reducing serotonin reuptake and increasing synaptic serotonin levels.
Elevated basal cortisol levels are reported as a common pathophysiological feature in patients with IBS, reflecting HPA axis dysregulation.

Low-intensity exercise reduces cortisol levels and may improve IBS symptoms, whereas high-intensity exercise (above roughly 60% VO2max) proportionally increases cortisol release and HPA axis activation, potentially worsening IBS symptoms.
One cited study found intestinal dysbiosis in 73% of IBS patients compared with only 16% of healthy individuals.

Probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium longum has been shown to significantly improve intestinal symptoms and mood in patients with IBS by modulating microbiota structure and restoring SCFA levels.

Exercise interventions, particularly aerobic exercise, indirectly alleviate inflammation and intestinal dysfunction by increasing abundance of beneficial gut bacteria such as Akkermansia; long-term aerobic exercise increases Firmicutes abundance and SCFA levels, improving intestinal barrier and brain function.

High-intensity exercise, such as marathon running, increases the abundance of Actinobacteria and improves lipid metabolism, while involuntary exercise may not achieve the same beneficial microbiota shifts as voluntary exercise.
A basic study using continuous wave Doppler ultrasound of fingertip blood flow found increased sympathetic nervous system activity in patients with IBS compared to healthy individuals.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 intervention studies (1,253 patients) found that exercise training reduced muscle sympathetic nerve activity, with a dose-response relationship such that individuals with higher baseline sympathetic activity showed greater reductions.
Dysbacteriosis of the intestinal flora occurred in 73% of patients with IBS compared to only 16% of healthy individuals, indicating significantly reduced microbial diversity in IBS.

Clinical interventions have shown that probiotic supplementation with Bifidobacterium longum significantly improves intestinal symptoms and mood in patients with IBS by modulating microbiota structure and restoring short-chain fatty acid levels.

In a basic study recording vagal preganglionic neurons in rats, exercise training significantly increased resting activity of vagal preganglionic neurons and enhanced excitatory neuronal responses, indicating increased vagal tone.

A basic study showed that exercise significantly reduces expression of the serotonin transporter in specific brain regions such as the rostral ventromedial medulla, reducing serotonin reuptake and increasing synaptic serotonin levels.
Elevated basal cortisol levels have been reported as a common pathophysiological feature in patients with IBS, reflecting dysregulation of the HPA axis.

Repeated low-intensity exercise has been shown to reduce cortisol levels and improve IBS symptoms, whereas high-intensity exercise (above ~60% VO2max) causes a proportional increase in cortisol that may worsen IBS symptoms.
Strenuous exercise leads to increased intestinal permeability, gastrointestinal damage, and mild endotoxemia, contrasting with the benefits of low-intensity activities like yoga.

Long-term aerobic exercise (e.g., running or cycling) improves intestinal barrier and brain function by increasing the abundance of Firmicutes and short-chain fatty acid levels, whereas high-intensity exercise such as marathon running increases Actinobacteria abundance and improves lipid metabolism.
No serious adverse events directly related to exercise intervention were reported in any of the 10 included trials, supporting short-term safety of exercise therapy for IBS.
Psychiatric comorbidities such as anxiety and depression are significantly more prevalent in patients with IBS than in healthy individuals.

Pharmacological interventions such as anticholinergics and neuromodulators for IBS show modest overall efficacy, complicated by a placebo effect of up to 37.5%, and fewer than 25% of US patients with IBS achieve complete symptom remission.

Introduction of the AskMayoExpert (AME) ME/CFS care process algorithm was associated with a 21.6 percentage-point absolute increase in concordance between clinic referral and specialist ME/CFS diagnosis.
Referrals to the ME/CFS specialty clinic were 1.39 times more likely to result in a concordant specialist ME/CFS diagnosis after algorithm introduction compared to before.
The odds of achieving referral-diagnosis concordance were 2.69 times higher after introduction of the AskMayoExpert algorithm compared to before.
The difference in diagnostic concordance between pre- and post-intervention groups was statistically significant by both a Z-test for two proportions and Fisher's exact test.
Cohen's d of approximately 0.5 indicated a moderate effect size of the AskMayoExpert algorithm on referral-diagnosis concordance.
The 95% confidence interval for the difference in proportions of diagnostic concordance pre- vs post-intervention ranged from 4.08% to 39.1%, excluding zero and confirming statistical significance.

Both total referrals to the ME/CFS specialty clinic and the percentage of concordant diagnoses increased significantly after the algorithm's introduction, with concordance improving from 55.3% to 76.9%.

The AskMayoExpert ME/CFS algorithm was accessed 580 times during the study period by a multidisciplinary group of providers including consultants, advanced practice providers, and residents/fellows across more than a dozen specialties.
The ME/CFS AskMayoExpert topic ranked 263 out of 1143 topics for number of views over 12 months, above both the average and median views per topic.

PET imaging using markers of activated microglia such as translocator protein binding showed elevated neuroinflammation in widespread brain regions of ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, correlating with cognitive dysfunction and fatigue severity.

Proinflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 are elevated in ME/CFS and implicated in glial activation and neuroimmune crosstalk that disrupts neurotransmitter systems and contributes to mental fatigue.
Mitochondrial metabolism is perturbed in ME/CFS, including impaired oxidative phosphorylation and altered energy metabolite profiles, potentially limiting ATP available for cognitive function.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy studies found elevated brain lactate and other markers of energetic stress in ME/CFS patients, consistent with disrupted energy metabolism underlying fatigue.
fMRI studies documented aberrant functional connectivity between the default mode network and salience network in ME/CFS, networks implicated in attentional switching and cognitive control.

Ultra-high-field MRI showed reduced connectivity within ponto-cerebellar regions and between the cerebellum and cerebral cortex in ME/CFS, areas important for cognitive coordination and integration of cognitive/physiological signals.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found consistent deficits in immediate memory, information processing speed, and attentional capacity in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.

A systematic review of digital biomarkers of fatigue across chronic diseases found that only activity counts have been consistently investigated, indicating limited development and validation of digital biomarkers relevant to ME/CFS fatigue.

Across the 16 reviewed studies, processing speed and sustained attention were the most consistently discriminative cognitive domains distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls using computerized/digital testing.

Neuroimaging studies using fMRI/PCASL and machine learning classification found convergent evidence of altered neural activity or cerebral perfusion in attention- and limbic-regulation regions, and ML models could differentiate ME/CFS from Gulf War Illness based on multi-regional activation patterns.

Preliminary studies of low-intensity mind-body practices such as gentle yoga, Tai Chi, and Qigong suggest potential benefits for fatigue severity, mood, and perceived cognitive function in ME/CFS, possibly via parasympathetic activation and reduced sympathetic overdrive.

Digital psychological interventions (internet-based ACT, virtual CBSM, telerehabilitation) mostly targeted broader symptom burden with cognitive outcomes as secondary endpoints, and evidence for direct improvement in objective neuropsychological performance remains limited.
Social media (e.g., Reddit) analyses of ME/CFS patients revealed heterogeneity in how brain fog is defined and experienced, with overlap with dissociation, fatigue, and effort intolerance.

Studies of virtual world platforms (e.g., Second Life) demonstrated feasibility of cognitively accessible social support platforms for ME/CFS, indirectly addressing cognitive load and environmental overstimulation.

Persistent inflammatory/stress-related signaling, including altered cytokine profiles or HPA axis dysfunction, is proposed to promote maladaptive metacognitive beliefs and reduced regulatory flexibility contributing to brain fog via disrupted interoceptive processing.
At the hardest disparity (275 arcseconds), ME/CFS patients had significantly slower reaction time than controls after adjusting for age and sex.
At medium disparity (550 arcseconds), ME/CFS patients showed significantly slower reaction time than controls after adjusting for age and sex.
At the easiest disparity (1100 arcseconds), ME/CFS patients showed significantly slower reaction time than controls after adjusting for age and sex.
ME/CFS patients had a less steep RT-slope across disparities than controls, with the gap doubling by the third game round.
While controls significantly improved their RT-slope from round 1 to round 3 with repeated task exposure, ME/CFS patients only showed a non-significant trend of improvement.

In round 1, the RT gain between the harder and easier disparities (GAIN1 and GAIN2) was significantly greater in ME/CFS patients than controls, indicating greater visual-cognitive difficulty at task onset.
ME/CFS patients showed significant improvement in GAIN1 and a strong trend of improvement in GAIN2 between round 1 and round 2, unlike controls whose gains remained stable across rounds.
In round 2 pairwise comparisons, controls' reaction time remained significantly faster than ME/CFS patients despite proportional improvement in both groups.

The Chalder Fatigue Scale showed a weak-to-moderate positive correlation with reaction time at the hardest disparity (275 arcseconds) across all game rounds in ME/CFS patients, with the strongest correlation in round 1.
Successful binocular fusion rate was identical between ME/CFS patients and controls, indicating this parameter does not differentiate the groups.
Age was a significant covariate influencing reaction time results, while sex/gender had no significant effect, requiring statistical adjustment for age given the unmatched cohorts.
Neither the binary anamnestic fatigue/brain fog/concentration questions nor other patient-reported outcome measures correlated with any VR-OTS reaction time metrics in ME/CFS patients.

Confirmatory factor analysis showed that five neurocognitive-sensory symptoms (brain fog, sensory hypersensitivity, sleep disturbances, visual disturbances, headaches) loaded significantly onto a single latent 'Brain' factor with excellent model fit.
SEM confirmed a single latent 'Autonomic' factor underlying cardiovascular problems, respiratory problems, temperature intolerance, and gastrointestinal complaints, with excellent model fit indices.

The Gut symptom group (gastrointestinal complaints and food intolerances) showed stronger internal statistical association than the Immune group (flu-like symptoms and susceptibility to infections), indicating greater symptomatic coherence.

A joint one-factor model combining Gut and Immune symptoms fit significantly worse than separately modeled one-factor Gut and Immune models, supporting Gut and Immune as distinct but related latent constructs.

In a logistic regression among ME/CFS patients, respiratory problems and temperature intolerance were each associated with roughly 4- to 4.5-fold higher odds of cardiovascular problems, and gastrointestinal complaints with roughly 2-fold higher odds.

GutScore and ImmuneScore were significantly associated, with more than half (54.4%) of participants with high GutScore also showing high ImmuneScore, indicating frequent co-occurrence of gastrointestinal and immune symptom domains.

Gastrointestinal complaints acted as a bridging symptom, loading moderately on the general Autonomic factor while also anchoring the independent Gut construct with a much higher loading, suggesting they reflect both generalized autonomic dysregulation and a distinct gastrointestinal dimension.
Muscle problems and breathing difficulties showed only a moderate co-occurrence with low internal consistency, indicating a partially overlapping but not unified symptom dimension.
The Immune symptom group (susceptibility to infections, flu-like symptoms) was confirmed as a coherent one-factor construct with a high factor loading and low residual variance.
PEM, assessed using CCC and ICC criteria for ME, was identified in 26.4% of retrospectively reviewed post-COVID syndrome patients.
Nearly all PCS patients (98.1%) reported fatigue, with a median Fatigue Severity Scale score of 6.3 indicating severe, clinically significant fatigue.
POTS was significantly more frequent among PCS patients with PEM than those without PEM in univariate analysis, though this association did not persist after multivariate adjustment.
Orthostatic hypotension was significantly more frequent among PCS patients with PEM in univariate analysis, but this association was not retained in multivariate analysis.
Palpitations were significantly more common among PCS patients with PEM in univariate analysis.

In multivariate logistic regression, COVID-19 infection occurring in 2020-2021 (pre-Omicron period) was independently associated with nearly six-fold higher odds of PEM compared to infection during 2022-2023 (Omicron period).
Higher FSS scores were independently associated with more than double the odds of PEM in multivariate analysis.
Absence of vaccination was significantly associated with PEM in univariate analysis but this association did not persist after multivariate adjustment.
The overall prevalence of POTS among PCS patients in this cohort was 7.3%, consistent with previously reported ranges.
The overall prevalence of orthostatic hypotension among PCS patients was 10.3%, consistent with previously reported ranges of 8-13.8%.
Palpitations were observed in 26.3% of PCS patients overall, in line with previously reported ranges of 25-50%, though a large meta-analysis reported a lower rate of 18%.
Pain interference scores significantly decreased from baseline to the 8-week post-intervention timepoint following the TLC programme.
Fatigue scores showed a non-significant trend toward improvement from baseline to 8-week follow-up, with no significant change by 13-week retention.
Sleep disturbance was the only outcome to show a mean worsening over time (T1 to T3), though this and the T1-T2 change were not statistically significant.
Pain catastrophising scores showed a non-significant decrease from baseline at both 8-week and 13-week follow-up.
Anxiety scores showed a non-significant decrease from baseline at both post-intervention and retention timepoints.
Across the three timepoints, individual outcome-category trajectories were predominantly improvements, with 16 positive versus 2 negative category-level changes recorded.
Programme attendance was high, with most participants attending nearly all sessions, supporting feasibility of the group-delivered format.
No adverse events were attributed to the TLC programme by participants or the clinical study team.
The large majority of focus group participants felt the TLC programme could substantially benefit other people living with long COVID.

Qualitative data indicated that participants applying somatic and cognitive strategies learned in the programme experienced reduced symptom intensity and improved sense of control ("meaningful wins"), including one participant reporting better management of migraine symptoms.

Prior literature cited by the authors reports sympathetic overactivation and diminished parasympathetic response in long COVID patients, suggesting sympathovagal imbalance and autonomic dysregulation as a potential underlying/contributing mechanism.
The authors note that autonomic dysregulation has similarly been implicated as playing a significant role in ME/CFS, drawing a parallel to the proposed mechanism underlying long COVID.

Survey completion declined markedly at post-intervention and retention timepoints despite high programme attendance, a pattern the authors attribute to cognitive fatigue and fluctuating symptoms in this population.
A 2025 Chinese cross-sectional study of 12,789 individuals found one-year PCC prevalence of 7.8%, with PEM occurring in 36.9% of participants, the second most common symptom after fatigue (60.1%).
Longitudinal follow-up showed that approximately 35.6% of patients still experienced exercise intolerance two years after infection.
Persistent exercise intolerance at 2 years was associated with poorer overall health outcomes including higher fatigue scores.
ME/CFS patients show reduced ATP production following exercise, associated with persistent fatigue and delayed recovery.
Na+/K+-ATPase (sodium-potassium pump) dysfunction, arising from diminished hormonal signaling, ROS suppression, and inadequate ATP supply, may drive PEM-related muscle weakness and hyperexcitability.
PEM patients show elevated blood levels of lactate, pyruvate, and lipid peroxidation products, which correlate positively with post-exertional fatigue.
Activated NLRP3 inflammasome processes pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into mature cytokines via caspase-1, promoting systemic inflammation in PEM.
Circulating SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein has been detected months after infection, suggesting persistent viral reservoirs may drive chronic immune activation in long COVID.
PCC patients with symptoms lasting more than 30 days show persistent SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells and heightened antibody affinity, suggesting continued viral antigen presence.
In overtraining animal models, serum IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α were significantly elevated and correlated positively with mitochondrial ROS levels.
Following exertion, ME/CFS patients show elevated peripheral pro-inflammatory cytokines accompanied by muscle fatigue, exhaustion, and cognitive impairment.

TSPO-PET imaging (e.g., [18F]DPA-714) shows widespread elevated brain TSPO signal in some PCC patients up to two years post-infection, most pronounced in those with persistent fatigue and cognitive symptoms.

Animal studies show sustained TSPO-PET signal elevation (at least 50 days) after SARS-CoV-2 infection driven by co-activation of microglia, astrocytes, and endothelial cells, persisting after peripheral viral clearance.
Systematic reviews report neuroinflammatory (TSPO) evidence in ME/CFS with significant individual variability, and some studies failed to detect notable differences in TSPO binding.

PCC patients show widespread cerebral glucose hypometabolism (FDG-PET) in prefrontal cortex, cingulate cortex, insula, hippocampus, brainstem, and cerebellum, extending beyond regions with reduced perfusion, suggesting intrinsic neuronal mitochondrial dysfunction.

MRS studies show significantly elevated brain lactate concentrations and choline/creatine ratio in ME/CFS patients, indicating increased anaerobic glycolysis and altered phospholipid metabolism linked to neuroinflammation and oxidative stress.
Vagus nerve stimulation mitigates central inflammation via the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, presenting a potential therapeutic target for PEM-related cognitive symptoms.
Inhibiting peripheral inflammation has been shown to significantly improve cognitive function following exercise.
In animal models, inhibiting microglial activation significantly reduced brain IL-1β and TNF-α expression while improving cognitive impairments and fatigue-like behaviors after exercise.

A 2025 Chinese cross-sectional study of 12,789 individuals found a one-year Post-COVID Condition prevalence of 7.8%, with post-exertional malaise affecting 36.9% of participants, the second most common symptom after fatigue.
Longitudinal follow-up shows that about 35.6% of patients still experience exercise intolerance two years after infection, associated with poorer overall health and higher fatigue scores.

PET imaging with TSPO tracers ([18F]DPA-714) shows widespread elevated brain TSPO signal in some PCC patients up to two years post-infection, most pronounced in those with persistent fatigue and cognitive symptoms.

Animal studies show sustained elevation of TSPO-PET signal (lasting at least 50 days) after SARS-CoV-2 infection, driven by co-activation of microglia, astrocytes, and endothelial cells that persists after peripheral viral clearance.

Systematic review evidence in ME/CFS shows neuroinflammatory (TSPO) changes similar to PCC, but with significant individual variability, and some studies failing to detect differences in TSPO binding.

FDG-PET imaging reveals widespread cerebral hypometabolism in PCC patients in the prefrontal cortex, cingulate cortex, insula, hippocampus, brainstem, and cerebellum, correlating with cognitive scores independent of blood flow reduction.

Magnetic resonance spectroscopy in ME/CFS patients shows significantly elevated brain lactate concentration and choline/creatine ratio, indicating increased anaerobic glycolysis and altered membrane phospholipid metabolism linked to neuroinflammation and mitochondrial oxidative stress.

Wirth and Steinacker (2026) describe how Na+/K+-ATPase dysfunction in PEM—arising from reduced hormonal signaling, ROS suppression, and inadequate ATP—causes membrane depolarization, impairing action potential generation and causing muscle hyperexcitability, contributing to myasthenia.
In overtraining animal models, serum IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α were significantly elevated and correlated positively with mitochondrial ROS levels.
Vagus nerve stimulation has been shown to mitigate central inflammation via the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, suggesting a potential therapeutic target for cognitive symptoms in PEM.

In chronic arthritis patients, insular cortex functional connectivity is closely associated with subjective fatigue and pain scores, implicating the insula in integrating peripheral pathology with subjective symptom experience.

In chronic pain patients, decision-making shows heightened sensitivity to punishment, and posterior insular activity strongly correlates with fatigue and pain ratings, evidencing a link between reward-system dysfunction and interoceptive dysregulation.
Blood levels of lactate, pyruvate, and lipid peroxidation products are elevated in PEM patients and correlate positively with post-exertional fatigue.
Exogenous lactate supplementation may mitigate hypoxia-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular apoptosis in experimental studies.
Circulating SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein has been detected months after infection and may act as a persistent PAMP driving chronic immune activation in PEM/PCC.
PCC patients with symptoms lasting more than 30 days show persistent SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells and heightened antibody affinity, suggesting continued presence of viral antigen.
The ERRγ-GLS1 axis regulates GPX4-mediated clearance of lipid peroxides by modulating the GSH/GSSG ratio, linking mitochondrial ROS damage to lipid peroxidation control.

Among 55 patients with hypermobile EDS who underwent CT angiography of the chest, abdomen, pelvis (and sometimes head), aneurysms were found in 4 patients (7.3%), located in the thoracic aorta, splenic artery, or circle of Willis.
The presence of aneurysms in this hEDS cohort was not significantly associated with traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

Postmortem genetic testing on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded liver tissue identified a pathogenic COL3A1 variant confirming vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome as the cause of fatal aortic rupture in a pregnant woman.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome carries a markedly elevated risk of maternal mortality, particularly when undiagnosed prior to pregnancy.
Following the genetic diagnosis, at-risk relatives were started on celiprolol therapy as preventive management for vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Postmortem genetic testing using formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue was demonstrated as a viable method to diagnose vEDS when conventional (fresh/frozen) samples were unavailable.
Genetic testing identified a pathogenic COL3A1 variant (c.2438G>A) confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in a patient presenting with stroke.
The patient presented with simultaneous cerebral infarction and subarachnoid hemorrhage caused by middle cerebral artery dissection, an unusual dual vascular event attributable to vEDS.

The authors recommend that clinicians consider vEDS in young stroke patients with arterial dissection, particularly those with distinctive facial features or relevant family history, even when full diagnostic criteria are not met.
Col3a1G938D/+ mice recapitulate features of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, including a high risk of aortic rupture that accelerates at puberty onset, particularly in males.
Both genetic knockout and pharmacological blockade of the androgen receptor eliminated the sex difference in aortic rupture survival in the VEDS mouse model.
Treatment with a dual androgen receptor and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist provided near-complete and durable protection from aortic rupture in both male and female mice.
Gene pathways related to extracellular matrix organization and cell-ECM interactions targeted by dual AR/MR inhibition largely overlapped with those modulated by isolated MR antagonism alone.
Selective targeting of mineralocorticoid receptor signaling alone was an effective therapeutic strategy in both sexes and avoided the sexual side effects seen with AR antagonism in males.
EDS patients with ocular manifestations had a significantly increased risk of combined cardiovascular comorbidities compared to EDS patients without ocular manifestations.
Among ocular manifestations examined, EDS patients had significantly increased risk for 70% of the included cardiovascular outcomes when ocular disease was present.
Myopia was one of the ocular diagnoses conferring the highest relative risk for subsequent cardiovascular comorbidity in EDS patients.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension was among the ocular manifestations conferring the highest relative risk for subsequent cardiovascular comorbidity in EDS patients.
Dry eye disease was among the ocular manifestations conferring the highest relative risk for subsequent cardiovascular comorbidity in EDS patients.
Cerebral, coronary, and intracranial arterial events were the highest-risk cardiovascular outcomes among EDS patients with ocular manifestations.
EDS patients with ocular manifestations had significantly higher hospitalisation rates than those without ocular manifestations.
EDS patients with ocular manifestations had significantly higher emergency department visit rates than those without ocular manifestations.
Among the specific cardiovascular outcomes assessed, cerebral arterial events were among the highest-risk outcomes in EDS patients with ocular manifestations compared to those without.
Coronary arterial events were among the highest-risk cardiovascular outcomes for EDS patients with ocular manifestations relative to those without.
Intracranial arterial events were among the highest-risk cardiovascular outcomes in EDS patients with ocular manifestations compared to those without.
Overall, EDS patients with ocular manifestations showed significantly increased risk for 70% of the ten cardiovascular comorbidities examined compared to those without ocular manifestations.

The review states that pathological alterations of the myodural bridge complex are increasingly linked to cranio-cervical disorders including chronic cervicogenic headaches, Chiari malformation Type I, cervicogenic dizziness, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome-associated symptoms.

The authors demonstrate proof-of-concept use of a new semi-automated Fiji/ImageJ macro to quantify collagen fibril diameter and shape metrics from TEM images of dermal samples from a subject with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (VEDS).

The macro standardizes collagen fibril measurement via wand-based ROI detection with geometric validation, calculating area-equivalent diameters, ellipse-derived major/minor axes, shape consistency indices, and spatial localization, while excluding oblique or irregular fibril profiles via built-in quality thresholds.
Myalgia was the most common accompanying symptom in children with juvenile hypermobility syndrome, seen in about a fifth of patients.
Children with juvenile hypermobility syndrome reported reduced overall quality of life, with a median PedsQL total score of 74 out of 100.
Emotional and school functioning subscales of the child-reported PedsQL were among the lowest-scoring domains, indicating notable impact on emotional well-being and schooling.
Parents reported a similarly reduced quality of life for their children, with a median parent-reported PedsQL total score of 77.1.
The knee was the most frequently affected joint among children diagnosed with joint hypermobility syndrome.
Deficient lysosomal degradation of glycosaminoglycans (GAG) was identified as the cause of mucopolysaccharidoses.
A defective enzyme involved in GAG biosynthesis was found to underlie a variant form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Impaired sulfation of glycosaminoglycan chains was implicated as the cause of diastrophic dysplasia.
Impaired glycosaminoglycan chain elongation was identified as the mechanism underlying Desbuquois dysplasia.
Defective formation of the tetrasaccharide linker connecting GAG chains to the core protein causes a distinctive group of phenotypes termed linkeropathy.
Many disorders of defective GAG synthesis remain poorly documented phenotypically, making clinical suspicion and molecular interpretation challenging.

Despite distinct clinical and radiological features, disorders of abnormal GAG synthesis share common skeletal manifestations including distal humeral hypoplasia, misshapen proximal femora, accelerated carpal ossification, and malsegmentation of the short tubular bones.
The JAK2 V617F somatic mutation is associated with the formation of thoracic aortic aneurysms.
Higher JAK2 V617F variant allele frequency (VAF) is described as a valuable biomarker of thoracic aortic aneurysm risk.

The JAK2 V617F mutation is accompanied by increased cytokine production, pro-inflammatory leukocytes, and elevated MMP expression, mechanisms that drive elastin degradation classically associated with thoracic aortic aneurysm development.
Germline mutations in COL3A1 are described as a classic genetic cause of thoracic aortic aneurysm formation via Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vascular type).
No existing studies have examined whether an increasing JAK2 V617F variant allele frequency influences the rate of aneurysm growth, identifying this as a research gap.

EMG recruitment of the extensor carpi ulnaris during sustained gripping was significantly lower in individuals with chronic wrist hypermobility compared to healthy controls, regardless of forearm position.

EMG recruitment of the extensor carpi radialis brevis/longus during sustained gripping was significantly lower in individuals with chronic wrist hypermobility compared to healthy controls, regardless of forearm position.

EMG recruitment of the flexor carpi ulnaris during sustained gripping was significantly lower in individuals with chronic wrist hypermobility compared to healthy controls, regardless of forearm position.
Individuals with chronic wrist hypermobility showed higher flexor carpi radialis EMG activity than healthy controls, potentially a compensatory mechanism for volar wrist stability.
Grip force was lower in individuals with chronic wrist hypermobility compared to healthy controls.
No EMG activity differences were found across supination, pronation, and neutral forearm positions, either within or between the CWH and control groups.

Midcarpal instability and benign joint hypermobility syndrome were the most prevalent underlying etiologies among wrists with chronic wrist hypermobility, present in 100% and 44% of cases respectively.
ACL laxity measured at 134 N showed a significant group × time interaction, with the Pilates group returning toward baseline postpartum while the control group's pregnancy-related increase persisted.
ACL laxity measured at 200 N showed a significant group × time interaction, with laxity normalizing more in the Pilates group than in controls at six weeks postpartum.

Generalized joint hypermobility, assessed via the Beighton score, showed a significant group × time interaction, decreasing toward baseline postpartum in the Pilates group while remaining elevated in controls.
Pelvic girdle pain-related disability, measured with the Pelvic Girdle Questionnaire, showed a significant group × time interaction, decreasing more markedly in the Pilates group than in controls.
Daily step count showed a significant group × time interaction, increasing substantially more in the Pilates group compared to controls at six weeks postpartum.
Clinical cohorts of lipedema patients report a clustering of connective tissue laxity and joint hypermobility alongside other systemic manifestations.
Lipedema patients show co-occurrence of chronic widespread pain as part of a broader multisystem symptom cluster.
Gastrointestinal disturbances are reported among the systemic comorbidities associated with lipedema.
Thyroid dysfunction, autoimmunity, endocrine-gynecological alterations, and vitamin D deficiency are reported as recurrent comorbid features in lipedema cohorts.
Histopathological and microvascular studies describe alterations in extracellular matrix organization, stromal components, and endothelial structures in lipedema-affected tissue.
Pain scores decreased progressively from preoperative baseline through 2 weeks and 6 months postoperatively following patient-specific implant augmentation eminoplasty.
Maximal incisal opening (MIO) decreased significantly after surgery and remained reduced at 6-month follow-up, with no significant change between 2 weeks and 6 months.
Two of eleven patients (18.2%) developed right-sided postoperative infection that ultimately required implant removal after conservative treatment failed.
No clinical recurrence of TMJ dislocation or open-lock was documented in any patient during the available 6-month follow-up period.
FRRM, measured under symmetrical loading of the first and lesser metatarsals, showed excellent within-session reliability with an ICC of 1.00.
FRRM correlated strongly with a biomechanical reference construct combining superior-inferior translations at the first tarsometatarsal and medial naviculo-cuneiform joints.
FRAM, measured under isolated loading of the first metatarsal, also demonstrated excellent within-session reliability with an ICC of 0.97 but with higher absolute measurement error than FRRM.
FRAM showed a moderate positive correlation with the biomechanical reference construct, weaker than that observed for FRRM.
Symmetric loading of the first and lesser metatarsals engaged proximal first ray joints more effectively than isolated loading, which predominantly mobilised the first tarsometatarsal joint.

Arthrometer-based assessment of first ray mobility is sensitive to loading mode, and symmetric loading provides a more biomechanically representative evaluation than traditional isolated loading approaches.

Functional analysis of the MYH11 c.5544_5548del, p.(D1848Efs*60) variant demonstrated that it operates through a loss-of-function mechanism leading to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay, rather than the gain-of-function mechanism previously assumed.
Gain-of-function variants in MYH11 are associated with thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections (TAAD), a mechanism distinct from the loss-of-function variant found in this patient.

Loss-of-function variants in MYH11, such as the one carried by the patient, are linked to autosomal recessive Megacystis-Microcolon-Intestinal Hypoperistalsis Syndrome (MMIHS); as a heterozygous carrier, the patient is asymptomatic for MMIHS.

The child, initially suspected of Marfan Syndrome due to joint hypermobility at age 3 and later misdiagnosed based on the MYH11 variant, was found on complete clinical and genetic reinterpretation at age 7 to never have fulfilled the established clinical diagnostic criteria for Marfan Syndrome.
Offspring prenatally exposed to any maternal autoimmune or autoinflammatory disorder had a 15% higher risk of a major psychiatric disorder compared to unexposed offspring.
Offspring prenatally exposed to any maternal autoimmune or autoinflammatory disorder had an 18% higher risk of a neurodevelopmental disorder compared to unexposed offspring.
Maternal autoimmune thyroiditis during or before pregnancy was associated with more than double the risk of autism spectrum disorder in offspring, one of the largest effect sizes in the study.
Maternal pernicious anemia was associated with more than double the risk of other behavioral or emotional disorders (F98) in offspring.

Maternal hypermobility syndrome, grouped with polymyalgia rheumatica and Sjogren's syndrome as 'SIC', was associated with a 70-99% higher risk of certain neurodevelopmental disorders or milder regulatory disturbances in offspring.

When AD/AIDs were grouped by main affected body system, connective tissue autoimmune/autoinflammatory disorders and endocrine AD/AIDs were the categories mainly associated with offspring's mental health diagnoses.

Maternal type 1 diabetes mellitus was associated with a 70-99% higher risk of certain neurodevelopmental disorders in offspring, and this association was not completely explained by adverse birth factors.
Maternal systemic vasculitis was associated with a 70-99% higher risk of certain neurodevelopmental disorders or milder regulatory disturbances in offspring.
Maternal acute thyroiditis was associated with a 70-99% higher risk of certain neurodevelopmental disorders or milder regulatory disturbances in offspring.
Maternal Crohn's disease was associated with a 70-99% higher risk of certain neurodevelopmental disorders or milder regulatory disturbances in offspring.

Maternal SIC-group conditions (polymyalgia rheumatica, Sjögren's syndrome, and hypermobility syndrome, grouped together due to their individual rarity) were associated with a 70-99% higher risk of certain neurodevelopmental disorders or milder regulatory disturbances in offspring.
Autonomic symptom burden measured by COMPASS-31 was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia impact, as measured by the Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ-R), was significantly higher in the FMS group than controls.
Central sensitization symptoms, as measured by the Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI), were significantly higher in FMS patients than controls.
The choroidal vascularity index did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Subfoveal maximum choroidal thickness did not differ significantly between FMS patients and controls.
Subfoveal mean choroidal thickness did not differ significantly between FMS patients and controls.
CVI was not correlated with COMPASS-31, FIQ-R, or CSI scores within either the FMS or control group.
In multivariable regression, age was independently associated with choroidal vascularity index, while fibromyalgia status and COMPASS-31 total score were not.

In a case series of three patients with refractory fibromyalgia, a combined protocol of pulsed electromagnetic field therapy, medical ozone insufflation, and targeted nutritional supplementation led to substantial pain relief and significant improvement in quality of life sustained at 30-day follow-up.
Conventional treatments for fibromyalgia are described as often having limited efficacy and significant side effects, motivating exploration of alternative therapeutic strategies.
Between-segment (different dermatome) gentle brushing significantly reduced heat pain perception, indicating a supraspinal touch-pain modulation effect.
Within-segment (same dermatome) brushing and deep pressure/compression conditions did not produce significant touch-pain modulation.
Fibromyalgia patients and pain-free controls showed no significant differences in touch-pain modulation, contrary to the hypothesis that FM patients would show reduced modulation.
Childhood trauma history and depression were the strongest predictors of the degree of touch-pain modulation, more so than fibromyalgia diagnosis itself.

The pattern of results suggests that touch-pain modulation relies on supraspinal (central) neural mechanisms rather than purely segmental spinal circuits, and these mechanisms appear preserved in fibromyalgia.
The patient was diagnosed with MCAS based on characteristic symptoms, elevated serum tryptase, and adequate response to MCAS-directed therapies.

In this MCAS patient, intraprocedural administration of the mydriatic agent tropicamide during cataract surgery was temporally associated with development of periocular swelling and erythema on the first postoperative day, despite prophylactic antihistamine and anti-inflammatory treatment.

The authors propose that the periocular reaction may have been triggered not by tropicamide itself but by one or more excipients such as benzalkonium chloride, known to induce mast cell activation in susceptible individuals.

Standard prophylactic treatment (oral and IV antihistamines, intraoperative subconjunctival dexamethasone, postoperative anti-inflammatory medications) failed to prevent a severe periocular inflammatory reaction in this MCAS patient undergoing cataract surgery.

MRGPRX2, a mast cell receptor mediating IgE-independent activation and degranulation, is implicated in the pathogenesis of atopic dermatitis and mediates mast cell activation in the HDM+SEB mouse model.

Oral treatment with the MRGPRX2 antagonist INCB000262 for 4 weeks attenuated HDM+SEB-induced atopic dermatitis disease phenotype in MRGPRX2 knock-in mice, improving skin thickness, transepidermal water loss, tissue weight, and clinical score.

HDM+SEB-induced skin transcriptome changes in the mouse model exhibited a mast cell activation signature consistent with that seen in human atopic dermatitis lesional skin, and this signature was attenuated by INCB000262 treatment.
Jun o 1 was found to exist as multiple isoforms that assemble into oligomers, unlike the homologous cypress allergen Cup a 1, which shows isoforms without oligomerization.
IgE binding to Jun o 1, including its ability to activate mast cells, was critically dependent on the combined presence of both protein and carbohydrate (glycan) determinants.

Jun o 1 showed greater IgE-binding inhibition of Juniperus oxycedrus extract than Cup a 1 in sera from Cupressaceae-sensitized allergic patients native to J oxycedrus regions, indicating stronger IgE cross-reactivity/specificity.
Among Cupressaceae-sensitized patients from J oxycedrus's autochthonous regions, the highest rate of monosensitization was to J oxycedrus itself.

The authors conclude that Jun o 1 is a relevant and potential major allergen in cypress allergy, sharing structural/immunogenic similarity with Cup a 1 that drives cross-reactivity while also having unique IgE-reactive protein and glycan determinants.
The mast cell activation test (MAT) to egg showed an area under the ROC curve of 0.749 for distinguishing baked egg allergic from tolerant children.
MAT to egg showed an AUC of 0.704 for distinguishing loosely cooked egg allergic from tolerant children.
The optimal cut-off of MAT gave sensitivity/specificity of 52%/89% for baked egg allergy and 70%/66% for loosely cooked egg allergy.
MAT's overall diagnostic accuracy was 68% for both baked and loosely cooked egg allergy, lower than that achieved by other diagnostic tests.
MAT results depended on the presence of allergen-specific IgE and only outperformed sIgE testing when sIgE levels were at least 1 KU/L.
BAT and MAT results to egg were moderately correlated with each other.
Egg-specific IgE levels, specific activity, and avidity for egg allergens were directly correlated with mast cell activation test response.
Egg-specific IgG4/IgE ratios were inversely correlated with mast cell activation test response to egg, suggesting IgG4 blocking of IgE-mediated mast cell activation.
MRGPRX2, a mast cell-expressed GPCR, mediates non-IgE-dependent mast cell degranulation and is proposed as a key contributor to the pathogenesis of refractory chronic urticaria.
MRGPRX2 recognizes a broad range of ligands including exogenous cationic compounds, neuropeptides, and certain pharmacological agents, enabling mast cell activation independent of IgE.
Antihistamines and omalizumab are first- and second-line therapies for chronic urticaria, but a significant proportion of patients develop recalcitrant disease despite these treatments.
In chronic spontaneous urticaria, gut microbiota show depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing taxa such as Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and Bifidobacterium.
Pro-inflammatory Proteobacteria, particularly Enterobacteriaceae, are relatively enriched in the gut microbiota of chronic spontaneous urticaria patients.
Metabolic shifts in chronic urticaria include depletion of SCFAs and unsaturated fatty acids, which may lower the mast cell activation threshold.
Compromised intestinal barrier function in chronic urticaria may allow translocation of endotoxins such as LPS, promoting systemic immune dysregulation.
Multi-omics and Mendelian randomization studies provide convergent evidence linking gut dysbiosis to systemic inflammation and mast cell instability in chronic urticaria.

The review evaluates microbiome-targeted interventions, including probiotics and faecal microbiota transplantation, as potential novel adjuvant therapies for chronic urticaria, while noting translational challenges.
Chamaecrista nomame extract significantly inhibited mast cell degranulation and the release of inflammatory mediators in vitro.
Luteolin was identified as the primary active anti-allergic compound in CN extract, modulating FcεRI-mediated signaling in mast cells.
In an ovalbumin-induced murine asthma model, CN treatment markedly reduced airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and immune cell infiltration, with efficacy comparable to corticosteroids.
Transcriptomic analysis of bone marrow-derived mast cells showed that luteolin suppresses proinflammatory cytokine production by downregulating NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways.
CN extract and luteolin significantly inhibited cytokine release from house dust mite-stimulated human peripheral blood mononuclear cells, supporting clinical relevance.
OVA sensitization significantly increased OVA-specific IgE, IgG1, and IgG2a antibody levels compared with unsensitized controls.
High salt intake (NaCl diet/water) produced no additional increase in OVA-specific IgE, IgG1, or IgG2a beyond that caused by sensitization alone.
In sensitized mice, high salt intake caused a marked reduction in rectal temperature, indicating enhanced anaphylaxis severity compared with the sensitized normal-diet group.
Sensitized mice on the high-salt diet (SN group) showed elevated serum zonulin levels compared with other groups, indicating impaired intestinal barrier integrity.
Jejunal histology in the high-salt sensitized (SN) group showed villus damage consistent with intestinal barrier impairment.
Serum mMCP-1, a marker of mucosal mast cell activation, increased with OVA sensitization and was highest in the high-salt sensitized (SN) group.

In pregnancies exposed to anti-seizure medications, folic acid supplementation was associated with a lower risk of a composite adverse offspring outcome (preterm birth, low birth weight, major congenital anomalies, fetal death, or neurodevelopmental delay).
Folic acid supplementation in ASM-exposed pregnancies was associated with a markedly lower risk of fetal death.
No significant difference in offspring outcomes was observed between preconception initiation and first-trimester initiation of folic acid supplementation.
Compared to no supplementation, a folic acid dose of 0.4 mg/day was protective against fetal death in ASM-exposed pregnancies.
Doses of folic acid exceeding 0.4 mg/day further reduced the risk of composite adverse offspring outcomes in ASM-exposed pregnancies compared to no supplementation.
Folic acid doses above 1 mg/day showed a trend toward decreased preterm birth risk in ASM-exposed pregnancies compared to no supplementation.
Compared with 0.4 mg supplementation, folic acid doses above 1 mg/day were associated with a lower risk of low birth weight.
No association between folic acid supplementation and adverse offspring outcomes was observed in pregnancies not exposed to anti-seizure medications.
Serum DAO levels were significantly higher in chronic urticaria patients than in healthy controls.
Serum lactic acid levels were significantly higher in chronic urticaria patients than in healthy controls.
Histamine, IFABP, sCD14, endotoxin, zonulin, and calprotectin levels did not differ significantly between CU patients and healthy controls.
sCD14 levels were reduced in anti-TPO-positive CU patients.
The histamine/sCD14 ratio was significantly elevated in anti-TPO-positive CU patients, suggesting amplified mast cell signaling under impaired innate immune regulation.
The lactic acid/sCD14 ratio was significantly elevated in anti-TPO-positive CU patients.
In anti-TPO-positive CU patients, the IFABP/sCD14 ratio was significantly elevated, suggesting amplified epithelial barrier signaling relative to innate immune regulation.
In anti-TPO-positive CU patients, the zonulin/sCD14 ratio was significantly elevated compared to baseline, indicating amplified barrier-related signaling.
Severe anti-TPO-positive CU patients had significantly lower sCD14 levels than severe anti-TPO-negative patients.
NLR was significantly lower in severe anti-TPO-positive CU patients compared with severe anti-TPO-negative patients.
UAS7 disease activity scores were significantly higher in severe anti-TPO-positive CU patients compared with severe anti-TPO-negative patients.
Serum histamine was significantly higher in severe anti-TPO-positive CU patients compared with severe anti-TPO-negative patients.
Across included studies, PGAD etiology was most often linked to neuropathic/structural causes including sacral radiculopathy, Tarlov cysts, and pudendal or small-fiber neuropathy.
Central neurobiological mechanisms and psychosocial contributors were also implicated alongside peripheral/structural causes in PGAD.

Diagnostic practice for PGAD was inconsistent, with most studies using symptom-based criteria aligned to ISSWSH or Leiblum-Nathan frameworks, variably combined with imaging, neurophysiology, or small-fiber testing.

Reported interventions for PGAD (pelvic-floor physiotherapy, cognitive-behavioral approaches, gabapentinoids, benzodiazepines, neuromodulation, and selected surgical decompressions for defined lesions) showed mixed outcomes with limited follow-up and safety reporting.

High-frequency (10 kHz) spinal cord stimulation for painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy has been evaluated against optimized medical management in randomized comparative studies and was associated with sustained pain reduction and functional improvement through 24 months of follow-up.

Ultrasound-guided pulsed radiofrequency, a nondestructive field-based neuromodulation limiting tip temperature to under 42°C, has shown generally short- to mid-term benefit for focal entrapment-type neuropathic pain after positive diagnostic blocks, with heterogeneous protocols across small randomized trials and observational cohorts.
For hereditary transthyretin amyloid polyneuropathy, disease-modifying approaches including nucleic acid-based therapies are increasingly incorporated into contemporary clinical care.

The authors propose categorizing peripheral neuropathy into seven pathophysiologic phenotypes to structure a stepwise diagnostic and management algorithm, including small-fiber neuropathy and autonomic neuropathy as distinct categories.
TNF-alpha alone reduced collagen accumulation in a 3D fibroblast-derived tissue model.
IL-1beta alone reduced collagen accumulation, tissue strength, and stiffness in the 3D tissue model.
IL-18 alone had minimal effect on collagen accumulation, strength, or stiffness of the 3D tissue.
TNF-alpha combined with TGF-beta1 counteracted TGF-beta1-mediated increases in collagen, tissue strength, and stiffness.
IL-1beta combined with TGF-beta1 counteracted TGF-beta1-mediated increases in collagen, tissue strength, and stiffness.
IL-18 combined with TGF-beta1 had minimal effect on TGF-beta1-mediated collagen and mechanical increases, unlike TNF-alpha and IL-1beta.
TGF-beta1 alone stimulated collagen accumulation and increased extracellular matrix strength and stiffness in the 3D fibroblast tissue model.
None of the three pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-18, IL-1beta) increased collagen alone or in combination with TGF-beta1, despite their pro-inflammatory nature.
TGF-β1 treatment alone increased collagen accumulation and tissue strength and stiffness in the 3D fibroblast-derived tissue model.
TNF-α treatment altered the overall tissue morphology of the 3D collagen-rich fibroblast tissue construct.
IL-1β treatment altered the overall tissue morphology of the 3D collagen-rich fibroblast tissue construct.
The authors conclude their 3D collagen-rich tissue model is useful for studying cytokine-mediated cross-talk between immune cells and fibroblasts relevant to fibrotic and connective tissue processes.
Among 700 patients with IBS, 38.6% (270 patients) met criteria for insomnia based on an Insomnia Severity Index score of 15 or higher.
IBS patients with insomnia had more severe gastrointestinal symptoms as measured by IBS-SSS compared to those without insomnia.
IBS patients with insomnia had greater somatic symptom severity as measured by PHQ-15 compared to those without insomnia.
In hierarchical linear regression, higher ISI (insomnia severity) scores were independently associated with higher anxiety and depressive symptom scores.
Presence of functional dyspepsia was independently associated with higher insomnia severity (ISI) scores in IBS patients.
Presence of fibromyalgia was independently associated with higher insomnia severity (ISI) scores in IBS patients.
Older age was associated, to a lesser extent, with higher insomnia severity (ISI) scores in IBS patients.
Plasma EV concentration was significantly higher in both LC-ME/CFS and pan-ME/CFS compared with COVID-recovered controls, with no difference between the two ME/CFS groups.
The association between diagnostic group and EV concentration remained significant after adjusting for age, sex, and vaccination status.
Mean plasma EV size did not differ significantly among COVID-recovered, LC-ME/CFS, and pan-ME/CFS groups.
The proportion of CD45+ (leukocyte-derived) EVs was significantly increased in both LC-ME/CFS and pan-ME/CFS compared with COVID-recovered controls, robust to covariate adjustment.
CD20+ (B cell–derived) EVs were significantly reduced in LC-ME/CFS and pan-ME/CFS compared with COVID-recovered controls.
CD3+ (T cell–derived) EVs did not differ significantly across the COVID-recovered, LC-ME/CFS, and pan-ME/CFS groups.
CD14+ (monocyte/macrophage-derived) EVs were significantly increased in both LC-ME/CFS and pan-ME/CFS compared with COVID-recovered controls, surviving FDR correction and covariate adjustment.
CD16+ (NK cell–derived) EVs showed no significant group differences in unadjusted or adjusted analyses.
CD144+ (endothelial-derived) EVs showed no significant differences across pandemic-era groups.
CD41+ (platelet-derived) EVs were significantly elevated in both LC-ME/CFS and pan-ME/CFS compared with COVID-recovered controls, robust to FDR correction and covariate adjustment.
CD45−CD144−CD41−CD56+ (neural-associated) EVs showed a nominal increase in LC-ME/CFS versus COVID-recovered controls, but this did not survive FDR correction or covariate adjustment.
Total plasma EV mitochondrial membrane potential positivity did not differ significantly among COVID-recovered, LC-ME/CFS, and pan-ME/CFS groups.

Mitochondrial membrane potential positivity was significantly elevated in total leukocyte-, B cell-, monocyte/macrophage-, and NK cell-derived EV subsets in pan-ME/CFS compared with COVID-recovered controls, surviving FDR correction and covariate adjustment.
No significant differences in mitochondrial membrane potential were found in CD144+ (endothelial) or CD41+ (platelet) EVs across pandemic-era groups.

Mitochondrial membrane potential alterations across immune, endothelial, and platelet EV subsets were not statistically significant in LC-ME/CFS, suggesting these alterations are preferentially seen in pan-ME/CFS rather than LC-ME/CFS.
In the prepandemic cohort, plasma EV concentration did not differ significantly between pre-ME/CFS and healthy controls.
Mean EV diameter was smaller in pre-ME/CFS compared with healthy controls at nominal significance, but this did not survive FDR correction.
CD45+ EVs were significantly higher in pre-ME/CFS versus healthy controls at nominal significance, but this did not persist after FDR correction.
CD20+ (B cell-derived) EVs were significantly increased in pre-ME/CFS compared with healthy controls, surviving FDR correction.
CD3+ (T cell-derived) EVs, though present at low levels, were nominally higher in pre-ME/CFS but did not remain significant after FDR correction.
CD14+ (monocyte/macrophage) and CD16+ (NK cell) EVs did not differ between pre-ME/CFS and healthy controls.
CD144+ (endothelial) and CD41+ (platelet) EVs did not differ between pre-ME/CFS and healthy controls.
CD56+ (neural-derived) EVs, though low abundance, were significantly reduced in pre-ME/CFS compared with healthy controls, surviving FDR correction.
Total EV mitochondrial membrane potential positivity was significantly higher in healthy controls than in pre-ME/CFS, surviving FDR correction.

CD45+CD20+ (B cell-derived) EVs showed significantly higher mitochondrial membrane potential positivity in pre-ME/CFS compared with healthy controls, the most consistently significant mitochondrial signal across both cohorts.
Mitochondrial membrane potential positivity in CD14+ EVs did not differ between pre-ME/CFS and healthy controls.
CD16+ (NK cell) EVs showed a nominal increase in mitochondrial membrane potential positivity in pre-ME/CFS, which did not persist after FDR adjustment.
CD45−CD41+ (platelet-derived) EVs exhibited significantly higher mitochondrial membrane potential positivity in pre-ME/CFS than healthy controls, surviving FDR correction.

The mitochondrial membrane potential dye (MitoTracker Deep Red) signal was specific to mitochondria-containing EVs, as confirmed by FCCP-induced dissipation of membrane potential and by size-selective filtration.
Compared with healthy controls, people with ME/CFS reported markedly poorer subjective sleep quality across almost all PSQI domains, with 95% exceeding the clinical poor-sleep cutoff.
Daytime sleepiness was significantly higher in ME/CFS than controls, with 47% of ME/CFS participants showing excessive daytime sleepiness.
The proportion of ME/CFS participants with excessive sleepiness differed significantly across Bell scale severity subgroups.
Accelerometry-derived time in bed was significantly longer in individuals with ME/CFS than in matched controls.
Accelerometry-estimated sleep efficiency was significantly reduced in ME/CFS compared with matched controls.
Sleep onset latency was nearly doubled in ME/CFS relative to healthy controls.
Wake after sleep onset was significantly increased in ME/CFS compared with controls.
Despite spending nearly an extra hour in bed, total sleep time did not differ significantly between ME/CFS and controls.
Sleep disturbances (TIB, SE, SOL, WASO) appeared broadly similar across ME/CFS severity subgroups, with negligible effect sizes.
Night-to-night variability (CV) in total sleep time was significantly higher in ME/CFS than controls.
Night-to-night variability (CV) in sleep efficiency was markedly higher in ME/CFS than controls, with a very large effect size.
Night-to-night variability (CV) in wake after sleep onset was significantly higher in ME/CFS than controls.
In contrast to other parameters, night-to-night variability in bedtime and TIB was significantly lower in ME/CFS compared to controls.
Short-term night-to-night variability (RMSSD) was significantly greater in ME/CFS for total sleep time, sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, and wake after sleep onset.
Wake-up time instability (RMSSD) was elevated in ME/CFS, whereas bedtime instability was lower than controls, and TIB showed no substantial difference.

The Bayesian Variability Model, which isolates stable latent intraindividual variance, showed no significant group differences for wake-up time, TIB, TST, SE, SOL, or WASO, except that bedtime variability remained lower in ME/CFS.

The distribution of nights across sleep efficiency categories (appropriate/uncertain/inappropriate) differed significantly between ME/CFS and controls, reflecting frequent alternation between low- and high-efficiency nights in ME/CFS.

In sensitivity analyses adjusting for employment status, primary case-control differences in SE, SOL, WASO and variability indices remained similar, and employment status was not independently associated with sleep outcomes.

The paper cites prior genetic/transcriptomic studies reporting markedly elevated expression of the circadian clock gene NPAS2 in ME/CFS patients, though these studies were underpowered and lacked repeated rhythmic sampling.
Multiple studies report reduced plasma, salivary, and urinary cortisol levels and a flattened diurnal cortisol rhythm in ME/CFS patients, indicating HPA axis hypofunction.
ACTH responses to psychological and physiological stress tests were significantly blunted in ME/CFS patients while cortisol responses were relatively preserved, suggesting reduced central HPA drive.
Cortisol findings across ME/CFS studies are heterogeneous, with some cohorts showing only modest reductions or preserved/context-dependent cortisol output rather than stable hypocortisolism.

Low-dose dexamethasone suppression testing and prednisolone challenge showed greater cortisol suppression in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls, indicating enhanced glucocorticoid negative-feedback sensitivity.
Epigenetic studies found increased promoter methylation of the glucocorticoid receptor gene NR3C1 in ME/CFS, possibly linked to altered receptor regulation and childhood trauma.
Childhood trauma is estimated to increase the risk of developing ME/CFS by three- to eightfold.
More than half of ME/CFS patients report at least one episode of early childhood trauma.

Resting-state fMRI studies found altered functional connectivity in the prefrontal cortex, hippocampal/parahippocampal regions, and cingulate cortex in ME/CFS patients, significantly correlated with subjective fatigue severity.

Task-based MRI studies found a low-efficiency compensatory activation pattern and abnormal hemodynamic responses in cognitive networks of ME/CFS patients, reflecting decreased cognitive processing efficiency.

A rat central fatigue model using the modified multiple platform method plus alternate-day fasting reproduced ME/CFS-relevant features including reduced exploratory behavior, learning and memory impairment, physical fatigue, and hippocampal damage.

In a rat ME/CFS model with 35 days of chronic multifactorial stress, hippocampal CA1 showed structural and synaptic ultrastructural damage, with proteomics identifying differentially expressed proteins enriched in synaptic plasticity and neurotransmitter release pathways.

BALB/c mice repeatedly injected with inactivated Brucella abortus antigen showed significantly decreased CNS BDNF mRNA expression, suggesting reduced neuroprotective capacity and impaired synaptic plasticity.
In a Brucella-antigen-induced fatigue model, hippocampal atrophy was accompanied by reduced dentate gyrus neurogenesis, increased granule-cell apoptosis, and decreased BDNF expression.
Resveratrol treatment ameliorated hippocampal atrophy and reduced neurogenesis in a Brucella-antigen fatigue animal model by enhancing neurogenesis and suppressing apoptosis.

A comparable Brucella-antigen fatigue model study found elevated cytokine and oxidative stress markers in cortex and hippocampus but no detectable changes in neurogenesis, contradicting the reduced-neurogenesis finding of Moriya et al. (2011).
Early studies reported impaired natural killer cell function in ME/CFS patients.
