Uncommon clinical findings not previously reported in GZF1-related phenotype, such as umbilical hernia and congenital heart disease, were observed in the new patients.

Comparison of GZF1-related phenotype cases with Larsen syndrome case series (FLNB variants) allowed the authors to define a recognizable GZF1RP clinical spectrum comprising severe ocular defects, short stature, facial dysmorphism, joint hypermobility/dislocations, scoliosis, thoracic deformity, progressive hearing loss, umbilical hernia, and hypodontia.
Across included systematic reviews, joint hypermobility was consistently identified as a risk factor for musculoskeletal disorders in school-aged children.

Prevalence estimates for musculoskeletal disorders in school-aged children varied widely across conditions, from about 1% for scoliosis to over 20% for chronic pain and up to 70% for spinal pain in some populations.
Sedentary behaviors and psychosocial factors showed weaker associations with musculoskeletal disorders in children compared to other risk factors.
Multimodal scoliosis screening and footprint/posture indices for flatfoot were identified as valid assessment methods, though heterogeneity across studies limited comparability.

Exercise-based and psychological therapies, including Pilates-based programs and physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises, were found beneficial for musculoskeletal disorders in school-aged children.
Orthoses were reported beneficial only in symptomatic flatfoot, rather than broadly across flatfoot presentations.
The authors propose that fibromyalgia's apparent female predominance may partly reflect diagnostic and sociocultural biases rather than true epidemiological sex differences.

Men with fibromyalgia are proposed to be underdiagnosed due to sociocultural barriers to healthcare-seeking, clinician diagnostic bias, and heterogeneous symptom expression shaped by biological and psychosocial factors.

Men may delay seeking medical care for fibromyalgia symptoms due to cultural expectations of masculinity and often face skepticism about symptoms like diffuse pain, fatigue, and psychological distress.
Men with fibromyalgia may show differences in coping strategies and illness perception compared to women, despite sharing core symptoms across sexes.
Emerging evidence suggests possible small fiber pathology, reduced muscular strength, and gait impairments in men with fibromyalgia.
Psychological comorbidities are noted as part of the emerging neurophysiological and functional alteration profile in men with fibromyalgia.
Metabolic syndrome and its individual components, especially obesity, are reported to be highly prevalent among patients with fibromyalgia.
Both fibromyalgia and metabolic syndrome are associated with chronic low-grade inflammation as a shared pathophysiological mechanism.
Autonomic nervous system dysfunction is described as a shared feature contributing to both fibromyalgia and metabolic syndrome.
Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is proposed as a mechanism shared between fibromyalgia and metabolic syndrome.
Early-life stress is suggested as an environmental factor that may increase vulnerability to both fibromyalgia and metabolic syndrome by triggering persistent neuroendocrine and immune alterations.

The review highlights non-pharmacological strategies, including structured exercise, dietary interventions and microbiome-targeted approaches, as potentially beneficial for addressing shared mechanisms of fibromyalgia and metabolic syndrome.
Serum calcium levels were significantly lower in hemodialysis patients with fibromyalgia compared to those without.
Hemodialysis patients with fibromyalgia had significantly higher Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores, indicating greater symptom burden, than those without fibromyalgia.
FMS patients scored significantly lower on the SF-36 physical functioning domain than non-FMS hemodialysis patients.
FMS patients scored significantly lower on the SF-36 role-physical (role limitations due to physical health) domain than non-FMS patients.
FMS patients scored dramatically lower on the SF-36 role-emotional domain than non-FMS patients.
FMS patients scored significantly lower on the SF-36 mental health domain than non-FMS patients.
FMS patients scored significantly lower on the SF-36 vitality/energy domain than non-FMS patients.
FMS patients scored significantly lower on the SF-36 bodily pain domain than non-FMS patients.
FMS patients scored significantly lower on the SF-36 general health perceptions domain than non-FMS patients.
FMS patients scored significantly lower on the SF-36 social functioning domain than non-FMS patients.
Hemodialysis patients with fibromyalgia had significantly higher serum native thiol levels than those without fibromyalgia.
Hemodialysis patients with fibromyalgia had significantly higher serum total thiol levels than those without fibromyalgia.
Hemodialysis patients with fibromyalgia had significantly higher serum disulfide levels than those without fibromyalgia.
Thiol/disulfide ratio parameters did not differ significantly between hemodialysis patients with and without fibromyalgia.
Native thiol levels showed a weak positive correlation with FIQ symptom severity scores among hemodialysis patients.
Total thiol levels showed a weak negative correlation with SF-36 mental health subscale scores among hemodialysis patients.

In multivariable logistic regression adjusting for demographic and laboratory variables, total thiol level was independently associated with increased risk of fibromyalgia in hemodialysis patients, though with a small effect size and limited explanatory power.

No significant differences were found between FMS and non-FMS hemodialysis patients in demographic characteristics (age, sex, height, weight, dialysis duration) or in comorbid conditions (diabetes, hypertension, COPD, CAD, CHF), vascular access type, transfusion history, or Charlson Comorbidity Index.
Medication use, including phosphate binders, intravenous iron, calcitriol, paricalcitol, cinacalcet, and etelcalcetide, showed no significant differences between FMS and non-FMS hemodialysis groups.
Pregabalin exerts analgesic effects by binding voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing calcium influx and inhibiting release of excitatory neurotransmitters in the CNS.

At therapeutic doses, pregabalin often provides only partial pain relief and frequently causes side effects such as dizziness, somnolence, weight gain and peripheral edema that lead to treatment discontinuation.
A meta-analysis found that once-nightly sublingual cyclobenzaprine consistently improved pain response and global impression compared with placebo in fibromyalgia patients.
Cyclobenzaprine is associated with anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision), pronounced somnolence, and potential tachycardia/QTc interval prolongation.

Tizanidine, a centrally acting alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonist, inhibits norepinephrine release in the brainstem/spinal cord and inhibits release of excitatory amino acids (glutamate, aspartate) from spinal interneurons, enhancing presynaptic inhibition of motor neurons and producing muscle relaxation, sedation and anxiolysis.

A previous open-label, uncontrolled study reported that tizanidine improved pain, global assessment, fatigue, and Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) scores in fibromyalgia patients, though the study lacked a control group and had short follow-up.

Prior pregabalin RCTs in the fibromyalgia target population reported baseline self-reported pain intensity with a mean of 6.7 and SD of 1.5 on a 0-10 numerical rating scale, which informed this trial's sample size calculation.

This trial's primary hypothesis is that combination therapy with pregabalin and tizanidine provides superior analgesic efficacy compared with pregabalin monotherapy in fibromyalgia patients, to be tested via change in average pain intensity from baseline to week 12.
In August 2025, the US FDA approved a sublingual formulation of cyclobenzaprine hydrochloride for treatment of fibromyalgia in adults.
The global prevalence of fibromyalgia in the general population is estimated to range from 2% to 4%.

Nine of ten participants tolerated at least four weeks of continuous nocturnal wearable (EmbracePlus) monitoring, supporting feasibility of multi-week ambulatory ANS/sleep monitoring in migraine patients.

Nightly sleep measures and cardiovascular ANS measures (e.g., pulse rate, pulse rate variability, respiratory rate) did not significantly differ between nights preceding headache versus headache-free days.

Median total electrodermal activity (EDA), frequency of EDA peaks, storm frequency, and storm duration were numerically higher on nights preceding headache days than headache-free nights, though not statistically significant, with small-to-moderate effect sizes.

Individualized machine learning models predicting next-day headache from nocturnal wearable ANS/sleep features showed highly variable performance across participants (AUROC 0.28–0.81; AUPRC 0.19–0.76).
The best-performing individualized model (participant 1054, random forest) achieved clinically informative next-day headache prediction with AUROC 0.812 and AUPRC 0.760 at 45.5% headache prevalence.
Longer total sleep time and time in bed showed large positive correlations with higher Widespread Pain Index, higher Fibromyalgia Survey Score, and greater sleep disturbance.

Phasic EDA measures—frequency of EDA peaks, storm frequency, and storm duration—were positively correlated with both Widespread Pain Index and Fibromyalgia Survey Score, corresponding to medium-to-large effects.
EDA peak amplitude was positively and significantly associated with the Widespread Pain Index.
EDA peak amplitude showed only a non-significant trend toward positive correlation with the Fibromyalgia Survey Score.
Phasic EDA measures did not show statistically significant correlations with MIDAS disability score, PROMIS Fatigue, or PROMIS Sleep Disturbance scores.
The migraine cohort had a high baseline burden of nociplastic pain, with a median Fibromyalgia Survey Score near the clinical fibromyalgia threshold of 12.

The authors propose that sympathetic pathways mediating electrodermal activity originate in the hypothalamus, a region implicated in the pain-free premonitory phase of migraine, offering a mechanistic rationale for phasic EDA as a marker of pre-headache sympathetic arousal.
Multiple specific vaccines show elevated normalized VAERS Kawasaki disease adverse event frequencies in children aged 0, 1, and 2 years.

Six of the 30 vaccines with elevated KD safety signals are live, attenuated virus vaccines (MMR II, Priorix, ProQuad, RotaTeq, Rotarix, Varivax), consistent with a hypothesis that live attenuated viruses can activate mast cells.

18 of 24 remaining vaccines with elevated KD signals contain bacteria and/or Saccharomyces cerevisiae components in their manufacturing process, supporting a possible endotoxin/microbial contaminant hypothesis.

Coadministration of certain vaccine combinations was associated with normalized KD adverse event frequencies that differed from the sum of the individual vaccine frequencies, in some combinations exceeding the additive sum.
KD and MIS adverse event onset day distributions post-immunization are highly correlated, with most reports occurring 1-2 days after vaccination.
Four specific vaccines (Infanrix quinta, Infanrix hexa, Priorix, Bexsero) show greater male-versus-female imbalance in normalized KD adverse event frequency than other vaccines.
Different MMR-containing vaccine brands show discordant sex-specific KD adverse event frequencies, with Priorix showing much higher male-specific frequency than MMR II or ProQuad.
For the COVID-19 Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, more MIS adverse event reports were observed after the second dose than the first dose.

Specific COVID-19 Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine manufacturing lots (e.g., FK5127, FK5618, FL0007, FN4072) showed statistically elevated normalized MIS adverse event frequencies compared to the average across 34 high-volume lots.
The FcγR2α His167Arg variant (low-affinity IgG receptor) is associated with increased KD risk specifically in males.
No overall association was found between the FcγR2α rs1801274 polymorphism and MIS-C, but homozygous carriers developed severe cardiac dysfunction.
Increased TLR2 and TLR4 expression on peripheral neutrophils has been detected in some Kawasaki disease patients.
Some Kawasaki disease cases are associated with endotoxin exposure and elevated soluble CD14 (sCD14) levels.
Polyclonal expansion of TCRBV2- and TCRBV6-bearing T-cells occurs in Kawasaki disease patients, likely linked to endotoxin exposure.
Elevated Vβ2 T-cell expansion in some Kawasaki disease patients is consistent with a bacterial superantigen model of disease.
Kawasaki disease patients with abdominal symptoms are significantly more likely to be IVIG-resistant.
Kawasaki disease patients with abdominal symptoms are significantly more likely to have coronary artery aneurysms.
Monocyte-platelet aggregates, a marker of platelet activation, are significantly elevated during the acute stage of Kawasaki disease.
Platelet count and plateletcrit were found to serve as diagnostic markers for Kawasaki disease.
Cumulative prenatal and postnatal air pollution exposure to CO, NO, NO2, and NOx (but not O3) has a dose-dependent effect increasing Kawasaki disease incidence.
CCAD patients had a significantly higher prevalence of allergic rhinitis (79.2%) compared to other CRS phenotype groups.

CCAD histopathology is defined by an eosinophil-rich, stromal-dominant remodeling pattern with basement membrane thickening, fibrosis, and seromucinous gland hyperplasia, contrasting with epithelial-centric remodeling seen in non-eosinophilic CRS subtypes.

Transcriptomic analysis showed CCAD shares a type 2 inflammatory signature with the CC (concomitant central compartment disease) subtype, with high molecular similarity and only 19 differentially expressed genes between them.
Gene Set Enrichment Analysis identified mast cell activation as a pathway uniquely enriched in CCAD compared to other CRS subtypes.
GSEA also identified macrophage cytokine production as a pathway uniquely enriched in CCAD, distinguishing its local pathophysiology from other CRS subtypes.
Despite higher allergy burden, CCAD patients showed lower overall radiological (CT-based) opacification scores compared to other CRS phenotype groups.
Early oral introduction of ovalbumin in epicutaneously sensitized mice significantly reduced OVA-specific IgE levels compared to sensitized mice without oral tolerance induction.
Oral tolerance induction suppressed mast cell activation in epicutaneously sensitized mice.
Systemic Th2 cytokine levels were suppressed following early oral ovalbumin introduction in epicutaneously sensitized mice.
Despite achieving immune tolerance via oral ovalbumin introduction, the local skin inflammation at the site of epicutaneous sensitization remained unaffected.
Intestinal mast cell protease Mcpt1 expression was downregulated in mice given early oral ovalbumin introduction, indicating suppression of the intestinal mast cell axis.
Intestinal mast cell protease Mcpt2 expression was downregulated in mice given early oral ovalbumin introduction, indicating suppression of the intestinal mast cell axis.
Gasdermin C family member Gsdmc2 expression was downregulated in intestinal mast cells following oral tolerance induction with ovalbumin.
Gasdermin C family member Gsdmc4 expression was downregulated in intestinal mast cells following oral tolerance induction with ovalbumin.
mTiO2 nanoparticles were cytotoxic to bone marrow derived mast cells in a manner dependent on dose and exposure time.
SiO2 nanoparticles showed minimal cytotoxicity to BMMC at concentrations up to 100 µg/ml.
In the absence of antigen, neither SiO2 nor mTiO2 nanoparticles substantially altered degranulation or cytokine release from sensitized BMMC.
When co-cultured with antigen, SiO2 nanoparticles protected sensitized BMMC against antigen-induced degranulation.
SiO2 nanoparticles suppressed expression of mast cell surface activation markers (FcεRI, CD63/LAMP-3, CD107a/LAMP-1) in the presence of antigen.
In the presence of antigen, mTiO2 nanoparticles exacerbated BMMC degranulation and expression of surface activation markers.
Neurogranin (Ng) protein was detected within bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) under basal, unstimulated conditions, marking the first demonstration of Ng in mast cells.
BMMCs from Nrgn+/- heterozygous knockout mice showed a significant reduction in Nrgn mRNA compared with Nrgn+/+ wild-type BMMCs at baseline.
Ng protein levels were approximately 25% lower in Nrgn+/- BMMCs than in Nrgn+/+ BMMCs, but this reduction did not reach statistical significance.
Nrgn gene expression did not change across the allergen stimulation time course in either genotype, while the reduced Nrgn expression in Nrgn+/- BMMCs persisted throughout stimulation.
Ng deficiency had no effect on surface FcεRIα receptor levels in mature mast cells, indicating that downstream effects of Ng deficiency are not due to altered receptor expression.
Ng deficiency had no effect on surface c-kit receptor levels in mature mast cells.
Ng deficiency did not alter early-phase mast cell degranulation, as measured by β-hexosaminidase release after IgE/allergen (TNP-BSA + SCF) stimulation.
IL6 gene expression was significantly increased in Nrgn+/- BMMCs compared with Nrgn+/+ BMMCs at 120 minutes following allergen stimulation.
IL13 gene expression was significantly increased in Nrgn+/- BMMCs compared with Nrgn+/+ BMMCs at 180 minutes following allergen stimulation.
TNF gene expression showed a significant genotype (column) effect, being higher in Nrgn+/- BMMCs than Nrgn+/+ BMMCs following allergen stimulation.
CCL1 gene expression showed a non-significant biological increasing trend in Nrgn+/- BMMCs compared with Nrgn+/+ BMMCs following allergen stimulation.
No difference in CCL2 or CCL3 gene expression was observed between Nrgn+/- and Nrgn+/+ BMMCs following allergen stimulation.
IL-6 secretion was approximately 1.6-fold higher in Nrgn+/- BMMCs than Nrgn+/+ BMMCs at 6 hours after allergen stimulation.
IL-13 secretion was significantly elevated in Nrgn+/- BMMCs compared with Nrgn+/+ BMMCs after allergen stimulation.
TNF secretion was significantly elevated in Nrgn+/- BMMCs compared with Nrgn+/+ BMMCs after allergen stimulation.
Secretion of chemokines CCL1, CCL2, and CCL3 was significantly increased in Nrgn+/- BMMCs compared with Nrgn+/+ BMMCs following allergen stimulation.
Rcan1, another negative regulator of calcineurin, showed increased gene expression in Nrgn+/- mast cells following allergen stimulation, suggesting a compensatory mechanism for reduced Ng.

Both systemic OVA-specific IgE and OVA-specific Th2 cells were required together for sneezing and IgE-producing cell formation in cervical lymph nodes and nasopharynx-associated lymphoid tissue after intranasal OVA challenge.

Rag2-deficient mice, which lack mature B and T cells, failed to develop AR symptoms or IgE-producing cells after OVA-Th2/OVA-IgE sensitization and OVA challenge, indicating a requirement for adaptive lymphocytes.
Aid-deficient mice, which cannot undergo class-switch recombination to IgE, failed to develop AR symptoms or IgE-producing cells after sensitization and OVA challenge.
Stat6-deficient mice, lacking IL-4/IL-13 signaling required for IgE class switching, failed to develop AR symptoms or IgE-producing cells after sensitization and OVA challenge.
In imiquimod-induced psoriatic mice, Alkannin treatment reduced epidermal hyperplasia, vascular dilation, and splenomegaly.
Alkannin treatment altered the Th17 to Treg cell ratio in psoriatic mice.
Alkannin reduced proinflammatory cytokine levels in the psoriatic mouse model.
In vitro, Alkannin inhibited β-hexosaminidase release from mast cells in a MrgprX2-dependent manner.
Alkannin downregulated expression of inflammation-related cytokines in mast cells in vitro.
Alkannin reduced intracellular Ca2+ levels in mast cells in a MrgprX2-dependent manner.
SPR, CETSA, DARTS, and molecular docking assays showed that Alkannin directly binds to MrgprX2.

Oral sodium R-lipoate (NaRLA), particularly at the high dose, improved psoriasis-like symptoms (erythema, scaling, skin thickness) and reduced PASI scores in imiquimod-induced psoriatic mice, comparable to methotrexate.
NaRLA treatment reduced body weight loss, splenomegaly, and histopathological deterioration, and decreased oxidative stress markers in the imiquimod psoriasis mouse model.
NaRLA decreased the elevated expression of IL-23 in psoriatic mouse skin tissue.
NaRLA decreased the elevated expression of IL-17A in psoriatic mouse skin tissue.
NaRLA markedly inhibited phosphorylation of nuclear factor-κB p65 in psoriatic mouse skin tissue.
NaRLA downregulated TNF-α levels in psoriatic mouse skin tissue.
NaRLA downregulated IL-1β levels in psoriatic mouse skin tissue.
One cited study found significantly lower Faecalibacterium prausnitzii levels in IBS patients compared with healthy controls.
Increased Proteobacteria abundance and reduced Faecalibacterium prausnitzii have been observed in both IBS and IBD.
A metagenomic analysis of 1792 participants showed the microbiome had significant overlap between IBS and IBD but was distinct enough to distinguish the two diseases.
Lower SCFA levels reduce receptor activation in gut epithelial cells, impairing NLRP3 inflammasome activation and reducing IL-18 production, weakening mucosal immunity.

Reduced SCFA availability and expansion of mucus-degrading bacteria may lower tight junction protein expression, increasing paracellular permeability and disrupting the epithelial barrier in both IBS and IBD (more pronounced in IBD).
In IBS-D, increased fecal tryptophan and tryptamine levels have been observed, suggesting altered microbial tryptophan metabolism and serotonergic involvement in diarrhea-predominant symptoms.
In IBS, TLR4 and TLR5 expression are increased, promoting low-grade inflammatory cascades without macroscopic inflammation, in contrast to the marked NF-κB and Th1/Th17 activation seen in IBD.

Dysbiosis reduces bacteria with 7α-dihydroxylation activity, leading to increased primary bile acids and decreased secondary bile acids, reducing anti-inflammatory signaling and contributing to visceral hypersensitivity.

A multicenter study of 1426 participants found Ruminococcus gnavus-associated dysbiosis and biofilm formation more pronounced in IBS than in ulcerative colitis, with biofilm detected in 57% of IBS cases versus 34% of UC cases.
CEACAM6 receptor is overexpressed in the epithelium of Crohn's disease patients, allowing adherent-invasive E. coli (AIEC) to bind and invade gut epithelial cells; this has not been described in IBS.

AIEC strains expressing propanediol dehydratase (PduC) are enriched in CD microbiomes and drive T-cell-mediated intestinal inflammation via CX3CR1+ phagocyte-dependent Th17/IL-1β induction; PduC inhibition reduced inflammation in animal models.

NOD2 mutations impair NF-κB activation in Paneth cells, reducing antimicrobial peptide production, while ATG16L1 mutations reduce autophagy; both impair microbial control and are linked to Crohn's disease but not to IBS.

IBS-C patients show higher respiratory methane levels associated with greater abundance of fecal Methanobrevibacter smithii, linked to intestinal methanogen overgrowth and delayed transit; methanogenesis pathways were reduced in IBD versus controls.

IBS-D patients show higher respiratory hydrogen sulfide levels associated with greater abundance of H2S-producing bacteria (Fusobacterium, Desulfovibrio), and H2S can trigger visceral pain via TRPA1 receptor activation and increase paracellular permeability at high concentrations.

In a study of 2375 participants, anti-CdtB and anti-vinculin antibody levels were higher in IBS-D and lower in IBS-C, with IBS-C levels not differing significantly from healthy controls, supporting a post-infectious autoimmune mechanism damaging interstitial cells of Cajal and enteric neurons.

An Australian study failed to confirm that anti-CdtB and anti-vinculin antibodies could distinguish IBS-D from organic gastrointestinal disease, and another study found no significant differences between IBS subtypes and healthy controls.

In IBS, increased translocation of microbial antigens such as LPS activates mast cells located near submucosal sensory nerve fibers, which release mediators that sensitize visceral afferent nerves and influence abdominal pain severity and frequency, whereas in IBD mast cell activation is part of a broader inflammatory response rather than the main pain mechanism.
Mast cells release nerve growth factor (NGF), inducing neuroplasticity and contributing to chronic visceral hypersensitivity in IBS.
Fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin are among the most sensitive tests for distinguishing IBD from non-IBD conditions and are elevated in IBD while normal in most IBS patients.
Elevated ASCA titers identify Crohn's disease patients with high specificity but low sensitivity.
Positivity for ASCA IgA, ASCA IgG, anti-OmpC, and anti-CBir1 has been detected in 65% of Crohn's disease patients up to 6 years before diagnosis.
A meta-analysis of 60 studies estimated sensitivity and specificity of the ASCA(+)/pANCA(-) pattern for Crohn's disease at 55% and 93% respectively.
In a small cohort of ASCA-negative patients, 44% were positive for ALCA or ACCA, yielding a sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 90% for distinguishing CD from UC.
A multi-species bacterial panel based on metagenomic data from 5979 fecal samples achieved an AUC of 0.91 for distinguishing IBD from IBS, numerically higher than fecal calprotectin (AUC 0.86).
Anti-CdtB has shown a sensitivity of 43.7% and specificity of 91.6% for distinguishing IBS from IBD.
A meta-analysis of 53 RCTs showed probiotic combinations had beneficial effects on global IBS symptoms and abdominal pain, though no definitive conclusions on overall efficacy could be drawn.
A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial showed VSL#3 significantly reduced recurrence of chronic pouchitis and onset of acute pouchitis after surgery in UC patients.
A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study showed high-dose VSL#3 added to mesalamine significantly increased remission rates compared with placebo in mild-to-moderate UC.
Genistein treatment reduced ear thickening, scratching behavior, and spleen-to-body weight ratio in an MC903-induced murine atopic dermatitis model.
Genistein decreased serum IgE and IL-4 levels in the MC903-induced AD mouse model.
Genistein suppressed mast cell degranulation and release of β-hexosaminidase, histamine, MCP-1, tryptase, TNF-α, and calcium in LAD2 human mast cells.
Genistein directly binds the D127 and R226 sites of TRAM with high affinity, acting as an inhibitor of this key TLR signaling molecule in mast cells.
Genistein inhibits mast cell activation via the PLCγ1-IKKβ-NF-κB pathway downstream of TRAM, suppressing NF-κB signaling activation.
The NLRP3 rs10754558 polymorphism was significantly associated with CSU susceptibility across codominant, dominant, recessive, and multiplicative genetic models.
Under the codominant model, C/C genotype carriers had a 5.2-fold increased risk of CSU versus G/G carriers and 1.9-fold higher risk versus C/G carriers.
In the dominant model, carriers of at least one C allele (C/C or C/G) had a 3.4-fold higher risk of CSU relative to G/G genotype carriers.
Under the recessive model, the C/C genotype was associated with a 2.7-fold increased risk of CSU compared with combined C/G and G/G genotypes.
In the multiplicative (allelic) model, carriage of the minor C allele conferred a 2.3-fold higher risk of CSU compared with the major G allele.
In unstimulated whole blood cultures, IL-1β levels did not differ significantly between CSU patients and healthy controls.
Following LPS stimulation, IL-1β production was significantly higher in whole blood cultures from CSU patients than from healthy controls.
In unstimulated cultures, IL-18 levels were comparable between CSU patients and controls.
Following LPS stimulation, IL-18 production was significantly higher in CSU patients compared with controls.
A significant modest positive correlation was found between LPS-stimulated IL-1β and IL-18 production in CSU patients, but not in healthy controls.

In the codominant model, C/C carriers of NLRP3 rs10754558 showed significantly higher LPS-stimulated IL-1β and IL-18 production than C/G and G/G carriers, and higher UAS7 scores in C/C and C/G carriers versus G/G.
In the dominant model, carriers of at least one C allele had higher LPS-stimulated IL-1β and total serum IgE than G/G carriers.
In the recessive model, C/C carriers had significantly higher LPS-stimulated IL-1β and IL-18 production but paradoxically lower UAS7 scores than combined C/G+G/G carriers.
ASST-positive CSU patients had significantly higher UAS7 disease activity scores than ASST-negative patients.
Total serum IgE levels were significantly higher in ASST-positive than ASST-negative CSU patients.
UAS7 disease activity scores were not significantly correlated with BMI or total serum IgE concentrations in CSU patients.
Genotype and allele distributions of NLRP3 rs10754558 did not significantly deviate from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in the overall population or in CSU/control subgroups.
Differential expression analysis identified 96 DEGs in T2 asthma (30 up, 66 down) and 144 DEGs in non-T2 asthma (74 up, 70 down) relative to comparator groups.
GO and KEGG enrichment of T2 and non-T2 DEGs both implicated humoral immune response, IL-17 signaling, chemokine signaling, and acute inflammatory response pathways.

Machine learning consensus (LASSO, SVM-RFE, Random Forest) identified MS4A2 among six hub genes shared between T2 and non-T2 asthma, with elevated expression in asthma versus normal controls in the validation dataset.

TPSAB1 (mast cell tryptase alpha gene) was consistently upregulated in asthma versus healthy controls across the test and validation datasets, and correlated with resting mast cells by immune infiltration analysis.
FCER1A showed the most significant upregulation among the five hub genes in neutrophilic asthma samples compared with healthy controls in the GSE143303 test set.
TFF3 showed the most significant upregulation among hub genes in paucigranulocytic (non-T2) asthma samples relative to healthy controls.
TSPAN13 was upregulated in both neutrophilic and paucigranulocytic asthma versus healthy controls and correlated with CD4 memory resting T cells.

ROC curve analysis using the external validation dataset showed AUC values greater than 0.6 for all five hub genes, indicating moderate-to-high diagnostic performance for distinguishing asthma from healthy controls.
CIBERSORT immune infiltration analysis showed that proportions of macrophages and T cells were higher in both T2 and non-T2 asthma bronchial samples compared to controls.
Immune infiltration correlation analysis showed strong associations between MS4A2, TPSAB1, and FCER1A expression and resting mast cell abundance in both T2 and non-T2 asthma groups.

Single-cell RNA-seq analysis of scRNA-seq data (GSE164015) demonstrated that MS4A2, TPSAB1, and FCER1A were predominantly and significantly upregulated specifically in mast cells among 11 annotated bronchial cell types.

In human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cell culture, TFF3 and TSPAN13 mRNA were significantly increased after 24h stimulation with house dust mite (HDM), PM2.5, or toluene diisocyanate (TDI), whereas MS4A2, FCER1A, and TPSAB1 showed no detectable upregulation since they are mainly expressed in mast cells rather than epithelial cells.

In a murine multi-endotype asthma model, HDM sensitization produced eosinophilic airway inflammation with elevated BALF total cells and eosinophils, PM2.5 induced predominantly neutrophilic inflammation, and TDI induced mixed eosinophil/neutrophil infiltration, each with increased inflammatory scores versus filtered-air controls.

RT-qPCR in lung tissue from the HDM, PM2.5, and TDI mouse asthma models confirmed marked increases in expression of the five bioinformatically-identified hub genes, consistent with the human transcriptomic datasets.

The authors' core conclusion is that three classic mast cell marker genes (MS4A2, FCER1A, TPSAB1) are consistently upregulated in both type 2 and non-type 2 asthma, indicating that mast cell activation is a shared pathological event across asthma endotypes rather than being restricted to type 2 inflammation.

The paper cites prior literature that inherited copy number differences in α-tryptase-encoding TPSAB1 are associated with risk of severe anaphylaxis, and that TPSAB1 transcripts positively correlate with FeNO in severe asthma patients.
Whole exome sequencing identified a novel, de novo heterozygous missense variant in TGFBR1 (c.1051G>T, p.Asp351Tyr) within the kinase domain, confirming a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome Type I.

According to ACMG guidelines, the c.1051G>T variant was classified as pathogenic based on PP3-moderate, PM2-supporting, PM5-supporting, and PS2 criteria, and had not been previously reported in population databases.
In silico prediction tools (PolyPhen-2, PROVEAN, SIFT, CADD) consistently predicted the p.Asp351Tyr variant to be damaging/deleterious to TGFBR1 protein function.

AlphaFold3-based structural modeling predicted that the p.Asp351Tyr TGFBR1 mutant forms new hydrogen bonds with SMAD2, suggesting increased binding affinity, while interaction with SMAD3 remained largely unchanged.

Immunofluorescence staining showed significantly increased nuclear phosphorylated SMAD2/SMAD3 signal in smooth muscle cells of the patient's diseased aortic tissue compared with control aorta, indicating TGF-beta pathway hyperactivation.
Histopathological staining of the patient's aortic wall revealed severe medial disorganization, elastic fiber fragmentation/loss, and increased collagen deposition compared to control aortic tissue.

The patient underwent open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair and shortly thereafter developed an acute Type B aortic dissection, illustrating extreme post-surgical fragility of the residual aorta in Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
The patient was discharged on oral bisoprolol (5 mg daily) as lifelong prophylactic therapy following her two major aortic operations.

A cited 2025 study (Abdul Nabi et al.) reported significant sex-based differences in Loeys-Dietz syndrome, with males generally more susceptible than females to severe macrovascular complications such as AAAs and dissections.
A cited large-cohort study (Calderon-Martinez et al.) found that patients with pathogenic TGF-beta pathway variants face an exceptionally high and early risk of extra-aortic arterial events.
A patent ductus arteriosus was missed on the patient's initial screening echocardiograms and was only identified and surgically ligated incidentally during her second thoracic aortic operation.
Gut microbiome alpha diversity (Shannon index) was significantly lower in people with ME/CFS compared to controls after accounting for age, sex, and stool storage time.
Pielou evenness of the gut microbiome was significantly lower in ME/CFS in a simplified model of disease status alone.
Microbial community dominance (relative abundance of the most abundant ASV) was significantly higher in people with ME/CFS.
Faith's phylogenetic diversity of the gut microbiome did not differ between ME/CFS and controls.
The Firmicutes:Bacteroidetes ratio, a common dysbiosis marker, was significantly lower in people with ME/CFS than controls.
Overall gut microbial community structure (beta diversity: Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, weighted and unweighted UniFrac) differed significantly between people with ME/CFS and controls.
Live and dead bacterial cell counts from stool did not differ between people with ME/CFS and controls.
Fecal tryptophan and several aromatic amino acid metabolites, including the AHR agonists indole and indole acetate, were elevated in stool of people with ME/CFS compared to controls.
Fecal phenyllactate concentration was associated with disease status and disability status in a simplified model, though the full model was non-significant.
373 bacterial ASVs, mostly from the Class Clostridia, showed significant correlations with at least one fecal tryptophan metabolite.
The subset of gut bacteria correlated with tryptophan metabolites showed lower alpha diversity (Shannon index, dominance) in people with ME/CFS.

Community structure (beta diversity: Bray-Curtis, unweighted UniFrac, Jaccard) of the tryptophan-metabolite-correlated bacterial subcommunity differed significantly between ME/CFS and controls, driven by centroid shift rather than dispersion.
Ex vivo stool culture supernatants from ME/CFS and control participants showed no difference in their capacity to activate AHR in a luciferase reporter cell line.
Induction of AHR target genes AHRR and CYP1A1 in Caco2 cells by ex vivo stool culture supernatants did not differ between ME/CFS and control samples.

Participants (ME/CFS and controls combined) reporting neurocognitive symptoms showed elevated AHR agonist activity in ex vivo stool cultures compared to those without such symptoms, independent of ME/CFS diagnosis.
AHRR and CYP1A1 gene expression in Caco2 cells treated with stool culture supernatants were elevated in samples from individuals reporting neurocognitive symptoms, regardless of ME/CFS diagnosis.
Prior to FDR correction, indole, indoleacetate, and 4-hydroxyphenylacetate were elevated in stool of participants reporting neurocognitive symptoms.
Enterolactone was significantly lower in stool samples of participants reporting neurocognitive symptoms.
People with ME/CFS scored significantly lower on the Karnofsky Performance Scale, reflecting greater functional impairment, than controls.
SF-12 physical and mental component summary scores were both significantly lower in ME/CFS cases compared to controls.
Infection was the most commonly self-reported trigger of ME/CFS onset among study participants.
ME/CFS patients reported significantly greater frequency and severity of gastrointestinal symptoms compared with matched controls.
A prior diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome was reported by 53% of ME/CFS patients compared with 8% of controls.

GI symptom burden correlated with fatigue, cognitive difficulties, flu-like symptoms, pain, sleep disturbances, neurological complaints, and sensory sensitivities in ME/CFS patients, independent of illness duration.
CRP levels were higher in ME/CFS patients who had greater GI symptom burden.
CRP correlated with GI, fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, and flu-like symptom burden in ME/CFS patients, an association not seen in controls.
ME/CFS patients with greater flu-like symptom expression showed higher IgM responses to dietary gliadin.
ME/CFS patients with greater flu-like symptom expression showed higher IgM responses to bacterial lipopolysaccharide.

Participants emphasized that self-management support should be individualised and accessible, with attention to timing, readiness, and flexible delivery formats such as digital, hybrid, or modular approaches.
Participants reported gaps in continuity of follow-up care for ME/CFS and experiences of stigma from healthcare providers.
Peer support and practical adaptive strategies such as pacing and symptom tracking were highlighted as valuable components of self-management for ME/CFS.

Existing self-management support was found to be poorly aligned with patients' physical and cognitive limitations, lacked consistent structured follow-up, and often conveyed contradictory guidance on activity management.
At baseline, ME/CFS patients showed significantly higher quantitative sensory testing warm detection thresholds than PCC patients, indicating greater thermal small-fiber sensory dysfunction.
At baseline, ME/CFS patients reported a higher burden of autonomic symptoms on COMPASS-31 than PCC patients.
At baseline, ME/CFS patients had lower cardiovascular hemodynamic composite scores than PCC patients.
No cognitive domain or clinical symptom measure differed significantly between ME/CFS and PCC at baseline.
Small fiber symptom severity was positively correlated with autonomic symptom burden at baseline.
Small fiber symptom severity was positively correlated with fatigue severity at baseline.
Greater fatigue burden was associated with lower processing speed performance at baseline.
Greater fatigue burden was associated with lower attention performance at baseline.
Greater fatigue burden was associated with lower executive function performance at baseline.
Autonomic symptom burden was moderately, borderline-significantly correlated with fatigue at baseline.
At follow-up, no domain-level between-group differences remained across sensory, autonomic, cognitive, or clinical symptom domains, indicating convergence of ME/CFS and PCC profiles over time.
Parasympathetic function composite scores increased significantly from baseline to follow-up across the combined cohort.
Sympathetic function composite scores decreased significantly from baseline to follow-up across the combined cohort.
CHEPs responses increased markedly from baseline to follow-up, consistent with apparent improvement in small-fiber nociceptive responses, though this may partly reflect regression to the mean.
Small-fiber symptom burden improved (decreased) from baseline to follow-up.
QST cold sensory thresholds worsened modestly from baseline to follow-up, indicating incomplete, modality-specific sensory change.
Verbal memory scores improved significantly from baseline to follow-up, though this may reflect practice effects from repeated testing.
Processing speed scores decreased significantly from baseline to follow-up in the covariate-adjusted longitudinal model.
Older age was significantly associated with lower parasympathetic function in the covariate-adjusted longitudinal model.

Unadjusted models suggested differential follow-up change between ME/CFS and PCC in hemodynamic function and autonomic symptom burden, but this did not remain significant after adjustment for baseline disease duration.
Lower baseline CHEPs values predicted greater follow-up increase in CHEPs, consistent with regression to the mean rather than necessarily true recovery.
Lower baseline processing speed values predicted greater follow-up change in processing speed.

Metabolomic profiling of camel milk identified 1654 metabolites, of which 39 candidate compounds meeting ADME/drug-likeness criteria targeted 102 genes overlapping with CFS/ME disease targets, suggesting multi-target therapeutic potential.

Topological analysis of the protein-protein interaction network identified 10 hub targets (INS, IL1B, TNF, IL6, POMC, BDNF, IL10, IFNG, LEP, NR3C1) clustering into neuroendocrine, immune-inflammatory, and energy metabolism domains relevant to CFS/ME.

KEGG pathway enrichment of the 102 overlapping targets highlighted serotonergic synapse, neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, cAMP signaling, calcium signaling, AGE-RAGE signaling, and multiple immune-related pathways as candidate mechanisms of camel milk action in CFS/ME.
Chronic restraint/forced-swim stress reduced daily food intake in model mice, and camel milk treatment significantly restored intake to control-comparable levels.
Model mice had significantly lower body weight than controls, and camel milk treatment reversed this weight loss to a level not significantly different from control.

Model mice showed significantly shorter exhaustive swimming time under load compared to controls, indicative of physical fatigue, and camel milk treatment significantly prolonged swimming endurance back to control levels.
Immobility time in the tail suspension test was significantly increased in model mice, reflecting despair-like behavior, and camel milk administration significantly reduced this immobility time.
Plasma L-lactate was significantly elevated in model mice versus controls, and camel milk treatment significantly lowered lactate levels.
Plasma urea was elevated in model mice compared to controls, and camel milk treatment significantly reduced urea levels.
Lactate dehydrogenase activity was significantly higher in model mice than controls, and camel milk intervention normalized this activity to control-comparable levels.
Plasma TNF-α was significantly elevated in model mice versus controls due to chronic stress, but camel milk treatment showed only a non-significant trend toward reduction.
Plasma IL-17 was significantly elevated in model mice versus controls, but camel milk treatment produced only a non-significant trend toward reduction.
The anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 was significantly decreased in model mice versus controls, and camel milk treatment restored IL-10 to control levels.
Chronic stress significantly reduced total CREB/GAPDH protein ratio in the brain of model mice, and camel milk treatment restored total CREB expression to control-comparable levels.

Unlike total CREB, the phosphorylated CREB (p-CREB, Ser133)/GAPDH ratio did not differ significantly among control, model, and camel milk groups, indicating the CFS/ME deficit lies in total CREB pool rather than phosphorylation status.

Brain BDNF mRNA was significantly upregulated in model mice compared with controls, a change interpreted as a maladaptive compensatory response rather than neuroprotection, and camel milk treatment normalized BDNF expression back to control levels.

Brain DRD2 (dopamine D2 receptor) mRNA was significantly downregulated in model mice compared with controls, consistent with anhedonia/fatigue symptoms, and was restored to control levels by camel milk treatment.

Brain OPRM1 (mu-opioid receptor) mRNA was significantly downregulated in model mice compared with controls, consistent with pain/fatigue symptoms, and camel milk treatment restored expression to control levels.

Skeletal muscle AKT/GAPDH protein ratio was reported as significantly higher in model mice than controls in the Results section, and camel milk further increased this ratio to a level comparable to control; note the Discussion section states the opposite (AKT downregulation in model mice reversed by CM), indicating an internal inconsistency in the paper.

Skeletal muscle GLUT4 mRNA was reported as significantly upregulated in model mice versus controls in the Results section, and camel milk treatment restored GLUT4 expression to control levels; the Discussion section conversely describes GLUT4 downregulation in model mice reversed by CM, an internal inconsistency.
Camel milk administration significantly increased skeletal muscle glycogen content compared with the model group, indicating improved energy storage status.
No significant difference in muscle ATP levels was observed between the camel milk-treated group and the control group.

Chronic stress significantly reduced total CREB protein (CREB/GAPDH ratio) in brain tissue of model mice compared to controls, and camel milk treatment restored it to control levels without affecting p-CREB.
Phosphorylated CREB (Ser133) to GAPDH ratio did not differ significantly among control, model, and camel milk groups, indicating the phosphorylation status was not the limiting deficit.

Brain BDNF mRNA was significantly upregulated in the CFS/ME model group compared to controls, interpreted as a maladaptive compensatory response, and camel milk treatment normalized BDNF expression to control levels.

Dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2) mRNA in brain was significantly downregulated in CFS/ME model mice versus controls, consistent with anhedonia/fatigue symptoms, and camel milk restored expression to control levels.
Mu-opioid receptor (OPRM1) mRNA in brain was significantly downregulated in CFS/ME model mice, consistent with pain and fatigue symptoms, and camel milk restored its expression to control levels.
Skeletal muscle AKT/GAPDH protein ratio was significantly higher in the CFS/ME model group than in controls, and camel milk further increased the ratio to a level comparable with controls.
Skeletal muscle GLUT4 mRNA expression was significantly upregulated in the CFS/ME model group compared to controls, and camel milk treatment restored GLUT4 expression to control levels.
Camel milk administration significantly elevated skeletal muscle glycogen content compared to the untreated CFS/ME model group.
Muscle ATP levels showed no significant difference between the camel milk-treated group and the control group, indicating this endpoint was not fully normalized or was not significantly altered.
Fatigued healthy individuals showed enrichment of Escherichia coli in their gut microbiome compared to non-fatigued individuals.
Potentially beneficial gut bacteria were reduced in fatigued healthy individuals relative to those without fatigue.
Functional profiling showed enrichment of KEGG orthologs related to oxidative stress in the gut microbiome of fatigued individuals.
Functional profiling showed depletion of energy-producing pathway-related KEGG orthologs in the gut microbiome of fatigued individuals.
The energy metabolite citrate was decreased in fecal samples of fatigued healthy individuals.

Some fatigue-associated bacterial alterations in healthy adults overlapped with gut microbial changes reported in external datasets on psychiatric disorders and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome.

A Raman spectroscopy-machine learning model using plasma spectral features, age, and sex classified ME patients versus healthy controls at baseline (T0) with AUC 0.85, accuracy 79%, specificity 82%, sensitivity 73%.

The RS-ML model applied 90 minutes after a standardized post-exertional stress test classified ME patients versus controls with AUC 0.83, accuracy 84%, specificity 90%, sensitivity 69%, halving false positives compared with T0.
At baseline, the plasma Raman peak at 829 cm-1, attributed to proteins, lactic acid, and citrate, showed increased signal intensity in ME patients compared with healthy controls.
At baseline, the Raman peak at 1124 cm-1, reflecting fatty acid/lipid trans-conformation, proteins and glucose, was increased in ME patients compared with controls.
At baseline, the Raman peak at 1009 cm-1, associated with phenylalanine, tryptophan, and urea, was reduced in ME patients compared with controls.
At baseline, the Raman peak at 1422 cm-1, corresponding to CH2-form lipids, was reduced in ME patients compared with controls.
At 90 minutes post-exertional stress, the Raman peak at 1133 cm-1, reflecting fatty acid/lipid trans-conformation, proteins and glucose, remained elevated in ME patients versus controls.
At 90 minutes post-exertional stress, the Raman peak at 1588 cm-1, associated with amide II proteins, was increased in ME patients compared with controls.

At 90 minutes post-exertion, the phenylalanine/tryptophan-associated Raman peak at 1009 cm-1 and the CH2-lipid peaks at 1409 and 1421 cm-1 remained reduced in ME patients versus controls, with the 1005 cm-1 region showing a stronger statistical difference after exertion than at rest.
Patients with ME reported lower physical and mental component scores on the SF-36 health survey compared with healthy controls.
All domains of the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory-20 (general, physical, mental fatigue, reduced activity, reduced motivation) were higher in ME patients compared with healthy controls.

DePaul Symptom Questionnaire (DSQ) scores, capturing autonomic/neuroendocrine-immune dysfunction, cognitive dysfunction, sleep disturbance and PEM, were higher in ME patients compared with healthy controls.
The ME patient cohort had a median illness duration of seven years (IQR 3-16), indicating a chronically affected population.
ME patients had significantly lower baseline circulating irisin than healthy controls.
Following a 90-minute mechanical stress challenge, the exertion-induced rise in circulating irisin was significantly smaller in ME patients than in healthy controls.
Self-reported weekly physical activity was markedly lower in ME patients compared with healthy controls.
ME patients scored significantly lower on SF-36 physical and mental health components than healthy controls.
ME patients had significantly higher general fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and PEM scores than controls.
Within the ME cohort, female patients had significantly higher baseline circulating irisin than male patients, whereas no such sex difference was seen in healthy controls.
Across the ME cohort, higher circulating irisin correlated positively with greater PEM severity as measured by the DSQ.
The positive correlation between irisin and PEM severity was significant in male ME patients but not in female patients, indicating sex-dependent modulation of this relationship.
Circulating TSP-1 levels did not differ significantly between ME patients and healthy controls at baseline or after the stress challenge.
Within the ME cohort, patients with moderate-to-severe fatigue had significantly higher baseline irisin levels than those with mild fatigue.
Patients with moderate-to-severe fatigue also had significantly higher baseline TSP-1 levels than those with mild fatigue, paralleling the irisin increase.

TSP-1 levels were not significantly influenced by medication exposure (corticosteroids, hormone therapies, aspirin, metformin, gabapentinoids, angiotensin-related drugs, vitamin D) or by comorbidity status (including fibromyalgia, cardiovascular/autonomic, endocrine, respiratory, GI, or neurological conditions) in the ME cohort.

In a multivariable regression adjusting for age, sex, BMI, and disease duration, baseline irisin was the only significant independent predictor of fatigue severity, with higher irisin associated with greater fatigue.

In Jurkat cells, irisin-induced impedance responses were significantly and dose-dependently attenuated by an HSP90α-neutralizing antibody, indicating irisin bioactivity partly depends on extracellular HSP90α.
Pre-treatment with TSP-1 inhibited irisin-induced cellular responses by approximately 40%, with the strongest suppression under simultaneous HSP90α blockade.
Reciprocal dose–response analysis demonstrated that TSP-1 inhibits irisin signaling in a concentration-dependent manner.
Recombinant TSP-1-induced cellular responses remained largely independent of HSP90α inhibition, suggesting TSP-1 signals via pathways distinct from irisin's HSP90α dependence.

Irisin inhibited TSP-1 activity under vehicle conditions, but this inhibitory capacity was markedly reduced after HSP90α neutralization, indicating reciprocal antagonism dependent on HSP90α availability.
Blockade of αvβ5 integrin with a specific antibody significantly reduced irisin-induced cellular responses, comparably to HSP90α inhibition.
TSP-1 signaling showed only partial dependency on αvβ5 integrin and minimal sensitivity to HSP90α inhibition, indicating use of alternative signaling pathways distinct from irisin.
In the CFS mouse model, 17 differential metabolites were identified in brain tissue compared with controls.
In the CFS mouse model, 17 differential metabolites were identified in fecal samples compared with controls.
Arachidonic acid metabolism was among the pathways altered in the brain and gut of CFS model mice.
Steroid biosynthesis, linked to HPA-axis regulation, was among the pathways disrupted in the CFS model.
Glycerophospholipid metabolism was among the membrane-lipid remodeling pathways altered in the CFS mouse model.
Ether lipid metabolism was among the membrane-lipid remodeling pathways altered in the CFS mouse model.
Primary bile acid biosynthesis was among the pathways altered in the gut of CFS model mice.
Pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis, relevant to energy metabolism, was disrupted in the CFS mouse model.
Brain-gut metabolomic changes suggested disturbances in neurotransmitter-related metabolism associated with the chronic fatigue syndrome model and partly normalized by GSLS.
Metabolomic alterations implicated HPA-axis-associated steroid metabolism in the fatigue phenotype, which was partly normalized by GSLS treatment.
Inflammation-related metabolic pathways were implicated as part of the brain-gut disturbances in the CFS mouse model and were partly normalized by GSLS.
Oxidative stress-related metabolism was implicated in the fatigue phenotype and was partly normalized following GSLS supplementation.

GSLS supplementation partially normalized the brain and fecal metabolic abnormalities induced by the chronic fatigue syndrome mouse model, supporting its potential as a functional food ingredient for vitality and metabolic resilience.
A long-term forced-swimming induction protocol was used in male C57BL/6 mice to establish a fatigue-like phenotype modeling chronic fatigue syndrome.

SJZD treatment for 30 days improved general symptoms in a multi-factor stress rat model of chronic fatigue syndrome, including body weight, food intake, intestinal propulsion and gastric emptying rates, and exhaustive swimming time.
SJZD treatment normalized abnormalities in oxidative stress and energy metabolism indices, including skeletal muscle ATPase content, in CFS rats.
SJZD exerted therapeutic effects on CFS rats via regulation of 7 differential fecal metabolites.
SJZD exerted therapeutic effects on CFS rats via regulation of 25 differential serum metabolites.
16S rRNA sequencing showed that SJZD increased the diversity and compositional richness of intestinal microbiota in CFS rats.
SJZD treatment decreased the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes (F/B) ratio in the gut microbiota of CFS rats.
Significant correlations were detected between the intestinal microbiota and serum/fecal metabolites as well as biochemical indices in CFS rats treated with SJZD.
ME/CFS is characterised by persistent, debilitating fatigue not explained by another medical diagnosis, often accompanied by cognitive difficulties, pain, and sleep disturbance.

Post-exertional malaise, a worsening of symptoms following physical or mental exertion, is a defining feature of ME/CFS that distinguishes it from other causes of fatigue and has important management implications.
Graded exercise therapy is contraindicated in ME/CFS because it may precipitate or worsen post-exertional malaise.
Management of ME/CFS typically requires a multidisciplinary approach involving medical, psychological, and rehabilitative support.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is described as an evidence-based intervention for chronic fatigue of any cause, not only for depression or anxiety, and should be considered in appropriate patients.
Post-viral fatigue, particularly following COVID-19 infection, has become an increasingly relevant issue in primary care, with uncertain long-term implications.
Hospital-based rehabilitation significantly reduced fatigue scores from baseline after 8 weeks of supervised exercise therapy.
Telerehabilitation significantly reduced fatigue scores from baseline after 8 weeks.
The unsupervised home exercise programme did not significantly reduce fatigue scores after 8 weeks.
Hospital-based rehabilitation significantly improved physical functioning (SF-36) scores after 8 weeks.
Telerehabilitation significantly improved physical functioning (SF-36) scores after 8 weeks.
The home exercise programme did not significantly improve physical functioning scores after 8 weeks.
All three groups (hospital-based rehabilitation, telerehabilitation, and home programme) showed significant within-group reductions in episodic disability after 8 weeks.
Hospital-based rehabilitation produced a significantly lower (better) fatigue, physical functioning, and disability score than telerehabilitation after 8 weeks.
Hospital-based rehabilitation produced a significantly greater improvement than the home programme after 8 weeks.
Telerehabilitation was significantly more effective than the unsupervised home programme in improving fatigue, physical function, and disability.
The authors concluded that hands-on, hospital-based physiotherapy was substantially more effective than telerehabilitation for managing long COVID-related chronic fatigue syndrome.
All 44 patients diagnosed with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome had provoked vulvodynia confined to the vestibule (vestibulodynia).
Patients with hypermobile features not fully meeting hEDS diagnostic criteria (i.e., Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder) showed similar patterns of genito-pelvic pain as those with full hEDS.
Among patients with provoked vestibulodynia, 31.6% (25/79) had posterior vestibular allodynia, suggesting hypertonic pelvic floor muscle dysfunction as the sole cause of their vestibulodynia.

Among patients with provoked vestibulodynia, 68.4% (54/79) had diffuse vestibular pain, suggesting an inflammatory, neuroproliferative, or hormonal etiology rather than isolated pelvic floor dysfunction.
Hypermobile features (hEDS/HSD) are common among patients presenting for evaluation of genito-pelvic pain.
Urinary frequency was reported in 74.1% (n=20) of hEDS patients undergoing urodynamic evaluation.
Urinary incontinence was reported in 14.8% (n=4) of hEDS patients.
Frequent urinary tract infections were reported in 25.9% (n=7) of hEDS patients.
Bladder pain was reported in 33.3% (n=9) of hEDS patients.
Nocturia was reported in 48.1% (n=13) of hEDS patients.
Weak urinary stream was reported in 51.8% (n=14) of hEDS patients, suggestive of voiding dysfunction.

Urodynamic testing showed no evidence of detrusor overactivity, stress urinary incontinence, or abnormal bladder compliance in hEDS patients, arguing against intrinsic bladder pathology despite prevalent LUTS.
One patient (in this cohort) had incomplete bladder emptying with a pre-study post-void residual of 500 mL.
About 18.5% of hEDS patients undergoing urodynamics showed pelvic floor dysfunction with active EMG activity noted during bladder emptying.
One patient with hEDS had incomplete bladder emptying with a pre-study post-void residual of 500 mL.
Pelvic floor physical therapy was the most commonly recommended intervention for hEDS patients with lower urinary tract symptoms.
Beta-3 agonists were the second most common treatment recommended for overactive bladder symptoms in hEDS patients.
The patient was found to be homozygous for five distinct TNXB variants on gene panel testing performed for suspected classical/pseudo-classical EDS.
In addition to the homozygous splice-region variants, the patient carried a mosaic TNXB missense variant, c.8012C>T (p.Ala2671Val).
RT-PCR of patient-derived RNA and minigene splicing assays showed that the TNXB variants generated an alternatively spliced transcript retaining intron 40 alongside the normal transcript.

Among the tested variants, c.12,210+5G>A produced the most pronounced intron 40 retention in minigene splicing assays and is predicted to generate an in-frame aberrant transcript affecting the fibrinogen C-terminal domain.
The patient presented with generalized joint hypermobility (knees, fingers, elbows, feet), soft/pliable skin, and a history of multiple elbow dislocations, consistent with an EDS phenotype.
The patient reported orthostatic dizziness and chronic constipation, findings interpreted as suggestive of autonomic nervous system involvement in the context of her connective tissue disorder.
Cardiovascular evaluation of the patient identified mild mitral valve regurgitation.
In addition to the homozygous variants, the patient carried a mosaic missense variant c.8012C>T (p.Ala2671Val) in TNXB.
The aberrant TNXB transcripts resulting from intron 40 retention are predicted to affect the fibrinogen C-terminal domain of the protein.
Intron 40 retention was more pronounced when multiple TNXB variants were combined than with individual variants alone in the minigene splicing assays.
Higher self-reported pain frequency over the past week was associated with progressively longer sleep latency in a dose-response manner, after adjusting for age.
Older age groups had lower odds of prolonged sleep latency in the ordinal regression model.

Greater pain frequency was associated with significantly increased odds of reporting frequent poor mental health days (≥14 days/month), with each incremental increase in pain frequency raising the odds by 35%.
Increasing age was associated with decreased odds of reporting poor mental health burden.

Greater pain frequency was associated with significantly increased odds of reporting frequent poor physical health days (≥14 days/month), with each incremental increase in pain frequency raising the odds by 82%.
Increasing age was associated with slightly decreased odds of reporting poor physical health burden.
Pain frequency was high in this hEDS sample, with over one-third of respondents reporting daily pain.

The authors note that patients with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome may have an increased genetic predisposition to coronary thrombosis, which combined with coronary manipulation and postoperative anticoagulation instability after Bentall surgery may raise thrombotic risk, particularly with mechanical valves.
Twenty days after Bentall surgery, angiography and intravascular ultrasound identified a thrombus at the ostium of the left anterior descending coronary artery in this vEDS patient.
Percutaneous coronary intervention successfully removed the LAD ostial thrombus and restored coronary blood flow in this postoperative vEDS patient.

The patient carried a homozygous nonsense mutation in LTBP3 (c.3574G>T, p.Glu1192*), classified as pathogenic, providing the genetic basis for his geleophysic dysplasia through disrupted TGF-β signaling.

The patient also carried a heterozygous COL5A1 missense variant (c.4172A>G, p.Lys1391Arg), classified as likely pathogenic by ACMG criteria and typically linked to EDS Type 1, yet the patient lacked the joint hypermobility and skin fragility characteristic of that condition, suggesting a milder or modifier effect.
The patient had low serum phosphate and ferritin levels, which were corrected with oral phosphate and iron supplementation.
The patient had significant dental caries affecting all primary teeth, hypomineralization of primary and permanent teeth, and multiple periapical abscesses.
Echocardiography at age 7 showed normal cardiac muscle and heart valve function, indicating no current cardiac involvement typically reported in GD.
DEXA scan showed a bone mineral density Z-score of 0.2, within the normal range.
Vitamin D and Vitamin K2 supplementation was initiated to support bone health in this patient with recurrent fractures.
Surgical fixation of the right tibial fracture was performed using an elastic stable intramedullary nail (ESIN), though the fracture recurred with angulation afterward.
Due to recurrent fractures with angulation deformity following ESIN fixation, a 3-point compression orthosis was applied to the right leg to correct the deformity.
The nonsense mutation is predicted to produce a truncated, nonfunctional LTBP3 protein, disrupting normal extracellular matrix composition in bone and other tissues.
A previously reported LTBP3 nonsense mutation (Y744X) has been associated with short stature and oligodontia in other cases, supporting the gene's role in skeletal and dental development.
LTBP3 knockout in mouse models has been shown to impact skeletal system development, supporting the gene's role in bone formation.

The patient's sister was also affected with similar clinical features of GD, while the parents showed no signs of GD or related connective tissue disorders, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance of the LTBP3 variant.

Ciprofloxacin exposure caused 44% mortality in vEDS mice due to aortic or arterial rupture (hemopericardium/hemothorax), whereas all vehicle-treated vEDS mice and wild-type littermates survived the 4-week study.
Aortic tissue from ciprofloxacin-treated vEDS mice showed decreased collagen content compared to vehicle-treated vEDS mice.
Aortic tissue from ciprofloxacin-treated vEDS mice showed decreased lysyl oxidase (LOX) levels compared to vehicle-treated vEDS mice.
Aortic tissue from ciprofloxacin-treated vEDS mice showed increased levels of MMP2 and MMP9 compared to vehicle-treated vEDS mice.

Aortic tissue from ciprofloxacin-treated vEDS mice showed increased apoptosis (cell death) compared to vehicle-treated vEDS mice.
Ciprofloxacin-treated vEDS mouse aortic tissue showed increased macrophage infiltration compared to vehicle-treated vEDS mouse aortic tissue.
Ciprofloxacin-treated vEDS mouse aortic tissue showed increased apoptosis compared to vehicle-treated vEDS mouse aortic tissue.
Generalized joint hypermobility, defined as a Beighton score ≥4, was found in 64% of ganglion cyst patients compared to 19% of controls and was an independent risk factor for ganglion cysts.
Manual occupation was significantly more prevalent among ganglion cyst patients than controls and was identified as an independent risk factor.
A significant positive dose-response trend was observed between increasing Beighton score categories and risk of ganglion cyst.
Body mass index did not differ significantly between ganglion cyst patients and controls.
Foot abnormalities including hypermobility, flat feet, and pronation are proposed as contributors to the cartilage degeneration process in knee osteoarthritis.

In the mixed intervention group (combined exercises and orthopedic insoles), sway length and mean speed with eyes open and closed improved, and the center of gravity ellipse area decreased significantly.
The largest clinical effect on postural sway length with eyes open was observed between the control and exercise groups.
The combined (mixed) intervention group showed large clinical effects versus control for sway length with eyes closed, ellipse area with eyes open, and mean speed with eyes closed.
Quality of life and functioning, as measured by KOOS domains (pain, symptoms, ADL, sports/recreation, QoL), improved significantly with statistically significant between-group differences.

The ellipse area of the center of gravity with eyes open decreased with a large effect size in the mixed group compared to controls.
Mean sway speed with eyes closed improved with a large effect size in the mixed group compared to controls.

No significant differences were found between the exercise-only group and the orthopedic insole-only group regarding symptoms, activities of daily living, sports/recreation, and quality of life outcomes.
The KOOS pain score showed a significant clinical effect favoring orthopedic insoles over exercise alone.
Serum TNF-alpha levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum MMP-3 levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum IL-6 levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Serum IL-6R levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
TNF-alpha serum levels showed a moderate positive correlation with FIQ disease-severity score in FMS patients.

IL-6R serum levels showed a moderate positive correlation with FIQ disease-severity score.
MMP-3 serum levels showed a weak positive correlation with FIQ disease-severity score.
All measured biomarkers correlated significantly with FIQ score in female patients, while only IL-6 showed a significant correlation with FIQ in male patients.
Serum creatine kinase (CK) showed a strong positive correlation with FIQ score in FMS patients.
Serum vitamin D levels showed a strong negative correlation with FIQ score in FMS patients.
Serum uric acid showed a moderate positive correlation with FIQ score.

AST, ALT, free T4, and TSH did not show significant correlations with FIQ score.
ROC curve analysis showed high diagnostic accuracy for TNF-α, IL-6, IL-6R, and MMP-3 in differentiating FMS patients from healthy controls, with TNF-α showing the highest AUC.
CRP levels were not found to be correlated with FIQ scores in fibromyalgia patients.
FIQ (Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire) scores were significantly higher in FMS patients than in healthy controls, confirming greater functional impairment.
The title indicates that luteolin and its methoxylated derivative methoxyluteolin may be preferable polyphenol candidates for infant allergies because they inhibit mast cell activation.
The authors conclude, based on their prior review of human data, that leukotrienes are unlikely to be important direct mediators of symptoms during severe anaphylaxis.

The paper reviews platelet-activating factor as a proposed mediator directly causing severe symptoms during mast cell activation in anaphylaxis, without stating a definitive conclusion in the abstract.
The authors state that patients die from mast cell activation during severe anaphylaxis, including during acute asthma exacerbations.
SMURF2 expression was markedly increased in mast cells from allergic rhinitis patients and in PBMCs/induced sputum from acute asthma patients.
SMURF2 was upregulated in mast cells following IgE-mediated activation, consistent with a role in FcεRI signaling.
SMURF2 was found to positively regulate IgE-dependent mast cell activation in in vitro experiments.
Mast cell-specific Smurf2 deficiency in mice attenuated passive systemic anaphylaxis, indicating a causal role for SMURF2 in anaphylactic responses.
Mast cell-specific Smurf2 deficiency in mice attenuated OVA-induced allergic airway disease.
SMURF2 interacted with NEDD4L and promoted its K27-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby enhancing Syk-mediated FcεRI signaling.
Degradation of NEDD4L by SMURF2 amplifies Syk-mediated signaling downstream of FcεRI, positioning SMURF2 as a positive regulator of mast cell activation.
The authors propose SMURF2 as a potential diagnostic marker and therapeutic target for allergic diseases including asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis.
Quercetin significantly suppressed IL-33-induced cytokine production, degranulation, and apoptosis in RBL-2H3 mast cells in vitro.
Overexpression of ST2 partially reversed the suppressive effects of quercetin on IL-33-stimulated mast cell activation, implicating ST2 as a mediator of quercetin's action.
