In nasal tissues of the mouse AR model, quercetin downregulated expression of IL-33/ST2/NF-κB pathway proteins relative to untreated diseased animals.
Mast cell-derived mediators including histamine, tryptase, chymase, cytokines, and chemokines drive inflammation, angiogenesis, tissue remodelling, and fibrosis in cardiac tissue.
Mast cells participate in atherosclerosis and destabilize atherosclerotic plaques, promoting plaque rupture and associated cardiovascular events.
Mast cells stimulate fibrosis following myocardial infarction.
MCAS presents with symptoms resulting from mediator release including flushing, hypotension, urticaria, angioedema, headache, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Mastocytosis and MCAS diagnosis is rendered by skin and/or bone marrow biopsy.

The review calls for guidance on selecting efficacious mast cell stabilizers that block external stimulus signals, inhibit intracellular signalling, and disrupt degranulation as emerging therapies for MC-related disease.
In a Belgian study, patients with IBS had roughly three times the risk of allergic rhinitis compared with individuals without IBS.
IBS patients experienced more severe allergic rhinitis symptoms compared with individuals without IBS.

IBS-diarrhoea patients sensitised to grass pollen had significant worsening of abdominal symptoms during pollination season, while those sensitised to house dust mite (a perennial allergen) showed no seasonal variation.
IBS is associated with increased intestinal mast cell density, enhanced mediator release upon stimulation, and closer anatomical proximity of mast cells to enteric nerve endings.
Mast cell-derived histamine and tryptase contribute to chloride secretion via PAR-2, a mechanism potentially promoting diarrhoeal symptoms in IBS.
Abdominal pain and diarrhoea are highly prevalent in mastocytosis, a clonal mast cell disorder, supporting the clinical relevance of mast cell-driven symptom generation.
Faecal tryptase is proposed as a biomarker that may help identify IBS patients with a mast cell-driven phenotype, though its clinical utility remains under investigation.
Mast cell stabilisers, antihistamines, and anti-IgE monoclonal antibodies (e.g., omalizumab) have shown symptom improvement in clinical trials for IBS.

Mast cell mediators including histamine, proteases, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes can increase the excitability of vagal and splanchnic afferent nerves, promoting peripheral sensitisation and nociceptor hyperexcitability.

Hyperplasia and activation of mast cells and eosinophils have been linked to heightened luminal sensitivity, altered motility and secretion, and increased intestinal permeability in translational models of IBS.
Middle cerebral arteries from ECM mice showed preserved constriction to serotonin (5-HT) compared to control mice, indicating intact smooth muscle contractile responsiveness.
Endothelium-dependent relaxation to methacholine in ECM MCAs was preserved and was inhibited by L-NAME, demonstrating intact endothelial nitric oxide signalling despite cerebral malaria.
Nitroprusside responses (assessing smooth muscle NO responsiveness) in MCAs were intact in ECM mice, indicating preserved smooth muscle function.
Plasma from ECM mice produced concentration-dependent vasoconstriction of aortic rings, and this constriction was enhanced when nitric oxide synthase was inhibited.

Blockade of 5-HT2A receptors with ketanserin abolished more than 80% of plasma-induced vasoconstriction in a sex-independent manner, indicating plasma serotonin is the predominant circulating vasoconstrictor.

Plasma or serotonin induced robust vasoconstriction when applied to the abluminal (adventitial) surface of arteries, but not when applied intraluminally, revealing a compartment-specific effect of serotonin on vascular tone.

Vasoconstrictive responses of aortic rings to plasma from ECM mice were similar to those from control mice, suggesting no major difference in circulating vasoregulatory molecules despite cerebral malaria infection.

The authors conclude that experimental cerebral malaria does not cause intrinsic endothelial or smooth muscle dysfunction of the middle cerebral artery, and propose that normal circulating serotonin levels could exert vasoconstrictive effects in disease states that compromise vascular barrier integrity.
Basophil activation testing showed polysulfone-specific upregulation of the activation markers CD63 and CD203c, confirming an immediate hypersensitivity reaction to the dialyzer membrane.

Reexposure to the polysulfone-based dialyzer during a subsequent hemodialysis session reproducibly elicited the same anaphylactic reaction as the initial exposure, strongly implicating the membrane as the causative agent.

Serum tryptase, though commonly used as a marker of mast cell activation in anaphylaxis, has limited diagnostic utility in chronic kidney disease patients because baseline levels may be chronically elevated from reduced renal clearance.
The EtOAc fraction of P. amarus showed the highest quantified content of phenolic compounds among the phytochemical classes screened.
The EtOAc fraction contained a considerable amount of flavonoids as quantified by the aluminum chloride colorimetric assay.

The EtOAc fraction of P. amarus produced a dose-dependent inhibition of histamine release from IgE/antigen-stimulated RBL-2H3 mast cells, with strong inhibition at 200 and 300 µg/mL comparable to cromolyn sodium.

Cell viability of RBL-2H3 mast cells remained above 80% for EtOAc fraction concentrations of 50-200 µg/mL but dropped below 80% at 300-400 µg/mL, indicating cytotoxicity only at higher concentrations.

Light microscopy showed that EtOAc fraction treatment (200 µg/mL) markedly reduced degranulation-associated morphological changes (rounding, granule loss) in stimulated mast cells compared to control.
EtOAc fraction (200 µg/mL) substantially lowered intracellular ROS production in activated mast cells compared to control, though less effectively than vitamin C.
EtOAc fraction treatment (200 µg/mL) significantly reduced IL-4 production by about 50% from activated mast cells compared to control, comparable to cromolyn sodium.

EtOAc fraction treatment (200 µg/mL) significantly reduced TNF-α production by about 50% from activated mast cells compared to control, though cromolyn sodium's suppressive effect on TNF-α was stronger.

In OVA-induced allergic mice, EtOAc fraction treatment (50 mg/kg) significantly decreased serum IgE levels that had been elevated by OVA sensitization, comparable to the dexamethasone positive control.
In OVA-induced allergic mice, EtOAc fraction treatment (50 mg/kg) significantly decreased serum histamine levels elevated by OVA sensitization, comparable to the dexamethasone positive control.
Oral EtOAc fraction (50 mg/kg) significantly reduced OVA-induced sneezing behavior by about half compared to the OVA-only group, while dexamethasone (1 mg/kg) produced a greater reduction.

Histological examination showed that EtOAc fraction (or dexamethasone) treatment reduced inflammatory cell (notably eosinophil) infiltration and bronchial wall thickening in lung tissue of OVA-induced allergic mice, partially restoring normal lung structure.
Duox2 expression is markedly upregulated in the colonic epithelium of mice with AOM/DSS-induced chronic colitis and associated fibrosis.
In vivo knockdown of Duox2 using AAV-shRNA mitigated colonic shortening and decreased collagen content, fibrosis markers, and MDA (oxidative stress marker) levels in chronic colitis mice.
Epithelial Duox2 upregulation induces activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome and subsequent release of IL-33.
Paracrine IL-33 released from Duox2/NLRP3-activated epithelium mobilizes and activates mast cells, driving profibrotic factor release and epithelial migration.
Addition of an IL-33 neutralizing antibody in the epithelial-mast cell co-culture model attenuated mast cell activation and fibrosis-promoting effects.
Linarin dose-dependently inhibited compound 48/80-induced degranulation of RBL-2H3 mast cells, significantly reducing beta-hexosaminidase release.
Linarin suppressed phosphorylation of ERK1/2 in compound 48/80-stimulated mast cells.
Linarin suppressed phosphorylation of p38 MAPK in compound 48/80-stimulated mast cells.
Linarin treatment alleviated ovalbumin-induced nasal mucosa pathology in rats, including congestion, oedema, and inflammatory-cell infiltration.
Linarin treatment normalised spleen index in the allergic rhinitis rat model, suggesting improved immune function.
Linarin treatment showed no adverse effects on body weight, serum biochemistry, or histology of heart, liver and kidneys in rats.
Differential expression analysis of four integrated, batch-corrected GEO datasets identified 677 significantly differentially expressed genes between OA and control samples.
WGCNA identified 10 gene co-expression modules, with the turquoise module showing the strongest positive correlation with OA status.
Network target prediction using ChEMBL, SwissTargetPrediction, and SEA databases identified 93 unique molecular targets predicted to interact with TCDD.
Intersection of 93 predicted TCDD targets with 3,542 OA-related genes (from DEG/WGCNA integration) yielded 43 common genes considered candidate mediators of TCDD toxicity in OA.

KEGG enrichment of the 43 TCDD-OA intersection targets showed significant enrichment in neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, calcium signaling, serotonergic synapse, cGMP-PKG signaling, IL-17 signaling, chemokine signaling, cAMP signaling, arachidonic acid metabolism, and vascular pathways (VEGF signaling, vascular smooth muscle contraction).

An integrative machine learning framework of 127 algorithm combinations, validated across a training cohort and two independent external cohorts, identified PTPRC, PTGS1, CBR1, HTR2B, and PTGS2 as hub genes linking TCDD exposure to OA.
Feature selection frequency analysis across 89 converged algorithm combinations showed PTGS1 was selected with 100% frequency, the most stable hub gene identified.
ROC analysis showed PTGS1 had the highest diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing OA from control samples, followed by CBR1, HTR2B, PTGS2, and PTPRC.

In the transcriptomic (GEO-based) analysis PTGS2 appeared downregulated in OA, whereas PTGS1, CBR1, and HTR2B were upregulated and PTPRC showed no significant change; this contrasted with subsequent qPCR/IHC validation showing PTGS2 elevated in OA tissue.
SHAP analysis showed PTGS1 had the highest contribution to the OA prediction model, followed by CBR1, HTR2B, and PTGS2.
CBR1 expression was significantly positively correlated with activated dendritic cells and M1 macrophage infiltration in OA samples.
HTR2B expression showed the most extensive immune correlations among hub genes, positively associated with regulatory T cells and M2 macrophages in OA.
PTGS2 expression was negatively correlated with CD8+ T cells and natural killer cells in OA, suggesting a possible immunosuppressive role.

PTGS2 expression showed the strongest positive correlation with activated mast cells and the strongest negative correlation with resting mast cells among all hub gene-immune cell pairs analyzed in OA samples.
CBR1 expression was positively correlated with resting mast cells and negatively correlated with resting CD4 memory T cells in OA samples.
HTR2B expression was negatively correlated with activated mast cells in OA samples.
Comparing OA and control synovial samples, M0 macrophages, activated dendritic cells, and regulatory T cells were increased, while CD8+ T cells and resting mast cells were decreased in OA.
Molecular docking indicated favorable binding potential between TCDD and all four hub proteins, with PTGS2 showing the strongest predicted binding affinity, followed by CBR1, PTGS1, and HTR2B.

Molecular dynamics simulations showed that TCDD binding restricted local residue mobility in the binding pockets of all four hub proteins without disrupting overall protein stability, and all four complexes reached stable, energetically favorable conformations.

RT-qPCR and IHC validation in OA and healthy control synovial samples confirmed elevated PTGS1 and PTGS2 mRNA and protein expression in OA tissue, consistent with bioinformatics predictions and the established role of COX enzymes in OA.
The I-DN4 questionnaire score did not correlate with intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD), confirming its inaccuracy for diagnosing small fiber neuropathy in a cohort of 872 patients.
Among sensory symptoms, only burning sensation was found to be a moderate predictor of small fiber neuropathy risk, defined by reduced IENFD.

In a prior study of familial amyloid polyneuropathy patients, the author found that burning sensation intensity was inversely correlated with the severity of small fiber neuropathy lesions as assessed by quantitative thermal sensory testing and laser evoked potentials.
Not all forms of allodynia are attributable to small fiber dysfunction; most forms of mechanical allodynia are mediated by large-diameter A-beta fibers rather than small fibers.

Small fiber loss (reduced IENFD) is not always accompanied by pain, and conversely, pain involving small fibers can occur without measurable fiber loss (normal IENFD), a condition termed 'small fiber neuralgia' linked to small fiber hyperexcitability.
The DN4 questionnaire lacks specificity for screening small fiber neuropathy because it was designed to distinguish neuropathic from nociceptive pain, not neuropathic from nociplastic pain.
A family carrying a novel null variant in COL6A5 showed co-occurrence of Chiari malformation type 1 and small fiber neuropathy.
The novel COL6A5 null variant is implicated as a candidate genetic factor associated with small fiber neuropathy in this family.
The primary fibromyalgia study population was predominantly female (86%) versus male (14%), a ratio of approximately 6:1.
The majority (64.8%) of primary fibromyalgia patients were older than 35 years, while only 4% were under 20.
Cardiovascular and metabolic conditions collectively were present in 23.6% of primary fibromyalgia patients.
Hypertension was the most frequently reported comorbidity in primary fibromyalgia, affecting 16.3% of patients (10.3% isolated, 6.0% with concurrent diabetes).
Diabetes mellitus alone was reported in 4.7% of primary fibromyalgia patients.

Hypothyroidism was present in 9% of primary fibromyalgia patients, consistent with a proposed link between thyroid dysfunction and fibromyalgia via shared clinical features and central sensitization mechanisms.

Insomnia was reported by 35.5% of primary fibromyalgia patients, consistent with sleep dysfunction as both symptom and contributor to fibromyalgia via increased pain sensitivity and cortisol-mediated stress responses.
Vitamin D deficiency was highly prevalent (42.2%) among primary fibromyalgia patients, potentially contributing to increased pain perception, reduced muscle strength, and fatigue.

Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) was reported in 40.2% of primary fibromyalgia patients, exceeding rates commonly reported internationally, and is proposed to share pathophysiological mechanisms with fibromyalgia including central sensitization, autonomic dysregulation, and gut-brain axis disturbances.
Housewives constituted the largest occupational group among primary fibromyalgia patients (67.1%, n=202), possibly reflecting domestic/caregiving burden and gender roles in Palestinian society.
A strong negative correlation was found between occupation and sex among primary fibromyalgia patients, reflecting broader gender roles and occupational structure in Palestinian society.
A moderate negative correlation was found between occupation and age among primary fibromyalgia patients.
A weak positive correlation was identified between age and sex among primary fibromyalgia patients.
The ctgf promoter from the marine teleost Nibea coibor was characterized as a 3,185 bp sequence containing conserved cis-elements including TATA box, SP-1, Smad-3, and NF-κB sites.
Truncation assays identified a core functional region of the ctgf promoter spanning -785 to +166 bp that drives its transcriptional activity.
Site-directed mutagenesis of the SP-1 binding site in the ctgf promoter enhanced promoter activity, suggesting SP-1 normally acts as a repressor of ctgf transcription.
Mutation of the Smad-3 binding site at position -290 bp in the ctgf promoter suppressed promoter activity, indicating Smad-3 is a positive regulator of ctgf transcription.
Mutation of the NF-κB binding site at position -262 bp in the ctgf promoter suppressed promoter activity, indicating NF-κB is a positive regulator of ctgf transcription.
TGF-β1 treatment of swim bladder cells stably transfected with a ctgf promoter-driven EGFP reporter increased ctgf promoter activity in concert with promoted collagen synthesis.
In the UUO mouse model, TG2 expression increased progressively with kidney injury severity, correlating with cortical thinning, collagen I, α-SMA, P21 expression, and Sirius Red-stained fibrosis.

Cysteamine (TG2 inhibitor) dose-dependently reversed TGF-β-induced upregulation of fibronectin, periostin, collagen IV, TNF-α, and integrin-α5 in hPTECs and produced similar effects in NIH3T3 fibroblasts.
TGF-β markedly increased apoptosis in hPTECs, and cysteamine significantly attenuated this apoptotic response in a dose-dependent manner at 2 mM and 4 mM.

Proteomic profiling of hPTEC-derived EVs identified 537 differentially expressed proteins across control, TGF-β, and TGF-β+cysteamine conditions, with 184 proteins statistically significant by one-way ANOVA.

DEP clusters showed distinct enriched pathways: clusters 1/3 linked to TGF-β activation/regulation and ECM organization, cluster 2 to Rho GTPase and Wnt signaling/cytoskeletal dynamics, and cluster 4 to Notch signaling and ECM organization.
LTBP2 was significantly downregulated in EVs following TG2 inhibition with cysteamine, implicating regulation of TGF-β activation in the fibrosis remodeling phase.
The collagen alpha-1(XVIII) chain, previously reported upregulated in EVs from CKD patients, was significantly suppressed in EVs after TG2 inhibition in this study.

Tenascin X expression decreased following TGF-β activation while tenascin C expression increased after TG2 inhibition, indicating differential regulation of tenascin family ECM proteins by TG2 activity.
CTGF showed reversible expression in EVs, increasing with TGF-β stimulation and decreasing with TG2 inhibition, supporting its role in both fibrosis progression and resolution.

IGFBP-5 exhibited a reversible EV expression pattern following TG2 inhibition, suggesting a potential role as a kidney fibrosis biomarker, consistent with prior reports of elevated IGFBP-5 in CKD patient plasma.
Periostin exhibited reversible EV expression in response to TGF-β stimulation and TG2 inhibition, supporting its relevance as a therapeutic target and biomarker of kidney fibrosis.
PAI-1 was associated with fibrosis-related EV pathways, consistent with its known role in inhibiting plasmin-mediated ECM degradation and promoting matrix accumulation in kidney fibrosis.

Cluster 2 EV DEPs enriched for lamellipodium assembly and Arp2/3 complex-mediated actin nucleation showed significantly decreased expression after TG2 inhibition, suggesting TG2 inhibition affects cytoskeletal remodeling linked to fibroblast migration.
Genetic testing identified a COL1A2 p.Gly358Ser mutation in the neonate, consistent with a molecular diagnosis of type II osteogenesis imperfecta.

The neonate's phenotype (survival with a relatively stable clinical course) despite carrying a mutation typically associated with lethal type II OI suggested a severe but non-lethal phenotype closer to type III OI, highlighting limitations of the Sillence classification.

Intravenous zoledronic acid (0.05 mg every six months, first dose day 42 of life) with calcium and vitamin D supplementation was well tolerated, with only transient post-infusion fever and no new fractures at short-term follow-up.
Pain management escalated from paracetamol to intermittent morphine infusion due to persistently elevated EDIN neonatal pain scores, with morphine successfully tapered without withdrawal symptoms.
Echocardiography identified a small membranous ventricular septal defect as an extra-skeletal comorbidity in the neonate with osteogenesis imperfecta.
Cranio-cervical CT of the neonate showed turribrachycephaly, severe osteopenia with calvarial thinning, widened sutures, and diffuse bone erosions, consistent with severe osteogenesis imperfecta.

Prenatal ultrasound in the current pregnancy detected intrauterine growth restriction and lower limb deformities, with femoral length at the third percentile at 27 weeks and overall fetal growth at the first percentile by 37 weeks, prompting suspicion of a severe skeletal dysplasia.

Bisphosphonates such as zoledronic acid inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, increasing bone mineral density and reducing fracture incidence, but do not correct the underlying collagen genetic defect and carry potential long-term risks such as delayed fracture healing and osteonecrosis.
Rare functional variants in FBN2 were present in 9 of 42 (21%) individuals with type 1b spontaneous spinal CSF leaks.
FBN2 rare functional variants were significantly enriched in patients with type 1b spinal CSF leak compared with the Mendel discovery control cohort.
FBN2 rare functional variants were significantly enriched in patients with type 1b spinal CSF leak compared with the Belgian whole-exome validation cohort.
FBN2 rare functional variants were significantly enriched in patients with type 1b spinal CSF leak compared with the Belgian thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection validation cohort.
FBN2 variants found in patients showed non-random clustering, being enriched in the TGF-β binding protein-like (TB) domains of fibrillin-2.
Two of three tested FBN2 variant protein fragments showed reduced integrin-mediated adhesion to human dural fibroblasts in vitro compared with wild-type fibrillin-2 fragments.
CRISPR-Cas9 mouse models carrying Fbn2 variants equivalent to the human TB domain variants showed increased predisposition to dural rupture upon controlled leak induction testing.
Nine of 42 individuals (21%) with type 1b spontaneous spinal CSF leak carried rare functional variants in FBN2, establishing a substantial candidate-variant prevalence in this cohort.
The authors conclude that rare deleterious FBN2 variants may cause type 1b spontaneous spinal CSF leak and recommend incorporating FBN2 genetic testing into clinical practice for these patients.
A LASSO logistic regression model using 16S rRNA microbiome data distinguished IBS patients from healthy controls with sensitivity above 80% and specificity above 90%.
A random forest classifier combining shotgun metagenomics and untargeted urinary metabolomics distinguished pediatric IBS patients from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.93.

Resting-state functional connectivity classification of IBS versus matched healthy controls achieved 75% accuracy with a wide confidence interval, the lowest point estimate among the three neuroimaging ML studies reviewed.
An SVM model using functional connectivity strength features classified IBS versus healthy controls with 91.9% accuracy in a smaller single-site cohort, without a reported confidence interval.

A spatiotemporal graph convolutional network applied to dynamic functional connectivity achieved 83.51% classification accuracy under five-fold cross-validation, and its interpretability module identified altered brain regions but could not determine causal direction or effect sign.
Combining 16S rRNA microbiota profiling with urinary metabolomics improved IBS classification (AUC 0.74) relative to either modality alone (microbiota AUC 0.54, near chance; metabolomics AUC 0.65).
Longitudinal multiomics integration achieved a higher headline AUC of 0.82 for IBS classification and identified subset-specific mechanisms not visible in any single modality.

A logistic regression model using validated psychological and symptom inventories classified IBS versus healthy controls with balanced accuracy 0.93, recall 1.0, and precision 0.91, but this was estimated on a very small held-out test set.

A logistic regression model using psychological and quality-of-life features classified IBS versus healthy controls with an AUC of 0.86 under 10-fold cross-validation, reported with an explicit confidence interval in a larger sample.

A model integrating baseline gut microbiome and brain neuroimaging features predicted cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) response in IBS patients with an AUROC of approximately 0.96, alongside bidirectional posttreatment brain-gut-microbiome changes associated with symptom improvement, but this has not been externally replicated.

Across microbiome and neuroimaging ML studies, classifier discrimination between IBS and clinically overlapping disorders such as functional dyspepsia is consistently weaker than discrimination between IBS and healthy controls, limiting real-world differential diagnostic utility.
IBS patients often show elevated sympathetic activity as reflected by an increased low-frequency/high-frequency HRV ratio, which is linked to symptom severity.
IBS-C patients show more pronounced parasympathetic reductions whereas IBS-D patients are characterized primarily by sympathetic overactivation, indicating subtype-specific autonomic patterns.
About 65% of IBS patients report concurrent autonomic symptoms such as orthostatic hypotension and palpitations.
Reduced parasympathetic activity is associated with abdominal pain severity scores in IBS.
Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) improves autonomic function while relieving rectal hypersensitivity and abnormal defecation in IBS.
A systematic review found the prevalence of anxiety and depressive symptoms in IBS to be 39.1% and 28.8%, respectively.
IBS patients show reduced gray matter density in the anterior/medial thalamus, which may be linked to subclinical anxiety or depression.
Oxytocin administered at doses of 20 mU/min or higher elevates thresholds for visceral perception in IBS patients, likely via action on visceral afferents.
Polymorphisms in the serotonin transporter gene are strongly linked to IBS risk, particularly IBS-D, in Caucasian and Asian populations with high rectal mucosal serotonin levels.
IBS disease severity correlates with a fecal microbiota profile of reduced bacterial richness and diversity.
Colonizing germ-free animals with fecal microbiota from IBS patients induces visceral hypersensitivity and alters intestinal permeability and GI transit time.
IBS patients show higher mucosal innervation density and more TRPV1-positive nerve fibers than controls, correlating with hypersensitivity to rectal distension and heat.

Postinfectious IBS patients show elevated GAS5 lncRNA in colonic extracellular vesicles, which upregulates NMDA receptor subunit NR2B by inhibiting miR-23a/b, mediating visceral hypersensitivity; GAS5 blockade or miR-23 precursor supplementation reverses hyperalgesia in mice.
Both IBS patients and controls with early adverse life events (EALs) exhibited a heightened cortisol response to visceral stress relative to those without EALs.
In an IBS rat model, chronic acute combined stress decreased hippocampal BDNF expression, linked to depression- and anxiety-like behaviors, which antidepressant treatment could reverse.
Lactobacillus rhamnosus reduced stress-induced anxiety- and depression-like behaviors by modulating forebrain GABA levels via the vagus nerve in an animal model.
Chronic lesion of gut-innervating vagal afferent neurons alters anxiety behavior and anxiety-associated gene networks in the amygdala of male rats.
In rats, electrical vagus nerve stimulation blocks serotonin-driven endocannabinoid release in the duodenum, inhibiting visceral nociceptive transmission.

5-HT3 receptor antagonists such as alosetron alleviate IBS-D symptoms but their constipating effects limit use in IBS-C, while 5-HT4 agonists such as tegaserod enhance intestinal motility to treat IBS-C.

The beta3-adrenoceptor agonist GW427353 stimulates receptors on human enteric neurons and adipocytes, prompting somatostatin release, which activates SST2 receptors on enteric neurons to reduce neuronal excitability.
Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis causes persistent intestinal motility disorders through functional changes in enteric glial cells.
Individualized HRV-guided training may be more effective than traditional high-intensity interval training for improving autonomic balance in IBS.
Sympathetic nervous system dysfunction is associated with mucosal immune alterations in IBS, and this SNS dysfunction may be induced by early-life stress.
Serum IL-11 levels were significantly higher in female ME/CFS patients compared to age-matched healthy female controls.
Serum MMP-9 levels were significantly elevated in female ME/CFS patients compared to age-matched healthy female controls.
Stimulation of cultured human mast cells with recombinant EBV protein significantly increased MMP-9 release compared to untreated cells, with LPS as a positive control also inducing MMP-9 release.
Fifteen percent of the women with ME/CFS developed rheumatoid arthritis during the 16-year follow-up.
Ten percent of the participants were diagnosed with cervical or breast cancer during the follow-up period.
Five percent of participants experienced a premature myocardial infarction during follow-up.
Five percent of participants developed bronchial asthma during the 16-year follow-up.
Twenty percent of the participants were diagnosed with clinical depression during the follow-up period.
ME/CFS symptoms progressed in 15% of the participants over the 16-year follow-up period.
Five percent of the participants reported infertility during follow-up.
Fifteen percent of the participants developed arterial hypertension during the follow-up period.
Over the 16-year follow-up, 85% of the women with ME/CFS developed significant somatic or psychiatric conditions, with only 15% reporting no symptom worsening or new diagnosis.
Gut microbiome alpha-diversity did not differ significantly between ME/CFS, long COVID, and healthy control groups.

Beta-diversity analyses showed small but statistically significant disease-associated differences in gut microbiome community composition among ME/CFS, long COVID, and healthy controls, though with broad overlap between groups.
Differential abundance testing found stronger microbiome signals when comparing each disease group to healthy controls than when directly comparing ME/CFS to long COVID.
Sutterella was enriched in both ME/CFS and long COVID gut microbiomes relative to healthy controls.
Terrisporobacter was depleted in both ME/CFS and long COVID gut microbiomes relative to healthy controls.
Lachnospiraceae was depleted in both ME/CFS and long COVID gut microbiomes relative to healthy controls.

Predicted metagenomic functional profiling revealed shared disease-versus-control alterations in pathways involving anaerobic acetate/H2 carbon flow, inositol/polyol degradation, phosphonate/C1-related metabolism, and lysine-derived fermentation in both ME/CFS and long COVID.

Regression analyses showed the gut microbiome had the strongest associations with fatigue-related and physiosomatic symptom domains, while affective, cognitive, and gastrointestinal symptom domains showed weaker associations.
Predicted functional pathways related to lysine-derived fermentation showed shared alterations in both ME/CFS and long COVID compared to healthy controls.
Regression analyses found that microbiome variation showed the strongest associations with fatigue-related and physiosomatic symptom domains.
Affective, cognitive, and gastrointestinal symptom-domain scores showed comparatively weaker associations with microbiome variation than fatigue-related and physiosomatic domains.
Differential abundance analysis found weaker and fewer signals when directly comparing ME/CFS to long COVID than when each disease group was compared separately to healthy controls.
Plasma extracellular vesicle concentrations were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Of 424 proteins detected in plasma EVs, 11 showed different levels between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, though this did not survive correction for multiple testing.
The ME/CFS-associated EV proteins were predicted to mainly originate from erythroid cells, hepatocytes, and plasma B cells based on tissue expression data.
The paper states that each SARS-CoV-2 reinfection may increase the risk of long-term disability, with 5%–8% of infections resulting in Long COVID.

The review states that evidence shows increased risks of neurodegenerative, autoimmune, and cardiovascular disorders after SARS-CoV-2 infection, involving immune dysregulation, chronic inflammation, autonomic dysfunction, and tissue injury.
The paper reports that millions of people in Europe and North America face long-term work disability due to Long COVID and ME/CFS, worsening labor shortages and increasing social costs.
The paper notes that in Germany alone, hundreds of thousands of individuals are affected by post-infectious syndromes, causing billions in lost productivity.

Electroacupuncture treatment significantly improved behavioral performance in CFS model rats as measured by the general semi-quantitative score, Morris water maze test, open field test, and exhaustive treadmill test.
Compared with healthy controls, CFS model rats showed abnormal cellular morphology, disorganized cell arrangement, and reduced Nissl bodies in the hippocampal CA1 region on HE and Nissl staining.
Electroacupuncture treatment ameliorated the hippocampal CA1 pathological changes observed in model CFS rats.

18F-FDG PET/CT imaging showed that mean and maximum standardized uptake values in the anterior-dorsal and posterior hippocampus were significantly decreased in model CFS rats compared to healthy controls, indicating impaired glucose metabolism.
Electroacupuncture treatment significantly increased both SUV-mean and SUV-max in the anterior-dorsal and posterior hippocampal subregions relative to the untreated model group.
Nearly half of patients diagnosed with EDS or HSD reported moderate to severe pain at the time of diagnosis.
Older age was an independent predictor of moderate to severe pain at diagnosis in EDS/HSD patients.
A diagnosis of hypermobile EDS was independently associated with greater odds of moderate to severe pain compared to other subtypes/HSD.
Presence of headache was independently associated with increased odds of moderate to severe pain in EDS/HSD patients.
Use of pain medications, particularly paracetamol and NSAIDs, was strongly associated with higher pain severity among EDS/HSD patients.

A homozygous likely pathogenic missense variant in COL1A1 (p.Glu684Lys) was identified in a 10-month-old boy presenting with an arthrochalasia-like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome phenotype, with both parents confirmed as heterozygous carriers.

The recurrent homozygous COL1A1 p.(Glu684Lys) variant is associated with a phenotypic spectrum ranging from a severe neonatal form with respiratory distress and recurrent fractures to a milder classical EDS-like presentation, with this case representing intermediate severity.

Collagenopathies such as autosomal recessive arthrochalasia-like EDS should be considered in the differential diagnosis of congenital hypotonia, even when initially suggestive of a neuromuscular disorder.

In patients who returned to sport after primary ACL reconstruction, each additional positive test on the Beighton Score was associated with a 10% higher adjusted hazard of sustaining a second ACL injury (graft rupture or contralateral ACL injury).
Each additional positive Beighton Score test was independently associated with a 15% higher adjusted hazard of graft rupture specifically.
The number of positive Beighton Score tests was not significantly associated with the adjusted hazard of contralateral ACL injury.
The highest proportions of second ACL injury were observed among patients with total Beighton Scores of 9 (21.4%), 5 (21.1%), and 7 (18.4%).

Graft ruptures occurred earlier after return to sport (median 7.6 months) than contralateral ACL injuries (median 28.0 months), suggesting the two second-injury types follow distinct temporal patterns.
Loss of function of the zinc transporter ZIP13 (SLC39A13) causes connective tissue abnormalities, impaired bone and tooth development, and spondylodysplastic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome Type 3 in humans.
ZIP13 is predominantly localized to the Golgi apparatus, where it regulates metal homeostasis and modulates zinc-dependent TGF-beta and bone morphogenic protein signalling pathways.
Emerging evidence indicates ZIP13 transports both zinc and iron, functioning as a metal distributor that regulates intracellular metal allocation in a context-dependent manner.
Recent studies expand ZIP13's functional role beyond connective tissue to adipose tissue biology, skeletal muscle maintenance, cardiac homeostasis, and stem cell differentiation.
Joint hypermobility, along with low energy availability and low body mass index, is identified as an individual risk factor that may increase musculoskeletal injury risk in dancers.
Emerging but limited evidence suggests dance therapy may provide benefits as a non-pharmacological intervention for chronic musculoskeletal conditions, particularly fibromyalgia.
Oxygen-ozone autohaemotherapy is proposed to activate the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway in fibromyalgia patients.
Biomarker analyses across reviewed studies indicate reduced oxidative stress markers following O2-O3-AHT in fibromyalgia patients.
O2-O3-AHT is proposed to enhance mitochondrial resilience/function as part of its multi-target action in fibromyalgia.
Small fibre pathology/dysfunction is implicated as a neuropathic component of fibromyalgia that O2-O3-AHT may target.
Clinical studies reviewed report improvements in pain, sleep quality, fatigue, and overall functional status in fibromyalgia patients treated with O2-O3-AHT.
Case reports describe haemolysis and renal failure associated with the use of excessive ozone concentrations above 60 μg/mL during oxygen-ozone autohaemotherapy.
Hyperkalaemia was documented as an adverse event in patients with complex comorbidities including hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease undergoing O2-O3-AHT.
Myocardial infarction and ischaemic events were reported, attributed to vasoconstrictive and pro-thrombotic effects of the therapy.
Cerebral gas embolism was reported in patients with patent foramen ovale undergoing O2-O3-AHT.
Autonomic reactions were reported to be related to rapid reinfusion rates during O2-O3-AHT.
Anaphylactic reactions were reported, linked to materials used in the equipment during O2-O3-AHT.
Infectious complications following oxygen-ozone autohaemotherapy were reported as a result of breaches in aseptic protocol rather than the therapy itself.

The true incidence of serious adverse events from oxygen-ozone autohaemotherapy cannot be reliably quantified because of the absence of prospective registries and reliable denominator data, and a frequently cited historical low estimate is of uncertain methodology.
Mandatory screening for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is identified as a key safety measure to reduce haemolytic risk before oxygen-ozone autohaemotherapy.
Adherence to recommended ozone concentrations of 10-40 μg/mL, rather than excessive concentrations above 60 μg/mL, is recommended as a safety measure to reduce adverse events.
Controlling reinfusion rates to below 50 drops per minute is recommended to reduce autonomic reactions during oxygen-ozone autohaemotherapy.
The review concludes that current evidence does not show a pattern of frequent serious unexpected harm from oxygen-ozone autohaemotherapy when a standardised protocol is followed.
Nearly half of the fibromyalgia patients studied had severe IBS symptoms based on the IBS-SSS.
Fibromyalgia patients with severe IBS had higher widespread pain index and symptom severity scale scores compared with those with mild-moderate IBS, indicating a more severe FM phenotype.
Fibromyalgia patients with severe IBS had increased anxiety and depressive symptoms and reduced sleep duration compared to those with mild-moderate IBS.

Skin biopsy showed that fibromyalgia patients with severe IBS had a higher prevalence of reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density, particularly at proximal biopsy sites, compared with those with mild-moderate IBS.

IBS symptom severity scores were negatively correlated with proximal intraepidermal nerve fibre density in fibromyalgia patients, indicating that greater gastrointestinal symptom severity is linked to more pronounced small fibre loss.

IBS severity identifies a clinically more severe fibromyalgia phenotype associated with small fibre pathology, suggesting a possible interaction between gastrointestinal dysfunction and peripheral nerve involvement, though mechanistic pathways remain unclear.
Across included studies, fibromyalgia patients most frequently showed reduced gut microbial diversity.
Butyrate-producing taxa, notably Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, were depleted in fibromyalgia patients across included studies.
Shifts (compositional changes) in Bifidobacterium and Prevotella abundance were reported in fibromyalgia patients.

Pooled meta-analytic evidence shows individuals with a history of any childhood trauma have about 1.6-fold greater odds of having IBS, with physical and sexual trauma as particularly strong predictors.
ACE prevalence is higher among IBS patients (63%-80%) than healthy controls (48%-59%) across multiple cultures and continents.
The relationship between ACE burden and IBS risk shows a dose-response pattern, with each additional ACE increasing IBS likelihood and severe IBS symptoms linked to exposure to four or more ACEs.

Meta-analytic data show the ACE-IBS association is significant in females but not in males, although some large clinical studies find the association in both sexes with different predominant trauma types.

Somatization mediates the relationship between childhood abuse and the severity of abdominal pain and bloating in IBS patients.
Disturbance of Self-Organization (DSO) symptoms mediate the impact of childhood adversity on IBS symptoms and are associated with greater IBS severity than PTSD symptoms alone.
Lower birth weight is identified as a significant predictor of IBS development in adulthood.
Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery is associated with slightly increased odds of IBS in young adulthood in population studies.
Childhood gastroenteritis and other early inflammatory events (UTIs, cow's milk protein allergy) are established risk factors for post-infectious IBS and other functional GI disorders.

IBS patients with a history of early adverse life events show HPA axis hyperresponsiveness to visceral stressors such as endoscopy, with higher and more prolonged cortisol release, an effect more linked to trauma history than IBS diagnosis itself.

In female rats, unpredictable early life stress induces visceral hypersensitivity associated with upregulated CRF and glucocorticoid receptor in the central amygdala, and knockdown of CeA CRF or CRF1R antagonism reverses this hypersensitivity.
In the hypothalamic PVN, early life stress activates resident mast cells that release histamine, which activates neighboring CRF neurons via histamine H2 receptors, driving visceral hypersensitivity.

Early life stress reduces expression of the glial glutamate transporter EAAT-1 in the spinal cord, impairing glutamate reuptake and promoting central sensitization.

Early life stress expands intestinal stem cells and biases their differentiation toward enterochromaffin cells via NGF-TrkA activation and Wnt/β-catenin crosstalk, increasing mucosal serotonin availability and contributing to visceral hyperalgesia.

Early life stress induces a sex-dependent phenotypic switch in enteric glia, particularly in males, making them resemble the female phenotype, linked to altered prostaglandin and endocannabinoid signaling.

Decreased levels of analgesic GABA-containing bacterial lipopeptides are linked to visceral hypersensitivity in both prenatally stressed mice and IBS patients.

A higher number of benevolent childhood experiences is associated with reduced odds of developing IBS.
A post hoc analysis found that a history of childhood abuse did not predict response to paroxetine treatment in IBS patients.

Exclusive breastfeeding has been shown to be a protective factor against early disorders of gut-brain interaction.

Disinhibition of PVN-projecting GABAergic neurons in the anteroventral bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, leading to increased excitability of PVN CRF neurons, was identified as a mechanism underlying visceral hypersensitivity in an ELS model.

The Lewis rat strain, which exhibits inherent stress sensitivity and susceptibility to inflammation, shows baseline visceral hypersensitivity and morphological gut alterations compared to other strains, modeling the genetic vulnerability component of IBS.

Levetiracetam was tried but was not effective for the patient's attacks.

Diabetic gastroparesis is estimated to affect 5–12% of individuals with long-term diabetes when systematic gastric emptying evaluation is used, but only 0.16% of patients had a documented diagnosis in a large US administrative database of over 43 million records lacking objective testing.
In a large US cohort using clinical diagnosis without systematic gastric emptying testing, gastroparesis prevalence was 4.6% among type 1 diabetes patients versus 1.3% among type 2 diabetes patients.
Among identified etiologies of gastroparesis in large national claims databases applying strict diagnostic criteria, diabetic etiology accounted for approximately 57.4% of all reported cases.

Risk correlates for diabetic gastroparesis include long disease duration, poor glycemic control, presence of other diabetic complications (especially peripheral and autonomic neuropathy), prior bariatric surgery, and female sex, while psychological factors such as anxiety, depression, and somatization may modulate symptom severity independent of objective gastric emptying findings.

In diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia and reduced trophic factors, particularly reduced stem cell factor (SCF) signaling through KIT/c-KIT, cause loss or dysfunction of interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs), leading to dysregulated gastric emptying, a condition termed 'cajalopathy' considered the most common alteration in diabetic and idiopathic gastroparesis.
Reduced expression of the enzyme heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) promotes loss of interstitial cells of Cajal and the development of gastroparesis.

Constipation is present in approximately one-third of patients with gastroparesis and can exacerbate gastric symptoms via altered intestinal transit and retrograde feedback signals, reflecting a pan-enteric motility disturbance.

Gastric emptying scintigraphy diagnostic thresholds for delayed gastric emptying are >90% retention at 1 hour, >60% at 2 hours, and >10% at 4 hours, with the 4-hour timepoint considered most sensitive and specific for severity stratification.

Small-particle size diets have been shown to improve symptom severity and quality of life compared with a standard soft diet in diabetic gastroparesis, despite showing similar effects on objective gastric emptying.
Metoclopramide is the only FDA-approved drug for gastroparesis but its use is limited to less than 12 weeks due to risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia.

The selective 5-HT4 receptor agonist prucalopride may improve nausea, early satiety, bloating, and quality of life in selected patients with gastroparesis, though it carries gastrointestinal side effects.

GLP-1 receptor agonists slow gastric emptying and may worsen gastroparetic symptoms and late hyperglycemia if insulin bolus timing is not adjusted, sometimes requiring dose reduction, discontinuation, or switching therapies in symptomatic diabetic gastroparesis.
Gastric per-oral endoscopic myotomy (G-POEM), which reduces pyloric resistance, improves symptoms in refractory diabetic gastroparesis with success rates around 70% at 1 year in small series.

Hybrid closed-loop automated insulin delivery (AID) systems can increase time-in-range and reduce hypoglycemia in patients with diabetic gastroparesis, with improvements comparable to those seen in patients without gastrointestinal complications, though data remain limited and largely observational.

Delayed and erratic gastric emptying in diabetic gastroparesis produces a temporal mismatch between prandial insulin action and nutrient absorption, causing early postprandial hypoglycemia followed by late postprandial hyperglycemia.
Exposure to urban acoustic environments worsened patient global impression of change with a large effect size compared with the broadband sound comparator and silence control conditions.
Urban acoustic environment exposure worsened pain intensity with a medium effect size relative to the active comparator (broadband sounds) and attention-placebo control (silence).

Urban acoustic environment exposure worsened static quantitative sensory testing measures (e.g., pressure pain detection thresholds and intensity ratings) with a medium effect size compared with control conditions.
Pain intensity during the trial was predicted by pain catastrophizing, a prespecified psychological covariate.
Recent meta-analyses using Rome IV criteria estimate global IBS prevalence between 13.28% (probability-sampling studies) and 17.14% (overall), with a higher prevalence among women.
In IBS-D, increased 5-HT release from enterochromaffin cells activates ENS 5-HT3/4 receptors, driving colonic hypermotility and accelerated transit.
IBS-C patients show reduced 5-HT levels, which is associated with delayed colonic transit and gastric emptying.
Stool consistency correlates positively with colonic transit time in IBS, supporting a functional link between ENS-mediated motility and bowel habit.
Mast cell-derived histamine activates neuronal TRPV1 channels in the ENS, inducing visceral hypersensitivity in IBS.
Eosinophils enhance ENS synaptic plasticity via NGF, contributing to IBS pathophysiology.
SCFAs and PYY regulate intestinal sensitivity in IBS, with SCFAs inhibiting colonic peristalsis and PYY increasing 5-HT synthesis.
Abdominal distension in IBS correlates positively with orofecal transit time, while pain and flatulence do not, suggesting sensory and motor ENS pathways are independently regulated.

Abnormal proliferation and activation of enteric glial cells in the colonic myenteric plexus directly affects colonic contractility in IBS-D rats, and inhibiting EGC activation ameliorates motor dysfunction.
Purines released from enteric neurons act on EGC P2Y1 receptors, forming a neuron-glia signaling axis that regulates colonic contractility and contributes to IBS-D pathogenesis.

Spore-forming bacteria promote 5-HT synthesis in enterochromaffin cells; resulting 5-HT elevation activates 5-HT3 receptors on sensory afferents, amplifying pain signaling and contributing to abdominal pain and diarrhea.
Reduced Lactobacillus abundance lowers 5-HT levels, weakening propulsive signals and predisposing to constipation in IBS.
Gut bacteria modulate dopamine metabolism, and activation of dopamine D2 receptors attenuates visceral hyperalgesia in IBS.
The probiotic Saccharomyces boulardii directly alters myenteric neuron neurochemistry, suggesting bacterial-neuronal interactions can reset distorted ENS signaling in IBS.

In visceral hypersensitivity-predominant IBS, dysbiosis triggers IL-6/TNF-alpha release and mast cell histamine activation that stimulates TRPV1 channels on sensory neurons, distorting pain signal gain.
Rifaximin, a non-absorbable antibiotic, reduces ENS hyperexcitability in diarrhea-predominant IBS by suppressing fermentative gas-producing bacteria.
Tricyclic antidepressants are effective in IBS, particularly reducing abdominal pain and diarrhea, by modulating serotonergic and noradrenergic signaling in the CNS and ENS.

High-fiber diets increase microbial fermentation to SCFAs such as butyrate, which enhance excitatory enteric neuron activity, induce neuroplasticity, and strengthen peristalsis, proposed as beneficial in IBS-C.
High-fat diets trigger inflammation and altered neuronal receptor sensitivity, leading to ENS "desensitization" and impaired gut motility.
Colonic PYY+ neuropod cells express TLR5, which senses bacterial flagellin and triggers vagal activation via NPY2R to regulate feeding, a mechanism proposed to explain rapid symptom onset in IBS.
FMT trials for IBS and IBD show inconsistent outcomes, highlighting the need for biomarker-guided donor selection rather than broad, unstratified application.

The authors hypothesize that IBS subtypes reflect a shift in cholinergic/nitrergic excitatory-inhibitory balance: cholinergic excitation predominance in IBS-D and nitrergic inhibition predominance in IBS-C.
Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is caused by a dominant R206H mutation in ACVR1, present in 97% of cases, leading to heterotopic ossification triggered by inflammatory flare-ups.

Allele-selective siRNA targeting mutant ACVR1, conjugated to docosanoic acid (DCA), produced a profound reduction of heterotopic ossification in a murine FOP model using both post-trauma and pre-trauma intervention strategies.
Combination siRNA therapy targeting both mutant ACVR1 and a key inflammatory regulator outperformed modulation of either target alone in reducing heterotopic ossification.

DCA-conjugated allele-selective siRNA targeting mutant ACVR1(R206H), given alone, produced profound reduction of heterotopic ossification in a murine FOP model using both post-trauma (responsive) and pre-trauma (preventative) dosing strategies.
Combination therapy pairing the ACVR1(R206H)-selective siRNA with an siRNA targeting a key inflammatory regulator outperformed modulation of either target alone in reducing heterotopic ossification.

A newly engineered class of lipophilic divalent siRNAs, capable of simultaneously targeting both the ACVR1 and inflammatory pathways with a single compound, showed superior muscle accumulation and therapeutic efficacy compared to single-target siRNAs.
siRNA treatment inhibited key signaling pathways within muscle-resident fibroadipogenic progenitors (FAPs), leading to a significant reduction in cartilage, bone, and connective tissue formation.

Allele selectivity of the siRNA is essential because wildtype ACVR1 is crucial for multiple functions including skeletal homeostasis and development, so sparing the wildtype allele avoids disrupting normal ACVR1 function.
Blocking neuronal nitric oxide synthase in the insular cortex with NPLA enhanced the pressor and tachycardic responses to acute restraint stress in rats.
Scavenging NO with carboxy-PTIO in the insular cortex also enhanced the pressor and tachycardic responses to restraint stress.
Inhibiting sGC with ODQ in the insular cortex enhanced the pressor and tachycardic responses to restraint stress.
Inhibition of nNOS with NPLA in the insular cortex reduced the restraint-induced rise in circulating corticosterone.
Scavenging NO with carboxy-PTIO in the insular cortex reduced the restraint-induced rise in circulating corticosterone.
Unlike NPLA and carboxy-PTIO, sGC inhibition with ODQ in the insular cortex did not alter the restraint-induced corticosterone rise, indicating the nNOS effect on corticosterone is sGC-independent.
Restraint-induced drop in tail skin temperature was not altered by intra-insular cortex microinjection of NPLA, carboxy-PTIO, or ODQ.
The involvement of nNOS in stress-induced corticosterone release from the insular cortex occurs through a mechanism independent of its downstream target soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC).
High-fat diet promoted subsynovial connective tissue (SSCT) thickening in a rabbit model of carpal tunnel syndrome.
High-fat diet upregulated the profibrotic gene TGF-beta in subsynovial connective tissue in the carpal tunnel syndrome rabbit model.
Additional fibrotic genes showed sex-specific differential expression in response to high-fat diet in the SSCT.
Although overall carpal tunnel syndrome prevalence is higher in women, men show a greater incidence of the condition under metabolic dysfunction.
Skin punch biopsy showed markedly reduced epidermal nerve fiber density at the thigh and calf compared to age-matched normative values, indicating small fiber sensory neuropathy.
Nerve conduction studies revealed a mixed chronic distal demyelinating and axonal peripheral neuropathy.

Head-up tilt testing showed resting tachycardia and severe symptomatic orthostatic intolerance with a sustained fall in systolic blood pressure and further heart rate acceleration on tilt, indicating autonomic dysfunction.
FDG-PET/MRI showed hypometabolism in bilateral anterior and mesial temporal, superior parietal, and lateral occipital lobes, anterior cingulate cortices, and cerebellar hemispheres.
Volumetric MRI analysis showed left hippocampal and temporal hippocampal volumes less than 5% of age-matched controls.
Serum GAD65 antibody titer was mildly elevated above the reference range, raising suspicion of autoimmune encephalopathy.
Lumbar puncture revealed an elevated CSF total protein level, otherwise normal CSF studies.
Treatment with monthly IVIg over five months produced overall initial clinical improvement in this patient with PASC-related peripheral, autonomic, and central nervous system involvement.
Long COVID-19 patients with fatigue showed a significant dissociation over time in the NOL index (a composite HRV/autonomic measure) compared to control participants, consistent with dysautonomia.
Long COVID-19 patients without fatigue showed only a non-significant trend toward dissociation in NOL index over time compared to controls.
No significant difference in NOL index change over time was found between the two long COVID-19 groups (with vs without fatigue).
Long COVID-19 patients with fatigue had significantly higher Nijmegen (hyperventilation/breathing pattern) scores than those without fatigue.
Long COVID-19 patients with fatigue had significantly higher PCL-5 (post-traumatic stress) scores than those without fatigue.
Loss of taste and smell occurred at similar frequency in long COVID-19 patients with and without fatigue, with no significant difference between groups.
The 30-second sit-to-stand ('30 s of up and down') test result did not significantly differ between long COVID-19 patients with and without fatigue.

Prior literature cited in the discussion reports that HRV is inversely correlated with CRP and inflammatory markers, suggesting a link between autonomic dysfunction and inflammation relevant to COVID-19.
The authors hypothesize that SARS-CoV-2 may gain access to the central nervous system by binding ACE2 expressed on cerebral capillary endothelium, contributing to autonomic dysfunction.
An estimated 10% of COVID-19 survivors continue to experience symptoms weeks to months after initial infection, a condition termed PASC or 'long-haulers'.
Older age, comorbid medical conditions, and greater COVID-19 severity are reported risk factors for PASC, though young and previously healthy individuals with mild COVID-19 are also at risk.
Elevated cardiac troponin, indicating myocardial injury, was reported in approximately 20-40% of hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19.

In a large cardiac autopsy series, SARS-CoV-2 RNA was localized to cardiac interstitium and infiltrating macrophages rather than cardiomyocytes, with zero confirmed myocarditis cases by Dallas criteria.

Among nearly 250 intubated patients, myocardial injury (troponin elevation) was less common in COVID-19 ARDS than in non-COVID-19 ARDS after accounting for degree of critical illness and organ dysfunction.
Troponin elevation in COVID-19 was consistently associated with elevated inflammatory markers including CRP, d-dimer, ferritin, and fibrinogen.

In a series of 100 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, right ventricular dysfunction was the most common echocardiographic abnormality, occurring in nearly 40% and associated with clinical decompensation.
A multi-center international cohort of over 300 hospitalized COVID-19 patients found RV dysfunction in about 26%.
Speckle-tracking echocardiography found reduced basal longitudinal strain in 52% of patients in a single-center study, more common among obese, Black, hypertensive, and diabetic patients.
Shi and colleagues found troponin elevation associated with a threefold to fourfold higher risk of death in a Wuhan cohort of COVID-19 patients.
Lombardi and colleagues validated the troponin-mortality association in a multi-center Italian cohort of over 600 patients, with a hazard ratio of 1.7.
In a diverse New York City cohort of over 2000 patients, Smilowitz and colleagues found the risk of death was twofold higher among patients with troponin elevation.
Metkus and colleagues found troponin elevation was no longer associated with mortality after controlling for age, sex, and multiorgan system dysfunction.

In a multi-center international echocardiography study of over 300 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, only troponin elevation combined with echocardiographic abnormalities, not troponin elevation alone, was significantly associated with higher in-hospital mortality.
Early case reports estimated COVID-19 myocarditis prevalence at about 7%, but larger multi-center retrospective cohort studies found the true prevalence to be 1% or less.

Huang and colleagues found abnormal T1/T2 signaling and late gadolinium enhancement on CMR, indicating myocardial edema and fibrosis, in 26 patients with persistent cardiac symptoms 50 days after COVID-19 symptom onset.
Puntmann and colleagues found ongoing myocardial inflammation by CMR in 60% of 100 unselected COVID-19 patients at a median follow-up of 71 days, two-thirds of whom had not been hospitalized.
STEMI rates fell by approximately 20% during the COVID-19 pandemic, likely due to patients avoiding hospital care for fear of infection.

In a CMR study of 26 competitive athletes post-COVID-19, 15% had findings suggestive of myocarditis and an additional 30.8% had late gadolinium enhancement without T2 elevation suggesting prior myocardial injury.
Brito and colleagues found that more than 1 in 3 of 54 previously healthy college athletes recovering from COVID-19 showed imaging features of resolving pericardial inflammation.

A registry of 789 professional athletes undergoing a return-to-play cardiac screening protocol after COVID-19 found imaging evidence of inflammatory heart disease in only 0.6% (5 athletes), with no adverse cardiac events after return to play.
In a cohort of 143 discharged COVID-19 patients in Italy, 87% reported ongoing fatigue and dyspnea at 60 days post-discharge.

Halpin and colleagues found patients requiring ICU-level care were more likely than general ward patients to report persistent fatigue (72% vs 60.3%) and breathlessness (65.6% vs 42.6%) after discharge.
A Michigan cohort found 33% (159 of 488) of discharged COVID-19 patients endorsed ongoing cardiopulmonary symptoms including cough and dyspnea at 60 days, though the study had high loss to follow-up.
In a non-hospitalized US cohort of 272 individuals, 35% reported not being back to their baseline health at 14-21 days after COVID-19 diagnosis.
Approximately 20% of young individuals aged 18-34 without comorbid conditions continued to report ongoing symptoms at 14-21 days after COVID-19 diagnosis.
Approximately 20% of individuals reported chest pain and 14% reported palpitations at 60 days after COVID-19 infection.

A rising number of patients and case studies note a relationship between COVID-19 and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), hypothesized to arise from SARS-CoV-2's interaction with the ACE2 protein on neurons disrupting blood pressure regulation and causing dysautonomia.
Management of POTS and dysautonomia centers on education, exercise, salt/fluid repletion, with midodrine used to improve vascular tone and beta-blockers or ivabradine used to manage palpitations.

A 38-year-old woman with post-acute COVID-19 sequelae experienced resolution of brain fog, dyspnea, and fatigue after undergoing enhanced external counterpulsation (EECP) therapy three times weekly for five weeks.

EECP-induced pulsatile shear stress is associated with improved systemic endothelial function through modulation of vasodilating agents like nitric oxide and pro-inflammatory agents like tumor necrosis factor alpha.

A CDC study following 274 COVID-19 patients at two to three weeks post-diagnosis found that 34% reported at least one persistent symptom, most commonly cough, fatigue, congestion, dyspnea, confusion, and chest pain.

A prospective cohort study of 1,733 patients in Wuhan, China found that 76% reported at least one symptom at six-month follow-up, most commonly fatigue/muscular weakness, dyspnea, sleep difficulties, and anxiety/depression.
Puntmann et al. performed cardiac MRI in 100 COVID-19 patients approximately 71 days after diagnosis and found abnormal findings in 78% of patients.

Huang et al. assessed pulmonary function in 57 patients one month after discharge and found DLCO below 80% predicted in 53% of patients, with higher incidence in severe versus non-severe infection, and severe patients had a six-minute walk distance 56 meters shorter than non-severe patients.

Zhou et al. assessed cognitive function and inflammatory markers in 29 patients two to three weeks after COVID-19 infection, finding significant decreases in sustained attention along with significant elevations in C-reactive protein.
A study performing brain MRI in 51 COVID-19 patients three months after discharge found decreased cerebral blood flow and changes in white and gray matter in patients with severe infection.

A leading hypothesis for PASC pathophysiology proposes that SARS-CoV-2 infects endothelial cells via the angiotensin-converting enzyme-2 receptor, triggering inflammatory cytokine release and compromising the epithelial-endothelial barrier.

In patients with underlying cardiovascular disease, EECP has been shown to significantly improve Canadian Cardiovascular Society angina class, Duke Activity Score Index, Seattle Angina Questionnaire scores, and six-minute walking distance, markers associated with mortality benefit.

A study showed EECP improved exercise endurance in patients with low-to-normal exercise endurance and in COPD patients, with significant improvements in maximum oxygen uptake (VO2-MaxKg) after three weeks of EECP therapy.
Acute sleep deprivation prior to ischemia/reperfusion increased left ventricular developed pressure in isolated rat hearts.
Acute sleep deprivation prior to ischemia/reperfusion increased rate pressure product in isolated rat hearts.
Acute sleep deprivation before ischemia/reperfusion reduced myocardial infarct size compared to the ischemia-reperfusion-only group.

Chemical sympathectomy with 6-hydroxydopamine before sleep deprivation abolished the sleep-deprivation-induced reduction in infarct size, resulting in infarct size not different from the ischemia-reperfusion-only group.
Fibromyalgia patients with a diagnosis of PTSD reported significantly higher total AdAS spectrum (autistic traits) scores than fibromyalgia patients without PTSD.
AdAS spectrum total scores were significantly correlated with Trauma And Loss Spectrum-Self Report (TALS-SR) total scores in the fibromyalgia sample.
The non-verbal communication domain of the AdAS spectrum showed a particularly significant correlation with TALS-SR scores.
The hyper-hypo reactivity to sensory input domain of the AdAS spectrum correlated significantly with several domains of the TALS-SR.
Among 100 patients with unexplained late-onset action tremor, ataxia, or parkinsonism, two (2%) carried an FMR1 premutation, with one male patient having 83 CGG repeats.
The second identified premutation carrier, a female patient, showed CGG repeat mosaicism with 32 and 58 repeats.
The authors note that autonomic dysfunction may be an important, though not primary, part of the clinical spectrum in FXTAS patients alongside tremor, ataxia, and parkinsonism.
The authors suggest that a positive family history of involuntary movement disorders and/or autism spectrum disorders in younger cousins should raise suspicion for probable FXTAS.
There was no significant main effect of ASD diagnosis on overall respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA), a parasympathetic index, during the TSST-F paradigm.
The rate of change in RSA across baseline, preparation, social interaction, and recovery periods of the TSST-F did not differ significantly between ASD and TD groups.

A significant diagnosis-by-age interaction showed that the increase in RSA with older age seen in typically developing youth was blunted in youth with ASD, indicating a slower developmental rise in parasympathetic regulation.
There was no significant main effect of ASD diagnosis on pre-ejection period (PEP), a marker of sympathetic activity, during the TSST-F.
A diagnosis-by-age interaction model for PEP was not significant, indicating sympathetic reactivity by age did not differ between ASD and TD groups.
Across both ASD and TD groups, greater parent-reported social problems on the CBCL were associated with lower mean RSA, independent of diagnosis.
Self-reported state anxiety (STAIC) and overall ASD symptom severity (SRS total) were not significant predictors of RSA or PEP.
Children with ASD were rated by parents as having significantly more social problems on the CBCL and higher overall ASD symptom severity on the SRS-2 compared to TD peers.
Youth with ASD self-reported greater state anxiety following the TSST-F peer interaction than TD youth.

An exploratory three-way interaction of diagnosis, age, and time on RSA was not statistically significant, but the estimated effect size fell in the small-to-medium range, suggesting the study may have been underpowered to detect it.
Autistic adults reported significantly greater self-reported ANS dysfunction than matched neurotypical adults.
Autistic adults reported significantly higher trait-anxiety than neurotypical adults, whereas depression and state-anxiety did not differ significantly between groups.
Depression and state-anxiety scores did not differ significantly between autistic and neurotypical adults in Study 1.
After controlling for trait-anxiety via ANCOVA, the group difference in ANS dysfunction between autistic and neurotypical adults was no longer significant.
Trait-anxiety was significantly linked to ANS dysfunction independent of group in the ANCOVA model.
Mediation analysis showed trait-anxiety significantly mediated the relationship between autism group status and ANS dysfunction.
State-anxiety and depression did not significantly mediate the relationship between autism group status and ANS dysfunction in Study 1.
In the general population sample, depression, anxiety, and stress scores were positively correlated with ANS dysfunction, but autistic traits were not.
Autistic traits were not significantly correlated with ANS dysfunction in bivariate analysis of the general population sample.
Multiple regression showed that anxiety, stress, and being female were unique significant predictors of greater ANS dysfunction, whereas depression and autistic traits were not.
Anxiety and stress, but not depression, significantly mediated the relationship between autistic traits and ANS dysfunction in the general population sample.
After accounting for anxiety and stress as mediators, the direct effect of autistic traits on ANS dysfunction was no longer significant.
There was a significant overall (total) effect of autistic traits on ANS dysfunction, controlling for age and sex, before mediators were accounted for.
Autistic traits were significantly associated with greater anxiety and stress, which in turn were associated with greater ANS dysfunction.
Across both studies, depression showed minimal or no link with ANS function once anxiety and stress were accounted for.
Children with ADHD (ADHD-only and ADHD+autism) had significantly longer reaction times on the response-conflict task than those without ADHD.
Neurotypical children had faster reaction times than children with ADHD-only, autism-only, or comorbid ADHD+autism, with no significant differences among the three clinical groups.
Children with autism (autism-only and ADHD+autism) had significantly lower accuracy on the response-conflict task than those without autism.
Children with ADHD (ADHD-only and ADHD+autism) had significantly lower accuracy on the task than those without ADHD.
Children with autism showed an earlier-peaking (reduced latency) cue-locked parietal P3 compared to children without autism.
Children with autism showed reduced amplitude of the cue-locked parietal P3 compared to children without autism, suggesting reduced processing of the informative cue stimulus.
Children with autism showed a delayed (longer-latency) fronto-central target-N2 compared to those without autism, suggesting slower conflict processing.
During high-demand (but not low-demand) trials, children with ADHD showed reduced target-N2 amplitude compared to children without ADHD.
Children with ADHD showed longer inter-beat intervals (slower heart rate) in relation to the cue stimulus than those without ADHD, indicating hypo-arousal.
Children with autism showed shorter inter-beat intervals (faster heart rate) in relation to the cue stimulus than those without autism, indicating hyper-arousal.
Children with ADHD-only had reduced average heart rate throughout the task compared to children with autism-only, ADHD+autism, and (marginally) neurotypical children.
Children without ADHD showed a significant heart rate acceleration after the cue stimulus, whereas children with ADHD showed no significant change in heart rate in response to the cue.
Children with ADHD had longer inter-beat intervals (slower heart rate) in relation to the target stimulus than those without ADHD.
Children with autism had shorter inter-beat intervals (faster heart rate) in relation to the target stimulus than those without autism.

Children with ADHD-only had marginally longer inter-beat intervals around the manual button-press than children with autism-only, ADHD+autism, or neurotypical children, with a significant main effect of autism also observed on response-locked IBI.
During the manual response, children without ADHD showed faster heart rate (shorter IBIs) in high-demand versus low-demand trials, whereas children with ADHD showed no such demand-related modulation.
A mediation analysis showed that the relationship between ADHD and slower reaction times was statistically mediated by reduced heart-rate acceleration following the cue stimulus.
Across the whole sample, larger heart-rate accelerations after the cue stimulus were associated with faster (shorter) reaction times.

Children with comorbid ADHD+autism showed marginally lower task accuracy than children with ADHD-only, supporting an interactive model of comorbidity in addition to the additive pattern seen across electrophysiological and behavioral measures.
Half of the affected children met ADOS-2 diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder, far exceeding general population ASD prevalence.
Two of five deletion-carrying parents showed elevated autism traits on the Broad Autism Phenotype Questionnaire, with a third scoring just below threshold.
The majority of affected children and about half of affected parents showed repetitive behavior severity comparable to individuals with idiopathic ASD.
All affected children showed deficits in adaptive functioning on the Vineland-III, with most scoring at least two SD below the population mean on one or more subscales.
Children with the 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 deletion showed medium-to-large increases in postural sway length and variability compared to matched control children.
Adult deletion carriers (parents) showed large increases in postural sway length compared to matched control adults.
A subset of participants showed selective executive dysfunction, with reduced ability to flexibly shift response sets relative to processing speed.
Verbal memory abilities were largely intact across the cohort, though a minority scored below average, including one subject markedly impaired on recognition memory.
Whole-exome sequencing identified 526 high-confidence potentially damaging variants in 453 distinct genes across affected children, averaging 100 PDVs affecting 88 genes per child.
132 potentially damaging variants were predicted to be de novo, with 99 genes carrying exclusively de novo variants in the affected children.

Subject 3 carried a de novo in-frame deletion in APBB1, a gene that interacts with CYFIP1 and is associated with ASD, in a subject who was near ADOS-2 threshold for ASD and had global developmental delay.

Subject 2 carried a missense variant in GOLGA2, which interacts with CYFIP1 and, in mouse models, affects brain morphology and causes ataxia; this subject had a disturbed motor phenotype, ASD, and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

Subject 7 had a de novo missense variant in MEOX1, which interacts with CYFIP1 and plays a role in sclerotome/somite development, in a child with connective tissue defects, congenital malformations, epilepsy, and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

Subjects 2 and 3 carried the same missense variant in FAT3, which interacts with CYFIP1 and TUBGCP5 and is linked to Hirschsprung disease, raising concern for gastrointestinal issues despite not being on ASD/clinical panels.

Subject 9 carried a variant in SPAST, whose protein product Spastin interacts with both NIPA1 and NIPA2, in a child with hypotonia, motor delay, and autism; SPAST variants are separately linked to hereditary spastic paraplegia and ASD with spastic paraplegia.
Subject 5 inherited a stop-loss variant in the connective tissue disorder gene FLCN from the deletion-carrying parent, and both had a history of musculoskeletal findings.
Subject 5, who had significant joint hyperextensibility, inherited a frameshift variant in the collagen gene COL5A3 from the deletion-carrying parent.
Subject 7, who had joint hyperflexibility, inherited a missense variant in the collagen gene COL21A1 from the non-deleted parent.
Subject 7 also inherited a missense variant in COL6A2, a gene associated with Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy 1, coinciding with joint hyperflexibility.
Subject 9 had an in-frame deletion in COL4A3, inherited from the deleted parent, coinciding with flat feet and a history of constipation; COL4A3 is separately implicated in renal failure disorders.

The same COL6A6 missense variant was found in Subjects 9 and 11; COL6A6 has been implicated in skin disorders, and both subjects had cutaneous findings (flat feet-related connective changes and birthmarks respectively).

Subject 11 had a de novo missense variant in CDK19, a gene associated with bilateral congenital retinal folds, microcephaly, and intellectual disability, consistent with this subject's intellectual disability.

Affected children carried on average 17 ASD-associated genes with potentially damaging variants, and the child with the most such variants also had the most severe repetitive behavior and ADOS-2 scores.
