NIPA1 protein was predicted to interact with 11 other proteins, three-quarters of which are BMP superfamily members or receptors involved in bone morphogenesis and developmental signaling.

NIPA2 protein was predicted to interact with 19 other proteins, including BMP superfamily members, BMP receptors, and SMAD signal transducers, implicating it in TGFB/BMP-mediated developmental signaling.

Four of five probands inherited the 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 deletion maternally and one paternally; the paternally-inherited case was the most severely affected (ataxia, wheelchair use, non-verbal, impaired cognition), suggestive of a parent-of-origin effect.
Most subjects presented with dysmorphic features and connective tissue findings, including abnormal ears, ptosis, joint hypermobility, scoliosis, flat feet, and delayed wound healing.
Subject 7 had a PDV in GLI2, a gene on the clinical cleft palate testing panel, coinciding with craniofacial malformation involving the mouth.
Subject 11 had a PDV in FOXE1, a gene on the clinical cleft palate testing panel, coinciding with craniofacial malformation involving the mouth.
MLC1 variants were flagged by clinical gene panels as candidate contributors to macrocephaly and motor delay in Subject 9, and to epilepsy in Subject 7.

Subject 5 inherited a stop-loss variant in the connective tissue disorder gene FLCN from the parent carrying the 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 deletion, and both individuals had a history of musculoskeletal findings.
Subject 5, who had significant joint hyperextensibility, inherited a frameshift variant in the collagen gene COL5A3 from the parent with the deletion.

Subject 7, who had joint hyperflexibility, inherited missense variants in COL21A1 and COL6A2 from the non-deleted parent, with COL6A2 variation being associated with Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy 1.

Subject 9 had an inframe deletion in COL4A3 and a missense variant in COL6A6 inherited from the parent with the deletion; COL4A3 variation is implicated in renal disorders and the subject had a history of constipation and flat feet.
Subject 11 carried the same COL6A6 missense variant found in Subject 9 and presented with birthmarks on the thigh and forehead, consistent with the gene's implication in skin disorders.

Subject 11 had a de novo missense variant in CDK19, a gene associated with bilateral congenital retinal folds, microcephaly, and intellectual disability, consistent with the subject's intellectual disability.
MLC1 gene panel variants were identified as candidate contributors to macrocephaly and motor delay in Subject 9 and to epilepsy in Subject 7.
Subjects 7 and 11 carried potentially damaging variants in the cleft-palate testing panel genes GLI2 and FOXE1, respectively, corresponding with craniofacial malformations involving the mouth.
NIPA1 protein was predicted to interact with 11 other proteins, of which 45% were BMP superfamily members and 27% were BMP receptors, implicating NIPA1 in BMP signaling and bone morphogenesis.
NIPA2 protein was predicted to interact with 19 other proteins, including 42% SMAD superfamily members, implicating NIPA2 in TGF-beta/SMAD signaling affecting bone morphogenesis.

CYFIP1 protein interacts with partners involved in cytoskeleton organization, actin filament binding, cell-matrix adhesion, MAP kinase signaling, glucose uptake stimulation, and translational repression.
In silico STRING network analysis of the four 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 region genes and their interacting proteins identified 11 nodes and 34 edges representing shared functional protein-protein associations.

The 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion was found to be the most common cytogenetic abnormality among more than 10,000 consecutive patients referred for genetic services with features of ASD or other neurodevelopmental disorders.

A systematic review of over 200 reported individuals with the 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion found developmental delay in 73%, speech delay in 67%, motor delay in 42%, dysmorphic ears/palatal anomalies in 46%, writing/reading/memory impairment or verbal IQ ≤75 in 50-60%, general behavior problems in 55%, and abnormal brain imaging in 43%.

Four of five probands inherited the 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 deletion maternally, while one (Family E) inherited it paternally; the paternally-inherited case was the most severely affected (ataxia, wheelchair use, non-verbal, impaired cognition), suggesting a possible parent-of-origin effect.
Dysmorphic craniofacial features were common in the cohort, with five participants showing abnormal ear findings (broad, soft, fleshy, or overfolded ears) and six participants showing ptosis.
Joint hyperextensibility was common in the cohort, with unrelated individuals scoring at least 6/9 on the Beighton hypermobility scale.

Affected adult parents showed a large increase in postural sway center-of-pressure (COP) path length relative to age- and sex-matched control adults and a medium increase in anterior-posterior sway variability.
Of the potentially damaging variants identified in affected children, 132 were predicted to be de novo, occurring across 99 distinct genes that were exclusively de novo.
Youth with ASD showed reduced resting sympathetic activity compared to typically developing controls.
Youth with ASD showed reduced resting parasympathetic activity compared to typically developing controls.
The ASD+Anxiety group and the Anxiety Alone (non-ASD) group differed from each other in sympathetic activity at rest.
The ASD+Anxiety group and the Anxiety Alone (non-ASD) group showed similar parasympathetic activity at rest.
In NICU male infants aged 34-42 weeks postmenstrual age, higher positive heart rate skewness (toward accelerations) was associated with increased risk of later autism spectrum disorder diagnosis.
In males with at least 4 days of HR data, ASD prevalence was 11% among those in the top 5th percentile of HR skewness compared to an overall prevalence of 5%.
The association between high positive HR skewness and increased ASD risk was significant in male infants but not observed in females.
Preterm infants at early postmenstrual ages showed negative HR skewness reflecting decelerations, which increased (became less negative) with maturation.
Overall, the live birth rate among women with rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases was 97%.
Pregnancy complications, including miscarriage, premature delivery, small-for-gestational-age infants, and pregnancy-related diseases, occurred in 39.1% of pregnancies excluding twin pregnancies.
Infants born to mothers with connective tissue diseases had significantly lower mean gestational age at birth compared with infants born to mothers with inflammatory joint diseases.
Infants born to mothers with connective tissue diseases had significantly lower mean birth weight than infants born to mothers with inflammatory joint diseases.
Infants born to mothers with connective tissue diseases had significantly lower mean birth length than infants born to mothers with inflammatory joint diseases.

Three children born to mothers with connective tissue diseases had affected development, including one case of autism spectrum disorder, one of congenital heart disease, and one of bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

Across 51 studies comparing autistic and neurotypical participants, 60.8% reported evidence of group differences in resting-state autonomic arousal measures (heart rate, pupillometry, or electrodermal activity).
Findings of hyperarousal, particularly using indices of parasympathetic function, were the most commonly reported pattern of autonomic difference in autistic individuals during resting-state.
Findings of hypo-arousal and autonomic dysregulation were also consistently present across studies of autistic individuals, alongside the more common hyperarousal findings.
The experimental context of resting-state measurement played a role in whether studies detected autonomic differences between autistic and neurotypical participants.
A PVP-based amorphous solid dispersion tablet of nifedipine achieved rapid dissolution, releasing 35% of the drug dose within 15 minutes in a monophasic dissolution medium.
The HPMC-nifedipine amorphous solid dispersion exhibited very slow dissolution compared to the PVP-based formulation.
The Soluplus-nifedipine amorphous solid dispersion system showed no nifedipine release at all over 120 minutes of dissolution testing.

In biphasic dissolution medium, the PVP-nifedipine amorphous solid dispersion tablet produced a release profile comparable to that of the pre-split/ruptured nifedipine soft capsule currently used off-license for autonomic dysreflexia.

Outpatient (same-day discharge) vagus nerve stimulation implantation was feasible and safe in 26 adult patients with drug-resistant epilepsy and severe intellectual disability, some of whom also had autism, with no surgery-related complications or hospital admissions within one month.
Maternal allergic inflammation (ovalbumin challenge) increased microglia levels in the fetal brain of offspring.
Offspring of allergically-inflamed mothers had increased mast cell numbers in the hippocampus on the day of birth.
Maternal allergic challenge produced region-, time-, and sex-specific changes in microglia measures in offspring.
Offspring of ovalbumin-exposed mothers exhibited abnormal social behavior later in life.
Offspring of ovalbumin-exposed mothers exhibited hyperlocomotion.
Offspring of ovalbumin-exposed mothers showed reduced cognitive flexibility.
Children in the dysregulated sleep group showed fewer nonspecific skin conductance responses compared to children with more regulated sleep.
Children in the dysregulated sleep group had lower tonic skin conductance levels in the afternoon compared to children with more regulated sleep.
The blunted afternoon arousal pattern may reflect a broader dysregulation profile that co-occurs with dysregulated sleep and elevated autism symptom severity, rather than sleep per se.
Surgically closed ASD patients had significantly lower SDNN (a global heart rate variability measure) than healthy controls.
SDANN was significantly reduced in surgically closed ASD patients compared with controls.
RMSSD, a marker of parasympathetic (vagal) activity, was reduced in both surgically and percutaneously closed ASD patients compared with controls.
pNN50 was significantly lower in surgically closed ASD patients than controls, reflecting reduced vagal tone.
The HRV triangular index was significantly lower in surgically closed ASD patients than in controls.
Both surgically and percutaneously closed ASD patients had a lower maximum heart rate during 48-h Holter monitoring than controls.
Surgically closed ASD patients had a higher occurrence of incomplete right bundle branch block compared to controls.
A larger atrial septal defect size before closure was negatively correlated with pNN50, suggesting larger defects are associated with reduced parasympathetic tone.
No correlation was found between age at ASD closure and any HRV parameter.
Surgically closed ASD patients had a larger right atrial end-systolic volume index than controls, indicating persistent right atrial remodelling years after closure.

Overall, patients with a surgically or percutaneously closed ASD continue to show sympathovagal imbalance with impaired HRV more than a decade after closure, with sympathetic dominance and parasympathetic withdrawal most pronounced in the surgical group.
Some studies report that children with autism spectrum disorder pay less attention to another person who is in distress.

Functional neuroimaging studies in ASD adolescents suggest the emotional sharing dimension of empathy is preserved, but a deficit in emotional self-regulation may prevent them from experiencing empathic concern.
Children with conduct disorder and callous-unemotional traits show a clearly reduced autonomic nervous system response to others' distress or suffering.
Functional neuroimaging studies show that atypical patterns of brain activity at 15 months of age can predict later severe conduct disorder.
Neural regions involved in emotional processing (anterior cingulate cortex, insula, amygdala) show reduced activation to empathy-eliciting stimuli in children with callous-unemotional traits.
The genetic nature of callous-unemotional traits is highlighted across several studies cited in the review.
Rab39b knockout mice showed a persistent ~10% reduction in body weight compared to wild-type littermates, beginning at postnatal day 7 and maintained through adulthood.
The body weight loss in Rab39b KO mice was linked to a significant reduction in abdominal adipose tissue volume, measured by MRI.
GluA2 AMPAR subunit maturity ratio (mature/immature glycoform) was significantly decreased in Rab39b KO hippocampal neurons compared to WT, indicating ER retention.
GluA3 AMPAR subunit maturity ratio was more strikingly decreased than GluA2 in Rab39b KO hippocampal neurons.
In contrast to GluA2/GluA3, the GluA1 AMPAR subunit maturity ratio was increased in Rab39b KO neurons, suggesting increased homomeric GluA1 AMPAR trafficking.
Lentiviral re-expression of RAB39B (CherryRab39b) in Rab39b KO neurons fully restored GluA1, GluA2 and GluA3 maturity ratios to wild-type levels.
Surface (non-permeabilised) GluA2 AMPAR density was decreased on Rab39b KO hippocampal neurons compared to WT.
Surface GluA3 AMPAR density was decreased on Rab39b KO hippocampal neurons compared to WT.
Surface GluA1 AMPAR density was increased on Rab39b KO hippocampal neurons compared to WT, consistent with increased GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPAR insertion.
Rab39b KO hippocampal CA1 dendritic spines failed to undergo the normal developmental reorganisation of density and morphology, remaining in an immature P20-like state at P30 and P90.
Re-expression of RAB39B, but not GluA2 alone, in Rab39b KO hippocampal neurons fully rescued spine density and morphology toward the mature WT state at 14 DIV.
GluA2 surface expression in Rab39b KO neurons was restored only by RAB39B re-expression, not by GluA2 overexpression alone.
Live imaging showed that Rab39b KO stable spines at 14 DIV retained a hyperdynamic rate comparable to immature WT spines at 7 DIV rather than to mature WT spines at 14 DIV.
Pharmacological blockade of Ca2+-permeable AMPARs with NASPM fully restored normal spine dynamics in Rab39b KO neurons to WT-comparable levels.
Cortical pyramidal neurons in Rab39b KO mice showed increased intrinsic excitability (spike frequency to current injection) without changes in resting membrane potential or input resistance.
AMPA-mEPSC frequency and decay time were decreased in Rab39b KO cortical pyramidal neurons compared to WT, with no change in amplitude.
The AMPAR rectification index, an indicator of Ca2+-permeable GluA2-lacking receptor presence, was increased in Rab39b KO cortical pyramidal neurons with no change in the AMPA/NMDA ratio.
Bath application of NASPM produced a greater reduction of AMPA current amplitude in Rab39b KO pyramidal neurons than in WT, confirming increased GluA2-lacking AMPAR insertion in KO synapses.
Ifenprodil sensitivity and NMDA-EPSC decay kinetics did not differ between Rab39b KO and WT neurons, indicating no alteration in NMDA receptor subunit composition.
In the emergence test, Rab39b KO mice showed significantly increased locomotor activity (path and velocity) compared to WT.
In the novelty test, Rab39b KO mice showed increased object investigation without loss of interest over 30 minutes, indicating reduced avoidance/increased curiosity toward novel objects.
Rab39b KO mice showed a significant deficit in short-term spatial working memory in the 8-arm radial maze task, failing to exceed chance-level correct responses after 10 days of training.
Rab39b KO mice showed reduced correct alternations in the spontaneous alternation task, indicating impaired short-term working memory.
In both standard and trace fear conditioning paradigms, Rab39b KO mice showed significantly reduced freezing during context and tone memory tests, indicating impaired associative memory.
Rab39b KO mice showed no deficit in spatial reference memory in the Morris water maze task compared to WT.
Cortical measurements at P20 and P90 showed no difference between Rab39b KO and WT mice, excluding the macrocephaly phenotype reported in a different Rab39b KO mouse model.

No significant differences in the weight of brain, testes, kidney, liver, spleen, heart, lung or stomach were observed between Rab39b KO and WT mice at P20 or P90, indicating the body weight loss is not due to generalized organ atrophy.
Rab39b KO mice did not display macrocephaly, contrasting with a prior report describing macrocephaly in a different Rab39b KO mouse model.
Food intake, water intake and body temperature did not differ between adult Rab39b KO and WT mice.
Glycaemic index and brain regional [18F]-FDG glucose uptake (cortex, striatum, hippocampus, thalamus, cerebellum) were not different between Rab39b KO and WT adult mice.
MRI imaging revealed a significant reduction in abdominal adipose tissue volume in Rab39b KO mice, which may account for their lower body weight.
Total protein levels of several molecules known to directly regulate spine formation, maturation and stabilisation did not differ between Rab39b KO and WT neurons.

Rab39b KO cortical pyramidal neurons showed increased firing (action potential) excitability in response to current injection compared to WT, without changes in resting membrane potential or input resistance.
Rab39b KO cortical pyramidal neurons showed decreased AMPA-mEPSC frequency and decay time compared to WT, with no change in amplitude.
The AMPAR rectification index was increased in Rab39b KO pyramidal cortical neurons, indicating a higher proportion of GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs, with no change in the AMPA/NMDA ratio.

Bath application of NASPM produced a greater reduction in AMPA current amplitude in Rab39b KO cortical pyramidal neurons than in WT neurons, confirming increased synaptic insertion of GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs.
Ifenprodil sensitivity and basal NMDAR-EPSC decay time did not differ between Rab39b KO and WT neurons, suggesting NMDA receptor subunit composition (including GluN2B) is unaltered.
In the Morris water maze test, Rab39b KO mice were indistinguishable from WT mice, indicating no deficit in spatial reference memory.
In the eight-arm radial maze working memory task, Rab39b KO mice failed to exceed chance-level performance after 10 days of training, unlike WT mice which performed well above chance.
In the spontaneous alternation task, Rab39b KO mice showed a significantly lower percentage of correct alternations than WT mice, indicating impaired short-term working memory.
In standard auditory fear conditioning, Rab39b KO mice showed no training deficit but had significantly reduced freezing during both context and tone memory tests 24h later compared to WT.

In trace fear conditioning, Rab39b KO mice froze significantly less than WT mice during conditioning and during subsequent context and tone memory tests, revealing a drastic associative memory impairment.
Rab39b KO mice showed increased locomotor activity (hyperactivity) in the emergence test, with increased path and velocity during progression and decreased time at rest.

In the novelty test, Rab39b KO mice showed increased scanning but decreased progression with no change in velocity, and showed excess, persistent approaches to a novel object without loss of interest, indicating increased curiosity/novelty-seeking and reduced avoidance behaviour.
Re-expressing GluA2 alone (via CherryGluA2 transfection) in Rab39b KO neurons failed to rescue dendritic spine morphology, density, or dynamics, in contrast to full rescue by RAB39B re-expression.

The authors note that two prior independent studies of Rab39b KO mice both identified abnormal activation of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway, a mechanism important for cell differentiation, proliferation and metabolism, which they did not directly test in their own model.
RR intervals were significantly shortened (indicating tachycardia) in autistic children compared to controls at rest.
HF-HRV, reflecting cardiovagal (parasympathetic) activity, was significantly lower in autistic children compared to controls both at rest and during orthostasis.
LF-SBPV, reflecting sympathetic vasomotor regulation, was significantly lower in autistic children compared to controls at rest and during orthostasis.
HF-SBPV was significantly lower at rest in autistic children compared to controls.
Plasma EGF levels were significantly lower in autistic children compared to controls, with no significant correlation to autonomic parameters.
Plasma VEGF levels showed no significant difference between autistic children and controls.
Complex heart rate dynamics assessed by symbolic dynamics parameters were similar between autistic children and controls.

Pooled meta-analysis across non-sibling control studies and all combined studies found lower total IgG in ASD with a confidence interval not including zero, but the model was not statistically significant due to high heterogeneity.
Meta-analysis found IgG4 subclass concentrations significantly elevated in ASD across all comparison groups, with notable variability in the sibling-control comparison.
Other IgG subclasses besides IgG4 showed no significant difference between ASD and comparison groups in the meta-analysis.
One study found that lower total IgG concentrations correlated with increased severity of disruptive/aberrant behaviors in children with ASD.
One study found that higher IgG4 concentrations were significantly associated with increased severity of social interaction impairments in ASD as measured by ADOS.
Two studies using archived neonatal blood specimens found that lower total IgG concentrations in the neonatal period were associated with increased risk of later ASD diagnosis.
Two studies examining cerebrospinal fluid IgG concentrations or IgG index found no significant difference between ASD and reference/control groups.
In one CSF study, increased protein was found in 33% of ASD cases, oligoclonal bands in 3%, and GAD65 autoantibodies in 6% of patients.

A double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial of a one-time IVIG dose in 12 children with ASD showed significant parent/teacher-rated improvements in ABC irritability, hyperactivity, social withdrawal and inappropriate speech, though physician-rated CPRS scores did not significantly improve.

In children with ASD and SPAD/hypogammaglobulinemia, IVIG treatment was associated with decreases in pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-12, and IL-23 and reduced IL-12 and IL-17/IFN-γ production upon mitogen stimulation, compared to normal controls.
TGF-β and soluble TNF receptor II increased in children with ASD and immunodeficiency following IVIG treatment compared to normal controls.

In a study of 78 children with ASD treated with IVIG 2 g/kg monthly for six months, 27% had complete elimination of the ASD phenotype, 42% had marked improvement, 29% had mild-to-moderate improvement, and 99% overall showed some improvement.
In the same 78-child cohort, 81% of children with epilepsy had seizure improvement and 72% had improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms with IVIG treatment.
Meta-analysis combining two studies (n=46) found IVIG treatment significantly improved ABC total score and irritability with a large effect size.
The same meta-analysis found ABC social withdrawal and hyperactivity subscales significantly improved with IVIG treatment with a medium effect size.
ABC stereotyped movements and inappropriate speech subscales were not found to significantly improve with IVIG when the two studies were combined in meta-analysis.
In a case series of 31 children with ASD and autoimmune encephalopathy, anti-Dopamine D2L and anti-tubulin antibodies from the Cunningham panel were predictive of response to IVIG treatment.

A case report of a 33-month-old boy with ASD and neurodevelopmental regression diagnosed with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis showed improvements in language and social skills by the third day of IVIG treatment.

Adverse events reported with IVIG in ASD treatment studies included headache (39%), vomiting (29%), worsening behaviors (16%), anxiety (13%), fever (13%), nausea (10%), fatigue (10%), and rash (5%), with 6% discontinuing due to AEs in one prospective uncontrolled study.

In a prospective open-label study of 14 children with ASD and immune abnormalities treated with IVIG, TNF-α production induced by TLR ligands (zymosan, flagellin, lipopolysaccharide) significantly decreased alongside clinical improvements.
Across the reviewed literature, six studies reported improvements in seizures with IVIG treatment in ASD, with one study noting seizure worsening when IVIG was discontinued.
Among sibling-controlled studies, one found total IgG and IgG4 higher in ASD versus TD siblings while another found no difference, illustrating inconsistency across studies using sibling controls.

A gradient boosting classifier trained on 120 non-contact pulse-wave-derived ANS activation features classified adult males with ASD versus TD adults with 68% mean accuracy, significantly above chance.
The classifier assigned significantly higher ASD-class probabilities to actual ASD participants than to TD participants.
At a probability threshold of 0.5, 76.4% of ASD participants and only 38.1% of TD participants were classified into the ASD group, a significant difference.
The classifier achieved average sensitivity 0.76, specificity 0.63, precision 0.63, and F1 score 0.68 for distinguishing ASD from TD adults using pulse-wave-derived features.
Adults with ASD reported significantly lower subjective 'happy' ratings than TD adults in response to the happy-inducing video clip.
Adults with ASD gave significantly higher 'unpleasantness' ratings than TD adults in response to the happy-inducing video clip.
Adults with ASD reported significantly higher 'fear' ratings than TD adults in response to the sad-inducing video clip.
Adults with ASD showed lower perspective-taking scores on the Interpersonal Reactivity Index than TD adults.
Adults with ASD showed higher personal distress scores on the Interpersonal Reactivity Index than TD adults.
Adults with ASD scored higher on every factor of the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20) than TD adults, consistent with reported alexithymic tendencies in ASD.
After Bonferroni correction, there was no significant correlation between IRI or TAS-20 questionnaire scores and the classifier-estimated probability of ASD classification.

The hit rate for correctly classifying the happy emotional state from pulse-wave-derived ANS indices was markedly lower in the ASD group than the TD group, with happy-clip responses more often confused with fear-clip responses in ASD.

The Grounded Delphi study produced a consensus definition describing autistic burnout as involving exhaustion, withdrawal, problems with thinking, reduced daily living skills, and an increase in the manifestation of autistic traits.
Autistic burnout is suggested to be caused by the chronic stress of masking autistic traits and living in an unaccommodating neurotypical world.
Clinicians are advised that autistic burnout is a distinct condition from depression, though further research is needed to confirm this separation.
Psychological treatments designed for depression could potentially worsen autistic burnout, according to the expert consensus.
Among 117 children with Autism Spectrum Disorder, 70 (59.83%) showed an abnormal increase in joint mobility (hypermobility) based on Beighton score assessment.
The average Beighton score across the studied autistic children was 5.33 with a standard deviation of 2.42.
Height showed a moderate negative correlation with the degree of hypermobility in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
Body weight showed a moderate negative correlation with the degree of hypermobility in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
Age showed a moderate negative correlation with the degree of hypermobility in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
BMI showed a moderate negative correlation with the degree of hypermobility in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
Lyme disease is caused by genospecies within the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato complex, with the specific causative species differing by geographic region (North America versus Europe).

The spirochete's fragmented genome encodes numerous differentially expressed outer surface lipoproteins that are central to its ability to persist in the enzootic cycle and to cause disease in humans.
Tissue damage and the clinical manifestations of Lyme disease arise from the host inflammatory response elicited by the spirochete and its constituents.
Deposition of spirochetes into human dermal tissue produces a local inflammatory response manifesting as erythema migrans, the hallmark skin lesion of early Lyme disease.
A small proportion (about 10%) of Lyme disease patients go on to develop a poorly defined fibromyalgia-like illness termed post-treatment Lyme disease (PTLD).
Post-treatment Lyme disease symptoms do not improve with prolonged antimicrobial therapy.
A pooled meta-analysis of 7 studies found that 80% of COVID-19 patients had at least one long-term symptom, sign, or abnormal laboratory finding beyond two weeks after acute infection.
Fatigue was the most common long-term effect of COVID-19, pooled prevalence 58%.
Headache was reported as a long-term effect in 44% of COVID-19 patients pooled across studies.
Attention disorder was reported in 27% of COVID-19 patients as a long-term neuropsychiatric effect.
Hair loss (telogen effluvium) was reported in 25% of COVID-19 patients as a long-term effect.
Dyspnea was reported in 24% of COVID-19 patients as a long-term respiratory effect.
Abnormal chest X-ray or CT findings persisted in 34% of COVID-19 patients on long-term follow-up.
D-dimer was reported elevated in 20% of COVID-19 patients during long-term follow-up.
NT-proBNP was reported elevated in 11% of COVID-19 patients during long-term follow-up.
C-reactive protein was reported elevated in 8% of COVID-19 patients during long-term follow-up.
Serum ferritin was reported elevated in 8% of COVID-19 patients during long-term follow-up.
Procalcitonin was reported elevated in 4% of COVID-19 patients during long-term follow-up.
Interleukin-6 (IL-6) was reported elevated in 3% of COVID-19 patients during long-term follow-up.
A couple of the included studies reported that fatigue as a long-term COVID-19 effect was more common in female patients.
One study reported that postactivity polypnoea and alopecia were more common among female patients with long-term COVID-19 effects.
Decreased diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide (pulmonary function abnormality) was present in 10% of patients in this meta-analysis.
Cough was reported as a long-term effect in 19% of COVID-19 patients.

The authors note that post-COVID-19 symptoms partly resemble myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (severe fatigue, pain, neurocognitive disability, sleep disruption, autonomic dysfunction, post-exertional symptom worsening), and speculate SARS-CoV-2 could join the list of viral triggers implicated in ME/CFS.
Adults were reported to have double the risk of a new psychiatric disorder diagnosis after COVID-19, most commonly anxiety disorders, insomnia, and dementia.

In an early study of 96 patients with post-viral fatigue syndrome, creatine kinase was mildly elevated and muscle biopsies were largely indistinguishable, with enterovirus RNA detected in skeletal muscle of some patients up to 20 years after disease onset.

Preedy and colleagues found a 15% reduction in muscle RNA content (mg RNA/mg DNA) in 22 patients with acute-onset PVFS, implying reduced muscle protein synthetic potential, while plasma carnosinase and creatine kinase were normal.

Exercise-induced neutrophilia strongly correlated with plasma creatine kinase in healthy women but this correlation was absent in CFS patients, suggesting disrupted stress-induced neutrophil mobilization in CFS.

Using 31P MRS, CFS patients reached exercise exhaustion much more rapidly than controls and had relatively reduced intracellular ATP at exhaustion, though muscle phosphocreatine levels did not differ between groups.

Other 31P MRS trials reported significantly reduced maximal rate of post-exercise phosphocreatine resynthesis in CFS patients versus sedentary controls, and decreased resting phosphocreatine-to-phosphocreatine-plus-phosphate ratio with increased pH during exercise, though not all studies replicated impaired phosphocreatine resynthesis.
Brooks and colleagues found a trend toward reduced hippocampal creatine levels in CFS patients compared with controls (8.6 mM vs. 10.9 mM), suggesting impaired brain creatine metabolism.

Children with CFS showed markedly altered cerebral blood flow (lower in temporal/occipital lobes, higher in basal ganglia and thalamus) alongside a notable elevation of the choline-to-creatine ratio compared with healthy children.

Cardiac bioenergetic studies in 12 CFS patients found a lower mean phosphocreatine-to-ATP ratio than controls, consistent with cardiac impairment, and a prolonged half-time for phosphocreatine recovery after exercise.
In 89 women with CFS, greater pain was associated with reduced gray matter volume and decreased N-acetyl aspartate-to-creatine ratio in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.

A whole-brain MRS study found creatine levels in the parietal cortex were lower in CFS patients than controls (6.4 mM vs. 7.3 mM, p=0.03), while creatine in the putamen was higher in patients than controls (6.3 mM vs. 5.7 mM, p=0.01), indicating region-specific brain creatine variation, alongside an elevated choline-to-creatine ratio in the left anterior cingulate correlating with fatigue.

CFS patients showed higher brain temperatures than healthy controls in several brain regions, suggesting neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and aberrant neuronal communication may contribute to metabolic perturbations.
Elevated urinary creatine excretion has been identified as a metabolomic signature of fibromyalgia, correlating with both fatigue and pain severity.
A metabolomics study of 34 women with ME/CFS found elevated urinary creatinine and decreased serum glycine, suggesting increased utilization of creatine to form ATP.

In the UK ME/CFS Biobank cohort of 272 people with CFS and 136 healthy controls, patients with severe CFS had lower creatine kinase levels than both healthy controls and non-severe CFS patients, a difference persisting after adjustment for sex, age, BMI, muscle mass, disease duration, and activity levels.

Among 30 clinical parameters evaluated in the UK ME/CFS Biobank, only blood creatine kinase levels differed significantly between groups, being lower in CFS patients than healthy controls (59.93 U/L vs. 88.67 U/L; p=0.006).

A CFS-associated dysregulation of microRNA profiles included upregulation of NTRK1 (essential for neuronal development and survival) and downregulation of MECP2 and AGO2, genes involved in chromatin modification and RNA-mediated silencing respectively.

A randomized placebo-controlled double-blind trial of a polynutrient supplement containing creatine (1200 mg/100 mL) in 53 CFS patients over ten weeks found no significant differences between placebo and treated groups on any outcome measure.

In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 43 fibromyalgia patients, creatine monohydrate supplementation (20 g/day for 5 days, then 5 g/day for 16 weeks) increased muscle phosphoryl creatine levels and improved dynamic and isometric muscular strength, along with improved mental health domain of SF-36 and incidental memory, while other cognition, quality of life, and sleep measures were unchanged.

In a randomized controlled crossover trial of 21 mid-age women with CFS, three months of oral guanidinoacetic acid (2.4 g/day) significantly increased total muscle creatine levels compared with placebo (36.3% vs. 2.4%; p<0.01), improved quadriceps strength and maximal oxygen uptake, attenuated activity, motivation, and mental fatigue, and improved physical and mental SF-36 domains, but had no effect on general fatigue and musculoskeletal soreness.
A cross-sectional study of dietary habits in women with CFS found patients often avoid many creatine-rich foods such as meat, milk, and dairy products.
CFS patients were reported to have intakes below reference values for several animal-based nutrients, including vitamin D, vitamin A, calcium, zinc, and iron.
The creatine transporter SLC6A8 (CT1) is not present in astrocytic feet, which cover approximately 98% of the blood-brain barrier, implying limited uptake of circulating creatine into the brain.
A pooled meta-analysis of 7 studies found that 80% of COVID-19 patients had at least one persistent symptom beyond two weeks after infection.
Fatigue was the most common long-term effect of COVID-19, affecting 58% of patients across pooled studies.
Headache was reported in 44% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Attention disorder was reported in 27% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Hair loss (telogen effluvium-type) was reported in 25% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Dyspnea was reported in 24% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Abnormal chest X-ray or CT findings persisted in 34% of patients after COVID-19.
D-dimer was reported elevated in 20% of long-term COVID-19 patients.
NT-proBNP was reported elevated in 11% of long-term COVID-19 patients.
C-reactive protein was reported elevated in 8% of long-term COVID-19 patients.
Serum ferritin was reported elevated in 8% of long-term COVID-19 patients.
Procalcitonin was reported elevated in 4% of long-term COVID-19 patients.
Interleukin-6 was reported elevated in 3% of long-term COVID-19 patients.
Cough was reported in 19% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Decreased diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide was present in 10% of patients after COVID-19, indicating residual pulmonary dysfunction.
Fatigue, and separately post-activity polypnea and alopecia, were reported as more common in females than males in some of the included studies.
Adults were reported to have double the risk of being newly diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder (most commonly anxiety, insomnia, and dementia) after a COVID-19 diagnosis.
Anosmia was reported in 21% of patients as a long-term neuropsychiatric/sensory effect of COVID-19.

The authors note that post-COVID-19 symptoms resemble chronic fatigue syndrome/ME, including severe fatigue, pain, neurocognitive disability, poor sleep, and symptoms suggestive of autonomic dysfunction that worsen with minor exertion.
The authors speculate that SARS-CoV-2 could be added to the list of viral agents (including Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, enterovirus, and herpesvirus) implicated in causing ME/CFS.
Three of four controlled trials found that high-dose IV vitamin C significantly reduced fatigue compared with control groups.
In all observational before-and-after studies a reduction in fatigue was reported, and in the four studies with statistical comparison of pre-post values the reduction was significant.
IV vitamin C had no effect on acute post-operative fatigue in one of the controlled trials.
In a herpes zoster study using 7.5 g IV vitamin C every second or third day, fatigue improved in 78.2% and impaired concentration improved in 81.8% of patients.

In advanced lung cancer patients, fatigue continued to increase in the control group despite best supportive therapy, whereas it decreased significantly in the group receiving vitamin C plus hyperthermia.
Patients with idiopathic CFS have significantly elevated markers of oxidative stress, including reactive oxygen species, malondialdehyde, and F2-isoprostane, compared to healthy controls.
Patients with idiopathic CFS show reduced antioxidant parameters, including total antioxidant activity, catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione activity, compared to healthy controls.

In patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and low disease activity, fatigue severity was associated with increased F2-isoprostane, which remained a significant predictor of fatigue severity after adjusting for age, BMI, pain, and depression.

In cancer patients, an exercise intervention after completion of radiation or chemotherapy reduced fatigue, with reductions in total and affective fatigue correlating with decreases in plasma 8-hydroxy-deoxyguanosine, behavioral/sensory fatigue changes correlating with protein carbonyls, and increased antioxidant capacity correlating with reduced affective, sensory, and cognitive fatigue.

In a pilot study of COVID-19 patients requiring intensive care, high-dose IV vitamin C significantly improved oxygenation, reduced IL-6 (a marker of cytokine storm), and showed a trend toward reduced mortality in severely ill patients.
A retrospective cohort study found a significant reduction in mortality and improvement of oxygen status with high-dose vitamin C in COVID-19 patients.

A review of long COVID reported abnormal chest CT/X-ray in 34% of patients six months after infection, along with elevated markers of D-dimer, NT-proBNP, C-reactive protein, serum ferritin, procalcitonin, and IL-6, implicating circulatory, cardiac, and inflammatory involvement.

First observations point to IgG autoantibodies widely associated with myopathies, vasculitis, and antiphospholipid syndromes in SARS-CoV-2 infected subjects, suggesting autoimmune involvement in persistent post-COVID symptoms.

In a cohort of 1733 patients six months after hospitalization for COVID-19 in Wuhan, 63% suffered from fatigue or muscle weakness, 26% from sleep disturbances, and 23% from anxiety or depression, with more severely ill patients showing more impaired pulmonary diffusion capacity and abnormal chest imaging.

A systematic review and meta-analysis identified more than 50 long-term effects of COVID-19; 80% of individuals with confirmed COVID-19 continued to have at least one symptom beyond two weeks post-infection, with the five most common being fatigue (58%), headache (44%), attention deficit disorder (27%), hair loss (25%), and dyspnea (24%).

Genetically determined differences in the vitamin C transporter have been described in patients with COVID-19, contributing to variability in oral vitamin C absorption that IV administration circumvents.
Vitamin C deficiency is frequent during acute severe infections, particularly in patients with pneumonia and COVID-19, likely due to high consumption of the vitamin during infection.

In COVID-19, oxidative stress and SARS-CoV-2 endothelial invasion via ACE receptors trigger neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, leading to immune thrombosis, embolism, and microcirculatory dysfunction.

Early observations suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infected subjects develop IgG autoantibodies associated with myopathies, vasculitis, and antiphospholipid syndromes, suggesting an autoimmune contribution to persistent symptoms.
Genetically determined differences in the vitamin C transporter have been described in patients with COVID-19, potentially affecting oral vitamin C resorption, which IV administration can circumvent.
Vitamin C, an important endogenous antioxidant, is reduced in chronic inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and cancer.

SARS-CoV-2 penetrates endothelial cells via ACE receptors, triggering endothelial damage, neutrophil infiltration, and formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), contributing to immune thrombosis and microcirculatory dysfunction.
Vitamin C is essential for macrophage phagocytosis of spent neutrophils; when this clearance fails, neutrophil necrosis leads to NET formation and circulatory disorders.

In an Italian cohort of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 87% had persistence of at least one symptom at 60 days after discharge, with fatigue, worsened quality of life, dyspnea, joint pain and chest pain being most common.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients continued to experience breathlessness and excessive fatigue at 3 months after discharge.
The prevalence of residual COVID symptoms differed sharply by care setting: about 35% among outpatients versus about 87% among hospitalized cohorts.

Failure to return to work at 14-21 days after a positive COVID test was 35% overall, increasing with age and number of comorbidities, and obesity plus psychiatric conditions were associated with more than two-fold odds of not returning to work.

Fever and chills from acute COVID largely resolved (97% and 96%) but cough, fatigue and shortness of breath remained unresolved in a substantial minority, and loss of taste/smell took about 8 days to resolve.
A meta-analysis found the five most common manifestations of long COVID were fatigue, headache, attention disorder, hair loss and dyspnea.
The risk of long COVID is about twice as common in women compared to men, and patients who develop long COVID are on average about four years older than those who do not.

Having more than 5 symptoms during the acute stage of COVID-19 was associated with increased risk of developing long COVID, and fatigue, headache, dyspnea, hoarse voice and myalgia were the symptoms most commonly associated with long COVID.

Two main symptom patterns were identified in long COVID: one dominated by fatigue, headache and upper respiratory complaints, and another with multi-system complaints including ongoing fever and gastrointestinal symptoms.
A Survivor Corps patient-reported survey found that 26.5% of people with long COVID experienced painful symptoms.
More than 50% of people were suffering from fatigue at 10 weeks of follow-up after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
There was no association found between development of post-COVID fatigue and either COVID-19 severity or the level of inflammatory markers.
Female sex and a diagnosis of depression/anxiety were more common among those who developed post-COVID fatigue.

Up to 40% of patients who recovered from SARS in 2003 developed chronic fatigue syndrome, proposed to involve chronic oxidative and nitrosative stress, low-grade inflammation, and impaired heat shock protein production.
SARS-CoV-2 infection can lead to pulmonary complications including chronic cough, post-COVID/post-ARDS pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, and pulmonary vascular disease.

Cardiac complications reported after COVID-19 include labile heart rate/blood pressure responses, myocarditis, pericarditis, impaired myocardial flow reserve, myocardial infarction, cardiac failure, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, aneurysms, accelerated atherosclerosis and thromboembolic disease.
SARS-CoV-2 has been detected in cerebrospinal fluid, indicating neuro-invasive potential, and recovered COVID-19 patients show possible disruption of micro-structural and functional brain integrity.

In a British study of neuropsychiatric manifestations of COVID-19, stroke and altered mental status were the commonest findings, while psychiatric symptoms from encephalopathy/encephalitis and primary psychiatric diagnoses were noted commonly in younger patients.
Acquired focal or multifocal peripheral nerve injury was observed in COVID-19 ARDS patients who had received prone ventilation.
Severe SARS-CoV-2 infection can result in autoreactivity against a variety of self-antigens.
COVID-19 associated coagulopathy can result in both arterial and venous thrombosis.
The paper notes that EBV has been associated with malignancies, autoimmune diseases, and chronic fatigue syndrome as background context for this case.
A young woman with no prior medical history developed cholestatic hepatitis, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia, and splenomegaly, attributed in the case work-up to EBV infection.
The authors state that while EBV commonly elevates liver enzymes, cholestatic hepatitis as a manifestation is exceedingly rare, with only a few prior cases reported.
The authors note that haemolytic anaemia is a common EBV complication that is typically Coombs-positive, making this patient's Coombs-negative presentation atypical.

COVID-19 is described as being able to cause dysautonomia, including POTS, via vagus nerve damage, presenting with intermittent tachycardia, fluctuating blood pressure, and chronic cough or GI complaints.
POTS has been observed in recovered COVID-19 patients who continue to experience significant disability 6-8 months after acute infection.
Severe post-COVID fatigue combined with brain fog and other poorly defined chronic complaints resembles myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome.
Intracortical GABAergic dysfunction has been proposed as a contributing mechanism underlying long-COVID fatigue.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported persistent symptom across post-acute COVID-19 cohort studies, occurring in 30-72% of patients.

An Italian cohort of 143 hospitalized COVID-19 patients found 84.7% reported at least one persistent symptom, most commonly fatigue (53.1%), dyspnea (43.4%), joint pain (27.3%), and chest pain (21.7%).

In a 6-month follow-up study of 1733 patients, 63% reported fatigue or muscle weakness, 26% sleep difficulties, 23% anxiety or depression, up to 29% abnormal 6-minute walk distance, and 13% developed acute kidney injury despite no AKI during acute illness.

Persistent lymphocytopenia, particularly affecting CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ subsets, may be evident up to 6 weeks post-symptom onset, especially among patients with severe acute COVID-19, compared with healthy controls.

A retrospective cohort study of 236,379 COVID-19 patients estimated a 33% incidence of neurological or psychiatric diagnosis within 6 months post-infection, with 12% receiving a first-time diagnosis, rising to 46% among ICU-admitted patients.
Memory impairment with or without delirium during the acute phase affected up to 44% of COVID-19 survivors.
The cumulative incidence of thrombosis and hemorrhage at day 30 post-discharge were reported to be 2.5% and 3.7%, respectively, in a US cohort.
The odds of venous thromboembolism following hospital discharge were estimated to be 60% higher in the post-acute COVID-19 setting compared with 2019.
Cardiac MRI performed 24-71 days post-infection suggested myocardial inflammation or scarring in 15-60% of patients, including those with asymptomatic or mild acute illness.
Recovered COVID-19 patients showed an increased rate of major adverse cardiovascular events at a median follow-up of 140 days.
Myocardial injury, indicated by elevated troponin, was detected in 30% of patients at 3-month follow-up after COVID-19 infection.
Production of autoantibodies against type I interferon has been associated with severe COVID-19.
Several patients presented with abnormally low vitamin D and increased parathyroid hormone levels 8 weeks after COVID-19 onset, potentially impacting bone health.
Up to one-fifth of long-COVID patients report hair loss, possibly attributable to telogen effluvium from direct viral infection or stress response.
Between 18% and 50% of SARS-CoV-2 survivors screened positive for at least one neuropsychiatric domain in cross-sectional and cohort studies.

SARS-CoV-2 can persist in the gut for weeks after diagnosis even without prominent GI symptoms, which may explain some long-term GI symptoms such as dyspepsia and post-infectious IBS-like manifestations.
In a retrospective cohort of 158 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients, persistent pulmonary damage at 2 months after infection was associated with sustained elevation of IL-6.
Chun et al. found higher levels of Lipocalin-2 in 61 prevalently non-critical COVID-19 patients at 2 months, suggesting ongoing neutrophil activation potentially amenable to targeted therapy.
Sonnweber et al. found persisting hyperferritinemia in ~38% of 109 patients with mild-to-critical COVID-19, significantly associated with severe lung pathology.
Han et al. found lung fibrotic-like changes in 35% of 114 severe COVID-19 patients up to 6 months after infection.
Several small cohorts of critically ill COVID-19 patients showed reduced diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) persisting up to 3 months after infection.

Mo et al. found abnormal pulmonary function in 110 discharged COVID-19 patients: DLCO impairment in 47.2%, reduced total lung capacity in 25.0%, FEV1 abnormality in 13.6%, FVC abnormality in 9.1%, FEV1/FVC abnormality in 4.5%, and small airway dysfunction in 7.3%.
Mao et al. reported that approximately 36.4% of COVID-19 patients presented neurological symptoms, supporting the neuro-invasive potential of SARS-CoV-2.
Negrini et al. found that long-term neurological symptoms and general cognitive decay were associated with length of stay in the ICU.

Gallus et al. found that among 48 mild COVID-19 patients at about 1 month follow-up, 8.3% reported hearing loss, 4.2% tinnitus, 8.3% dizziness, 2% spinning vertigo, 2% dynamic imbalance, and 6.3% static imbalance.
At 2 months follow-up, 58.7% of 179 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients presented moderate neurocognitive decline, while 39.1% also showed psychiatric morbidity.
Pilotto et al., in a retrospective cohort of 165 moderate-to-severe COVID-19 patients, found that long-term neurological/cognitive symptoms persisted in about 37% of patients at 6 months follow-up.
The same Pilotto et al. cohort found hyposmia present in ~15% of 165 patients at up to 6 months of follow-up.
Lu et al. prospectively examined 60 mild-to-critical COVID-19 patients and found brain micro-structural changes in 50% of recovered patients at 3 months.
A prospective study of 138 severe COVID-19 patients found 5.8% had moderate-to-severe olfactory dysfunction and 4.3% had a significant taste disorder at 2 months follow-up.

Fjaeldstad found that among 109 mild COVID-19 patients with chemosensory loss at ~1 month, only 44% fully recovered olfactory function (28% no improvement), and 50% fully recovered gustatory function (20% no improvement).
Moein et al. found smell loss in ~37% of 82 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients at 2 months of follow-up.
Sudre et al. analyzed 4,182 incident non-severe COVID-19 cases logged in the COVID-19 Symptom Study App and found women aged 50-60 were at greatest risk of developing long-COVID.
Female sex (mean age 47.22) was reported as a risk factor for poor health-related quality of life among Chinese COVID-19 patients.

D'Cruz et al. and Taboada et al., in prospective cohorts of 119 and 91 severe/critical COVID-19 patients respectively, found dyspnea on exertion in 57%, asthenia in 37%, myalgia in 37%, and arthralgia in 29% up to 2 months, with a general decrease in quality of life (mobility, usual activities, self-care, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression) in 67% of patients at up to 6 months.
Taboada et al. found that at 6 months follow-up only 16% of severe/critical COVID-19 patients were completely free of persistent symptoms.

Tenforde et al., in a Multistate Health Care Systems Network survey of 270 COVID-19 patients including those with milder outpatient illness, found that 35% had not returned to their usual state of health 14-21 days after symptom onset.
Carvalho-Schneider et al. found that about 66% of 150 mild/moderate COVID-19 patients presented at least one persistent symptom at 2 months follow-up, with dyspnea in 30% and asthenia in 40%.
Cirulli et al. found that ~24% of 233 mild COVID-19 patients had at least one persistent symptom after 3 months.

Mahmud et al., in a cohort of 355 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients, found that about 46% developed long-term symptoms at 1 month follow-up, with symptoms significantly higher among females and fatigue as the main long-term symptom.

In an Italian cohort of 143 discharged mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients, only 12.6% were completely free of symptoms at ~2 months, 32% had 1-2 symptoms, and 55% had 3 or more, with chronic fatigue (53.1%), dyspnea (43.4%), joint pain (27.3%), and chest pain (21.7%) most common.

In two prospective cohorts of severe/critical COVID-19 patients (n=119 and n=91), dyspnea on exertion, asthenia, myalgia, and arthralgia persisted up to 2 months after symptom onset, with quality of life reduced in two-thirds of patients by 6 months.
At 6 months follow-up only 16% of severe/critical COVID-19 patients in Taboada et al.'s cohort were completely free of persistent symptoms.
Among 270 interviewed COVID-19 patients including those with milder outpatient illness, 35% had not returned to their usual state of health 14-21 days after symptom onset.
Among 196 mild-moderate COVID-19 patients evaluated by Pellaud et al., 63% of those who returned home reported persistent symptoms at 1 month after symptom onset.
In 150 mild/moderate COVID-19 patients followed prospectively, about 66% presented at least one persistent symptom at 2 months, with dyspnea in 30% and asthenia in 40%.

Cirulli et al. found that ~24% of 233 mild COVID-19 patients had at least one persistent symptom at 3 months, including difficulty concentrating, fatigue, memory loss, confusion, headache, palpitations, chest pain, pain with deep breaths, dizziness, and tachycardia.
A British Medical Association survey of 3,729 doctors found that a third had seen or treated patients with long-term COVID-19 symptoms.
Davido et al. reported that most patients they evaluated for persistent post-COVID symptoms were young women (sex ratio 4:1) around 40 years old with no significant prior medical history.
Female sex (mean age 47.22 years) was identified as a risk factor for poor health-related quality of life in Chinese COVID-19 patients.
Sudre et al. analyzed 4,182 incident cases of non-severe COVID-19 logging symptoms prospectively and found that women aged 50-60 were at greatest risk of developing long-COVID.

In a large cohort of 355 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients, about 46% developed long-term symptoms at 1 month follow-up, and post-COVID features were significantly higher among females, with fatigue the main long-term symptom.
Persistent fatigue was reported in about 12% of a cohort of 1,002 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients.

Analysis of 150 tweets from moderate-to-severe COVID-19 patients found the 10 most common long-term symptoms to be chronic fatigue (62%), dyspnea (19%), tachycardia/palpitations (13%), chest pain (13%), sleep disorders (10%), cough (9%), headache (7%), and joint pain, fever, and unspecified pain (6% each).

In 143 hospitalized mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients followed for an average of 2 months, only 12.6% were completely symptom-free, 32% had 1-2 symptoms, and 55% had 3 or more, with chronic fatigue (53.1%), dyspnea (43.4%), joint pain (27.3%), and chest pain (21.7%) most common; initial dyspnea predicted long-term symptoms.
A retrospective study of 206 mild-to-moderate COVID-19 patients detected chronic pain in approximately 40% of patients at 2 months follow-up.

A cross-sectional study of 46 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients found an extremely low outlier ratio of total protein, albumin, and globulin at 2 months follow-up, indicating persistent abnormal liver function.
Lymphopenia, elevated D-dimer, and elevated C-reactive protein at 2 months follow-up were associated with persistent fatigue, dyspnea, and anosmia in COVID-19 patients.
Raman et al. reported organ abnormalities at 3 months follow-up in the heart (26%), liver (10%), and kidneys (29%) of COVID-19 patients.

In 120 relatively non-severe COVID-19 patients assessed by questionnaire 100 days after initial symptom onset, dyspnea (42%), chronic fatigue (55%), memory loss (34%), concentration disorders (28%), and sleep disorders (30.8%) were reported.
By examining 9,989 mild-to-severe COVID-19 patients, persistent neuropsychiatric, pulmonary, metabolic, and coagulopathic phenotypes were identified at 6 months follow-up.
Fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, muscle and joint pain, headache, insomnia, and palpitations were reported as persistent long-term symptoms in children and adolescents up to 6-8 months after COVID-19.
At 6 months follow-up, high blood pressure and persistence of prehypertension were detected in approximately 13% of mild COVID-19 children.
In larger pediatric cohorts, approximately 53-70% of children had at least one persistent symptom 100 days or more after COVID-19 diagnosis.

The authors propose that women's risk of developing long-term COVID-19 is approximately double that of men among patients aged 40-50, with risk levels becoming similar between sexes after age 60, a pattern resembling autoimmune disease sex distribution around menopause.

The authors hypothesize that long-term COVID-19 symptoms are associated with the coronavirus' ability to trigger a persistent massive inflammatory response ('cytokine storm'), warranting future cytokine network analyses in recovered patients.
The median duration of SARS-CoV-2 viral shedding is reported as 12-20 days, with evidence that fecal shedding may be prolonged compared to respiratory secretions.
A case-report of three women described telogen effluvium (temporary hair shedding) as a long-term COVID-19 symptom occurring 3 months after infection.
Between 10% and 65% of survivors who had mild or moderate COVID-19 present symptoms of post-COVID-19 syndrome persisting for 12 weeks or more.
At six months after COVID-19, subjects report an average of 14 persistent symptoms.
The most common persistent symptoms reported in post-COVID-19 syndrome are fatigue, dyspnoea, anxiety, depression, and impaired attention, concentration, memory and sleep.

The authors hypothesize that an abnormal or excessive autoimmune and inflammatory response may be an important underlying biological mechanism of post-COVID-19 syndrome, though the mechanisms remain unknown.

Post-COVID-19 syndrome is described as a heterogeneous condition that includes post-viral chronic fatigue syndrome, multi-organ sequelae, and effects of severe hospitalisation/post-intensive care syndrome, occurring irrespective of initial COVID-19 severity.
About 30.3% of 185 surveyed COVID-19 patients reported unabating long COVID symptoms at least 30 days after testing positive.
Among long-term subjects at least 90 days post-COVID diagnosis, 66.7% of long COVID subjects were positive for EBV reactivation versus only 10% of control subjects, a significant difference.
Among short-term subjects 21-90 days post-diagnosis, 66.7% of long COVID subjects showed EBV reactivation versus 11.1% of controls, a significant difference.
EBV EA-D IgG antibody titers correlated significantly with the number of reported long COVID symptoms across all 68 subjects.
EBV VCA IgG titers did not show a significant relationship with number of long COVID symptoms.
EBNA-1 IgG titers did not show a significant relationship with number of long COVID symptoms.

EBV DNA PCR testing of subjects negative on antibody titers identified additional reactivation cases, raising overall reactivation rates to 73.3% in long-term and 77.8% in short-term long COVID groups.
The most frequently reported symptoms among EBV-reactivation-positive long COVID subjects were fatigue, insomnia, headaches, myalgia, and confusion/brain fog.
Some long COVID subjects with EBV reactivation experienced skin manifestations including COVID toes, and tinnitus/hearing loss, resembling known EBV-associated dermatologic and otologic conditions.
A prior clinical study in Wuhan reported that ganciclovir, an anti-herpesvirus drug blocking EBV replication, reduced the risk of death in patients with severe COVID-19 disease.
Spironolactone has been found in vitro to inhibit EBV viral capsid antigen synthesis and capsid formation, and is also being studied as a potential SARS-CoV-2 therapeutic.
Extended administration of valacyclovir is known to reduce the frequency of EBV-infected B cells and has been theorized as a treatment to eradicate EBV from the body.

Prior studies found high rates of EBV reactivation during acute severe COVID-19, including 55.2% of hospitalized patients in Wuhan, 95.2%/83.6% of ICU/SICU patients in Italy, 82% of ICU patients in France, and 78% of ventilated ICU patients in Austria.
EBV reactivation was found to be associated with longer median ICU stay in COVID-19 patients (15 days vs 8 days) in a French study.
Olfactory dysfunction affects up to 61% of patients with active COVID-19, with higher prevalence in young adults, women, and Caucasians, and lower prevalence in children and the elderly.
A population-based postal survey found 12% of COVID-19 survivors had persistent olfactory dysfunction (PVOD) at a median follow-up of 117 days.

In an online survey of sudden-onset olfactory dysfunction in active COVID-19, median recovery time was 15 days, with 52.6% achieving full recovery by day 15, while 46% and 19% reported partial or no recovery, respectively, at a median 31-day follow-up.
Persistence of olfactory dysfunction beyond 20 days from onset significantly predicted the risk of developing post-viral olfactory dysfunction.
Among patients with severe olfactory dysfunction at 20 days, 20% still had the problem at 60 days follow-up, whereas those with moderate OD at 20 days had improved by 60 days.
CT imaging showed olfactory cleft obstruction in 3 of 16 anosmic COVID-19 patients, supporting a conductive mechanism of olfactory dysfunction.

MRI showed olfactory cleft obstruction paralleled olfactory dysfunction early in COVID-19, and both improved together at one month in most patients, though a subset remained affected by PVOD despite resolution of olfactory cleft obstruction.
Olfactory cleft opacification on CT was found in 73.9% of recovered COVID-19 patients with olfactory dysfunction persisting beyond one month.
66.9% of COVID-19 patients with anosmia did not report nasal congestion, distinguishing COVID-19-related anosmia from typical viral-rhinitis anosmia.

Non-neuronal olfactory epithelial cells (sustentacular, microvillar, Bowman's gland, horizontal basal cells, olfactory bulb pericytes) express ACE2 in significantly higher quantities than surrounding olfactory epithelium, providing the main entry route for SARS-CoV-2 in the olfactory system.
TMPRSS2, the protease that primes SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, is co-expressed with ACE2 in the same non-neuronal olfactory epithelial cell types.
Higher ACE2 expression in adults compared with children correlates with the higher prevalence of COVID-19 disease in adults.

Release of proinflammatory cytokines, especially TNF-α, in response to olfactory epithelial injury causes initial desensitization of olfactory sensory neurons followed by neuronal loss, producing sensorineural olfactory dysfunction.

Neuropilin-1 (NRP1), abundantly expressed in olfactory sensory neurons and mitral cell axons but not in the olfactory epithelium, is a host factor that binds primed SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and mediates cell entry, potentially explaining viral presence in the CNS despite OSNs lacking ACE2.

An in silico study found NRP1 abundantly expressed in brain regions involved in olfaction, including olfactory tubercles and para-olfactory gyri, supporting a hypothesized retrograde axonal transport route for SARS-CoV-2 CNS invasion similar to herpes simplex virus.

MRI of COVID-19-recovered patients with persistent olfactory dysfunction beyond one month showed olfactory bulb shape changes in 54.2% of cases, abnormal bulb signal intensity (diffusely increased signal, hyperintense foci, or microhaemorrhages) in 91.3%, olfactory filia clumping in 34.8%, filia thinning/scarcity in 17.4%, and primary olfactory cortex signal abnormality in 21.7%.
A modified alcohol sniff test using 10% ethanol showed 75% sensitivity as a screening tool for COVID-19 in a Phase II trial, with an odds ratio of 6.56.

In an objective olfactory assessment of 91 patients at a mean of 57.94 days post-infection, there was poor correlation between measured olfactory performance and patients' self-assessment, with 51.35% of hyposmic patients unaware of their impairment.
In vitro studies showed the protease inhibitor camostat mesylate inhibits SARS-CoV-2 cell entry, suggesting potential therapeutic use during active COVID-19 to reduce the incidence/severity of PVOD.

Olfactory training (repeated odorant exposure) is described as a cost-effective intervention for sensorineural olfactory loss, with both traditional and modified protocols showing significant improvement in olfaction, though neither has established superiority.
High-concentration odorants demonstrated higher efficacy than low-concentration odorants in olfactory training for post-infectious olfactory dysfunction.

In vitro studies show camostat mesylate, a protease inhibitor, blocks SARS-CoV-2 cell entry and is proposed as a potential therapeutic during active COVID-19 to prevent post-viral olfactory dysfunction.

Nasal lavage with an ACE-2 antagonist or angiotensin receptor blocker is hypothesized to reduce viral load in COVID-19, which the authors propose could decrease incidence and severity of post-viral olfactory dysfunction.
BSG and PIKfyve are additional molecules identified as contributors mediating SARS-CoV-2 infection, beyond ACE-2/TMPRSS2 and NRP1.
High concentration odorants demonstrated higher efficacy than low concentration odorants in olfactory training for post-infectious olfactory dysfunction.

An ongoing registered trial (NCT04495816) is comparing an Omega-3 fatty acid supplement versus placebo for olfactory dysfunction, based on preclinical mouse and post-surgical human data suggesting improved olfaction return.
An ongoing registered trial (NCT04484493) is comparing mometasone furoate nasal spray plus olfactory training versus olfactory training alone for olfactory improvement over 3 weeks.

An ongoing four-arm trial (NCT04422275) is testing budesonide nasal lavage versus placebo combined with high or low concentration essential oil olfactory training, assessed via UPSIT and quality-of-life scales.
An ongoing trial (NCT04569825) is comparing intranasal steroid drops (Ophtamesone) versus normal saline drops for recovery rate and time of anosmia.

An ongoing open-label trial (NCT04528329) is comparing early dexamethasone use (initiated at first evidence of high inflammatory markers) versus late dexamethasone use (initiated on clinical deterioration) for time to recovery.

An ongoing trial (NCT04361474) is comparing budesonide saline nasal irrigation with olfactory rehabilitation versus saline irrigation with olfactory rehabilitation alone, measuring ODORATEST score improvement after 30 days.

An ongoing trial (NCT04657809) is testing a bioadhesive fast-dissolving film containing 100IU insulin versus placebo film for smell sensation improvement measured by butanol threshold test at 4 weeks.

Plasma viscosity was significantly increased in acute COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls and compared to Long COVID/PASC, but Long COVID/PASC patients showed no significant difference in viscosity compared to controls.

SAA1 plasma concentrations measured by ELISA were significantly elevated in both acute COVID-19 and Long COVID/PASC patients compared to healthy controls, with no significant difference between the two COVID groups.

Platelets from Long COVID/PASC patients showed hyperactivation (increased CD62P and PAC-1 marker binding) with an additional feature of platelet clumping, similar to previously reported findings in acute COVID-19.
Platelet poor plasma from Long COVID/PASC patients contained considerable anomalous (amyloid) microclots detectable by thioflavin T staining, comparable to those seen in acute COVID-19 plasma.

Unlike plasma from healthy controls and T2DM patients, which was fully digested by a single trypsinization step, plasma from acute COVID-19 and Long COVID/PASC patients formed a visible, fibrinolytic-resistant pellet deposit requiring a second trypsin digestion step to solubilize.

Proteomic analysis of fibrinolysis-resistant pellet deposits showed a significant fold increase in α2-antiplasmin in Long COVID/PASC samples compared to both controls and acute COVID-19 samples, while antiplasmin levels in the fully digested supernatant were similar across all groups.

SAA4, a constitutively expressed acute phase protein normally partitioned onto HDL, was undetectable in digested control plasma but showed a 17-fold increase in the fibrinolysis-resistant pellet deposits of Long COVID/PASC samples.

Mass spectrometry proteomics confirmed that fibrinogen alpha chain concentration was increased in the digested supernatant of acute COVID-19 samples compared with controls and Long COVID/PASC, while the beta and gamma chains were unchanged across groups.

Proteomic analysis of digested pellet deposits showed increased levels of coagulation factor XIII and the α and β fibrinogen chains in Long COVID/PASC samples compared to fully digested control plasma and to acute COVID-19 pellet deposits.
Plasminogen levels were slightly increased in the pellet deposits of Long COVID/PASC samples relative to control and acute COVID-19 samples.
Von Willebrand Factor levels were increased in both acute COVID-19 and Long COVID/PASC samples, which may promote greater platelet activation and adhesion to the endothelium.
Proteomics of fully digested plasma supernatants showed fold-change increases in Complement C1r subcomponent-like protein and SAA1 in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus samples compared to control samples.

Comparison of digested plasma supernatants from T2DM and Long COVID/PASC samples revealed significant fold changes in complement C1q subcomponent subunit B and two keratin proteins (type I and II cytoskeletal).
Among non-hospitalized, lab-confirmed COVID-19 positive participants, 68.7% reported at least one persistent symptom at 30 days or longer post-infection.
PASC prevalence increased with longer follow-up, from 59.6% at 30–59 days to 77.1% at ≥60 days post-diagnosis.
Fatigue and shortness of breath were the most commonly reported symptoms among individuals with PASC, each affecting 37.5% of participants.
Brain fog and stress/anxiety were each reported by 30.8% of participants with PASC.
Only 6 participants reported stress/anxiety as their sole symptom, indicating the overall PASC prevalence estimate is not driven by this non-specific symptom.

Individuals with PASC were more likely to have less education, at least one pre-existing chronic condition (particularly seasonal allergies), and greater self-reported acute illness severity compared to those without PASC.
Females had a higher proportion of PASC than males (73% versus 63%), but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
No difference in PASC prevalence was observed based on age or BMI.

Sensitivity analyses using multiple imputation to account for loss to follow-up produced lower estimated PASC prevalence as the assumed dropout bias increased, ranging from 68.0% (delta=0%) to 43.9% (delta=75%).
At ≥60 days follow-up, half of participants reported 3 or more symptoms and a quarter reported 7 or more symptoms, with a median of 3 symptoms overall among those with PASC (range 1-20).
Oxygen-ozone autohemotherapy (O2-O3-AHT) reduced PASC-related fatigue by a mean of 67% across the treated cohort.
Despite the cohort being predominantly female, the therapeutic effect of O2-O3-AHT on fatigue was not significantly influenced by sex distribution.
About two fifths (approximately 40%) of the treated cohort achieved near-complete recovery from PASC-associated fatigue following O2-O3-AHT.
An estimated 10% of COVID-19 survivors continue to experience protracted symptoms weeks to months after initial infection, a condition termed PASC.
Age, comorbid medical conditions, and severity of acute COVID-19 are suspected risk factors for developing PASC, though young and previously healthy individuals with mild COVID-19 are also at risk.
Management of PASC centers on symptom recognition, clinical evaluation, supportive treatment, and attention to comorbid medical conditions.
All patients (100%) had very high serum ferritin concentrations 60 days after hospital discharge for Covid-19.
All patients (100%) had very high serum D-Dimer levels 60 days after hospital discharge for Covid-19.
87% of patients had clinically significant low hemoglobin levels 60 days after hospital discharge.
72% of patients had clinically significant low serum albumin levels 60 days after hospital discharge.
73% of patients had elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate 60 days after hospital discharge.
73% of patients had elevated CRP 60 days after hospital discharge, indicating persistent pro-inflammatory cytokine predominance.
More than 27% of patients had persistently elevated LDH levels, supporting ongoing cellular damage.
Male patients had significantly higher ESR levels than female patients, otherwise no gender differences in blood markers were observed.
Fatigue and dyspnea are described as the most frequent symptoms of Long-COVID.
The Fatigue Assessment Scale (FAS, score range 10-50, substantial fatigue defined as score ≥22) was used as a validated self-report tool to identify patients with fatigue for study inclusion.
Muscular weakness was objectively confirmed using the 1-minute sit-to-stand test, with weakness defined as repetitions below 70% of predicted values.
Persistent alterations in ferritin, hemoglobin, albumin, CRP, ESR, LDH and D-Dimer 60 days after acute Covid-19 indicate an ongoing hypercatabolic/hypermetabolic state underlying PASC symptoms.
Cited literature suggests SARS-CoV-2-induced IL-1β and IL-6 stimulate hepcidin synthesis, and the virus itself has hepcidin-mimetic action, driving hyperferritinemia and iron dysmetabolism.
SARS-CoV-2 nonstructural protein ORF3a is proposed to digest the heme group of mitochondrial cytochrome-C, dissociating iron and causing mitochondrial/cellular metabolic impairment.
Cited literature indicates SARS-CoV-2 infection activates MAPK phosphorylation cascades, which regulate autophagy and viral mRNA translation.

The authors recommend prophylactic nutritional therapy, including personalized nitrogen/protein and amino acid intake with anabolic vitamin and mineral cofactors, as first-line care to counteract the hypercatabolic state in PASC.
The authors recommend that prophylactic anticoagulant therapy be considered and discussed with patients given persistent D-Dimer elevation and possible long-term thromboembolic risk in PASC.
Nearly 20% of previously young, healthy outpatients with COVID-19 do not return to their usual state of health within 3 weeks of infection.
Approximately 75% of COVID-19 survivors hospitalised in a Chinese cohort had at least one persistent symptom 6 months after acute illness.
Beyond the first 30 days after infection, non-hospitalised COVID-19 patients had a higher risk of death compared with those without COVID-19.
Patients hospitalised with COVID-19 had a higher risk of death beyond 30 days compared with patients hospitalised with seasonal influenza.
Nearly a quarter of COVID-19 survivors perform below the lower limit of normal on the 6-minute walk test 6 months after acute illness.
In a large international survey, 85% of respondents self-reported cognitive impairment that affected daily life and return to work.
Nearly one in four patients hospitalised with COVID-19 reports substantial depression or anxiety symptoms lasting at least 6 months after acute illness.
Among hospitalised patients, decreased DLCO (about 33%) and reduced total lung capacity (about 17%) are the most common pulmonary impairments at 6 months after acute COVID-19.
Patients with more severe initial COVID-19 pneumonia had significantly lower percentage of predicted DLCO at 4-month follow-up compared with less severe patients.
