There is no consistent association between dyspnoea and abnormalities on chest imaging, pulmonary function tests, or initial disease severity in COVID-19 survivors.
Fatigue is common in survivors of ARDS, affecting approximately 70% of patients at 1-year follow-up.

Fatigue after acute respiratory failure is not consistently associated with severity of illness or ICU length of stay, but frequently co-occurs with cognitive, mental health, and physical function impairments.
Autonomic dysfunction occurs in patients with PASC, making timely completion of autonomic function tests such as the tilt table test important for proper diagnosis and treatment.
A systematic review (Michelen et al) reported pooled proportions of weakness (41%), malaise (33%), and decreased sensation (11%) among COVID-19 survivors.

A 2018 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that ICU survivorship clinics improve outcomes for patients after ICU discharge, citing heterogeneity in services and study design.

Beginning early rehabilitation within 48 hours of ICU admission is associated with improvement in strength and independent walking in the hospital, though the long-term effects of early intervention remain uncertain.
About one-third of patients recovering from COVID-19 report that persistent symptoms affect their ability to return to work up to 7 months after acute illness.
Black, Asian, and minority ethnic groups in Europe and North America have an increased risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and poorer outcomes, including higher mortality, from COVID-19.
About 30% of COVID-19 outpatients or hospitalized patients report persistent symptoms after the acute infection.
Patients who go on to develop PASC generally show higher pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, including TNFα, than those who recover.
Persistent SARS-CoV-2 viral proteins and RNA have been detected in intestinal biopsies, suggesting a hidden viral reservoir may drive PASC.
Activation or dysregulation of the complement system has been implicated in the development of PASC.
During acute COVID-19, autoantibodies targeting the type I interferon system contribute to pathogenesis and development of severe disease.
A subset of children with SARS-CoV-2-associated multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C) develop autoreactive antibodies against MAP2K2 and the lupus antigen (La).
Adults with COVID-19 show increased levels of autoreactive antibodies similar to those found in rheumatoid arthritis, which may drive PASC development.

Male COVID-19 patients show higher plasma pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, while female patients display more robust T cell activation.

Patients with post-polio syndrome, which shares many features with chronic fatigue syndrome, show increased plasma levels of TNFα, IL-6 and IL-8.
A polymorphism in the FcγRIIa gene (FcγRIIa-131HH) is associated with enhanced autoimmune markers and persistent clinical symptoms following dengue virus infection.

Anxiety was the second most common post-acute COVID-19 symptom, documented in 25.8% of patients.
Depression was documented in 24.0% of patients during the post-acute COVID-19 period.
Fatigue was documented in 23.4% of patients in the post-acute COVID-19 period and was one of the symptoms with perfect NLP extraction precision.
Joint pain was documented in 21.0% of patients during the post-acute COVID-19 follow-up period.
Shortness of breath was documented in 20.8% of patients during the post-acute COVID-19 period.
Headache was documented in 20.0% of patients during the post-acute COVID-19 period.

Visual changes, documented in 5.8% of patients, were highlighted as a post-acute COVID-19 symptom not previously identified in large-scale studies.

The final 355-symptom PASCLex lexicon, applied via a rule-based NLP system (MTERMS), achieved high precision (46/50 top symptoms >0.90, average 0.94) and moderate recall (0.84) for extracting post-acute COVID-19 symptoms from clinical notes in a held-out validation cohort.

Starting from 157,245 UMLS concepts, iterative manual review and consolidation across 26,117 COVID-19 patients' clinical notes yielded a final lexicon of 355 consolidated post-acute COVID-19 symptoms mapped to 1520 UMLS concepts and 16,466 synonyms.

The post-acute COVID-19 clinical follow-up cohort had a higher proportion of females overall, with a greater share of females under age 50 (49.9%) compared to males under 50 (37.3%), and both sexes showed a unimodal age peak in the 50s.
COVID-19 survivors who required hospitalization scored significantly lower on multiple SF-36 quality-of-life domains compared to those who were not hospitalized.
Participants with moderate or severe acute COVID-19 disease scored significantly lower than those with mild disease on five SF-36 domains.
Participants with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) had significantly lower quality-of-life scores across seven of the eight SF-36 domains compared to those without PASC.

COVID-19 survivors with pre-existing chronic medical conditions had significantly lower quality-of-life scores in physical, energy/fatigue, and general health domains than those without chronic conditions.
Female COVID-19 survivors reported significantly lower Pain scale scores (i.e., more pain) than male survivors.
There was no significant difference in any of the eight SF-36 scales between Hispanic and non-Hispanic COVID-19 survivors.
No significant differences were found in any of the eight SF-36 scales between participants tested 15-44 days post-PCR-positive and those tested 175+ days post-PCR-positive.
Obese COVID-19 survivors had reduced Physical Functioning, Role Limitation due to Physical Health, Energy/Fatigue, and General Health scores compared to normal-weight or underweight participants.
When included as continuous covariates in ANCOVA models, BMI and age were not significantly related to PASC, hospitalization, or chronic conditions status with regard to SF-36 scores.
Emotional Well-Being scores on the SF-36 were not significantly impacted in any patient subgroup, including those with PASC, despite significant physical impacts.
Role Limitations due to Emotional Problems were significantly reduced in hospitalized patients and in those with PASC, distinguishing this from the unaffected Emotional Well-Being scale.
Across cohorts reporting general symptoms, fatigue was the most frequently reported long COVID feature, with a median prevalence of 45.1%.
Dyspnea was the most commonly reported respiratory symptom of long COVID, with a median prevalence of 35.1% across cohorts.
Decreased diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide was the most commonly reported pulmonary function finding in long COVID cohorts.
Insomnia was the most commonly reported sleep impairment finding, with a median prevalence of 31.9% across cohorts.
Hepatic steatosis was the most commonly reported gastrointestinal finding in the small subset of cohorts assessing liver findings, though it is also common in the general population.
Elevated circulating D-dimer concentration was the most commonly reported laboratory abnormality in long COVID cohorts.
Anxiety was the most commonly reported behavioral abnormality among long COVID cohorts.
Depression was the most commonly reported emotion/mood abnormality among long COVID cohorts.
Hypertension was the most commonly reported cardiovascular finding among long COVID cohorts.
Cognitive impairment was the most commonly reported cognitive dysfunction finding among long COVID cohorts.
Alopecia was the most commonly reported dermatological finding among long COVID cohorts.
Parenchymal consolidation was the most commonly reported pulmonary imaging finding among long COVID cohorts.
Myalgia was the most commonly reported pain-category finding among long COVID cohorts.
Anosmia was the most commonly reported smell/taste abnormality among long COVID cohorts, though terminology for loss of smell/taste varied widely across studies.
Blurred vision was the most commonly reported ocular abnormality among long COVID cohorts.
Diarrhea was the most commonly reported gastrointestinal symptom among long COVID cohorts.
Fever was the most commonly reported finding in the reproductive/genitourinary/endocrine/metabolism category, though reported at low prevalence overall.
Dysphagia was the most commonly reported finding in the neuropsychiatric findings category, at low prevalence.
Among the 31 phenotypic terms reported in at least 10 cohorts, nausea was the least commonly reported, with a median prevalence of 3.9%.

Curators mapped descriptions from 59 publications and 81 cohorts of long COVID patients to 287 distinct Human Phenotype Ontology terms, representing signs, symptoms, laboratory, and imaging abnormalities.

Ten phenotypic abnormalities identified in long COVID were also reported in Post-Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS), and while most manifestations occurred at similar frequencies between the two conditions, dyspnea was more commonly reported in COVID-19 patients.

A prior patient-led survey of 3,762 respondents with illness lasting more than 28 days documented 205 distinct phenotypic features of long COVID, far more than the 84 signs/symptoms and 19 lab/imaging measures reported by clinical systematic reviews.
A cited systematic review concluded that 73% of individuals who had acute COVID-19 experienced at least one persistent symptom, though study heterogeneity limited comparability.

A preprint systematic review of 15 studies with at least 100 patients each identified 55 symptoms of long COVID, none of which were assessed by all 15 studies, underscoring extreme heterogeneity in symptom assessment.
Hospitalized COVID-19 survivors were significantly more likely to develop PASC than those who were not hospitalized.
Participants with moderate COVID-19 (1-5 L oxygen) were equally as likely to develop PASC as those with severe COVID-19 (>5 L oxygen).
Overall, 49% of participants who completed follow-up (37 of 75) developed PASC at any point during follow-up, with surveillance up to 8 months post-infection.

Persistent symptoms attributed to COVID-19 increased over time, being reported by 55% of participants at 25-89 days, 67% at 90-174 days, and 64% overall (90% among hospitalized patients) after 175 days post-infection.
Participants with PASC had a lower mean total SF-36 quality-of-life score than those without PASC.

PASC participants scored lower than non-PASC participants across all eight SF-36 subdomains, with the largest gaps in physical functioning, role limitations due to physical health, and general health.
Obesity, older age, male sex, and Hispanic/Latinx ethnicity were identified as risk factors for severe COVID-19 in this cohort.
Average BMI was substantially higher in participants with moderate or severe COVID-19 compared to those with mild disease.
Males were disproportionately represented among participants who suffered severe COVID-19 despite being a minority of the overall cohort.
The majority of Hispanic or Latino participants in the cohort were hospitalized for COVID-19.
Among participants with only mild COVID-19, there was no significant difference in age, gender, BMI, or underlying health conditions between those with and without PASC.
Physical examinations were normal in nearly all participants with PASC despite their reported symptoms.

Non-infected adult controls who completed the symptom questionnaire reported no symptoms, supporting that reported PASC symptoms are attributable to SARS-CoV-2 infection rather than general pandemic-related factors.
New-onset alopecia recorded 3-6 months after a COVID-19 RT-PCR test was strongly associated with a positive past COVID-19 test in the overall cohort and specifically in women under and over 65.
A new diagnosis of non-specific chest pain 3-6 months post-test was indicative of past COVID-19 infection, particularly in those under 65.
Anosmia and dysgeusia recorded for the first time 3-6 and 6-9 months after testing were strongly indicative of past COVID-19 infection, particularly in patients under 65 and women under 65.
A new diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome after COVID-19 was associated with past positive infection in both the 3-6 and 6-9 month windows, more prominent in patients and women under 65.
New pneumonia diagnoses 3-6 months after testing were associated with past COVID-19 infection in the overall population and those over 65.
Shortness of breath newly recorded 3-6 and 6-9 months after testing was strongly associated with past COVID-19 infection, especially in those under 65.
New-onset palpitations 3-6 months after testing had a high confidence score for association with past COVID-19 infection.
A new formal diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus 3-6 months after testing was associated with past COVID-19 infection.
Iron deficiency anemia newly diagnosed in the 6-9 month window was associated with past COVID-19 infection among patients and women under 65.
Proteinuria newly recorded 3-6 months after testing was strongly associated with past COVID-19 infection in men under 65, suggesting persistent renal insult.
Syncope and collapse newly recorded 6-9 months after testing was associated with past COVID-19 infection in men under 65.
Anemia during pregnancy was identified with moderate-high confidence as newly associated with past COVID-19 infection in women under 65 in the 3-6-month window.
Chronic kidney disease was newly identified with moderate-high confidence as associated with past COVID-19 infection in patients and women over 65 in the 3-6-month window.
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction was newly identified with moderate-high confidence as associated with past COVID-19 infection in the over-65 cohort in the 3-6-month window.
Irregular menstrual cycle was newly associated with past COVID-19 infection in women under 65 (3-6-month window) and in the total cohort (6-9-month window).

A generic 'neurological disorders' phenotype (predominantly ICD code for symptoms/signs involving cognitive function and awareness) newly appeared in under-65 patients and was associated with past COVID-19 infection, suggesting ongoing cognitive dysfunction.
Rash and other non-specific skin eruptions were newly associated with past COVID-19 infection in men under 65 in the 3-6-month window.
Anemia of chronic disease was newly associated with past COVID-19 infection in women 65 and older in the 6-9-month window.
Disorders of the conjunctiva were newly associated with past COVID-19 infection in men under 65 in the 6-9-month window.
Dizziness and lightheadedness were newly associated with past COVID-19 infection in women older than 65 in the 6-9-month window.
Sensorineural hearing loss was newly associated with past COVID-19 infection in women over 65 in the 6-9-month window.

Vascular dementia was newly diagnosed with elevated confidence in patients and women over 65 in the 6-9-month window, and the authors suggest COVID-19 may have contributed to worsening of pre-existing cognitive decline leading to formal dementia diagnosis.

A composite nail disease phenotype (including leukonychia, onycholysis, onychomadesis, Mees' lines, Muehrcke's lines, and Beau's lines) was identified as newly associated with past COVID-19 infection, suggesting systemic infection with possible renal involvement.

This large, controlled EHR study did not confirm a broad association between COVID-19 and cutaneous eruptions other than nail changes and alopecia, ruling out some previously reported skin-related associations from poorly controlled observational data.
Female sex was identified as a risk factor for developing persisting symptoms after acute COVID-19.
Pre-existing comorbidities were identified as a risk factor for persisting symptoms after acute COVID-19.
Greater severity of the acute COVID-19 illness was identified as a risk factor for persisting symptoms, though symptoms also occur after mild disease.
Persisting symptoms after acute COVID-19 commonly include fatigue with exercise intolerance, exertional dyspnea, chest pain, and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
In a US observational cohort, 32.6% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients had ongoing morbidity 60 days after hospital discharge.
More than 70% of a large Chinese cohort experienced at least one persistent symptom at 6 months post-acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Only 12.6% of an Italian cohort of 143 discharged COVID-19 patients were completely symptom-free at a mean of 60 days after symptom onset.
A discharged COVID-19 cohort showed fatigue or muscle weakness in 63%, sleep difficulties in 26%, and anxiety or depression in 23% of patients.
Eight lymphoid-associated immunoinhibitory receptor genes were specifically upregulated in autopsy tissue from severe, terminal-stage COVID-19, correlating with viral load in lung tissue.
Exhaustion markers PD-1, CTLA-4, TIGIT and Tim-3 were increased in both lung-resident and circulating T cells of COVID-19 patients.
An increased population of lung-infiltrating CD8+ T cells showing transcriptional hallmarks of terminal exhaustion (CCL4, GZMB, MKI67, TYMS) was found in severe COVID-19 patients.
52% of 172 COVID-19 patients had antiphospholipid antibodies of various isotypes, and IgG fractions from these patients enhanced venous thrombosis when injected into mice.
68.7% (20/29) of ICU COVID-19 patients tested positive for autoantibodies related to autoimmune rheumatic diseases.

A high prevalence of autoantibodies against diverse immune-related proteins (cytokines, chemokines, complement proteins, immunomodulatory proteins, metalloproteinases, endothelial cell surface proteins) was observed in 194 COVID-19 patients.

Approximately 10% of 987 patients with life-threatening COVID-19 pneumonia had high-titer IgG autoantibodies against type I interferon-alpha2 and interferon-omega, seen only in severe and not mild/asymptomatic cases.
44% of a 31-patient COVID-19 cohort tested positive for antinuclear antibodies.
Proteome array profiling identified pathogenic autoantibodies targeting endoglin (CD105), MAP2K2 and casein kinases in MIS-C, implicating them in MIS-C immunopathology.
Gut microbiota composition was altered in COVID-19 patients and this dysbiosis persisted for up to 30 days after disease resolution.
Persistent SARS-CoV-2 in the gut of MIS-C patients was shown to drive zonulin-dependent loss of gut mucosal barrier integrity, contributing to hyperinflammation.
Elevated plasma angiotensin II levels have been associated with lung injury and pathogenesis in critically ill COVID-19 patients.
Pathological evidence showed residual SARS-CoV-2 virus persisting in the lungs even after three consecutive negative PCR test results.
In a cohort of 55 COVID-19 survivors assessed 3 months after recovery, 64% had persistent symptoms and 71% showed radiological or physiological lung abnormalities.
A longitudinal study found residual ground-glass opacity on lung CT in 94% of discharged COVID-19 pneumonia patients.

In a cohort of competitive athletes recovered from mostly mild/asymptomatic COVID-19, CMR imaging revealed myocarditis in 15% and prior myocardial injury in 31%.
The rate of venous thromboembolism in post-acute COVID-19 has been estimated at less than 5%, though based on studies with small sample sizes and inadequate follow-up.
Neurological deficits including strokes, seizures and Guillain-Barre syndrome were reported in more than a third (36.4%) of COVID-19 patients.
A systematic review of 43 studies (>18,000 patients) found diarrhea in 11.5%, nausea/vomiting in 6.3%, and abdominal pain in 2.3% of COVID-19 patients.

Gastrointestinal sequelae were observed in 44% of 117 COVID-19 patients at 90 days post-discharge, most commonly loss of appetite (24%), nausea (18%), acid reflux (18%) and diarrhea (15%).
Use of medications for autoimmune disease was associated with a modestly higher, but not statistically significant, odds of reporting ≥7 symptoms at COVID-19 enrollment compared to non-users.

Older age was associated with greater symptom persistence, particularly fatigue, in follow-up, in contrast to its lack of association with more severe acute disease presentation.
Female gender, smoking, obesity, fewer years of education, and lung disease requiring prescription medications were each associated with more severe COVID-19 presentation at enrollment.

Autoimmune disease medication users were less likely to complete the 30-day follow-up survey than non-users (37.6% vs 44.3% retention), and this differential loss to follow-up was more pronounced among those with additional comorbidities, suggesting the study's risk estimates may underestimate true risk.
Between 17% and 63% of both hospitalised and non-hospitalised COVID-19 patients report fatigue 6-12 months after infection, based on prior cohort studies cited in the protocol.

A longer duration of fatigue symptoms prior to treatment is associated with a less favourable response to CBT, motivating early intervention after COVID-19.
Severe fatigue in this trial is defined and screened using a cut-off score of ≥35 on the fatigue severity subscale of the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS-fatigue).
Fatigue is reported as the most common symptom among patients with long COVID, although most patients also report additional symptoms beyond fatigue.
82% of patients presenting at least 6 months after COVID-19 reported persistent fatigue.
61% of patients reported dyspnea on exertion at least 6 months after COVID-19.

Impairments in lung function tests were more common in patients who had been previously hospitalized for COVID-19 compared to those treated as outpatients.

Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein, a marker of astrocyte activation and injury, is elevated in patients with moderate-to-severe COVID-19.

A low-dose nitroglycerin patch (0.1 mg/h) applied at night and removed in the morning has been used to manage nocturnal hypertension in patients with autonomic dysfunction.

In a phase 2 clinical trial in patients with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, escalating doses of ampreloxetine followed by 20 weeks of open-label treatment increased plasma norepinephrine levels by 71%.
Passive heat applied via an abdominal heating pad reduced systemic blood pressure by approximately 20 mmHg in 12 patients with autonomic failure.
In a proof-of-concept study, overnight passive heat via a 38°C water-perfused heating pad under the back reduced systolic blood pressure by 28 ± 6 mmHg in patients with autonomic failure.
Heart rate variability inversely correlates with markers of inflammation in patients with coronary artery disease, cardiovascular risk factors, autoimmune disease, and traumatic brain injury.
Lungs of adults with pulmonary hypertension contain approximately twice the number of pericytes compared to non-hypertensive adults.
The inflammatory proteins tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-1β increase pericyte gap size, facilitating leukocyte migration across the vascular wall.

Entropy analysis of cardiac signals (integrated transformed probability signals, symbolic dynamics entropy, and copula parameters) identified features of cardiac autonomic dysfunction in patients with COVID-19.
Dysautonomia has been reported to persist for nearly a year following initial SARS-CoV-2 infection in some patients, at times severe enough to preclude return to work.
Low-dose β-blockers reduce heart rate and attenuate symptoms in some, but not all, patients with POTS.
Respiratory therapy and breathing retraining improve functional capacity, respiratory rate, breath-hold time, and quality of life among patients with autonomic dysfunction, including those with POTS.
A hyperadrenergic state with increased plasma norepinephrine levels helps maintain blood pressure while standing in patients with POTS.

Frequent sighing is a common symptom among patients with COVID-19 identified through large patient registries, and unexplained sighing is frequently associated with abnormal tilt table testing, suggesting a link to autonomic dysfunction.
A gain-of-function channelopathy involving If channels has been proposed as a contributor to inappropriate sinus tachycardia.

Pre-existing conditions characterized by heightened sympathetic tone—including systemic hypertension, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and chronic kidney disease—are associated with increased risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection and poorer outcomes.

Evening administration of eplerenone 50 mg lowered nocturnal blood pressure without worsening orthostatic hypotension in patients with autonomic dysfunction, suggesting excess mineralocorticoid secretion contributes to nocturnal hypertension.
A low-dose nitroglycerine patch (0.1 mg/h) applied at night and removed in the morning has been used successfully to manage nocturnal hypertension in autonomic dysfunction.

Passive heat applied via a heating pad reduced systemic blood pressure by ~20 mmHg in 12 patients, and overnight passive heat (38°C water-perfused pad) reduced systolic blood pressure by 28±6 mmHg in a proof-of-concept study of patients with autonomic failure.

In a phase 2 clinical trial of ampreloxetine (a selective, long-acting norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) in patients with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, escalating doses over 5 days followed by 20 weeks of open-label treatment increased plasma norepinephrine levels by 71%.

Bajic et al. identified features of cardiac autonomic dysfunction in COVID-19 patients using entropy analysis of integrated transformed probability signals, symbolic dynamics entropy, and copula parameters.

Using a smartphone-based COVID symptoms study database of 2.8 million users, Denis et al. identified orthostatic intolerance syndromes (resting or orthostatic hypotension and/or tachycardia) exclusively in women aged 26-50 years among long-term COVID-19 symptom reporters.

Johansson and colleagues described a small case series of patients developing a POTS-like syndrome approximately 3 months after COVID-19 diagnosis, with symptom onset following a period of post-acute illness quiescence.

In a rat model of pulmonary hypertension, the β-blocker nebivolol reduced endothelial cell proliferation and improved nitric oxide availability, reflecting its combined β1 antagonist and β2/β3 agonist vasodilating properties.
Lungs of adults with pulmonary hypertension contain approximately twofold greater number of pericytes compared with non-hypertensive adults.
Inflammatory proteins such as tumor necrosis factor and interleukin-1β increase pericyte gap size, facilitating leukocyte migration across the vascular wall.

Single-cell studies show that cells double-positive for ACE2 and TMPRSS2 have gene expression covariant with immune signaling genes and are enriched in antigen processing and presentation pathways, suggesting a mechanism for autoimmune responses in COVID-19.

Respiratory therapy and breathing retraining improved functional capacity, respiratory rate, breath hold time, and quality of life among patients with autonomic dysfunction, including those with POTS.

Anodal transcranial direct current stimulation using bifrontal electrode/coil positioning has been used to increase vagus nerve activity, and temporal cortex autonomic modulation has been reported to reduce sympathetic activity, increase baroreceptor sensitivity, and reduce heart rate at submaximal exercise.

Heart rate variability inversely relates to markers of inflammation in patients with coronary artery disease, cardiovascular risk factors, autoimmune disease and traumatic brain injury, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of parasympathetic tone.
During facial expression tasks, children with ASD showed greater autonomic nervous system changes than controls, mostly evidenced by non-linear HRV indices.
Autism severity and behavioral symptoms, as measured by CARS and ABC scales, were significantly correlated with HRV indices in children with ASD.
Autoimmune systemic disease (ASD) patients had a significantly higher prevalence of symptomatic COVID-19 than the general Italian population across all three macro-areas studied.

ASD patients with pre-existing interstitial lung involvement had a significantly higher prevalence of COVID-19 than those without such lung involvement.

ASD patients treated with biological DMARDs showed a significantly lower prevalence of COVID-19.
Scleroderma patients undergoing low-dose aspirin therapy had a significantly lower rate of COVID-19 compared to those not on aspirin.

A biallelic ELFN1 frameshift mutation is associated with a novel clinical entity combining developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, autistic features, pyramidal signs, joint laxity, and dysmorphic features.
Whole exome sequencing followed by Sanger sequencing identified an 8 bp frameshift deletion in ELFN1 (c.42_49delGGCCGCCA; p.(Ala15Profs*241)) as the disease-causing variant in the affected siblings.
The ELFN1 frameshift variant showed an autosomal recessive segregation pattern, being homozygous in the three affected patients and heterozygous in the parents and three unaffected siblings.
ELFN1 encodes a transmembrane leucine-rich repeat protein involved in signal transduction in neural cells and in ROD ON-bipolar cell synaptogenesis.
The authors recommend considering ELFN1 mutations in patients with neonatal- or infantile-onset epileptic encephalopathy even before the full syndromic clinical picture becomes apparent.

Segregation analysis showed the ELFN1 frameshift variant was homozygous in the three affected siblings and heterozygous in both parents and three unaffected siblings, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
In silico pathogenicity assessment tools, combined with segregation data, strongly supported a damaging effect of the frameshift variant on ELFN1 protein function.
ELFN1 encodes a transmembrane leucine-rich repeat protein involved in signal transduction in neural cells and in synaptogenesis of ROD ON-bipolar cells.

The authors recommend considering ELFN1 gene mutations as a diagnostic possibility in patients with neonatal or infantile-onset epileptic encephalopathy before the full clinical phenotype becomes apparent.

People with autism spectrum disorder show an increased abundance of Lactobacillus species in their gut microbiota.

Autistic children show decreased levels of the beneficial species Coprococcus in intestinal microflora compared with healthy controls.

Adult autistic patients show significantly increased serum IL-1beta compared with healthy controls, inversely correlated with socialization scores.
Adult autistic patients show significantly increased serum IL-6 compared with healthy controls, inversely correlated with socialization scores.

Disturbances in the maternal gut microbiome causing in-utero inflammation promote neurodevelopmental abnormalities in mouse offspring, supporting a maternal-microbiome route to increased ASD-like risk.
Autism spectrum disorder patients commonly exhibit gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain in addition to core psychological features.
Germ-free mouse models show impaired neurogenesis and altered morphology in the hippocampus and amygdala, supporting a role for gut microbiota in nervous system development.
Germ-free mice show disrupted microglia morphology and processes, resulting in disturbed activation and response to pathogens.
Short-chain fatty acids produced by gut microbiota act as signaling molecules and affect microglial maturation within the CNS.
