Germ-free mice show decreased serum serotonin levels compared with conventionally colonized mice.
Germ-free mice exhibit decreased expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a factor responsible for maintaining and promoting neurogenesis.
Germ-free mice present with cognitive impairment, problems with sociability, and depressive and anxious behaviors, linking absent gut microbiota to behavioral phenotypes.
H2A.Z protein levels are significantly elevated in PAX3+ neural progenitor cells in the DRG of Elp1 conditional knockout embryos at E11.5.
Western blot analysis shows H2A.Z levels are significantly elevated in the brains of Elp1 CKO embryos at E17.5 compared to controls.
Although total H2A.Z is elevated in Elp1 CKO brains, acetylated H2A.Z levels remain normal, resulting in a reduced ratio of acetylated to total H2A.Z.

H2A.Z is also elevated in the retina of adult Pax6-Cre; Elp1 CKO mice, showing an approximately twofold increase, suggesting H2A.Z upregulation is a general consequence of Elongator loss across tissues.
Quantitative RT-PCR shows H2a.z transcript levels are only slightly, non-significantly elevated in Elp1 CKO embryos, indicating H2A.Z protein elevation is not driven by increased transcription.

The E3 ubiquitin ligase UBR1, which normally degrades H2A.Z, is decreased 60-fold at the protein level (with normal transcript levels) in Elp1 CKO embryos, suggesting reduced UBR1-mediated degradation contributes to elevated H2A.Z.
SIRT1 protein levels, assessed by IHC in the DRG and western blot in the brain, are normal in Elp1 CKO embryos, ruling out SIRT1 downregulation as the mechanism for elevated H2A.Z.
Notch target genes are significantly more misregulated (49%, 21 of 43) than the overall transcriptome background level of misregulation (20%, 5201 of 25,697 genes) in Elp1 CKO embryos.

In vivo administration of the HDAC inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) to pregnant dams during neurogenesis (E8.5, E10.5, E12.5) fully rescues the number of TrkA+ DRG sensory neurons in Elp1 CKO embryos to control levels by E17.5.
Notch3 expression is elevated in the DRG/neural tube of Elp1 CKO embryos at E11.5, and its expression is significantly reduced following TSA treatment.
Hes1, a Notch target gene, showed normal expression in Elp1 CKO embryos at E11.5 and did not change in response to TSA treatment.
Western blots show similar H3K14 acetylation levels in the brains of E17.5 Elp1 CKO embryos and controls, indicating no global histone acetylation deficit.

Transcriptome analysis shows roughly equal proportions of up- and downregulated genes in Elp1 CKO embryos, indicating that elevated H2A histones do not disproportionately suppress gene expression or induce widespread heterochromatin formation.
The study confirms significantly reduced numbers of Pax3+ neural progenitors at E11.5 and TrkA+ sensory neurons at E12.5 in Elp1 CKO embryos, replicating prior findings from this model.
ADINR lncRNA expression was significantly higher in peripheral blood of ASD children compared with healthy controls and remained significant after Bonferroni correction.

ANRIL lncRNA expression was significantly higher in ASD children compared with controls and remained significant after Bonferroni correction, showing the highest fold difference of the assessed genes.
DILC lncRNA expression was nominally higher in ASD children compared with controls, but this did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction.
NKILA lncRNA expression was significantly higher in ASD children compared with controls and remained significant after Bonferroni correction.

CHAST lncRNA expression was nominally higher in ASD children compared with controls, but did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction; CHAST over-expression has also been reported in schizophrenia.
PACER lncRNA expression showed no significant difference between ASD children and healthy controls.
DICER1-AS1 expression showed no significant difference between ASD children and healthy controls.
HNF1A-AS1 expression showed no significant difference between ASD children and healthy controls.
ATG5 expression showed no significant difference between ASD children and healthy controls.
CEBPA expression showed no significant difference between ASD children and healthy controls, despite ADINR regulating this locus.
ATG5 expression was correlated with age among ASD patients but not among healthy controls.
DICER1-AS1 expression was correlated with age among ASD patients but not among healthy controls.
DILC expression was correlated with age among ASD patients but not among healthy controls, suggesting age-related modulation specific to ASD.
Among ASD cases, ADINR expression showed the strongest co-expression correlation with NKILA expression.
Among healthy controls, ADINR expression showed a robust co-expression correlation with CHAST expression, differing from the ADINR-NKILA correlation pattern seen in ASD cases.
ANRIL showed the greatest diagnostic power (AUC=0.857) for distinguishing ASD from healthy status among the assessed genes.
NKILA showed the second-best diagnostic power (AUC=0.757) for distinguishing ASD from healthy status.
Significant differences in respiratory sinus arrhythmia were found between sensory-based subtypes during baseline and during tactile, tone, and movement sensory stimuli.
Changes in respiratory sinus arrhythmia during auditory stimulation and during recovery periods predicted sensory subtype membership.

Children with an adaptive sensory responsivity subtype differed physiologically from those with sensory processing dysfunction, but ANS and cortisol variables did not distinguish between subgroups with different patterns of sensory processing dysfunction.
Males with FXS showed a significant overall main effect of group on interbeat interval compared to typically developing males, consistent with shorter IBI (hyperarousal).
A significant group-by-age interaction showed that IBI increased more each month in typically developing children than in children with FXS, indicating slower cardiac maturation in FXS.
By 29 months of age, children with FXS exhibited significantly shorter IBI than typically developing children, marking the emergence of detectable hyperarousal.
Males with FXS showed a significant overall main effect of group on RSA relative to TD males, consistent with reduced parasympathetic regulation.
A significant group-by-age interaction indicated that RSA increased more each month in TD children than in FXS children, showing slower parasympathetic maturation in FXS.
By 24 months of age, children with FXS showed significantly lower RSA than TD children, marking the earliest detectable emergence of hyperarousal in this measure.
Shorter IBI at 24 months (IBI intercept) predicted higher later anxiety symptoms across the combined FXS/TD sample.
IBI intercept at 24 months did not significantly predict later ASD symptom severity.
Slower developmental change (slope) in IBI across early childhood predicted higher later anxiety symptoms.
Developmental slope of IBI did not significantly predict later ASD symptom severity.
Lower RSA at 24 months (RSA intercept) predicted higher later ASD symptom severity.
RSA intercept at 24 months did not significantly predict later anxiety symptoms.
Developmental slope (change over time) in RSA did not significantly predict either later ASD or anxiety symptoms, contrary to prior studies in non-syndromic and high-risk ASD populations.
Across multiple models, diagnostic group (FXS vs TD) significantly predicted higher ASD symptom severity but not anxiety symptom severity.
Developmental level (cognitive ability) was significantly correlated with RSA developmental slope, indicating a link between cognitive maturation and autonomic development.
Developmental level was strongly, negatively correlated with ASD symptom severity, i.e., lower cognitive ability was associated with more severe ASD symptoms.
Developmental level was marginally correlated with RSA intercept (baseline RSA at 24 months).

Children with ADHD (ADHD-only and autism+ADHD) showed significantly lower cardiac sympathetic index than those without ADHD during a 3-minute resting-state period, indicating sympathetic hypo-arousal.
During the passive auditory oddball task, children with ADHD (with or without co-occurring autism) had reduced cardiac sympathetic index compared to children without ADHD.

Children with ADHD-only (but not those with co-occurring autism+ADHD) showed specifically reduced CSI during the 30-second breaks of the passive oddball task compared to neurotypical, autism-only, and autism+ADHD groups.

Children with autism (autism-only and autism+ADHD) had significantly reduced cardiac vagal index compared to children without autism during the initial pre-block break and second block of the passive oddball task, indicating reduced parasympathetic activity/hyper-arousal.
During the active response-conflict (POP) task, children with autism (autism-only and autism+ADHD) showed reduced cardiac vagal index across the entire task compared to children without autism.

Across the whole sample, both sympathetic and parasympathetic activation (CSI and CVI) were greater during active task blocks of the oddball paradigm compared to silent breaks, and CSI was higher in the second block than the first.

During the active response-conflict (POP) task, CSI was higher during breaks than during task blocks across all participants, suggesting increased parasympathetic regulation during sustained-attention demands.
Across all experimental conditions, CSI and CVI were strongly negatively correlated with each other in the clinical sample, indicating a reciprocal sympathetic-parasympathetic balance.
More severe hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms (but not inattention) were associated with reduced CSI and increased CVI among children with autism, ADHD, or both.
More severe autism symptoms, particularly social-communication deficits, were associated with reduced CVI and increased CSI, consistent with autonomic hyper-arousal.
Children with higher global functioning scores displayed increased CVI.

A two-step cluster analysis on averaged CSI and CVI identified a 'Low-CSI' cluster, into which almost all ADHD-only children were assigned, and a heterogeneous 'Low-CVI' cluster containing subsets of both autism-only and autism+ADHD children.

Children in the 'Low-CVI' (hyper-arousal) cluster had significantly more severe autism symptoms (SCQ Total, Social, and Communication scores) than those in the 'Low-CSI' (hypo-arousal) cluster, but reduced hyperactivity/impulsivity.
The 'Low-CVI' (hyper-arousal) cluster displayed more severe generalised and social anxiety and reduced global functioning scores compared to the 'Low-CSI' (hypo-arousal) cluster.

Children with co-occurring autism and ADHD did not show a unique autonomic arousal profile but instead displayed both the reduced CVI pattern seen in autism-only and the reduced CSI pattern seen in ADHD-only, supporting an additive rather than interactive model of comorbidity for arousal dysregulation.
The incidence of ASD in Russian children has increased with age, from 5 per 10,000 under age 2 to 18 per 10,000 at age 4.
Calcium deficiency was found in 45.1% of children with ASD.
Lithium deficiency was found in 30-35% of children with ASD.
Potassium deficiency was found in 70% of children with ASD.
Nutritional deficiencies in children with ASD exacerbate neuropsychiatric symptoms, including metabolic disorders, delayed physical and mental development, fatigue, and endocrine dysfunction.

Eating disorders in children with ASD negatively affect nutritional status and aggravate the course of gastrointestinal diseases, which themselves involve inflammatory and functional GI disorders, altered immune status, altered autonomic nervous system tone, and altered gut microbiota composition.
Nutritional adjustments in children with ASD can improve non-verbal IQ and decrease clinical manifestations of autism.
Incidental vertebral fusion occurred most frequently in the cervical spine, followed by the thoracic and lumbar regions.
The C2-C3 level was the most common site of incidental vertebral fusion, followed by T3-T4 and C3-C4.
In the cervical region, Pfirrmann degeneration scores of upper adjacent segments decreased significantly with increasing distance from the fusion site.
In the cervical region, Pfirrmann degeneration scores of lower adjacent segments also decreased significantly with increasing distance from the fusion.

In the thoracic region, only the first close upper-segment Pfirrmann measurement decreased significantly with distance from fusion, while second/third close and mean scores showed no significant change.
In the thoracic region, Pfirrmann scores of lower adjacent segments decreased significantly with increasing distance from the fusion.
In the lumbar region, upper adjacent segment Pfirrmann measurements and mean scores generally showed no significant change with distance from fusion.
In the lumbar region, the first close lower-segment Pfirrmann measurement and the mean Pfirrmann score decreased significantly with distance from fusion, while the second close measurement did not.

Disks adjacent to the fused vertebra showed the greatest degeneration, indicating that hypermobility near the fusion site is the main driver of adjacent segment change, particularly in the cervical spine.
Older patients showed more pronounced intervertebral disk degeneration than younger patients, which the authors attribute to age-related worsening of hypermobility rather than aging alone.
The authors cite prior literature indicating that hypermobility syndrome accelerates the rate of degeneration in segments adjacent to spinal fusion.

Prior literature reports reoperation rates for adjacent segment disease after fusion ranging from 1.4% to 16.8%, with overall ASD frequency reported between 5.6% and 30%, including a seven-year follow-up study showing about 25% subsequent ASD incidence and 5.6% requiring reoperation.
Persons with epilepsy on carbamazepine monotherapy did not show a significant reduction in the time-domain HRV parameter SDRR compared to those on other anti-seizure drugs.
PWE on carbamazepine monotherapy had significantly lower RMSSD, a time-domain marker of parasympathetic (vagal) heart rate variability, than those on other anti-seizure drugs.
PWE on carbamazepine monotherapy had significantly lower SDSD, another parasympathetic HRV index, compared to other anti-seizure drug monotherapy.
pNN50, a parasympathetic HRV index, was significantly lower in PWE on carbamazepine monotherapy than in those on other anti-seizure drugs.
Frequency-domain measures of heart rate variability did not differ significantly between PWE on carbamazepine and those on other anti-seizure drug monotherapy.
Frequency-domain measures of heart rate variability did not differ significantly between persons with epilepsy on carbamazepine monotherapy and those on other anti-seizure drug monotherapy.
Heart rate response to deep breathing, a parasympathetic function test, did not differ significantly between the carbamazepine and other-ASD groups.
Heart rate response to the Valsalva maneuver did not differ significantly between persons on carbamazepine versus other anti-seizure drugs.
Heart rate response to tilt-testing did not differ significantly between the carbamazepine group and the other-ASD group.

Blood pressure responses to Valsalva maneuver and tilt-testing, markers of sympathetic function, were not significantly different between persons on carbamazepine and those on other anti-seizure drugs.

The authors conclude that reduced parasympathetic activity associated with carbamazepine monotherapy may increase risk of Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy (SUDEP), suggesting caution in prescribing it to at-risk patients.
The patient's acute respiratory distress was due to bilateral pneumothoraces associated with bilateral apical bullae, a pulmonary complication relevant to Rett syndrome.
Rett syndrome is characterised, among other features, by autonomic dysfunction, oral-motor impairment, and gastrointestinal disturbance in addition to autistic-type behaviour.
Patients with Rett syndrome can present acutely due to aspiration secondary to poor gag or swallow reflexes, in addition to unassociated acute conditions.

Without adjusting for cell type or medication, 22qDel carriers showed 390 significantly differentially expressed genes relative to controls, with more genes downregulated (251) than upregulated (139).

Gene ontology analysis of genes differentially expressed in 22qDel carriers versus controls implicated biological adhesion and immune pathways including regulation of T cell activation and adaptive immune response.
22qDup carriers showed six significantly upregulated genes relative to controls, including five genes within the 22q11.2 locus and one gene outside the locus (CDH6).

CDH6, which encodes cadherin-6 involved in cell adhesion, platelet aggregation, and angiogenesis in the developing brain, was significantly upregulated in 22qDup carriers relative to controls, and this remained significant after adjusting for cell-type proportions.

Between 22qDel and 22qDup carriers there were 141 significantly differentially expressed genes (117 downregulated, 24 upregulated), including 28 22q11.2 locus genes, with GO enrichment for cell adhesion and wound healing.

A WGCNA co-expression module (dark red) enriched for platelet-associated genes and immune cell markers (mast cells, B cells, dendritic cells, M0 macrophages, neutrophils, plasma cells, gamma delta T cells) showed graded expression across groups, lowest in 22qDel, intermediate in controls, and highest in 22qDup carriers.

The medium purple3 module, composed predominantly of 22q11.2 locus genes, showed graded expression differences across all three groups (lowest in 22qDel, intermediate in controls, highest in 22qDup) and weak enrichment for T-cell subtype markers.

The dark green co-expression module, enriched for multiple T-cell subtype markers, showed significantly reduced expression in 22qDel carriers relative to both controls and 22qDup carriers, consistent with known thymic dysplasia and T-cell deficits in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

Estimated CD8 T cell proportions were significantly decreased in 22qDel carriers compared to controls, and marginally decreased compared to 22qDup carriers, consistent with prior reports of T-cell deficits and thymic dysplasia in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.
22qDel carriers showed an increased proportion of activated mast cells and a corresponding decrease in resting mast cells relative to both controls and 22qDup carriers.
22qDel carriers showed significantly increased M1 macrophage proportions compared to both controls and 22qDup carriers.
22qDup carriers showed increased proportions of undifferentiated (M0) macrophages relative to both 22qDel carriers and controls.

After adjusting gene expression for estimated cell type proportion, the number of significantly DE genes outside the 22q11.2 locus dropped dramatically (from 362 to 3 for 22qDel vs controls, and from 113 to 8 for 22qDel vs 22qDup), indicating that most of the widespread transcriptomic differences were driven by cell composition rather than within-cell expression changes.
FUT7, which encodes an enzyme allowing white blood cells to accumulate at inflammation sites, remained significantly downregulated in 22qDel carriers versus controls after cell-type adjustment.

EDAR, which encodes a receptor that can activate NF-kappa-B transcription factors involved in inflammatory and immune responses, remained significantly downregulated in 22qDel carriers versus controls after cell-type adjustment.
HIST1H2BD, encoding an H2B family histone protein, was significantly upregulated in 22qDel carriers versus controls after cell-type adjustment.
SAPCD2, a gene involved in regulating cell division, was significantly downregulated in 22qDup carriers compared to controls after adjustment for cell-type composition.

No WGCNA co-expression modules derived from cell-type and medication-adjusted expression data were significantly differentially expressed between 22qDel, 22qDup, and control groups, supporting cell type as a major driver of the co-expression differences.

No significant associations were found between diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder or psychosis and cell type proportions, cell type- and medication-adjusted gene expression, or WGCNA module eigengene expression among 22qDel and 22qDup carriers.

No significant associations were found between cell type proportion, cell type-adjusted gene expression, or cell type-adjusted module eigengene expression and IQ, mean cortical thickness, or total cortical surface area.
A meta-analysis found that ASD diagnosis was associated with diminished baseline respiratory sinus arrhythmia and diminished RSA reactivity during social experiences.

Neonatal RSA indices in very preterm children predicted social competence at age three and at school age, and infants later diagnosed with ASD showed a blunted RSA developmental trajectory from 18 months.
Copy-number microduplications in the chromosome 15q11-q13 region, which encodes GABAA receptor subunits, have been associated with ASD.
Post-mortem studies found a decrease in GABAergic Purkinje neurons in cerebellum specimens from deceased ASD patients.
Functional alterations in the activity of excitatory networks involving the locus coeruleus are found in children with ASD.
In children with ASD, shorter sleep duration exacerbates the severity of both repetitive behaviors and social-communication deficits.
Delayed wave V latency in the auditory brainstem response at birth is associated with increased risk of subsequent ASD diagnosis, persisting through infancy, toddlerhood, and childhood.
Morphological studies demonstrate durable alterations in size, volume, and neuronal density in the superior olive, along with abnormal cell body shape and orientation, in individuals with ASD.
Congenital blindness is a significant risk factor for ASD, affecting approximately 50% of infants born without the ability to see.
Deficits in stabilizing visual fixation at 6-9 months predicted social-communication problems at 36 months.
A meta-analysis found a negative association between maternal breastfeeding and ASD, though the underlying mechanism remains unclear.
Reduced tactile-motor reactivity at 12 months during parent-child interaction was shown to be a risk factor for subsequent ASD diagnosis.
Aberrant structuring of the inferior olivary nucleus has been found in ASD populations in post-mortem studies.
Atypical structuring of the medullary arcuate nucleus, which is involved in cardiorespiratory regulation, has been noted in ASD.

Tractography machine learning analysis found altered white matter connectivity of brainstem tracts in ASD, alongside cerebellar-brainstem white matter tract abnormalities involving insufficient glial maturation and axonal growth differences in infancy and early childhood.
Children, adolescents, and adults with ASD display decreased sleeping time, delayed sleep latency, less efficient sleep, and an elevated risk for sleep disorders.
Pooled meta-analysis of 7 studies found that 80% of COVID-19 patients had one or more long-term symptoms beyond the acute phase.
Fatigue was the single most common long-term effect of COVID-19, present in 58% of patients across pooled studies.
Headache was reported in 44% of patients as a long-term effect, though with wide confidence intervals reflecting high heterogeneity.
Attention disorder was reported as a long-term effect in 27% of patients from a single cohort study.
Hair loss (telogen effluvium) was reported in 25% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Dyspnea was present in 24% of patients as a persistent long-term effect of COVID-19.
Ageusia (loss of taste) persisted in 23% of patients following COVID-19 infection.
Anosmia (loss of smell) persisted in 21% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Post-activity polypnea (rapid breathing after exertion) was found in 21% of patients in a single cohort study.
Joint pain was reported in 19% of patients as a long-term musculoskeletal effect of COVID-19.
Cough was reported in 19% of patients as a persistent respiratory symptom after COVID-19.
Chest pain or discomfort persisted in 16% of patients following COVID-19.
Memory loss was reported in 16% of patients, though with an extremely wide confidence interval reflecting high heterogeneity across studies.
Hearing loss or tinnitus was reported in 15% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Anxiety was reported in 13% of patients as a long-term neuropsychiatric effect of COVID-19.
Depression was reported in 12% of patients as a long-term neuropsychiatric effect of COVID-19.
Sleep disorder was reported in 11% of patients as a long-term effect of COVID-19.
Reduced pulmonary diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide was present in 10% of patients, lower than reported in other COVID-19 or SARS survivor cohorts.
Abnormal chest X-ray or CT findings persisted in 34% of patients after COVID-19.
D-dimer was elevated in 20% of patients as a persistent laboratory abnormality after COVID-19.
NT-proBNP was elevated in 11% of patients as a persistent cardiac laboratory abnormality.
C-reactive protein remained elevated in 8% of patients as a persistent inflammatory marker after COVID-19.
Serum ferritin remained elevated in 8% of patients as a persistent inflammatory marker after COVID-19.
Procalcitonin remained elevated in 4% of patients as a persistent laboratory abnormality after COVID-19.
Interleukin-6 remained elevated in 3% of patients as a persistent inflammatory marker after COVID-19.

Fatigue was reported to be more common in females in two studies, and post-activity polypnea and alopecia were more common in females in one additional study; the remaining studies did not stratify results by sex or age.
Adults were reported to have double the risk of being newly diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder after a COVID-19 diagnosis, most commonly anxiety disorders, insomnia, and dementia.

The authors note that post-COVID-19 fatigue and associated symptoms partly resemble myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), including severe fatigue, pain, neurocognitive disability, sleep disturbance, and features suggestive of autonomic dysfunction, and speculate that SARS-CoV-2 could be added to the list of viral triggers implicated in ME/CFS.

The review notes that long-term lung dysfunction and pulmonary fibrosis observed after COVID-19 parallel prior reports in SARS and MERS survivors, with 28% of SARS survivors showing decreased lung function/fibrosis at 1 year and 33% of MERS survivors showing pulmonary fibrosis.
Pooled analysis found elevated NT-proBNP in 11% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Pooled analysis found elevated C-reactive protein in 8% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Pooled analysis found elevated serum ferritin in 8% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Pooled analysis found elevated procalcitonin in 4% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Pooled analysis found elevated interleukin-6 in 3% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Health care related mental health impact was reported in 7% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New psychiatric illness was reported in 6% of post-COVID-19 patients across a large electronic health record cohort.
Red eyes were reported in 6% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Pulmonary fibrosis was reported in 5% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Discontinuous flushing was reported in 5% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New diabetes mellitus was reported in 4% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Sputum production was reported in 3% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Limb edema was reported in 4% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Dizziness was reported in 4% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New stroke was reported in 3% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Throat pain was reported in 3% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New mood disorders (e.g., depressive episodes) were reported in 2% of post-COVID-19 patients in a large EHR cohort.
Dysphoria was reported in 2% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New obsessive-compulsive disorder was reported in 2% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New hypertension was reported in 1% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Myocarditis was reported in 1% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Renal failure was reported in 1% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New post-traumatic stress disorder was reported in 1% of post-COVID-19 patients.
New arrhythmia was reported in 0.4% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Paranoia was reported in 0.3% of post-COVID-19 patients.
Fatigue was reported to be more common among female patients in two of the included studies.
Post-activity polypnea and alopecia (hair loss) were reported to be more common among female patients in one included study.
Adults were reported to have double the risk of being newly diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder after a COVID-19 diagnosis.

The authors speculate that post-COVID-19 fatigue symptoms resemble myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), and suggest SARS-CoV-2 may be added to the list of viral triggers of ME/CFS alongside Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, enterovirus, and herpesvirus.

For comparison, prior SARS survivor studies found that 28% had decreased lung function and pulmonary fibrosis signs one year after infection, and MERS survivors showed pulmonary fibrosis in 33% of cases.

Nearly half (45.2%) of renal transplant recipients developed clinical complications after acute COVID-19, most commonly shortness of breath, fatigue, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive impairment, and dry cough.
The majority of patients (71.2%) had at least one laboratory abnormality at initial post-COVID-19 evaluation.
Increased D-dimer levels were found in over a third of patients post-COVID-19, with a fifth showing levels more than twice the reference range.
Increased fibrinogen was observed in roughly a third of patients post-COVID-19.
Shortened activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), consistent with a procoagulant state, was found in half of patients post-COVID-19.
EBV reactivation was detected in about a quarter of patients following COVID-19, requiring mycophenolate dose reduction and, in some, IVIG.
BK virus reactivation occurred in 16.3% of patients post-COVID-19 and was more frequent in those with lower complement C3 and C4 levels.
CMV reactivation was detected in 8.7% of patients after COVID-19, with one severe case of ganciclovir/valganciclovir-resistant CMV colitis requiring foscarnet and letermovir.
Hypogammaglobulinemia was present in nearly a quarter of patients following COVID-19.
Complement C3 was decreased in a small subset of patients post-COVID-19.
Patients with elevated D-dimer post-COVID-19 had significantly longer time since transplantation than those with normal levels.
Decreasing the tacrolimus dose during acute COVID-19 had a protective effect against the later development of laboratory abnormalities, remaining significant on multivariate analysis.

Hospitalization for acute COVID-19, diabetes mellitus, and concomitant laboratory complications were the strongest predictors of post-COVID-19 clinical complications, while better allograft function (eGFR) decreased the probability.
In multivariate analysis, diabetes mellitus and lower eGFR (CKD-EPI) were the two independent predictors of clinical complications after COVID-19, with the overall model statistically significant.
A minority of patients developed allograft dysfunction (rise in creatinine or new/worsening proteinuria) after COVID-19; almost all had pre-existing chronic allograft dysfunction.
De novo donor-specific antibodies developed in 5.7% of patients following COVID-19, and some patients developed allograft rejection, suggesting a possible immunomodulatory effect of SARS-CoV-2.
Anemia worsened in a sizable minority of patients following COVID-19.
Leukopenia was present in 7.7% of patients post-COVID-19.
Thrombocytopenia was present in 8.7% of patients post-COVID-19.
Introduction of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents for post-COVID-19 anemia resulted in improved serum hemoglobin levels.
Low-dose aspirin (75 mg) was introduced in patients with persistently elevated D-dimers as prophylaxis against the procoagulant state.
Only 11.53% of renal transplant recipients who survived acute COVID-19 were completely free of clinical symptoms and laboratory abnormalities during follow-up.

Rehospitalizations increased over the 6-month follow-up, with 29 patients hospitalized for problems including leukopenia, viral reactivation, sepsis, pneumonia, urinary tract infections, diabetes, rhabdomyolysis, and psychotic reaction; three patients died from sepsis.
By 6 months post-COVID-19, most initial symptoms had substantially improved, with only small proportions still reporting fatigue, peripheral neuropathy, or hair loss.
At approximately 10 weeks after symptom onset, 85.4% of patients with confirmed COVID-19 reported severe fatigue on the CIS-Fatigue scale.
The overall CIS-Fatigue score improved significantly between the ~10-week and ~23-week follow-up assessments, though the change was modest.
Despite the modest improvement in continuous fatigue score, the proportions of patients classified as having normal, mild, or severe fatigue did not change significantly between the two timepoints.
Self-reported physical fatigue score decreased significantly between the ~10-week and ~23-week assessments.
Unlike physical fatigue, self-reported mental fatigue did not change significantly between the ~10-week and ~23-week assessments.
The proportion of long COVID patients receiving or seeking care from a medical professional increased significantly from T1 to T2.
The proportion of long COVID patients receiving or seeking care from an allied health care professional increased significantly from T1 to T2.
Participation in interdisciplinary rehabilitation programs among long COVID patients increased significantly between T1 and T2.
The confirmed-COVID-19 long COVID cohort was predominantly female, consistent with prior evidence that women are more prone to develop long COVID.
The number of self-reported symptoms decreased substantially from the acute infection phase to both follow-up timepoints, though a persistent symptom burden remained at 6 months.
Only a small minority of long COVID patients rated their health as good at either follow-up timepoint, despite most having reported good health prior to infection.

The authors note that median fatigue scores in this long COVID sample were equal to or higher than those reported in other chronic fatigue-associated diseases such as COPD, asthma, Q fever, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic sclerosis, despite the sample being younger and with fewer comorbidities.

About 10% of people with COVID-19-related smell and taste changes reported persistent problems including anosmia, hyposmia, parosmia, phantosmia, dysgeusia and reduced chemesthesis, despite most people recovering within weeks.
Prior post-viral smell alteration literature found that as many as 56% of patients experience parosmia and/or phantosmia.

Anosmia was associated with a shift towards more sugary, fatty, highly-processed foods (since basic tastes were still detectable) for some participants, while others reported an improved diet away from previously flavour-driven unhealthy eating.
Parosmia universally led to a much-reduced range of tolerable foods and raised widespread concerns about health among participants.

Participants reported widespread weight gain, weight loss, and malnutrition as consequences of altered smell and taste, contrasting with prior literature suggesting most people maintain adequate dietary intake.

Participants reported a broad range of negative emotional responses—including worry, disgust, confusion, frustration, depression, anxiety and hopelessness—linked to COVID-related smell and taste loss/distortion.

Inability to smell a romantic partner, or aversive parosmic distortion of a partner's scent/kisses, was a dominant theme negatively affecting intimacy, though a minority reported improved sexual disinhibition due to reduced smell sensitivity.

Participants consistently reported dismissive, unhelpful, or unempathetic responses from GPs, ENTs and dentists regarding their smell and taste loss, contributing to feelings of being medically abandoned.

In one longitudinally-followed participant narrative, smell training was associated with partial improvement in persistent metallic taste and parosmia over several months, though symptoms remained fluctuating and distorted.
Loss of ability to detect one's own body odour led to frequent paranoia about being malodorous, resulting in compulsive-like behaviours such as excessive showering, clothing changes and deodorising.
Loss of smell impaired occupational functioning for participants whose jobs relied on olfaction, such as nurses unable to detect bodily fluids, infected wounds, or other clinical odour cues.
Empiric treatment with combined H1/H2 histamine receptor antagonists reduced overall symptom burden in the majority of long COVID patients treated.
Unlike other symptom categories, dysautonomia (postural tachycardia) did not improve with HRA treatment.

CD8+ effector memory T cell counts were reduced below the normal median in the large majority of both long COVID and asymptomatic recovered participants, suggesting this reflects recovery from COVID-19 generally rather than long COVID specifically.
Reduced CD4+ effector memory T cell counts were more prevalent in long COVID patients than in asymptomatic recovered individuals and distinguished the two groups by ROC analysis.
PD-1 antigen density was significantly increased on CD4+ central memory T cells in all post-COVID participants, more markedly in long COVID patients.
PD-1 antigen density was significantly increased on CD8+ central memory T cells in all post-COVID participants, more markedly in long COVID patients.

CD28 costimulatory antigen density on CD4+ central memory T cells was increased specifically in asymptomatic recovered participants but not in long COVID patients, suggesting a marker of a healthy immune response to SARS-CoV-2.
CD57 antigen density did not differ significantly between long COVID, asymptomatic, and healthy participants.
Long COVID patients were almost universally polysymptomatic, with an average of 4.58 out of 11 symptom categories persisting for a mean of 269 days.
More than a third of long COVID patients had a prior history of atopy.
Standard hematologic and inflammatory blood tests (full blood count, ESR, CRP, D-dimer, renal and liver function) were normal in almost all long COVID patients.
In untreated long COVID patients followed without HRA, only a minority showed spontaneous symptomatic improvement while most remained unchanged or worsened.
SARS-CoV-2 antibody status did not correlate with spontaneous symptom resolution in untreated long COVID patients, nor did it predict response to HRA.
Neither T cell subset counts nor PD-1/CD28 antigen density predicted which patients would respond to HRA treatment.
Long COVID patients in this cohort were predominantly younger women with few comorbidities.
A meta-analysis of acute COVID-19 studies found an overall fatigue prevalence of 23% during the acute infection.
Prospective cohort studies showed declining fatigue rates over time post-COVID, from a peak of 8-29% acutely to 9-49% at 4 weeks and 4-35% at 8 weeks post-symptom onset.
Cross-sectional studies reported median fatigue rates declining from 50% at 4-7 weeks to 28% at 16-20 weeks, with 34% still reporting fatigue at 28 weeks post-symptom onset.
Persistent post-COVID fatigue was associated with functional disability, with 9%-40% of patients unable to return to work at 2-4 months post-symptom onset across three studies.

Acute illness severity markers including hospitalization, ICU admission, duration of hospital stay, duration of viral shedding, and dyspnea during hospitalization were exploratory predictors of fatigue at follow-up.
Across 15 studies of diverse pathogens (EBV, dengue, chikungunya, Ebola, Q fever, Giardia), disabling post-infective fatigue persisted at 6 months or more in 10%-35% of adolescents or adults.
A prospective case-control study found that minor symptomatic infections such as common colds did not increase the likelihood of developing chronic fatigue.

A systematic review of predictors of post-infective fatigue syndrome found the most consistent predictors were acute illness severity, host immune response markers including biochemical hepatitis, self-reported illness/fatigue severity, and functional impairment (days in bed or off school).

Some evidence across post-infective cohort studies implicated self-reported anxiety, perceived stress, neuroticism, negative illness beliefs, and premorbid distress as risk factors for chronic fatigue.

A prospective cohort of 4501 US college students followed for EBV infection found a 23% case rate of post-infective fatigue syndrome at 6 months, and premorbid psychological factors did not predict this outcome.

Nested case-control studies of well-characterized PIFS patients versus recovered controls found no evidence of ongoing pathogen replication beyond several weeks or of a consistent pattern of ongoing immune activation.
Autonomic dysfunction with sympathetic predominance is proposed as a perpetuating factor in idiopathic post-COVID fatigue/PIFS.
Endocrine disturbance with hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis attenuation is proposed as a perpetuating factor in idiopathic post-COVID fatigue/PIFS.

The largest included study, using the COVID Symptom Study smartphone app (n=4182), had an unusually high proportion of female participants (72%) despite no known sex difference in acute COVID-19 prevalence, suggesting selection bias.

RIPK1 overactivation in microglia and astrocytes contributes to MS pathology, particularly progressive disease, and appears among dysregulated genes shared between COVID-19 brains and chronic CNS diseases including MS.

COVID-19 brains showed extensive CD8+ T cell infiltration, microgliosis, and axonal damage comparable to that seen in long-term MS patients, with perivascular CD8+ clusters causing vascular immunopathology and BBB disruption.

Single-cell transcriptomics of CSF in neuro-COVID-19 patients showed increased activation of CSF T cells interacting with overactive NK and dendritic cells, upregulation of IL-1 and IL-12 pathways, and B cell enrichment compared with healthy donors.
B cells were enriched in the CSF of COVID-19 patients compared with controls, and a subset of intrathecal antibodies—especially anti-Spike—also targeted neural antigens.

A literature review identified 43 cases of acute transverse myelitis reported through January 2021 in association with COVID-19, with an estimated incidence of 0.5 per million, and 70% of COVID-19-associated myelitis cases showed longitudinally extensive lesions spanning more than three spinal segments.

A virus-host interaction analysis found that IL-17 receptor A physically interacts with the SARS-CoV-2 Orf8 protein and identified a genetic locus associated with COVID-19 severity whose biological effects relate to IL-17 signaling.
The IL1B gene is upregulated in blood and brain lesions of primary progressive MS patients, attributed to NLRP3 inflammasome overactivity.
Gain-of-function variants in NLRP3 and IL1B genes correlate with severity and progression of MS.
The use of beta-interferon formulations decreases the risk of COVID-19 in people with MS.
Zhang et al. found an enrichment of genetic variants causing impaired type I interferon immunity among patients with severe COVID-19.
Bastard et al. reported augmented levels of type I interferon neutralizing autoantibodies in severely ill COVID-19 patients.
High levels of antibodies against EBV antigens (EBNA1 and VCA) at least triple the risk of developing MS, and a history of infectious mononucleosis exerts a similar effect.

Screening of 104 moderate-to-severe COVID-19 cases found EBV was the only opportunistic virus detected, present in 95.2% of ICU patients and 83.6% of sub-ICU patients, with reactivation correlating with reduced CD8+ T and NK lymphocyte counts.
Gold and colleagues found that two-thirds of COVID-19 long-haulers had EBV reactivation, speculating this might contribute to the clinical manifestations of long-COVID.
Circulating CD8+ mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells occur at high frequency in both chronic fatigue syndrome and MS patients, linking intestinal dysbiosis to CNS inflammation.
A randomized clinical trial found no difference between placebo and three commonly prescribed medications (amantadine, modafinil, methylphenidate) in reducing MS-related fatigue.

EBV's ZTA transcription factor regulates ACE2 expression, peaking during EBV lytic replication in epithelial cells, and EBV reactivation was shown to facilitate ACE2-dependent coronavirus infection in pseudovirus assays.

Deletion of NRP1 exacerbates experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, the principal murine MS model, and NRP1 expression is increased in endothelial cells of active MS lesions in response to BBB disruption.

SARS-CoV-2 activates HERV-W and HERV-K Env transcription in T lymphocytes via Spike-ACE2 interaction; Env expression is strongly present in blood cells of COVID-19 patients but not healthy donors, correlates with IL-6, IL-17, CXCR1, and the T-cell exhaustion marker PD1, and predicts severe prognosis.

Four cases have been described in the literature in which typical multiple sclerosis onset (fulfilling McDonald 2017 criteria) occurred during or after COVID-19 in young people (three women, one man).
Serologically confirmed upper respiratory tract infection was associated with a threefold increase in the risk of MS exacerbation.

A large community-based study found that most pwMS with COVID-19 reported worsening of pre-existing neurological symptoms, and 20-35% developed new MS symptoms lasting for months, consistent with true relapses.
A smaller NYU MS Centre study reported a 21.1% rate of symptom recrudescence following COVID-19 in pwMS.

A retrospective study found a lower clinical relapse rate in pwMS with confirmed COVID-19 versus those without, though self-comparison of pre- and post-pandemic relapse rates showed no significant difference, suggesting selection bias.
pwMS receiving disease-modifying therapies were less likely to develop new MS symptoms during COVID-19 compared with untreated patients.
A complicated COVID-19 course occurred more frequently in pwMS not receiving any DMT, those on anti-CD20 agents (ocrelizumab, rituximab), or those recently given high-dose corticosteroids.
People with MS do not appear to have an increased risk of contracting SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with the general population.
Fatigue affects more than 75% of pwMS during the disease course, including the prodromal phase, and is often considered the worst symptom.
A randomized clinical trial found no difference between placebo and amantadine, modafinil, or methylphenidate in easing MS-related fatigue.
CD8+ mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells are found at high frequency in both chronic fatigue syndrome and MS patients, linking intestinal dysbiosis to CNS inflammation.
Genetic deletion of NRP1 worsens experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, the standard murine MS model.
NRP1 expression is increased in endothelial cells of active MS lesions in response to blood-brain barrier disruption.
High anti-HHV-6 antibody titers are epidemiologically associated with MS development risk, both independently and via interaction with anti-EBNA1 titers.

A case of para-infectious acute myelitis following COVID-19 in a man with lymphopenia and hypogammaglobulinemia showed high CSF HHV-6 viremia together with serum anti-MOG antibodies, suggesting viral synergy in triggering demyelination.

An in-silico analysis found that EBV-induced host gene expression signatures show the most significant overlap with SARS-CoV-2, suggesting mechanistic virus-virus interplay at the transcriptional level.
EBV's ZTA transcription factor regulates ACE2 expression, peaking during EBV lytic replication, and EBV reactivation facilitates ACE2-dependent coronavirus infection in pseudovirus assays.
NRP1 acts as a SARS-CoV-2 co-receptor and also facilitates EBV cell entry via interaction with EBV-gB protein, activating kinase pathways that positively feed back on viral infectivity.
SARS-CoV-2 Spike interaction with ACE2 on T lymphocytes activates HERV-W and HERV-K Env transcription in vitro.
HERV-W Env is strongly expressed in blood cells of COVID-19 patients but not healthy donors, correlates with inflammatory mediators and T-cell exhaustion markers, and predicts severe prognosis.

Four cases in the literature describe new MS onset (fulfilling McDonald 2017 criteria) in young people during or shortly after COVID-19, raising the possibility that SARS-CoV-2 acts as an environmental trigger.

A 28-year-old woman with a family history of MS developed active myelitis and disseminated white matter lesions with CSF oligoclonal bands 6 days after her first BNT162b2 vaccine dose, leading to an MS diagnosis.
In 555 pwMS receiving the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, adverse event frequency and characteristics were almost comparable to the non-MS population, though more numerous in younger patients.
Four cases have been reported in which typical clinical onset of multiple sclerosis (fulfilling 2017 McDonald criteria) occurred during or after COVID-19 in young patients.
Serologically confirmed upper respiratory tract infection was associated with a threefold increase in risk of MS exacerbation.

In a large community-based study, most pwMS who developed COVID-19 reported worsening of pre-existing neurological symptoms, and 20-35% developed new motor or sensory symptoms lasting months, considered true relapses that were worse than those triggered by non-COVID infections.
A smaller study from a New York University MS Center reported a 21.1% recrudescence rate of MS symptoms following COVID-19.
Disease-modifying therapies appear protective against SARS-CoV-2-induced MS relapses, as pwMS on DMTs are less likely to develop new symptoms during COVID-19 than untreated patients.

In a retrospective study of 125 relapsing-remitting pwMS (56 with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection), only 7.14% of the COVID-19 group experienced a clinical relapse compared with 26.09% of the non-COVID group.

A self-comparison analysis found no significant difference in relapse rate for each patient across comparable time windows before versus during/after the pandemic, undermining the between-group finding of a protective COVID-19 effect.
People with MS do not appear to have an increased risk of contracting SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with the general population.
Older age, male sex, and comorbidities negatively affect COVID-19 clinical course in pwMS, similar to the general population.
Fatigue was more frequent in pwMS with COVID-19 than expected, whereas respiratory and systemic symptoms did not differ from the general population.
Neurological disability and progressive disease course were linked to greater COVID-19 severity in pwMS, consistent with a frailer clinical status in this subgroup.
Type I interferon formulations showed a protective effect on COVID-19 course in pwMS, consistent with the role of interferons in restraining early SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A complicated COVID-19 course occurred more often in pwMS who were untreated, on anti-CD20 therapy (ocrelizumab, rituximab), or recently exposed to high-dose corticosteroids.

In 555 pwMS receiving the Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 vaccine, the frequency and characteristics of vaccine-induced adverse events were almost comparable to the non-MS population and more common in younger people.
In a cohort of 239 pwMS surveyed after BNT162b2 vaccination, vaccine reactions were even less common than in the Achiron cohort.
15.1% of pwMS reported new or worsening neurological symptoms after BNT162b2 vaccination, lasting more than 3 days in 55.6% of these cases.
Most studies have ruled out an increased long-term risk of developing MS as well as a short-term risk of neurological relapse in people with established MS following vaccination.

A 28-year-old woman with a family history of MS developed active myelitis and disseminated white matter lesions with positive CSF oligoclonal bands 6 days after her first BNT162b2 dose, and was diagnosed with MS.
Fingolimod, natalizumab, alemtuzumab, and anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies (ocrelizumab, rituximab) may reduce serological response to traditional (inactivated, conjugate, toxoid) vaccines in pwMS.
Anti-CD20 therapy has the greatest impact on antibody production after vaccination among MS DMTs, partly dependent on circulating B-cell levels at time of administration.
Following COVID-19, lower anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG titers were found in pwMS receiving fingolimod or anti-CD20 therapy, with anti-CD20 associated with a completely absent antibody response.

The largest study to date found significantly higher humoral response to the mRNA-1273 vaccine compared with BNT162b2 in pwMS, suggesting preferential use in those at risk of unsuccessful immunization.
Preliminary evidence showed that most ocrelizumab-treated pwMS who experienced COVID-19 were able to mount an efficient T-cell response toward SARS-CoV-2 despite B-cell depletion.
Serologically confirmed upper respiratory tract infections were associated with a threefold increase in the risk of MS exacerbation.

In a large community-based study, most people with MS who developed COVID-19 reported clinical worsening of pre-existing neurological symptoms, and 20-35% developed new MS symptoms lasting for months, considered true relapses that were worse than those triggered by non-COVID infections.
A smaller study from the New York University MS Centre reported a 21.1% neurological symptom recrudescence rate following COVID-19 in people with MS.
People with MS receiving disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) were less likely to develop new MS symptoms during COVID-19 compared with untreated patients.

A retrospective study found that only 7.14% of people with MS with confirmed COVID-19 experienced a clinical relapse compared with 26.09% of the non-COVID-19 group, though within-patient comparison before/during the pandemic showed no significant difference, suggesting selection bias.
Pooled analyses indicate that people with MS do not appear to have an increased risk of contracting SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with the general population.

Older age, male sex, and comorbidities were associated with a worse COVID-19 clinical course in people with MS, similarly to the general population, and neurological disability and progressive disease course were linked to greater COVID-19 severity.

Type I interferon formulations were associated with a protective effect against a complicated COVID-19 course in people with MS, whereas untreated patients, those on anti-CD20 agents (ocrelizumab, rituximab), or those recently given high-dose corticosteroids more often had a complicated course.

In a study of 555 people with MS receiving the Pfizer-BioNTech (BNT162b2) SARS-CoV-2 vaccine, the frequency and characteristics of vaccine-induced adverse events were almost comparable to the non-MS population, and were more numerous in younger people.
In a cohort of 239 people with MS surveyed by Lotan and colleagues, vaccine reactions to BNT162b2 were even less common than reported by Achiron et al.
Most studies have ruled out an increased long-term risk of developing MS as well as a short-term risk of neurological relapse in people with clinically defined MS following vaccinations in general.

A 28-year-old woman with a family history of MS developed active myelitis and disseminated white matter lesions with CSF oligoclonal bands, leading to a diagnosis of MS, 6 days after her first dose of the BNT162b2 vaccine.
In a study on BNT162b2 vaccination, 15.1% of people with MS reported worsening or new neurological symptoms that lasted more than 3 days in 55.6% of cases.
Fingolimod may attenuate or abolish humoral (antibody) response to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, especially in people with MS with reduced lymphocyte count at the time of administration.

Humoral response to SARS-CoV-2 vaccination is frequently absent in people with MS receiving ocrelizumab or rituximab, and when present depends on the time interval between the last drug infusion and vaccination.
Cladribine and other DMTs did not appear to interfere with post-COVID-19 or post-vaccination serological response in people with MS.

The largest study to date found significantly higher humoral response to the mRNA-1273 (Moderna) vaccine compared with BNT162b2 in people with MS, suggesting preferential use of mRNA-1273 in patients at risk of unsuccessful immunization.

In an immunological study of 20 B-cell depleted people with MS (19 on ocrelizumab, 1 on rituximab) following mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, despite significantly impaired antibody and memory B cell responses, a robust T-cell response was found with SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cell expansion exceeding that of healthy controls, especially in patients lacking IgG production entirely.

Masitinib, a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor that showed efficacy in phase 2B/3 trials for progressive MS, has been highlighted as a potent Coronavirus inhibitor, suggesting a repurposing opportunity for COVID-19.
Across the reviewed literature, the reported prevalence of post-acute COVID-19 syndrome ranged widely from approximately 20% to 95%.
Fatigue and dyspnea were the most commonly reported symptoms of PACS, occurring in more than half of studied populations.
US Veterans Affairs data estimated six-month mortality of about 8 per 1,000 non-hospitalized and 29 per 1,000 previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
UK NHS data found a significantly higher mortality rate (12.3%) among previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients at an average follow-up of 140 days.
Readmission rates after acute COVID-19 hospitalization were substantial, 29.4% in NHS data and 19.9% at 60 days in a separate VA study.

Higher body mass index, preexisting respiratory disease, older age, female sex, and Black/Asian/minority ethnicity were associated with increased risk of long-term COVID-19 sequelae, with acute illness severity (ICU admission) the strongest risk factor.

Residual cognitive dysfunction ('brain fog') affecting reasoning, spatial planning, problem solving, and verbal fluency was found in about one-third of non-hospitalized recovered individuals and up to two-thirds of those who required hospitalization; even mild-disease patients had more cognitive deficits than matched controls.
Anxiety and depression were reported in 12%-47% of PACS patients, with higher rates among those requiring hospitalization.
Symptoms consistent with PTSD were reported in roughly 10% of recovered COVID-19 patients, regardless of hospitalization status.
Chronic pain including myalgias, arthralgias, and headaches were common complaints in COVID-19 long-haulers with associated quality-of-life impact and use of pain medications.
Among patients who developed neurologic manifestations during acute COVID-19 infection, about nine in ten reported persisting neurologic deficits at six-month follow-up.

Cardiac magnetic resonance studies of COVID-19 survivors found ongoing cardiac inflammation in anywhere from 0% to 60% of participants, suggesting risk of long-term arrhythmias and heart failure even in seemingly healthy recovered patients.
COVID-19-positive individuals experienced prolonged relative tachycardia lasting on average 79 days after symptom onset, with 13.7% not returning to resting heart rate baseline until after 133 days.

A UK follow-up study found that previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients had roughly three times the risk of heart failure, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and stroke compared with matched controls at 140 days.
Development of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and orthostatic intolerance without hemodynamic effects has been described as a complication following COVID-19 infection.

Right ventricular dysfunction related to fibrotic lung damage, pulmonary hypertension, and/or clot burden was reported in COVID-19 survivors, with diastolic dysfunction incidence of roughly 32%-55% and pulmonary hypertension incidence of roughly 10%-35% up to 12 weeks after acute disease.
Reduced diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide was found in 21%-50% of patients after COVID-19, with female sex and ICU admission identified as risk factors for DLCO <60% of predicted at four months.
A study evaluating incidence of interstitial lung disease after COVID-19 hospitalization found that 4.8% of patients developed interstitial lung disease with an organizing pneumonia-like pattern.

A meta-analysis of 102 studies estimated the prevalence of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism after COVID-19 at roughly 15% and 8%, respectively, with higher rates among critically ill patients.

Hematologic complications appeared to decrease with time after recovery: cumulative incidence of thrombosis and bleeding at 30 days was only 2.5% and 3.7%, respectively, in one cohort, and a Belgian cohort found only a single symptomatic DVT/PE event at six weeks and none at six months.
Acute kidney disease was prevalent in hospitalized acute COVID-19 patients, with 35% not recovering to baseline renal function upon discharge.
One study found a greater rate of decline in glomerular filtration rate per year among recovered COVID-19 patients compared with a non-COVID-19 cohort.
5%-10% of patients developed diarrhea after resolution of acute COVID-19 disease.
Case reports described four patients developing cholangiopathies in the months following acute COVID-19 infection, with one requiring liver transplantation.
A report from Italy described nearly 50% of patients in a rehabilitation unit as malnourished after acute COVID-19 disease, and 90% as having some degree of dysphagia.
A follow-up study of hospitalized COVID-19 patients found a new diabetes diagnosis rate of 29 per 1,000 on average at 140 days.

Although most patients with abnormal thyroid function during acute COVID-19 hospitalization normalized on follow-up, 3%-5% developed antithyroid peroxidase antibodies and fewer than 2% developed subclinical thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism.

Patients undergoing surgery after COVID-19 infection have increased 30-day adjusted mortality; risk returns to baseline ≥7 weeks after recovery, but patients with persisting symptoms retain elevated mortality risk even beyond seven weeks.
The authors propose that long COVID may be related to reactivation of latent Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).
Impaired lymphocyte subpopulation counts and EBV load correlate with COVID-19 disease severity.
EBV can induce ACE2 expression, facilitating SARS-CoV-2 entry into epithelial cells.
More than half of COVID-19 survivors reportedly experience long-term symptoms (post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, PASC) or 'long-COVID'.
EBV-induced chronic fatigue syndrome has long been associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.
Mitochondrial function is essential for sustained cytotoxic T cell killing of virally infected cells, and EBV can itself infect T cells.

In SARS-CoV-2 infection, a subset of T cells with altered metabolism prone to mitochondrial apoptosis and lymphopenia, plus increased myeloid-derived suppressor cells, is associated with disease severity and altered VDAC1 expression.
A genetic and phenotypic causal analysis found accelerated biological ageing to be a key susceptibility factor for COVID-19, with altered Notch signalling and B cell functioning implicated.
EBV infection can alter mitochondrial dynamics and mitochondrial DNA replication.
EBV latent membrane protein 1 (LMP1) interacts with Drp1 to enhance glycolysis.
EBV induces metabolic reprogramming in monocytes with decreased autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis, enhancing apoptosis and reducing immune surveillance.
EBV modulates c-Myc activity and glutaminolysis/aerobic glycolysis, enhancing GLS-1 isoform activity in mitochondria, linked to its cancer association.
A Swiss outpatient cohort study found that 34.8% of participants had post-acute symptoms seven months after COVID-19 diagnosis.
Gut microbiota composition may affect how apparently healthy individuals respond to COVID-19, with cross-talk between gut microbiota and mitochondria (e.g., after exercise).

Physical activity is suggested as beneficial for mitochondrial and immune robustness via myokine-mediated inter-organ communication, potentially reducing susceptibility to viral-triggered fatigue syndromes.
A ketogenic diet is suggested as a possible aid via mitochondrial metabolic adaptation.
Existing pleiotropic drugs such as metformin or steroids, which modulate mitochondrial function, are proposed as potentially relevant to prevention/treatment of the described mitochondrial 'whammy'.
Mild calorie restriction is proposed as a possible way to enhance mitochondrial function and reduce inflammation.
The Three Principles/Innate Health psycho-spiritual education programme produced the largest mean reduction in fatigue severity compared with control of any intervention reviewed.
Group-based cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) produced large reductions in fatigue severity compared with control in two included trials.
Oriental Medicine Music Therapy significantly reduced fatigue severity compared with control.
Individual CBT delivered over a long series of one-to-one sessions significantly reduced fatigue severity compared with control.
Isometric yoga combined with pharmacological therapy significantly reduced fatigue severity compared with control.
Acupuncture significantly reduced fatigue severity compared with control, and the effect was sustained at follow-up.
A social/functional support intervention with no active participant input significantly reduced fatigue in a severely fatigued sample.
Operant learning showed a smaller, non-significant benefit for fatigue compared with control, with a confidence interval crossing zero.
Graded Exercise Therapy (GET), when adopted as a self-management strategy with counselling support, significantly reduced fatigue compared with control.
Self-regulation-based physical activity with motivational interviewing/counselling significantly reduced fatigue compared with control.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) showed little or no benefit for fatigue compared with control.
Tai Ji Quan showed essentially no benefit for fatigue compared with control.
Supportive listening showed no benefit for fatigue compared with control.
Mirtazapine showed little or no significant effect on fatigue severity compared with control.
Doxycycline was found to have little or no beneficial effect on fatigue, with mean differences favouring control in two studies.
Self-management supported by web diaries showed a significant, sustained reduction in fatigue at 6-12 month follow-up.
Multidisciplinary rehabilitation showed a significant, sustained reduction in fatigue at follow-up.
Across the 40 included studies, 18 of the reviewed fatigue management interventions showed no significant effect on fatigue symptoms.
Persistence of long COVID fatigue at around three months post-infection appears associated with moderate to severe depression and worsened quality of life.
Hospitalisation status does not appear to predict long Covid outcomes, and severity of acute COVID-19 is not predictive of long Covid outcomes.

Lower family income, poor health status, lack of physical activity, hypertension, and persistent COVID-19 symptoms are associated with recovery from fatigue-type long Covid symptoms, suggesting socio-economic determinants of long Covid outcomes.

Hyperglycemia during acute COVID-19, regardless of prior diabetes history, was a strong predictor of in-hospital mortality, associated with a sevenfold higher death rate than in patients with well-controlled glucose.
In UK Biobank participants, higher BMI was associated with an increased risk of COVID-19-related mortality.
Among ICU patients infected with SARS-CoV-2, higher BMI was strongly associated with greater risk of mortality.
In a cohort of 551 hospitalized COVID-19 patients in Italy, 46% were hyperglycemic and 27% normoglycemic, and even normoglycemic patients showed insulin resistance and increased cytokine levels.

GP73, a Golgi protein induced by infections, was increased during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, and injection of recombinant GP73 raised blood glucose in mice within 15 minutes via hepatic cAMP-PKA activation and gluconeogenic gene induction.
In the context of adipocyte dedifferentiation during SARS-CoV-2 infection, adiponectin levels are reduced while the proinflammatory adipokine leptin is increased.
