Among 30 patients with acute COVID-19, circulating CD26+ T-cell numbers decreased during acute illness, particularly with severe disease, and rose again in patients who fully recovered but not in those with prolonged disease or death; CD26+ cell counts correlated with hospital-free days.
Gastrointestinal symptoms of PASC, compared with respiratory symptoms, were associated with unique T-cell clonal and transcriptional dynamics.
A review of studies through mid-January 2022 found that vaccinated individuals were far less likely to develop PASC, particularly when vaccinated within a week of acute infection.
Fatigue, cough, and anosmia/dysgeusia are the three most prominent PASC symptoms, and each is strongly associated with type 2 diabetes.
A study of Italian healthcare workers found obesity to be a major risk factor for developing PASC.
Type 2 diabetes and high levels of acute SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia were identified as strong predisposing risk factors for developing PASC.
In a case-control study, patients with T2D who developed COVID-19 had a much greater likelihood of high fatigue scores postinfection than uninfected T2D controls.
Patients with T2D had poorer grip strength and increased inflammatory markers post-COVID relative to noninfected controls.

In a study of 145 patients with diabetes and 144 non-diabetic controls assessed a mean 7.2 months after COVID-19 hospitalization, the number of post-COVID symptoms was similar between groups, suggesting diabetes was not a risk factor for long-term post-COVID symptoms.
In a retrospective EHR cohort, a new diagnosis of anosmia and dysgeusia two or more months after a positive COVID-19 RT-PCR test was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A new diagnosis of chest pain two or more months after a positive COVID-19 RT-PCR test was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A new diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome two or more months after a positive COVID-19 RT-PCR test was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.
A new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes two or more months after a positive COVID-19 RT-PCR test was significantly associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.

CDC analysis of pediatric patients (<18 years) found new diabetes diagnosis incidence was significantly higher after COVID-19 than in matched patients without COVID-19 (in two independent claims databases) and higher than in patients with prepandemic non-COVID acute respiratory infections.

In a longitudinal cohort of 736 Spanish patients followed after COVID-19, new-onset diabetes was diagnosed in 7 patients (1.3%) at 1-year follow-up, and 15 of 189 previously diagnosed diabetics required treatment intensification.

In an autopsy series, SARS-CoV-2 was detected in at least one adipose tissue depot in 10 of 18 male individuals, and viral presence in adipose tissue was restricted to those who were overweight or obese.

Studies in hamsters and humans suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection suppresses de novo lipogenesis and reduces adiponectin and adipsin expression in mature adipocytes, phenomena typically associated with dysfunctional adipose tissue and T2D.
Higher plasma SARS-CoV-2 viral load was associated with lower absolute lymphocyte counts, increased C-reactive protein and IL-6, and worse prognosis.
In hospitalized PASC patients, dyspnoea, fatigue, and muscle weakness were each reported by approximately 53-63% of patients at 4-7 months after acute infection.
PASC symptoms of dyspnoea, fatigue, and muscle weakness were more common in women and in patients with more severe acute Covid-19, and dyspnoea was not explained by residual pulmonary abnormalities.
Bedridden, intensive-care patients with severe Covid-19 showed a ~30% decrease in rectus femoris cross-sectional area and ~20% reduction in anterior quadriceps compartment thickness after 10 days.
Knee-extensor and arm-flexor weakness was observed in 75-85% of a cohort of 41 previously hospitalized Covid-19 patients (aged 40-88).
Covid-19 patients with pre-existing sarcopenia took twice as long to be discharged and had an eight-fold higher mortality rate than those without sarcopenia.
Increased echogenicity in rectus femoris muscle of severe Covid-19 patients suggests qualitative tissue impairments such as fat infiltration and fibrosis contributing to muscle weakness.

Atrogin and muscle RING-finger protein-1 (MuRF1), components of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, are elevated in septic ICU patients, implicating this pathway in ICU-acquired muscle atrophy relevant to severe Covid-19.

Neuromuscular complications, including decreased muscle membrane excitability, are common in ICU patients (~40%), causing prolonged compound muscle action potential duration and slowed motor conduction velocities.

A single Covid-19 patient with critical illness myopathy showed necrotic muscle fibres, regeneration, disrupted sarcomeric ultrastructure, and myosinolysis (loss of myosin ATPase staining) on histopathology.

A comprehensive autopsy study found substantial infiltration of leukocytes, T-cells, and natural killer cells in skeletal muscle of patients who died of severe Covid-19, compared with critically ill patients without Covid-19.
Autopsies from 26 Covid-19 patients showed increased ACE2 and fibrosis-related gene expression, with two-fold higher diaphragm fibrosis compared to ICU patients without Covid-19.
Post-Covid-19 patients who had been mechanically ventilated for a median of 13 days showed poor cardiorespiratory fitness during rehabilitation, with peak oxygen uptake at ~50% of predicted values.
Skeletal muscle flow-mediated dilation during exercise is reduced and arterial stiffness is higher in young adults with Covid-19 compared with healthy controls.
A young Covid-19 patient studied before symptom onset showed lower ADP-stimulated mitochondrial respiration and attenuated ADP sensitivity, suggesting early skeletal mitochondrial dysfunction.

Circulating GDF15 was elevated in ~80% of patients hospitalized with Covid-19 compared with age-stratified healthy individuals, and higher levels were associated with viremia, hypoxaemia, soluble ACE2, mortality, and cardiovascular disease risk.
Plasma CRP, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-2 receptor, sTNFR1, and TNF-α were higher in severe Covid-19 cases compared with mild cases.
IL-6 has been identified as the best early biomarker for Covid-19 disease severity, followed by CRP, IL-10, IL-8, and IL-1β.
CRP levels correlate with Covid-19-related cachexia and may not return to pre-infection levels by 3 months post-infection, with implications for PASC.
Viral particles were detected in the diaphragm muscle of deceased patients with severe Covid-19, though overall viral load in skeletal/cardiac muscle at autopsy was low or negative in most cases.

A Dutch multicentre study found 36% of hospitalized Covid-19 patients were malnourished at admission, 73% were at high risk for sarcopenia, and one in five patients (over a third of ICU patients) lost more than 5 kg during hospitalization.

In ICU-admitted Covid-19 patients, hydrocortisone dose correlated with handgrip strength and walking distance, suggesting a possible link between corticosteroid medication and skeletal muscle function.

A more pronounced immune response to exercise and altered muscle metabolic function, with greater reliance on glycolysis for energy production, is evident in CFS/ME, which shares symptom overlap with PASC.

Higher skeletal muscle ACE protein content in women is speculated as a possible genotype-related factor contributing to PASC muscle symptoms, alongside low-grade inflammation, inactivity, and persisting viral load.

A meta-analysis of the literature found pooled prevalence estimates for common PASC symptoms including fatigue (64%), sleep disturbances (47%), dyspnea (39.5%), arthralgia (24.3%), cough (22.5%), headache (21%), anosmia (20%), mental health problems (14.5%), and chest pain (10%), with pooled pain prevalence of 42% and anxiety/depression prevalence of 38%.
In a cohort of 143 recovered COVID-19 patients, 87.4% reported persistence of at least one symptom (55% had three or more), most commonly fatigue, dyspnea, joint pain, and chest pain.
Patients assessed more than 100 days after hospital discharge commonly reported fatigue, dyspnea, memory loss, concentration disorders, and sleep disorders.
In an observational cohort of 1648 patients (488 completed the 60-day survey), substantial minorities reported cardiopulmonary symptoms, loss of taste/smell, ADL difficulty, and emotional impact.
A cohort followed at day 30 and 60 post-recovery found the most common symptoms at disease onset were flu-like symptoms, anosmia/ageusia, and fever.
A retrospective case series of 214 COVID-19 patients found 36.4% had neurologic manifestations, with cerebrovascular disease and conscious disturbance more likely in severe infection.

An online notification portal captured 153 COVID-19-associated neurological/psychiatric cases, with cerebrovascular events, altered mental status, and psychiatric disorders (including new-onset psychosis) predominating.

Among 1257 Chinese healthcare workers, those directly treating COVID-19 patients had more worsening depressive symptoms, anxiety, and general distress than peers not treating COVID-19 patients, and strong social support was protective.

Sudre et al. found Long COVID incidence to be higher among individuals aged 18-49 with greater risk associated with increasing age, higher BMI, female sex, and having more than five symptoms in the first week of acute illness.
Huang et al. and Jacobs et al. found that older patients experienced more PASC symptoms.
Several studies showed women more frequently report PASC symptoms from as early as four weeks up to six months after COVID-19 recovery.

Huang et al., Halpin et al., and Taquet et al. reported a direct correlation between increasing COVID-19 severity and more PASC symptoms, with ICU/invasive-ventilation patients more likely to report physical and mental problems.

A French study following patients 110 days post-discharge found no significant difference in fatigue, memory/concentration loss, or sleep disorders between ward-admitted and ICU-admitted patients, contradicting the reported severity-symptom correlation.
An Italian study surveying patients one month after discharge found an inverse relationship between duration of hospitalization and PASC symptom burden.
Patients managed at home for mild COVID-19 reported feeling more anxious and depressed, attributed to reduced perceived healthcare support and greater isolation/loneliness during recovery.

Mazza et al. found that women, patients who managed symptoms at home, and those with prior psychiatric history had higher self-reported PTSD, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms after COVID-19.

Taquet et al. found that patients surveyed 14-90 days post-discharge had twice the risk of a first-time psychiatric diagnosis, most commonly anxiety disorders, insomnia, and dementia, with prior psychiatric history contributing to distress.
Janiri et al. found no established association between prior psychiatric history and post-COVID psychological distress, instead identifying cyclothymic and depressive temperament as predictive.
A meta-analysis of post-COVID psychiatric symptoms reported prevalence of PTSD at 32.2%, depression at 14.9%, and anxiety disorders at 14.8%.
Rossi Ferrario et al. reported acute stress disorder, anxious/demoralization symptoms, depression, and troublesome grief as common post-COVID-19 psychological issues.
A study of hospital-discharged COVID-19 patients found 10% developed anxiety symptoms, 19% developed depressive symptoms, and 12% developed PTSD.
In a prospective study of 100 patients at a NeuroCOVID-19 clinic, the most common neurological symptom (81%) was non-specific cognitive impairment described as 'brain fog'.
Pathologists proposed that SARS-CoV-2-triggered migration of megakaryocytes to the brain blocks cerebral capillary blood flow, producing focal neurological impairment underlying 'brain fog'.

Stefano et al. proposed that SARS-CoV-2 damages mitochondrial energy metabolism via viral genome integration into the host mitochondrial matrix, producing a pro-inflammatory response that contributes to neuronal dysfunction and 'brain fog'.

Taquet et al. found that patients surveyed 14 to 90 days after hospital discharge for COVID-19 had twice the risk of receiving a first-time psychiatric diagnosis, most commonly anxiety disorders, insomnia, and dementia.

Janiri et al. found no significant association between prior psychiatric history and post-COVID psychological distress, but found that cyclothymic and depressive temperaments before infection predicted greater risk of psychological distress after recovery.
A meta-analysis reported post-COVID-19 psychiatric symptom prevalence of 32.2% for post-traumatic stress disorder, 14.9% for depression, and 14.8% for anxiety disorders.

Rossi Ferrario et al. reported that the most common post-COVID-19 psychological issues were acute stress disorder (18.6%), anxious and demoralization symptoms (26.7%), depression (10.5%), and troublesome grief (8.1%).
A study of COVID-19 patients discharged from hospitals found that 10% developed anxiety symptoms, 19% developed depressive symptoms, and 12% developed PTSD.
In a prospective study of 100 patients at a NeuroCOVID-19 clinic, 81% reported a non-specific cognitive issue commonly called "brain fog" as their most common neurological symptom.

Pathologists proposed that bone marrow-derived megakaryocytes migrate to the brain in response to SARS-CoV-2 activity, blocking capillary blood flow in the cerebral cortex and causing focal neurological impairment consistent with brain fog.

Stefano et al. proposed that SARS-CoV-2 damages mitochondrial energy metabolism via integration of the viral genome into the host cell mitochondrial matrix, and that resulting mitochondrial dysfunction with a pro-inflammatory response contributes to neuronal dysfunction and brain fog.

Mazza et al. found that women, patients who managed COVID-19 symptoms at home, and patients with a prior psychiatric history reported higher rates of PTSD, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms after recovery.

A French study following patients 110 days after discharge found persistent fatigue, memory/concentration loss, and sleep disorders in hospital-admitted patients, but no significant difference between ward-admitted and ICU-admitted patients.
An Italian study surveying patients one month after hospital discharge found an inverse relationship between duration of hospitalization and PASC symptom burden.
Alcohol and other substance use reportedly increased among long haulers as a coping strategy for stress caused by prolonged illness and psychosocial stressors.
UK COVID-19 symptom app data showed around 300,000 people reported symptoms lasting more than a month, and over 60,000 were still symptomatic after three months.

In an Italian cohort of 143 patients discharged after COVID-19, 87% still had at least one symptom at 60 days, with 13% symptom-free, 32% having one or two symptoms, and 55% having three or more, most commonly fatigue, dyspnea, joint pain, and chest pain, with quality of life worsening in about two-fifths of patients.
A Rome-based study of 143 COVID-19 patients discharged from hospital found that 53% reported fatigue an average of two months after symptom onset.
A study of patients in China found that 16% were still fatigued after recovery from COVID-19.

In a multistate telephone survey of symptomatic adults with a positive outpatient SARS-CoV-2 test, 35% had not returned to their usual state of health 2-3 weeks after testing, including one in five among those aged 18-34 with no chronic medical conditions.
Using the CFQ-11 chronic fatigue questionnaire in 128 patients, 52.3% (67/128) met criteria for fatigue, with a mean CFQ-11 score of 20 (±4.4) in that group.

The paper proposes that pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interferon-gamma contribute to compromised neurological regulation of the glymphatic system in post-COVID fatigue, analogous to chronic fatigue syndrome.
The paper proposes that interleukin-7, along with other pro-inflammatory cytokines, may compromise neurological regulation of the glymphatic system contributing to post-COVID fatigue.

Neuroinflammation caused by COVID-19 or systemic inflammation may activate the brain's innate immune system via humoral and retrograde neural signaling, largely involving the vagus nerve, as a proposed mechanism of post-viral fatigue.

Buildup of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the CNS, crossing the blood-brain barrier through circumventricular organs such as the hypothalamus, is proposed to cause autonomic dysfunction and, longer term, dysregulation of sleep/wake cycle, cognitive dysfunction, and unremitting fatigue characteristic of CFS/ME.
SARS-CoV-2 is proposed to enter the nervous system via widely distributed ACE-2 receptors, potentially explaining loss of smell/taste and brain fog in post-COVID patients.
A cited report suggests occlusion of brain capillaries by large megakaryocyte cells as a possible mechanism contributing to brain fog after COVID-19.

The recommended management of post-COVID fatigue is behavioral/supportive, emphasizing total rest, reduced sensory/cognitive stimulation, gentle low-level activity, adequate nutrition/hydration, and allowing extended time for recovery, as no specific medication exists.
Nearly 30% of the cohort of symptomatic COVID-19 patients developed persistent symptoms consistent with PASC at 60-90 days follow-up.
Hospitalization for the acute COVID-19 illness was independently associated with increased odds of developing PASC in adjusted analysis.
A history of diabetes was independently associated with increased odds of developing PASC.
Higher BMI was independently associated with a small but significant increased odds of developing PASC.
Patients with Medicaid insurance, compared to commercial insurance, had lower odds of developing PASC.
A history of solid organ transplant was independently associated with reduced odds of developing PASC, possibly reflecting dampened host inflammatory response due to immunosuppression.
Age, race/ethnicity, Social Vulnerability Index, and baseline functional status were not independently associated with developing PASC.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported persistent symptom among PASC patients at 60+ days follow-up.

The pattern of persistent symptoms differed by care setting: shortness of breath was the second most common symptom in hospitalized PASC patients, while loss of taste or smell was second most common in outpatient PASC patients.
Women showed a trend toward higher likelihood of developing PASC compared to men, though this was not statistically significant, in contrast to prior literature.
Patients hospitalized for COVID-19 had a higher rate of PASC (30.8%) than those treated as high-risk outpatients (26.5%).
Anosmia is reported as one of the predominant persisting symptoms in long COVID-19 patients, with or without prior hospitalization.
Dysautonomia, characterized by sympathetic/parasympathetic dysfunction, is proposed as the manifestation underlying neurological symptoms including anosmia in long COVID-19.
A genetic variation in ACE2 in the European population increases receptor expression, potentially predisposing Europeans to anosmia compared with Asians.

Soluble platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (sPDGFRβ), mainly expressed in brain pericytes that co-express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, has been proposed as a candidate biomarker of blood-brain barrier dysfunction.

Antibodies against ACE2 detected in long COVID-19 patients may downregulate soluble and membrane-bound ACE2 activity, shifting the angiotensin balance toward increased Ang II and enhanced immune activation.
Antinuclear, antiphospholipid, and anti-interferon autoantibodies have been detected following COVID-19 infection.
ACE2 receptor expression is more prevalent in adults than in children, which may explain the milder COVID-19 prognosis observed in young people.

Women are more likely than men to develop olfactory disorders in COVID-19, and anosmia risk increases with aging and female gender, possibly due to incomplete X chromosome inactivation leading to ACE2 overexpression.
ACE2 immunohistochemical expression was 200 to 700 times greater in sustentacular cells of the olfactory neuroepithelium than in nasal or tracheal epithelia.
ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are highly expressed on sustentacular cells of the olfactory epithelium, whereas ACE2 expression is absent on olfactory sensory neurons themselves.

A post-mortem study of two COVID-19 patients with anosmia showed focal atrophy of the olfactory epithelium, leukocytic infiltration of the lamina propria, and axonal damage in the olfactory nerve fibers.
Patients with anosmia persisting three months after COVID-19 diagnosis exhibited extensive destruction of the olfactory epithelium.
Viral RNA has been detected in the olfactory bulb of post-mortem COVID-19 patients, supporting neurotropism via the olfactory pathway.

ACE2 is highly expressed in adipose tissue, particularly visceral fat, suggesting a possible role of adipose tissue in determining COVID-19 severity and duration, though this link remains unclear in long COVID.
Neuropilin-1 (NRP-1), found in the olfactory system and olfactory epithelium neurons, may provide a second route for SARS-CoV-2 brain invasion in conjunction with ACE2.
SARS-CoV-2 has been shown to damage the integrity of choroid plexus epithelium in hippocampal-like brain organoids.

Dysautonomia may enhance afferent baroreflex failure, damaging the baroreceptor pathway from carotid body baroreceptors through vagal and glossopharyngeal fibers to the nucleus of the tractus solitarius.
The 60-140 nm diameter of SARS-CoV-2 is proposed to allow it to translocate through the blood-brain barrier and gain entry into the CNS.
64.8% of patients (168/259) reported persistent symptoms beyond 21 days after acute COVID-19 onset, while 35.13% remained asymptomatic.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported PASC symptom, seen in 71 patients (42.26%).
Respiratory complaints including breathlessness (22.61%) and cough (20.83%) were among the most frequent PASC symptoms.
Loss of smell, loss of taste, anxiety, and insomnia were also reported PASC symptoms at lower frequencies.
Patients with PASC symptoms had significantly higher BMI than those without PASC symptoms.
A past history of systemic hypertension was significantly more common among patients with PASC symptoms than those without.
Elevated systolic blood pressure at follow-up was significantly associated with the presence of PASC symptoms.
Persistent abnormalities on chest x-ray were significantly more frequent in patients with PASC symptoms.
No significant association was found between patient gender and the presence of PASC symptoms.
No significant association was found between patient age and the presence of PASC symptoms.
The severity category of acute COVID-19 illness (mild, moderate, severe) was not significantly associated with presenting with at least one PASC symptom.
CRP levels were not significantly elevated in patients with PASC symptoms compared to those without.
Neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio was not significantly elevated in patients with PASC symptoms compared to those without.
D-dimer levels did not significantly differ between patients with and without PASC symptoms.
Women were significantly more likely than men to report persistent symptoms of COVID-19 (72.4% vs 53.7% of respective groups had persistent symptoms).
Older age was significantly associated with greater self-reported COVID-19 illness severity, with median age increasing from 51 years in mild disease to 59 years in severe disease.
Patients with self-reported severe/very severe illness were far more likely to have been hospitalized than those with mild or moderate disease.
Negative psychological symptoms (anxiety and/or depression) were reported significantly more often by patients who had persistent COVID-19 symptoms than by those who did not.
Inability to resume normal activities within 1 month of illness onset was strongly associated with having persistent COVID-19 symptoms.
Just over one-third of the surveyed cohort (34.9%) reported persistent symptoms from their COVID-19 illness.
Despite over one-third of patients reporting persistent symptoms, only 2.3% of patients reported ever having been formally diagnosed with post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Fatigue was the most commonly reported persistent symptom across all severity levels of COVID-19.
Poor sleep quality was the second most commonly reported persistent symptom.
Anosmia was among the most commonly reported persistent symptoms.
Dysgeusia was among the most commonly reported persistent symptoms.
Dyspnea was among the most commonly reported persistent symptoms, likely reflecting respiratory complications more prevalent in hospitalized/severe patients.
Self-reported acute COVID-19 severity level did not differ significantly between women and men.
Persistence of symptoms (PASC) was not significantly associated with hospitalization status, a proxy for acute disease severity.

Nearly one-third of respondents reported being symptom free for a period before developing new symptoms, most commonly among those with milder initial disease, though this was not statistically significant across severity groups.
Objective neuropsychological testing showed no mean scores in the clinically Impaired range and a low base rate of Impaired individual test scores among PASC patients with cognitive complaints.
More than 20% of the sample showed Borderline (1-2 SD below normative mean) performance on some cognitive measures.
Mean scores on mood measures were frequently elevated among PASC patients.
Mood/anxiety measure scores significantly correlated with some objective cognitive measures and with the number of Borderline-range scores per participant.
Objective cognitive performance was not significantly correlated with premorbid vascular risk factors.
Objective cognitive performance was not significantly correlated with prior psychiatric diagnoses.
Subjective cognitive complaints reported by PASC patients did not correlate with objective neuropsychological test performance.
The authors suggest that fatigue and sleep issues may be additional contributing factors to cognitive complaints in PASC beyond mood/anxiety.

Exploratory factor analysis identified a single latent factor explaining 64.8% of the variance in 30 post-COVID symptoms, with positive loadings for all symptoms and loadings above 0.35 for 16 of them.
In Item Response Theory modeling, fatigue, psychiatric, and cognitive manifestations were the most discriminative symptoms of the PASC latent trait.
Greater PASC latent trait severity was associated with decreased body weight.
Greater PASC latent trait severity was associated with poorer objective physical performance.
Higher PASC latent trait severity was associated with elevated C-reactive protein blood levels, indicating persistent systemic inflammation.
Higher PASC latent trait severity was associated with elevated D-dimer blood levels, consistent with persistent coagulation/inflammatory activation.

The associations between the PASC latent trait and inflammatory markers/physical disability remained similar after excluding subjects with pro-inflammatory comorbidities, suggesting the findings are not solely driven by preexisting inflammatory conditions.
Individuals with significant long-COVID fatigue had significantly lower heart rate at peak exercise than those without fatigue.
Peak oxygen consumption per kilogram during cardiopulmonary exercise testing was significantly lower in individuals with long-COVID fatigue than in those without.
In multivariable logistic regression, higher peak exercise heart rate was independently associated with lower odds of long-COVID fatigue.
Long-COVID memory impairment was an independent risk factor for significant long-COVID fatigue.
A higher proportion of individuals with long-COVID fatigue reported sore throat during the acute COVID-19 illness compared to those without fatigue.
Individuals with long-COVID fatigue had a lower proportion of pre-existing hypothyroidism compared to those without fatigue.
Individuals with long-COVID fatigue had a significantly higher number of children than those without fatigue.
Individuals with long-COVID fatigue had a significantly lower peak exercise heart rate than those without fatigue.
Peak oxygen consumption per kilogram during cardiopulmonary exercise testing was significantly lower in individuals with long-COVID fatigue compared to those without.

Peak exercise heart rate was identified as an independent protective factor against long-COVID fatigue in multivariable logistic regression, with each 10 beats/minute increase associated with a 21% reduction in odds of fatigue.
Long-COVID memory impairment was an independent risk factor for significant long-COVID fatigue, associated with nearly a fourfold increase in odds.
The authors conclude that long-COVID fatigue may be related to autonomic dysfunction, impaired cognition, and decreased mood, suggesting a limbic-vagal pathophysiology.

An analysis of over 250,000 electronic health records found that more than one-third of individuals had at least one feature of post-COVID-19 condition recorded 3-6 months after a COVID-19 diagnosis, significantly more often than among individuals diagnosed with influenza.
Greater disease severity, female sex, and younger age were associated with a higher risk of developing post-COVID-19 condition.
Multiple studies across countries found fatigue or muscle weakness, sleep difficulties, and anxiety or depression to be among the most common symptoms persisting six months after COVID-19.

One year after acute infection, most COVID-19 survivors recover physically and functionally, but some continue to experience mobility problems, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or depression compared with non-COVID-19 controls.
Previously hospitalised COVID-19 patients had increased rates of multiorgan dysfunction compared with the general population.

The paper notes that distinguishing post-COVID-19 condition from an ongoing separate problem can be difficult, citing dysautonomia manifesting as abnormal heart rate variability as an example of a symptom that may be misattributed.
The causes of post-COVID-19 condition remain unclear, but persistent immune activation has been proposed as a possible contributing mechanism.

Evidence on the effectiveness of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination for treating post-COVID-19 condition is described as conflicting, despite proposals that vaccine-induced antibodies and T cells could help the immune system clear viral reservoirs.
More than one-third of patients with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection show involvement of the central or peripheral nervous system as part of long-COVID.
Observational studies incorporating patient-reported data record an approximately threefold higher incidence of neurological symptoms compared with other study designs.

Neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress processes are proposed as the leading pathophysiological mechanisms underlying neurological long-COVID sequelae, though supporting evidence remains very limited.
Persistent fatigue at 12 months was substantially more common in SARS-CoV-2 infected participants than new-onset fatigue in non-infected participants.
Of 22 symptoms assessed, 13 were found to be associated with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection based on relative risk comparisons at 12 months.

Factor analysis identified a neurocognitive/autonomic-type symptom cluster comprising brain fog, poor memory, dizziness, heart palpitations, and fatigue that loaded highly on the first underlying factor.
Shortness-of-breath and cough formed a distinct respiratory symptom cluster loading on the second underlying factor.
Loss of taste and smell showed only low to moderate correlation with the other post-COVID symptom clusters, suggesting a separate underlying mechanism.
Anxiety, depression and mood swings were not strongly related to prior COVID-19 infection, suggesting these psychological symptoms may not be core features of long COVID.
The article identifies fatigue as by far the most common symptom of Long COVID and discusses its pathogenetic classification and treatment approaches.
Among 17 long COVID patients referred for peripheral neuropathy evaluation, 59% had at least one objective test confirming neuropathy.
Skin biopsy testing was abnormal (consistent with small-fiber neuropathy) in 63% (10/16) of tested long COVID patients.
Electrodiagnostic testing (nerve conduction studies) was abnormal in only 17% (2/12) of tested long COVID patients, indicating large-fiber involvement was less common than small-fiber.
Autonomic function testing was abnormal in 50% (4/8) of tested long COVID patients, supporting autonomic small-fiber involvement.
At least 10 of 17 long COVID patients evaluated received a diagnosis of small-fiber neuropathy.
One patient was diagnosed with critical illness axonal neuropathy following COVID-19.
One patient developed multifocal demyelinating neuropathy 3 weeks after mild COVID-19.
At least 10 of 17 patients evaluated for long COVID-associated peripheral neuropathy received a diagnosis of small-fiber neuropathy.
Peripheral neuropathy symptoms in these long COVID patients most commonly began within one month of COVID-19 onset, even after mild acute infection.
The authors concluded that infection-triggered immune dysregulation was a common underlying mechanism for the observed post-COVID small-fiber and other peripheral neuropathies.
Despite an average 52% longitudinal improvement over follow-up, none of the patients reported complete resolution of their neuropathy, and the condition was often disabling.

The authors advocate Tai Chi, a multicomponent exercise involving breathing technique, balance and neuromuscular training, and stress management, as a rehabilitation tool for individuals recovering from COVID-19 and long COVID.

The authors note that Tai Chi has previously been shown to increase lung capacity, improve cognitive status and mental health, and improve quality of life in diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Approximately 10% of all COVID patients develop long COVID symptoms that may persist from 1 month to longer than 1 year, affecting any organ or system.

Physiological biosignal features recorded simultaneously with fMRI showed some statistically significant differences between High Arousal and Low Arousal states in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder, though overall classification performance was suboptimal.
Adults with schizophrenia showed significantly smaller SDNN (a heart rate variability measure) than neurotypical controls.
Adults with autism showed a nominal but non-significant reduction in SDNN compared to controls.
Heart rate differed significantly between groups overall, with a nominal (but not post-hoc significant) elevation in schizophrenia compared to controls.
Heart rate was strongly negatively correlated with SDNN across all three groups.
When heart rate was normalized by SDNN, group differences among schizophrenia, autism, and controls became stronger.
Low frequency power of the heartbeat was marginally lower in schizophrenia and autism than controls, but this did not survive multiple-comparisons correction.
There were no significant group differences in high frequency power of the heartbeat among schizophrenia, autism, and control groups.

Removing unmedicated schizophrenia participants weakened (rather than strengthened) the SDNN and low frequency power group differences, suggesting antipsychotic medication was not the primary driver of reduced HRV in schizophrenia.
Adults with autism reported marginally greater feelings of loneliness than neurotypical controls.
Loneliness scores in adults with schizophrenia were similar on average to controls, despite social deficits being a defining diagnostic feature.
